Examples: `0 * * * *` (every hour), `*/15 * * * *` (every 15 min), `0 2 * * *` (2 AM daily), `0 0 * * 0` (Sunday midnight). Capture output: `>> /tmp/job.log 2>&1`. Gotchas: minimal PATH, no shell init, no $HOME by default. Modern alternative: systemd timers (better logging, deps, calendar specs).

Webhook security: verify HMAC signature header (Stripe, GitHub, Slack include one). Compute HMAC-SHA256 of raw body with your shared secret; compare in constant time. Use raw body bytes, not parsed JSON (parsing rounds-trips can change bytes). Reject if timestamp is too old (replay protection). Don't trust headers from untrusted callers — IP allowlists less useful than HMAC.

Postgres JSONB: binary-stored JSON, indexable, queryable. `CREATE TABLE events (id serial, data jsonb)`. Query: `data->>'name'` (text), `data->'addr'->>'city'`, `data @> '{"type":"click"}'` (contains). GIN index for fast containment: `CREATE INDEX ON events USING gin(data jsonb_path_ops)`. Generally prefer columns for known fields, JSONB for the variable tail.

Postgres extensions: PostGIS (geo), pg_trgm (fuzzy text search), pgvector (AI embeddings), TimescaleDB (time-series), pg_stat_statements (query stats), pg_cron (in-DB scheduled queries), pg_partman (partition management), hstore (key-value). `CREATE EXTENSION name`. Check available: `SELECT * FROM pg_available_extensions`. Most managed Postgres providers offer common ones.

pgvector: Postgres extension for vector similarity search. `CREATE EXTENSION vector; CREATE TABLE items (id int, embedding vector(1536))`. Insert with embeddings from OpenAI/Cohere/local model. Query: `SELECT * FROM items ORDER BY embedding <=> '[...]' LIMIT 5`. Indexes: IVFFlat (faster build, recall tradeoff), HNSW (more memory, better recall). Pairs with Postgres full-text + structured data — usually no need for separate vector DB at small/medium scale.

Redis pub/sub: publishers send to channels, subscribers receive. `PUBLISH chan 'hi'`, `SUBSCRIBE chan`. No persistence — subscribers offline at publish time miss messages. For durable messaging, use Redis Streams instead. Use pub/sub for: cache invalidation across instances, live notifications, lightweight broadcast. For replay/durability/consumer groups: Streams (`XADD`, `XREADGROUP`).

OpenAI API: `from openai import OpenAI; client = OpenAI(); response = client.chat.completions.create(model='gpt-4o', messages=[{'role':'user','content':'hi'}])`. Stream: `stream=True`, iterate chunks. Tools (function calling) via `tools` param. Vision: include image_url in message content. Embeddings: `client.embeddings.create(model='text-embedding-3-large', input=text)`. Anthropic, Google, Mistral, etc. have similar APIs — many SDK-compatible.

Anthropic API (Claude): `from anthropic import Anthropic; client = Anthropic(); msg = client.messages.create(model='claude-sonnet-4-6', max_tokens=1024, messages=[{'role':'user','content':'hi'}])`. Tools: pass `tools=[...]` with JSON schemas, Claude returns `tool_use` blocks. Streaming: `stream=True`. Multimodal: text + image in content array. Long context: up to 200k tokens (1M on selected models). Caching for repeated context.

RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation): retrieve relevant context from a knowledge base, pass to LLM as part of prompt. Pipeline: chunk docs → embed → store in vector DB → at query time, embed query, find top-k, stuff into prompt. Improvements: hybrid retrieval (BM25 + vector), reranking (cross-encoder), query rewriting, citations in output, chunking strategies (semantic chunking, parent-child).

Prompt engineering: be specific (role, task, format, constraints), use examples (few-shot — show 2-5), structure with markdown (headers, lists), ask for step-by-step reasoning ('think step by step'), specify output format (JSON schema, code block). For complex tasks: decompose into sub-prompts, use chain-of-thought. Iterate empirically — small wording changes have large effects. Eval set + automated scoring beats vibes.

LLM tool use (function calling): give the model a list of functions with JSON schemas; it decides when to call them and produces structured arguments. Loop: send messages → model returns tool_use → you execute → return tool_result → model uses output to continue. Pattern enables: search, calculation, API calls, code execution. Anthropic and OpenAI both support; format differs slightly but concept identical.

LangChain: framework for composing LLM apps. Provides: model wrappers, prompt templates, output parsers, chains (sequential ops), agents (tool-using loops), memory, document loaders, vector stores. Reputation: powerful but heavyweight and abstraction-heavy — many devs prefer direct API calls + small libraries. Alternatives: LlamaIndex (RAG focus), Haystack, simple custom code. Use the right tool for your complexity level.

MCP (Model Context Protocol, Anthropic 2024): open standard for connecting LLMs to tools/data sources. Server exposes tools, resources, prompts; client (e.g., Claude Desktop, Claude Code) uses them. Transport: stdio (local) or SSE/HTTP (remote). Build a server in any language (TS/Python SDKs official). Lets you build once and use in any MCP-compatible client. Gaining wide adoption in late 2024/2025.

Vector embeddings: dense numeric representations of text/images/audio where similar items are close in vector space. Cosine similarity or dot product for comparison. Models: OpenAI text-embedding-3 (paid, strong), Cohere, voyage-3, open: sentence-transformers, BGE, nomic-embed, mxbai-embed-large. Dimension: 384-1536 typical. Trade-offs: smaller dim = cheaper storage/search; larger = better recall.

Docker compose example: `services:
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    environment: { POSTGRES_PASSWORD: dev }
    volumes: ['db_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data']
  api:
    build: .
    depends_on: [db]
    environment: { DATABASE_URL: postgres://postgres:dev@db:5432/postgres }
    ports: ['3000:3000']
volumes: { db_data: {} }`. Run: `docker compose up -d`, logs: `compose logs -f api`.

12-Factor App (Heroku, 2011): cloud-native app principles. Codebase (one repo, many deploys), Dependencies (declare explicitly), Config (in env), Backing services (treat as attached resources), Build/release/run (separate), Processes (stateless), Port binding (self-contained), Concurrency (process model), Disposability (fast start/stop), Dev/prod parity, Logs (event streams to stdout), Admin processes. Still mostly correct decades later.

Semantic Versioning (SemVer): MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. Bump MAJOR for breaking changes, MINOR for backwards-compatible features, PATCH for fixes. Pre-release: 1.0.0-beta.1. Build metadata: 1.0.0+sha. SemVer-range in npm: `^1.2.3` (any 1.x.x ≥ 1.2.3), `~1.2.3` (1.2.x). Pre-1.0: anything goes (0.x). Critique: most projects don't truly follow it; minor bumps break things.

Keep a Changelog: write CHANGELOG.md by hand (or generated). Sections per version (newest first): Added, Changed, Deprecated, Removed, Fixed, Security. Write for humans, not machines — describe what users care about, not commit list. 'Unreleased' section at top for pending changes. Tools: changesets, release-please, semantic-release for automation.

API versioning: URL path (`/v1/users` — simple, visible), header (`Accept: application/vnd.api.v1+json` — clean URLs, hidden from logs), query param (`?version=1`). Versionless API with field deprecation: GitHub-style, requires great communication. Breaking change strategy: ship new endpoint, deprecate old with sunset date, monitor usage. Don't break URLs in v1 forever — assume someone is depending on them.

Feature flags: ship code behind switches; toggle without redeploy. Use for: gradual rollouts, kill switches, A/B tests, internal vs external, dark launches. Tools: LaunchDarkly, GrowthBook (OSS), Unleash (OSS), PostHog, Statsig, ConfigCat. Cleanup is critical — old flags accumulate. Tag each flag with owner + expected removal date. Don't nest flag checks; flags create branching paths in code that must be tested.

Test doubles: stubs (return canned data), mocks (verify interactions), spies (record calls), fakes (working but simplified — in-memory DB), dummies (placeholders). Mock at boundaries (HTTP, DB, time, random); don't mock your own code. Over-mocking → tests pass while code is broken. Prefer integration tests with real dependencies in containers (testcontainers) when feasible.

TDD (Test-Driven Development): red (write failing test), green (minimum code to pass), refactor (clean up while green). Forces small steps, design through tests. Pros: regression safety, design pressure (testable code is decoupled), confidence to refactor. Cons: slower in unfamiliar domains, mocked-heavy tests can be brittle. Pragmatic: TDD where requirements are clear; spike + test for exploratory work.

SOLID principles (Robert Martin): Single Responsibility (one reason to change), Open/Closed (open for extension, closed for modification), Liskov Substitution (subtypes substitutable for base), Interface Segregation (many small interfaces > one fat), Dependency Inversion (depend on abstractions). Useful checklist, not gospel. Easy to over-apply — small classes everywhere bury logic in indirection. Apply when complexity warrants.

DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself, Hunt & Thomas): every piece of knowledge has a single, unambiguous representation. Critique: overapplied. Don't dedupe coincidental similarity — when two things may evolve differently, duplication is freer. WET (Write Everything Twice) and 'rule of three' (extract abstraction after third repetition) are sane refinements.

YAGNI (You Aren't Gonna Need It): don't build features until needed. Future-proofing usually doesn't match actual future needs. Hypothetical flexibility creates real complexity now. Counter-balance: leave hooks where extending is highly predictable. The most expensive code is code you wrote that's never used — and it slows you down forever.

KISS (Keep It Simple, Stupid): simpler designs win — fewer bugs, easier handoff, easier change. Complexity should justify itself. Symptoms of over-engineering: speculative generality, premature abstraction, deep inheritance, too many layers. Constraint = creativity. The simplest thing that could possibly work, then iterate. Rich Hickey's 'Simple Made Easy' is great companion reading.

MVC (Model-View-Controller): Model (data + domain logic), View (UI), Controller (mediates input → model → view). Origin: Smalltalk-80. Modern web: Rails, Django, Spring define MVC differently than original. React isn't really MVC — it's component-based with one-way data flow. MVVM, MVP are related variants. Pattern names obscure as much as they clarify.

Functional programming: emphasize pure functions, immutability, functions as values, expressions over statements, composition. Languages: Haskell (pure, lazy), Erlang/Elixir (concurrency), F#, Clojure (Lisp on JVM), OCaml. Multi-paradigm languages with strong FP support: Scala, Rust, Swift, modern JS/TS. Concepts: higher-order functions, currying, recursion + tail calls, algebraic data types (sum + product), pattern matching.

Why learn programming? Automate repetitive tasks. Build things others can use. Understand the increasingly digital world. Career flexibility — software touches every industry. Strong problem-solving skill that transfers. Joy of creation — turning ideas into working things from text. Accessible: free tools, free tutorials, vast community. Hard but worth it.

Starting to code: pick one language (Python is the gentlest, JavaScript if you want web). One project (something you want), not endless tutorials. Build, search when stuck, repeat. freeCodeCamp, The Odin Project, CS50 (Harvard, free). Code daily even briefly — consistency beats intensity. You'll feel stupid often — that's normal and necessary. Cycle through 'I get it' → 'I don't get it' → 'I get it' forever.

Dunder (double-underscore) methods are how Python objects hook into the language: `__init__` (construct), `__repr__` (unambiguous string, for devs), `__str__` (readable, for users), `__eq__` and `__hash__` (must agree — hashable objects need both, mutable ones usually unhash by setting `__hash__ = None`), `__lt__`/`__le__`/etc. (use `@functools.total_ordering` to derive the rest from `__eq__` + one), `__call__` (instance becomes callable), `__len__`, `__bool__`, `__contains__`. Implement protocols, not inheritance — duck typing means a class with `__iter__` IS an iterable.

`__init__(self, ...)` initializes an already-created instance — it does not return anything (returning non-None raises TypeError). The actual creator is `__new__(cls, ...)`, which you rarely override except for immutable types or singletons. Avoid heavy work in `__init__`; classmethod constructors (`from_json`, `from_dict`) are pythonic for alternative builds. Don't call `super().__init__()` only when there's no parent state to initialize — usually call it first.

`__repr__` should be unambiguous and ideally `eval`-able: `Point(x=1, y=2)`. `__str__` is for end users — drop it through and `print()` uses `__repr__` as fallback. Always implement `__repr__` for any class meant for debugging or logging — the default `<MyClass object at 0x...>` is useless. f-string `{obj!r}` forces repr, `{obj!s}` forces str.

`__eq__(self, other)` defines equality. If you override it, you should override `__hash__` too — they must satisfy: `a == b` implies `hash(a) == hash(b)`. Default `object.__hash__` is identity-based; override `__eq__` without `__hash__` and Python sets `__hash__ = None`, making instances unhashable (can't go in sets/dict keys). For value objects: hash a tuple of the identifying fields. Mutable objects should usually stay unhashable to avoid bugs when mutated inside a set.

`__call__` makes an instance behave like a function: `obj()` invokes `obj.__call__()`. Useful for stateful function-like objects (counters, memoizers), strategy objects, or decorators implemented as classes. Functions in Python are objects with `__call__`. Check `callable(x)` rather than `isinstance(x, types.FunctionType)`.

Iterables implement `__iter__` returning an iterator; iterators implement `__next__` raising `StopIteration` when exhausted. Generators (functions with `yield`) get both for free. An iterator is iterable (its `__iter__` returns self). Lists, tuples, dicts, files are iterables — each `iter()` call returns a fresh iterator. Custom iterables: usually return a generator from `__iter__` for simplicity.

Context managers implement `__enter__` (called on entering `with`, return value bound by `as`) and `__exit__(exc_type, exc_val, tb)` (called on exit, even on exception). Return truthy from `__exit__` to suppress the exception (rare — usually return None). Prefer `@contextlib.contextmanager` decorating a generator: code before `yield` is enter, after is exit, wrap in try/finally for cleanup.

Descriptors are objects with `__get__(self, obj, objtype)` and optionally `__set__`/`__delete__`. They power `property`, `classmethod`, `staticmethod`, ORM fields. Data descriptors (both get + set) override instance dicts; non-data descriptors don't. They live on the class, not the instance. Use them when you need reusable attribute behavior across many classes — for one class, `@property` is simpler.

A metaclass is the class of a class. `type` is the default metaclass. Define one by subclassing `type` and overriding `__new__`/`__init__`/`__call__`. Use `class Foo(metaclass=MyMeta): ...`. Used by ORMs (Django models), ABCs, enums. PEP 487's `__init_subclass__` and `__set_name__` cover most metaclass use cases in modern code — reach for a metaclass only when those aren't enough. Tim Peters: 'Metaclasses are deeper magic than 99% of users should ever worry about.'

`__slots__ = ('x', 'y')` on a class replaces the per-instance `__dict__` with fixed-slot storage — smaller memory, faster attribute access, prevents adding new attributes. Trade-offs: no class-level defaults stored in dict, no multiple inheritance with slotted bases that conflict, breaks `__weakref__` unless added. Worth it for classes with many instances (millions). dataclass: `@dataclass(slots=True)` (3.10+).

`TypeVar('T')` declares a type variable for generic functions: `def first(items: list[T]) -> T`. Constrain with `TypeVar('T', int, str)` or `bound=Comparable`. `covariant=True` / `contravariant=True` for variance. 3.12 added cleaner syntax: `def first[T](items: list[T]) -> T:` — no TypeVar import needed.

`Protocol` (PEP 544) brings structural subtyping (duck typing) to Python's type system. Define expected methods; any class with matching shape is a Protocol implementer — no inheritance needed. `@runtime_checkable` allows `isinstance` checks (slow, attribute-only). Use Protocols instead of ABCs when you don't control the implementing classes (e.g. third-party libs).

`TypedDict` types dictionaries with known string keys: `class User(TypedDict): id: int; name: str`. Two syntaxes: class-based or `User = TypedDict('User', {'id': int})`. `total=False` makes all keys optional; per-key `NotRequired[X]` / `Required[X]` for 3.11+. Stays a real dict at runtime — no validation, no methods. Pair with pydantic for runtime validation.

Subclass `Generic[T]` to create a generic class: `class Box(Generic[T]): def __init__(self, value: T): ...`. Use as `Box[int]`. 3.12+ uses syntactic generics: `class Box[T]: ...`. Generics enable static checkers (mypy, pyright) to track types through containers. Runtime: parameterization just stores info, no enforcement.

`Callable[[int, str], bool]` describes a function taking int and str, returning bool. `Callable[..., T]` matches any args, return T. For complex signatures with kwargs/defaults, use `Protocol` with `__call__`. `ParamSpec` (3.10+) preserves full parameter info: `def wrap[**P, R](f: Callable[P, R]) -> Callable[P, R]`.

`ParamSpec` (PEP 612, 3.10+) captures a callable's full parameter spec so decorators preserve types: `P = ParamSpec('P')`; `def log(f: Callable[P, R]) -> Callable[P, R]`. Inside, use `*args: P.args, **kwargs: P.kwargs`. Lets type checkers see decorated functions as their original signature instead of `(*args, **kwargs)`.

`Literal['red', 'green', 'blue']` constrains a value to specific literals — string enums without an Enum class. Useful for mode flags: `def open(mode: Literal['r', 'w', 'a']) -> ...`. Type checker narrows: after `if mode == 'r': ...`, mode is `Literal['r']` inside the branch.

`Final` marks a name as never-reassigned: `MAX: Final = 100`. Static checker errors if it's later rebound. `Final[int]` if you also want the type. On a class attribute, prevents override in subclasses. Doesn't enforce immutability of the value itself — `lst: Final = []` still lets you `lst.append(x)`.

`ClassVar[int]` marks a class-level attribute, not an instance attribute. dataclass uses this: `count: ClassVar[int] = 0` won't become a field. Tells type checkers (and dataclass machinery) the value lives on the class. No runtime enforcement — it's a hint.

`Optional[X]` is exactly `Union[X, None]` — sugar. PEP 604 added `X | None` (3.10+), now preferred. `Optional[X]` does NOT mean 'has a default'; it means 'may be None'. Common confusion: `def f(x: int = 0)` doesn't need Optional; `def f(x: int | None = None)` does.

`Self` (PEP 673, 3.11+) refers to the enclosing class — useful in alternative constructors and fluent builders: `def from_dict(cls, d: dict) -> Self`. Subclasses inherit the binding: `Child.from_dict(...)` is typed as `Child`. Before 3.11, you needed a bound TypeVar trick.

`Never` (3.11+) is the bottom type — used for functions that never return normally (always raise or loop forever). Equivalent to the older `NoReturn`. Type checkers use it for exhaustiveness: in a match/if-elif, an `assert_never(x)` call in the unreachable else catches missing cases at type-check time.

On a TypedDict, `NotRequired[X]` marks a key as optional, `Required[X]` as required (3.11+). Lets you mix in one class: `class Cfg(TypedDict): host: str; port: NotRequired[int]`. Pre-3.11 trick: split into two TypedDicts with `total=False`/`total=True` and inherit.

Structural pattern matching (PEP 634, 3.10+): `match value: case [x, y]: ... case {'name': n}: ... case Point(x=0, y=y): ... case _: ...`. Patterns: literals, captures (bare names), sequence, mapping, class, OR (`|`), guard (`if`), as-pattern (`pat as name`), wildcard `_`. Class patterns use `__match_args__`. Not just a switch — destructures and binds.

Walrus `:=` (PEP 572, 3.8+) assigns inside an expression: `while (line := f.readline()): ...` or `if (n := len(xs)) > 10: print(n)`. Useful in comprehensions to reuse a computed value: `[y for x in xs if (y := expensive(x)) > 0]`. Don't overuse — readability cost is real.

A decorator that takes arguments is a function returning a decorator: `def retry(n): def deco(f): @wraps(f) def wrap(*a, **kw): for _ in range(n): ... return wrap return deco`. Three nested defs. Always use `@functools.wraps(f)` on the inner wrapper to preserve `__name__`, `__doc__`, `__wrapped__`. Class-based decorators with `__call__` are an alternative.

`functools.partial(f, *args, **kwargs)` returns a new callable with some args pre-bound. `add5 = partial(operator.add, 5)`; `add5(3) == 8`. Useful for callbacks, mapping, deferring config. `partialmethod` is the descriptor variant for class bodies. Note: positional args bind left-to-right; can't skip middle args (use a lambda).

`@functools.lru_cache(maxsize=128)` memoizes a function — bounded LRU cache keyed on args. `maxsize=None` is unbounded. 3.9+ added `@functools.cache` (unbounded, no LRU eviction). Args must be hashable. Methods cache by `self` too — risks memory leaks; use `cached_property` instead for per-instance caching. `.cache_info()` / `.cache_clear()`.

`functools.reduce(f, iterable, [initial])` applies `f` cumulatively left-to-right: `reduce(lambda a,b: a+b, [1,2,3,4]) == 10`. Guido moved it out of builtins because most uses are clearer as a loop or `sum`/`max`/`min`. Justifiable for non-trivial associative ops and dict-merge tricks.

`@functools.wraps(f)` on a decorator's inner wrapper copies `__name__`, `__doc__`, `__qualname__`, `__module__`, `__dict__`, and sets `__wrapped__ = f`. Without it, your decorated function looks like `wrap` everywhere — broken docs, broken introspection, confused debuggers. Always use it.

`itertools.chain(*iters)` lazily concatenates iterables. `chain.from_iterable(iter_of_iters)` flattens one level — preferred over `chain(*xs)` when xs is large/lazy because the latter unpacks eagerly. Doesn't deep-flatten — use a recursive helper for nested structures.

`itertools.groupby(iter, key=None)` groups CONSECUTIVE equal-key elements — unlike SQL GROUP BY. Sort first if you want full grouping: `sorted(xs, key=k)` then groupby. Yields `(key, group_iter)` pairs; the group iterator is invalidated when you advance the outer loop, so materialize it (`list(g)`) if you need to revisit.

`itertools.cycle(iter)` repeats an iterable indefinitely (caches it after first pass — memory grows with the source). Pair with `islice` or `zip` to bound. Classic use: round-robin assignment, color cycling. Don't `list()` a cycle — it never ends.

`itertools.islice(iter, stop)` or `islice(iter, start, stop, step)` — slicing for iterators (which don't support `[a:b]`). No negative indices. Consumes the underlying iterator up to `stop`. Combine with `cycle`, `count` for bounded infinite generation.

Combinatorics from `itertools`: `combinations(it, r)` r-length unique unordered tuples; `permutations(it, r)` ordered; `product(*its, repeat=n)` cartesian product (nested for-loops); `combinations_with_replacement`. All are lazy. `product(range(2), repeat=8)` enumerates all 8-bit strings.

`collections.Counter(iter)` is a dict subclass that counts hashable items. `Counter('mississippi')` -> `{'i':4,'s':4,'p':2,'m':1}`. Methods: `.most_common(n)`, arithmetic (`c1 + c2`, `c1 - c2` — keeps positive only), `&` intersection min, `|` union max. Missing keys return 0 instead of raising KeyError. Don't use for negative or float counts — surprising behavior with arithmetic.

`defaultdict(factory)` creates default values on missing keys via `factory()`. `defaultdict(list)` for grouping, `defaultdict(int)` for counting, `defaultdict(set)` for deduped grouping. Watch: `d['k']` auto-creates `[]` even on read. Pass to JSON: serializes fine. Prefer `Counter` for pure counts, `dict.setdefault(k, [])` for one-off needs.

`collections.deque(iter, maxlen=None)` is a thread-safe double-ended queue. O(1) append/popleft/appendleft/pop. `maxlen` makes a sliding window — old items drop off the opposite end. Use for BFS queues, log tails, recent-N. List has O(n) for `pop(0)` — deque fixes that.

`OrderedDict` preserves insertion order — but since 3.7, regular `dict` does too. OrderedDict still differs: `move_to_end(k, last=True)`, equality compares order, supports `popitem(last=False)` (FIFO). Most code today uses plain dict; reach for OrderedDict when you need LRU-style reorder or order-sensitive equality.

`ChainMap(d1, d2, d3)` presents multiple dicts as one — lookups walk left-to-right, writes hit the first map only. Used by Python itself for variable scopes (locals + globals + builtins). Great for config layering (CLI > env > file > defaults). `.new_child()` pushes a fresh scope; `.parents` drops the first.

`namedtuple('Point', ['x', 'y'])` creates a tuple subclass with field names. Memory-light, immutable, unpacks like a tuple. Compare to `dataclass` (mutable by default, more features) or `typing.NamedTuple` (typed, class syntax). Use namedtuple for simple immutable records, NamedTuple if you want types, dataclass for richer behavior.

`@dataclass(frozen=True)` makes instances immutable — assignment raises `FrozenInstanceError`. Auto-generates `__hash__` based on fields (regular dataclasses get `__hash__ = None` if `eq=True`). Useful for value objects, cache keys, set elements. Internal mutation of mutable field values (list, dict) is still possible — frozen only blocks reassignment.

`@dataclass(kw_only=True)` (3.10+) makes ALL fields keyword-only in `__init__`. Or per-field: `field(kw_only=True)`. Solves the 'can't add a required field after one with a default' inheritance pain. `KW_ONLY` sentinel: fields below it become kw-only.

`field(default=..., default_factory=..., init=False, repr=False, compare=False, metadata={...})`. `default_factory=list` avoids the classic 'mutable default' bug (without it, `field(default=[])` raises). `init=False` for derived fields set in `__post_init__`. `metadata` is opaque to dataclasses — for your own use.

`__post_init__(self)` runs after the auto-generated `__init__`. Used to derive fields, validate, or call super-init. With `init=False` fields, set them here. With `InitVar[T]` you can declare init-only params — they're passed to `__post_init__` but not stored as attributes.

`Path('.').glob('*.py')` non-recursive; `rglob('*.py')` recursive (==`glob('**/*.py')`). Returns a generator of Path objects. Patterns: `*` any name part, `**` zero-or-more dirs, `?` single char, `[abc]` char class. No `{a,b}` brace expansion — use `chain` of globs. Anchored if pattern starts with `/`.

`Path('a.tar.gz').suffix == '.gz'`; `.suffixes == ['.tar', '.gz']`; `.stem == 'a.tar'`. `with_suffix('.txt')` swaps the LAST suffix only. To strip all: `p.with_suffix('').with_suffix('')`. `with_name(new)` replaces full filename, `with_stem(new)` keeps suffix.

`p.parent` is the directory; `p.parents` is a sequence of ancestors (`p.parents[0] == p.parent`, `p.parents[-1]` is the root). `p.anchor` is drive+root (`'C:\\'` on Windows, `'/'` on Unix). `p.parts` is a tuple of every segment. `p.is_absolute()`, `p.resolve()` (returns absolute, follows symlinks).

`await asyncio.gather(c1, c2, c3)` runs coroutines concurrently and returns results in order. `return_exceptions=True` captures exceptions as result values instead of cancelling siblings. By default, first failure cancels the rest and raises. Use `asyncio.TaskGroup` (3.11+) for stricter structured concurrency.

`asyncio.create_task(coro)` schedules a coroutine to run as a Task on the running loop and returns immediately. Hold the returned Task (or it may be GC'd mid-flight). `await task` retrieves the result. Use TaskGroup (3.11+) for safer lifecycle handling — cancels siblings on error and waits for all on exit.

`asyncio.Queue(maxsize=0)` is an async FIFO — `put`/`get` are awaitable. Classic producer/consumer pattern. `put_nowait`/`get_nowait` raise `QueueFull`/`QueueEmpty`. `task_done()` + `join()` to wait for all items to be processed. Also `LifoQueue`, `PriorityQueue`.

`asyncio.Semaphore(n)` limits concurrency to N — `async with sem:` blocks until a slot frees. Pair with `gather` to bound an N-wide fan-out. `asyncio.Lock` is mutex. `asyncio.Event` is broadcast. `asyncio.Condition` for wait-notify. All are NOT thread-safe — for thread coordination use `threading.*`.

`asyncio.run(main())` is the high-level entrypoint (3.7+) — creates a new loop, runs, cleans up. Don't call from inside a running loop (use `await` instead). The older `loop.run_until_complete(coro)` is lower-level and leaks loops if you forget to close. Avoid mixing `asyncio.run` and a custom loop.

`httpx` is a modern Python HTTP client: same API as `requests` but adds async (`AsyncClient`), HTTP/2, connection pooling, timeouts that actually work, and proper type hints. `requests` remains the de facto sync-only choice — battle-tested, huge ecosystem. `aiohttp` is async-only with both client and server. For new sync code, httpx is fine; for async-first, httpx or aiohttp.

`aiohttp` provides async HTTP client and server on asyncio. Server: routing, middleware, WebSocket, streaming. Client: connection pooling, sessions (always reuse one `ClientSession`), timeouts. Older than httpx, mature, but client API is more verbose. For client-only async needs, httpx is often simpler; for an async server, FastAPI/Starlette tend to win.

`concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor` runs callables in a thread pool — good for I/O-bound work, sidesteps the GIL during blocking I/O. `ProcessPoolExecutor` uses subprocesses — bypasses GIL, but args/results must be picklable, startup is expensive. Both expose `.submit()` (returns Future) and `.map()` (preserves order). `as_completed()` yields results in finish order.

The GIL (Global Interpreter Lock) is a CPython mutex that allows only one thread to execute Python bytecode at a time. Threads still help I/O-bound code (lock released around blocking I/O and many C calls). For CPU-bound parallelism: `multiprocessing`, native extensions that release the GIL (numpy), or PEP 703's experimental free-threaded build (3.13t, no-GIL). PyPy and Jython differ.

`multiprocessing.Pool(n)` creates worker processes. `.map(f, iter)`, `.imap`/`.imap_unordered` (lazy), `.apply_async`. Each worker is a fresh interpreter — `if __name__ == '__main__':` guard required on Windows/macOS (spawn start method). Args must be picklable. For CPU-bound parallelism that needs to bypass the GIL. ProcessPoolExecutor wraps this.

`multiprocessing.Queue` is a pickling-based IPC queue safe across processes. `Manager()` provides server-process-backed shared dict/list/Namespace — slower than Queue but supports mutation. `Value` and `Array` use shared memory directly for simple types. `shared_memory` module (3.8+) for zero-copy buffers.

`from abc import ABC, abstractmethod`. Subclass `ABC`, decorate methods `@abstractmethod`. Can't instantiate a class with unimplemented abstract methods — TypeError. Supports `@abstractclassmethod`, `@abstractproperty` (or stack `@property` + `@abstractmethod`). Use ABCs for explicit interface declaration; use Protocols for structural duck typing without inheritance.

`mypy` is the original Python static type checker. `mypy file.py` checks types per PEP 484. Flags worth turning on: `--strict` (sum of many), `--warn-unused-ignores`, `--no-implicit-optional`. Config in `pyproject.toml` under `[tool.mypy]`. Slower than pyright/ruff but features-complete. Plugin system for SQLAlchemy, Django, dataclasses.

`pyright` is Microsoft's Python type checker (TypeScript-style, in Node). Powers Pylance in VS Code. Much faster than mypy, better inference, stricter defaults. `basic` vs `strict` mode. Watches files, gives diagnostics in real time. Config in `pyrightconfig.json` or `pyproject.toml`. Often complements mypy — they disagree about some edge cases.

`ruff` is a fast (Rust) Python linter and formatter — replaces flake8 + isort + black + many plugins. 100x+ faster. Configure in `pyproject.toml` `[tool.ruff]`. Selects rule sets by code prefix (`E`, `F`, `I`, `B`, `UP`...). `ruff check --fix` auto-fixes safe rules; `ruff format` reformats (black-compatible). Now the default linter in many new projects.

`pyproject.toml` (PEP 518 + 621) is the standard Python project file. `[build-system]` declares build backend (setuptools, hatchling, poetry-core, flit-core). `[project]` metadata (name, version, dependencies, optional-dependencies, scripts, entry-points). `[tool.<name>]` per-tool config (ruff, mypy, pytest). Replaces setup.py, setup.cfg, requirements.txt, MANIFEST.in for most projects.

Modern Python packaging: `python -m build` produces a sdist (`.tar.gz`) and wheel (`.whl`) into `dist/`. `twine upload dist/*` publishes to PyPI (use API tokens, not username/password). Wheels are pre-built — fast installs. sdist is source — needs building on the user's machine. `cibuildwheel` builds wheels for all platforms in CI.

Build backends: setuptools (legacy default), hatchling (modern, hatch-recommended), poetry-core, flit-core, pdm-backend. Workflow tools: pip+venv (minimal), Poetry (lock file, virtualenv, publish), PDM (PEP-standard, fast), Hatch (envs+matrix), uv (Rust, blazing fast, now eating everyone's lunch). uv combines pip/pip-tools/venv/pipx in one tool.

`uv` (Astral) is a Rust-written Python package + project manager — 10-100x faster than pip. Drop-in `uv pip install`, `uv venv`, `uv run script.py`, `uv tool install` (replaces pipx), `uv python install 3.12` (replaces pyenv). `uv lock` / `uv sync` with `pyproject.toml`. As of 2025 it's the de facto fast path for new Python projects.

`pipx` installs Python CLI applications into isolated venvs and exposes them on PATH — keeps your global Python clean. `pipx install ruff`, `pipx install black`. `pipx run <pkg>` ephemeral run. `pipx upgrade-all`. Replaced by `uv tool install` in uv-based setups.

`breakpoint()` (3.7+) drops into the configured debugger — defaults to pdb. Set `PYTHONBREAKPOINT=ipdb.set_trace` (or `pudb.set_trace`, etc.) to override globally without editing code. `PYTHONBREAKPOINT=0` disables all breakpoint() calls — useful in production. Cleaner than the old `import pdb; pdb.set_trace()`.

`ipdb` is pdb + IPython niceties (syntax highlight, tab completion, magics). `pudb` is a full-screen TUI debugger — variable pane, breakpoints list, stack. `pdb++` (the package `pdbpp`) auto-replaces pdb with a nicer version. Set `PYTHONBREAKPOINT=ipdb.set_trace` so `breakpoint()` opens your preferred debugger.

`import dis; dis.dis(f)` disassembles a function/code object to CPython bytecode. Useful for understanding what `a if c else b` vs `c and a or b` actually compile to, or comparing two implementations. `dis.show_code(f)` summarizes consts/names. Bytecode is implementation-specific (CPython only) and changes between versions.

`ast.parse(source)` returns the abstract syntax tree of Python source. Walk with `ast.NodeVisitor` or transform with `ast.NodeTransformer`. `ast.unparse(tree)` (3.9+) converts back to source. Used by linters, formatters, codemod tools, and `eval`-safe arithmetic via `ast.literal_eval` (safe for literals only, never use `eval` on user input).

`inspect` introspects live objects: `inspect.signature(f)` gives a Signature with Parameter info; `inspect.getsource(f)`, `inspect.getfile(f)`, `inspect.getmembers(obj, predicate)`, `inspect.isclass`/`isfunction`/`iscoroutinefunction`. `inspect.stack()` / `currentframe()` for call-frame introspection (debuggers, loggers).

`weakref.ref(obj)` holds a non-owning reference — won't prevent GC. Call the ref to get the object or None if collected. `WeakValueDictionary` / `WeakKeyDictionary` build caches that don't pin their values/keys. `WeakSet`. Useful for caches, observer patterns, breaking reference cycles. Doesn't work on most builtins (int, str, tuple).

`if __name__ == '__main__':` runs the block only when the file is executed directly, not imported. The actual main module's name is `__main__`. A package with `__main__.py` lets `python -m pkg` run it. Console-script entry points (`[project.scripts]` in pyproject.toml) generate launchers — preferred over shebang scripts for installable packages.

`contextvars.ContextVar` provides per-context state — like thread-local but also async-task-safe. Each asyncio Task copies the current Context on creation. Used by logging (request IDs), tracing (OTel spans), DB connection scoping. `var.set(value)` returns a Token for `var.reset(token)`. Don't use threading.local for asyncio.

f-string features: `f'{x=}'` (3.8+) prints `x=<value>` — great for debug. Format spec after `:`: `{n:08d}` (zero-pad), `{x:.2f}` (2 decimals), `{x:,}` (thousands), `{x:>10}` (right-align), `{x:%}` (percent). Conversions: `{x!r}` repr, `{x!s}` str, `{x!a}` ascii. Nested format spec: `{x:{width}.{prec}f}`. Multi-line f-strings via implicit concatenation or parens.

Regex flags: `re.I` ignorecase, `re.M` multiline (`^`/`$` per line), `re.S` dotall (`.` matches newline), `re.X` verbose (whitespace and `#` comments ignored — great for readable patterns). Lookahead `(?=...)`, negative `(?!...)`. Lookbehind `(?<=...)`, negative `(?<!...)` — fixed-width only in `re`, variable-width in `regex` (3rd-party). Compile patterns reused often.

`subprocess.run(args, capture_output=True, text=True, check=True)` is the high-level API (3.5+). Use a list of args — pass `shell=True` ONLY when you genuinely need shell features, and NEVER with untrusted input (shell injection). `Popen` is the low-level building block — use for streaming or non-blocking IO. `timeout=` raises `TimeoutExpired`. `check=True` raises on non-zero exit.

`venv` is the stdlib (3.3+) virtual environment tool: `python -m venv .venv`. `virtualenv` is the older, faster, more-featured third-party tool (still supports old Pythons). `pyenv` manages multiple Python versions (compiles from source). `uv venv` is the new fast option and handles version install too. Activate with `source .venv/bin/activate` — or use `uv run` / `poetry run` to avoid activating.

`pickle` serializes arbitrary Python objects but is INSECURE — unpickling untrusted data is arbitrary code execution (pickle can be crafted to call `os.system`). Use only for trusted in-process or peer-controlled data. For interchange: JSON (human-readable, cross-language), msgpack (binary), protobuf (schema), CBOR. Never accept pickle over the network.

`df.merge(other, how=, on=, left_on=, right_on=)`. `how`: `inner` (default, intersection), `left` (all of left, NaN for missing right), `right` (mirror), `outer` (union), `cross` (cartesian, 1.2+). `indicator=True` adds a `_merge` column showing source. `validate='one_to_one'` / `'one_to_many'` etc. asserts the cardinality.

`df.melt(id_vars=['id'], value_vars=['a','b'], var_name='metric', value_name='value')` turns wide -> long. `df.pivot(index, columns, values)` turns long -> wide (fails on duplicates). `df.pivot_table(index, columns, values, aggfunc='mean')` aggregates duplicates. `stack`/`unstack` move the innermost axis level — works with MultiIndex.

MultiIndex: hierarchical row/column index. Build with `pd.MultiIndex.from_tuples`, `.from_arrays`, `.from_product`, or implicit via `groupby([...]).sum()`. Slice with `.loc[(outer, inner)]` or `pd.IndexSlice` for cross-level slicing. `.xs(key, level=)` cross-section. Beginners struggle — flatten with `.reset_index()` if you're not using it.

Window functions on Series/DataFrame: `df.rolling(window=7).mean()` fixed-size, `expanding().sum()` growing-from-start, `ewm(alpha=)` exponentially-weighted. `rolling('7D')` time-based on datetime index. `groupby().rolling()` per-group. `min_periods=` controls the leading-edge NaNs.

`polars` is a Rust-written DataFrame library with a lazy query API — multi-threaded, columnar (Arrow), often 10x faster than pandas on large data. Expression API differs from pandas: `df.select(pl.col('x').sum())`. `LazyFrame` builds a query plan, executes on `.collect()`. No index — flatter mental model. Solid choice for new analytical workloads.

`modin` is a drop-in `pandas` replacement that parallelizes via Ray/Dask — `import modin.pandas as pd`. `pyspark` (PySpark DataFrame) for distributed/cluster-scale. `dask.dataframe` partitions pandas across cores/machines with delayed execution. For single-node speed, polars usually beats them. For cluster, Spark.

`scipy` builds on numpy: `scipy.optimize` (minimize, root, curve_fit), `scipy.stats` (distributions, hypothesis tests), `scipy.signal` (filters, FFT helpers), `scipy.spatial` (KDTree, distance), `scipy.sparse` (sparse matrices), `scipy.integrate` (ODE solvers, quad), `scipy.linalg` (more than numpy.linalg). Pair with numpy + matplotlib + pandas as the classic SciPy stack.

`statsmodels` provides classical statistical models with R-like summaries: OLS/GLM/GLS regression, time series (ARIMA, VAR, SARIMAX), ANOVA, hypothesis tests, mixed-effects models. Pair with pandas. `model.fit().summary()` gives the publication-ready table. Compare to scikit-learn, which optimizes for prediction over inference (no p-values/confidence intervals by default).

`torch` is a tensor library with autograd and GPU support. Core: `torch.Tensor`, `nn.Module` (subclass + `forward()`), optimizers (`torch.optim`), data loading (`Dataset`, `DataLoader`). Dynamic graph (eager by default) — debug with normal Python. `model.train()/eval()` flips dropout/batchnorm. `torch.compile` (2.0+) for fast static compilation. Dominant in research, gaining in production.

TensorFlow: Google's ML framework. Keras (now `tf.keras`) is the high-level API — `Sequential`/`Model`, `.compile()`, `.fit()`. TF 2.x is eager-by-default with `@tf.function` for graph compilation. Stronger production story historically (TF Serving, TFLite, TF.js); has lost research mindshare to PyTorch. JAX rising in research too.

JAX is Google's numpy-on-XLA: pure-function transforms — `jit` (compile), `grad` (autodiff), `vmap` (auto-batch), `pmap` (multi-device). Functional style, no mutation. Composable transforms (`jit(grad(f))`). Backbone of recent research (Flax for NN layers, Optax for optimizers). Steeper learning curve than PyTorch but extremely flexible.

`Litestar` (formerly Starlite) is an ASGI framework — like FastAPI but with class-based controllers, layered DI, plugin system, and msgspec-fast (de)serialization. `Starlette` is the lightweight ASGI toolkit that FastAPI is built on — use directly when you want minimal magic. ASGI is the async successor to WSGI.

SQLAlchemy 2.0 unifies Core and ORM around `select()`/`insert()`/`update()`/`delete()` constructs. Mapped classes use `Mapped[T]` annotations and `mapped_column()` — type-checker-friendly. `Session.execute(select(User).where(...))` returns Result. Async support via `AsyncSession`. The legacy `Query` API still works but is deprecated for new code.

`Tortoise ORM` is an async ORM inspired by Django ORM — model classes, query API, migrations (aerich). Good for FastAPI/Starlette. `Peewee` is a sync, small, single-author ORM — readable source, lightweight, good for small projects. SQLAlchemy is the heavyweight standard. For new async code, SQLAlchemy 2.0's async or Tortoise.

Pytest fixtures: `@pytest.fixture` decorates a function; tests that name it as a parameter get its return value. `scope='function'|'class'|'module'|'session'`. `yield` in a fixture splits setup/teardown. `autouse=True` injects without naming. `params=[...]` parametrizes the fixture. Discover from `conftest.py` (shared across files in that dir tree).

`@pytest.mark.parametrize('a,b,expected', [(1,2,3), (4,5,9)])` runs the test once per row. Stack multiple `@parametrize` for cartesian product. `ids=` for nicer test names. `pytest.param(val, marks=pytest.mark.xfail)` per-row markers. Indirect parametrization passes values through a fixture.

Built-in fixtures: `monkeypatch` (set/delattr/setenv/setitem, auto-undone after test), `tmp_path` (per-test temp Path), `tmp_path_factory` (session-scoped temps), `capsys`/`capfd` (capture stdout/stderr), `caplog` (capture logging), `request` (test metadata), `pytestconfig`. Prefer `monkeypatch.setenv` over manual `os.environ['X']='y'`.

`tox` runs your test suite across multiple Python versions/dep sets in isolated venvs — config in `tox.ini` or `pyproject.toml`. `nox` is the same idea but configured in pure Python (`noxfile.py`) — more flexible than tox's INI. Both replaceable in CI by matrix builds; locally they're useful before pushing.

`contextlib`: `@contextmanager` turns a generator into a context manager (`yield` separates setup/teardown). `suppress(Exc)` swallows an exception in a block. `closing(thing)` ensures `.close()`. `redirect_stdout`/`redirect_stderr`. `ExitStack` lets you push context managers conditionally and unwind in reverse — replaces deeply nested `with`.

JS has two queues. Macrotasks: setTimeout, setInterval, setImmediate (Node), I/O, UI events. Microtasks: Promise callbacks, queueMicrotask, MutationObserver. Each macrotask is followed by the ENTIRE microtask queue draining before the next macrotask. `requestAnimationFrame` runs before paint, not on either queue. Long microtask chains can starve macrotasks — be careful with `await` loops over large arrays.

`requestAnimationFrame(cb)` schedules `cb` to run before the next paint — typically 60Hz. Browser pauses RAF in background tabs. Receives a high-resolution timestamp. For DOM-affecting work, RAF avoids layout thrash by batching reads/writes inside one frame. Cancel with `cancelAnimationFrame(id)`.

JS is prototype-based: every object has a `[[Prototype]]` pointing to another object (or null). Property lookup walks the chain. `Object.getPrototypeOf(obj)` reads it; `Object.setPrototypeOf` writes (slow, avoid). `obj.__proto__` is the legacy accessor. `class` syntax is sugar over prototypes. `Object.create(proto)` makes an object with the given prototype directly.

`this` rules in JS: 1) `obj.method()` -> this is obj. 2) `fn()` standalone -> undefined (strict) or global (sloppy). 3) `new Fn()` -> the new object. 4) `fn.call(x)` / `fn.apply(x)` / `fn.bind(x)()` -> x. 5) Arrow functions: NO own `this` — inherit from enclosing scope. Use arrows for callbacks where you want lexical this; avoid as methods on classes.

A closure is a function plus the variable environment where it was created. `function make(){ let n=0; return ()=>++n }` — the returned fn keeps a live reference to `n`. Classic pitfall: `for (var i=...) setTimeout(()=>log(i))` all log the final i (single binding). Use `let` (per-iteration binding) or an IIFE. Closures power module pattern, currying, hooks state.

Hoisting: `var` declarations are moved to top of function (initialized to undefined). `function` declarations are fully hoisted (callable before line). `let`/`const`/`class` are hoisted but uninitialized — accessing before the declaration is a ReferenceError (Temporal Dead Zone). Use `let`/`const`; the TDZ catches bugs `var` silently hides.

`async function` always returns a Promise; `await x` pauses the function until x settles, then resumes. Under the hood, the rest of the function after each `await` becomes a microtask callback. Throwing inside an async fn rejects the returned promise. `await` on a non-promise wraps it in `Promise.resolve` first. Top-level await works in ESM modules only.

`Symbol()` creates a unique value — useful as collision-free property keys. Not enumerable by `for..in` / `Object.keys`; use `Object.getOwnPropertySymbols`. Well-known symbols hook into language behavior: `Symbol.iterator` makes an object iterable (`for..of`), `Symbol.asyncIterator` for `for await..of`, `Symbol.toPrimitive` controls coercion. `Symbol.for(key)` accesses the cross-realm registry.

`function* g() { yield 1; yield 2; }` returns an iterator. `g().next()` advances, returns `{value, done}`. `yield expr` produces a value and pauses; `it.next(x)` resumes with `x` as the yield's result. `yield* other` delegates. Async generators (`async function*`) + `for await..of` for async streams. Used for lazy sequences, coroutines, redux-saga-style flows.

`WeakMap` keys are object references that don't prevent GC — entries auto-disappear when the key is collected elsewhere. Use to attach metadata to objects you don't own (DOM nodes, third-party objects). Not iterable, no .size. `WeakSet` is the same idea for sets. `WeakRef(obj)` (ES2021) for individual weak references; pair with `FinalizationRegistry` for cleanup hooks.

`new Proxy(target, handler)` wraps an object with trap functions: `get`, `set`, `has`, `deleteProperty`, `apply`, `construct`, etc. Used by Vue 3 reactivity, immer drafts, Mongoose-style models. `Reflect.get/set/...` mirror default behavior — call them from a trap to forward. Performance overhead is real; not for hot paths.

`structuredClone(value)` (modern browsers + Node 17+) deep-clones supporting Map/Set/Date/RegExp/Blob/ArrayBuffer/typed arrays/cyclic refs. Far better than `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x))` which loses dates, functions, undefined, cycles. Doesn't clone functions, DOM nodes, or class instances' prototype chain. Throws on unsupported types (Symbols, Error properties).

`Intl.NumberFormat('de-DE', {style:'currency', currency:'EUR'}).format(1234.56)`. `Intl.DateTimeFormat` for dates. `Intl.RelativeTimeFormat('en').format(-3, 'day')` -> '3 days ago'. `Intl.ListFormat`, `Intl.PluralRules`, `Intl.Segmenter` (grapheme splitting). Use these instead of hand-rolled formatting — handles locales correctly. Construct once, reuse — instantiation is expensive.

`BigInt`: arbitrary-precision integers. Literals: `123n`, or `BigInt(123)`. Can't mix with Number in arithmetic — throws TypeError. `JSON.stringify` doesn't serialize BigInt (throws). Slower than Number; use only when you actually need >2^53 precision (cryptography, ids, finance). Division truncates toward zero: `7n / 2n === 3n`.

Labels let you break or continue an outer loop from a nested one: `outer: for (...) { for (...) { if (cond) break outer; } }`. Rare in modern code — extract to a function and `return` instead. The only place labels are common is nested loops where extracting hurts readability.

Tagged template: `tag\`hello ${name}\`` calls `tag(strings, ...values)` where `strings` is an array of literal parts (with a `.raw` property) and `values` are the interpolations. Used by styled-components, lit-html, GraphQL `gql`, SQL builders. Lets you safely escape, syntax-highlight, or transform interpolated values.

ESM (ECMAScript Modules): `import`/`export`, static, async, native in modern browsers + Node 14+ (with `"type":"module"` or `.mjs`). CommonJS: `require`/`module.exports`, sync, Node's original — `.cjs` extension. UMD: wrapper that works as both AMD and CJS plus global — common in older browser libs. AMD (`define([deps], fn)`): legacy async loader (RequireJS). New code: ESM.

Node's `EventEmitter`: `.on(event, listener)`, `.emit(event, ...args)`, `.once`, `.off`. Default max listeners 10 — set higher with `.setMaxListeners` to suppress warnings, or fix the leak. Errors: emit `'error'` events; if unhandled, the process crashes. Modern alternative: `EventTarget` (cross-platform, AbortController-friendly). Always remove listeners you added in mounts/destroys.

Node streams: Readable (data source — `fs.createReadStream`, HTTP request), Writable (sink — fs.createWriteStream, HTTP response), Duplex (both — TCP socket), Transform (Duplex that transforms — zlib.createGzip). Pipe with `pipeline(src, t1, t2, dst, callback)` (handles errors and cleanup). Avoid manual `.pipe()` for production — error handling is leak-prone.

`cluster` forks worker processes that share server ports — primary distributes incoming connections. Pre-`worker_threads` way to use all cores. Largely superseded by process managers like PM2 (which clusters for you) or container orchestration (run N pods). For CPU work inside one process, prefer `worker_threads`.

`worker_threads` brings real threads to Node — for CPU-bound work without forking processes. Each worker has its own V8 isolate but can share `SharedArrayBuffer` and transfer `ArrayBuffer` zero-copy via `postMessage(value, [transferList])`. `MessageChannel` for direct worker-to-worker. Don't use for I/O — the event loop already handles that.

`import { promises as fs } from 'node:fs'` (or `import fs from 'node:fs/promises'`). Promise-based versions of readFile/writeFile/readdir/etc. Pair with `async/await`. Sync versions (`fs.readFileSync`) only for startup config. Streams for large files. `fs.watch` for file change events (platform quirks).

`readline` builds line-buffered interfaces over a Readable: `const rl = readline.createInterface({ input: process.stdin })`. `rl.on('line', cb)` per-line. For async iteration: `for await (const line of rl)`. Handles ANSI escapes, history (for terminals). `readline/promises` for promise API (`rl.question`).

Node `process` globals: `argv` (array of CLI args, [0]=node, [1]=script), `env` (process env vars), `cwd()`, `exit(code)` (immediate, may drop stdio buffers — prefer `process.exitCode = n` and let it drain), `stdin`/`stdout`/`stderr` (streams), `on('SIGTERM', ...)`, `on('uncaughtException', ...)` (log and exit, don't keep running).

`node:path`: `path.join('a','b')` joins with the OS separator; `path.resolve` resolves to absolute; `path.dirname`/`basename`/`extname`/`parse`. Always use `path.join` rather than string concatenation — Windows uses `\\`. For cross-platform POSIX-style paths use `path.posix`. ESM modules don't have `__dirname` — use `import.meta.url` + `fileURLToPath`.

`node:child_process`: `exec(cmd, cb)` runs through a shell, buffers output (max 1MB by default) — convenient but shell-injection risk. `execFile(file, args)` no shell, safer. `spawn(cmd, args)` streams stdio, no buffering — for large output. `fork('script.js')` for Node-to-Node with built-in IPC. Sync variants exist; avoid in event-loop code.

`perf_hooks` exposes high-res timing: `performance.now()` (sub-millisecond), `PerformanceObserver` for marks/measures and built-in events (gc, http, dns). `performance.mark('x')` + `performance.measure('span', 'x', 'y')`. `eventLoopUtilization()` to detect event-loop lag. Available as the `perf_hooks` module or the global `performance` in Node 16+.

`node --inspect script.js` enables the V8 inspector on port 9229 — connect with Chrome (`chrome://inspect`) or VS Code. `--inspect-brk` pauses before the first line. `--inspect=0.0.0.0:9229` for remote (firewall it). VS Code launch.json `"type":"node"` does it all under the hood.

Default V8 old-space heap is ~1.7GB on 64-bit Node. Raise with `--max-old-space-size=4096` (MB). Don't blindly increase — investigate the heap with `--heapsnapshot-signal=SIGUSR2` and Chrome Memory tab. OOM-killed in containers? Set both Node's flag AND the container memory request.

`npm` (default, with Node), `pnpm` (content-addressable store + hardlinks/symlinks — tiny disk usage, strict by default), `yarn` (Yarn 1 classic, Yarn Berry/2+ with PnP), `bun` (bundler + runtime + package manager in Zig, very fast). 2025: pnpm is the popular workspace choice, bun rising for speed, npm fine for most. Lockfiles: package-lock, pnpm-lock, yarn.lock, bun.lockb.

`npm run X` executes `scripts.X` from package.json with `node_modules/.bin` on PATH. Lifecycle: `preX`/`X`/`postX` run automatically around `npm X` — handy for build/test pipelines. Reserved scripts: `start`, `test`, `install` (and pre/post variants). `npm run` (no arg) lists all scripts. `--silent` suppresses npm's preamble.

Key package.json fields: `main` (CJS entry), `module` (ESM entry, bundler-only convention), `exports` (modern subpath map — replaces both), `types`/`typings` (TS declarations entry), `bin` (CLI executable mapping, installs to .bin), `scripts`, `dependencies`/`devDependencies`/`peerDependencies`/`optionalDependencies`, `engines` (node/npm version constraints), `type` (`module` for ESM-default).

pnpm workspaces: `pnpm-workspace.yaml` lists `packages: ['packages/*', 'apps/*']`. `pnpm -r run build` runs in each workspace. `pnpm add foo --filter @scope/pkg`. Internal deps use `workspace:*` protocol so versions stay linked. Faster than Yarn workspaces in practice; cleaner than npm 7+ workspaces.

Yarn 1 (classic) workspaces via `workspaces` in root package.json. Yarn 2+ (Berry): plugin architecture, Plug'n'Play (no node_modules — packages served from zip files via Yarn's resolver), zero-installs (commit `.yarn/cache`). PnP can break tools that scan node_modules — Yarn provides a node-modules linker for compatibility.

`"strict": true` in tsconfig enables: strictNullChecks, noImplicitAny, strictFunctionTypes, strictBindCallApply, strictPropertyInitialization, alwaysStrict, useUnknownInCatchVariables, noImplicitThis. Turn it on from day one — retrofitting is painful. Add `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` for the next safety level (array/dict access returns `T | undefined`).

TypeScript merges declarations of the same name across files: two `interface Foo`s combine their members; `namespace Foo` extends a class with statics or an interface with values; module augmentation (`declare module 'x' { ... }`) adds to a third-party module's types. Used to extend `Window`, Express's `Request`, etc.

`moduleResolution` options: `node` (CJS-era, with `.js`/`.ts` fallback), `node16`/`nodenext` (modern Node with package `exports` field, requires file extensions in imports), `bundler` (new, for Vite/esbuild/webpack — ignores extensions and exports), `classic` (legacy, don't use). Pick `bundler` for app code targeting a bundler, `nodenext` for libraries shipping to Node.

`paths` in tsconfig maps import specifiers: `"@/*": ["src/*"]`. Requires `baseUrl` (or in `bundler` mode, baseless paths are now supported). TS itself only rewrites for type-checking — your bundler/runtime must resolve them too. Use `tsc-alias` or a bundler plugin to translate paths in built output.

TS shipped legacy decorators (`experimentalDecorators: true`) used by Angular, NestJS, TypeORM. TS 5.0+ supports the Stage-3 ECMAScript decorator proposal natively (no flag), but the two syntaxes are incompatible — most frameworks still use experimentalDecorators. Stage-3 decorators have access via context object; legacy use parameter signatures.

`x as const` makes literals literal types and objects deeply readonly: `const a = [1,2] as const` is `readonly [1, 2]` instead of `number[]`. Useful for enum-like tuples, route maps, theme constants. Combine with `typeof` + `[number]` to derive union types from arrays.

`expr satisfies T` (TS 4.9+) checks that expr conforms to T WITHOUT widening expr's inferred type. Compare to `expr as T` (cast, no inference preserved) and `const x: T = expr` (variable type becomes T, losing narrow info). Perfect for config objects where you want `keyof typeof config` to be the narrow literal union, but still enforce schema.

Narrowing techniques: `typeof x === 'string'`, `instanceof Date`, `'key' in obj` (presence check), discriminated unions on a literal tag, equality narrowing (`x === null`), user-defined type guards (`function isUser(x): x is User`), `assertion functions` (`function assert(...): asserts x is T`). Avoid `as` casts when narrowing works.

Template literal types build types like strings: `type Greet = \`hello ${string}\``. Combine with utility types `Uppercase`/`Lowercase`/`Capitalize`/`Uncapitalize` and `infer` to parse strings at type level: route params, CSS units, event names. Powers libraries like tRPC and Hono's type-safe routing.

Mapped types iterate a key union: `type Readonly<T> = { readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] }`. Modifiers: `readonly`/`-readonly`, `?`/`-?`. Key remap via `as`: `{ [K in keyof T as \`get_${K & string}\`]: ... }`. Powers most utility types and many fluent APIs.

Conditional types: `T extends U ? X : Y`. Distribute over union types when T is a bare type parameter — wrap in `[T]` to disable: `[T] extends [U] ? X : Y`. Use with `infer` to extract types: `type ReturnType<T> = T extends (...a: any) => infer R ? R : never`. The basis for most utility types.

`infer` introduces a type variable inside `extends` clauses: `T extends Promise<infer U> ? U : T` peels a promise. Multiple infers in one extends. Built-ins built on infer: ReturnType, Parameters, Awaited, ConstructorParameters, InstanceType. Reads as 'capture this position into a name'.

Common TS utility types: Partial<T>, Required<T>, Readonly<T>, Pick<T,K>, Omit<T,K>, Record<K,V>, Exclude<T,U>, Extract<T,U>, NonNullable<T>, Parameters<F>, ReturnType<F>, ConstructorParameters<C>, InstanceType<C>, Awaited<T>, ThisParameterType, OmitThisParameter, ThisType, Uppercase/Lowercase/Capitalize/Uncapitalize (string), NoInfer (5.4+).

Project references split a TS codebase into independently-built sub-projects: each has `composite: true`, lists `references`, and `tsc -b` builds in dependency order with incremental cache. Faster than one mega-project, gives clean module boundaries. Used by large monorepos and the TypeScript compiler itself.

React Server Components render on the server (or at build) and ship serialized output to the client — zero JS for that component. Can `await` data directly, access server-only resources. Client components (`'use client'`) ship the JS and handle interactivity. Boundaries form a tree: a client component can have server children only via `children`/`props`. Next.js app router is the primary RSC consumer.

Rules of Hooks: 1) Call hooks at the top level — not in loops, conditions, or nested functions. React tracks them by call order. 2) Call only from React function components or other hooks. ESLint `react-hooks/rules-of-hooks` enforces this; `react-hooks/exhaustive-deps` warns on missing useEffect deps. Breaking these silently corrupts state between renders.

`<Suspense fallback={...}>` catches descendants that 'suspend' (throw a promise during render). The fallback shows while work is pending. Originally for lazy-loaded components (`React.lazy`); in modern React + RSC also for async data fetching and streaming. Pairs with `ErrorBoundary` for the failure case. Multiple nested Suspense boundaries enable progressive rendering.

Error boundaries are class components implementing `getDerivedStateFromError` and/or `componentDidCatch` — they catch errors in their subtree's render, lifecycle, and constructors. Don't catch: event handlers, async code (use try/catch), SSR, errors thrown in the boundary itself. No function-component API for this yet — use `react-error-boundary` library.

Next.js App Router (`app/` directory): file-based routing with React Server Components by default, nested layouts via `layout.tsx`, loading/error/not-found conventions, route handlers (`route.ts`), parallel and intercepting routes. Pages Router (`pages/`) is the legacy file-based system with `getServerSideProps`/`getStaticProps`. New projects: App Router.

Bundler/build-tool landscape: Webpack (mature, slow, plugin ecosystem), Rollup (libraries, clean ESM output, tree-shaking), esbuild (Go, blistering speed, ok plugins), Vite (dev: native ESM + esbuild; prod: Rollup), Parcel (zero-config), Turbopack (Webpack successor by Vercel, Rust), Rspack (Webpack-compatible Rust). For apps: Vite. For libraries: Rollup or tsup.

esbuild is written in Go with extensive parallelism — claims 10-100x faster than JS-based bundlers. Single binary, no node_modules. Bundles JS/TS/CSS, minifies, tree-shakes, code-splits. Plugin API is intentionally minimal. Tradeoff: fewer integrations than Webpack/Vite. Most use it indirectly through Vite/tsup.

Bun is a Zig-written JS runtime built on JavaScriptCore (Safari's engine), aiming to replace Node + npm + Webpack. Built-in bundler, test runner, package manager (`bun install`), TS support, SQLite, dotenv. Native APIs mostly Node-compatible. Pros: fast startup, fast installs. Cons: younger, some Node packages still break. Production use growing.

Deno (Ryan Dahl's Node redo) runs on V8 with Rust core. Native TS, secure by default (must grant `--allow-read`, `--allow-net`, etc.), URL-based imports (no node_modules), built-in formatter/tester/linter. Deno 2 added full npm compatibility and Node API support. KV store and Deploy edge runtime. Smaller ecosystem than Node but more cohesive.

Astro: content-first multi-framework — ships zero JS by default, opt-in 'islands' of interactivity. Great for marketing/blog. SolidJS: React-like JSX with fine-grained reactivity (signals), no virtual DOM, very fast. Qwik: 'resumable' — serializes app state in HTML and lazy-loads code on user interaction, near-zero JS on initial load.

ESLint flat config (`eslint.config.js`, v9 default) replaces `.eslintrc.*`: an array of config objects, each with `files`/`ignores`/`languageOptions`/`plugins`/`rules`. No more `extends`/`overrides` strings — import configs as objects. Plugins import as ESM. Migration: `npx @eslint/migrate-config`. Cleaner mental model, better composition.

Prettier is opinionated by design — limited config: `printWidth`, `tabWidth`/`useTabs`, `semi`, `singleQuote`, `trailingComma`, `bracketSpacing`, `arrowParens`. Config in `.prettierrc`/`.prettierrc.json`/`prettier.config.js` or `package.json`. Ignore via `.prettierignore`. Runs as editor format-on-save, pre-commit hook, or CI check (`--check`). Don't argue style — let Prettier decide.

Vitest is a Vite-native test runner with a Jest-compatible API — `describe`/`it`/`expect`, mocks, snapshots. Uses Vite's transform pipeline (fast, ESM-native, supports TS/JSX out of box) and runs tests in workers. Watch mode is sharper than Jest's. Migrating from Jest is usually a config swap. Jest still dominates older codebases.

`set -euo pipefail` is bash 'strict mode'. `-e` exits on any non-zero command (with caveats — does NOT trigger inside `if`, `&&`, `||`, `!`, or function calls in some contexts). `-u` errors on unset variables. `-o pipefail` makes a pipeline fail if ANY command failed (default: only the last). Add `IFS=$'\n\t'` to make word-splitting predictable. Combine with `trap 'echo err on $LINENO' ERR` for diagnostics.

IFS (Internal Field Separator) controls word splitting and `read`. Default is `<space><tab><newline>`. Set per-command: `IFS=, read -ra fields <<< "a,b,c"`. For loops over filenames: set `IFS=$'\n'` or use `find -print0` + `read -d ''`. Most 'mysterious' bash bugs trace back to unquoted expansion + IFS splitting on spaces in filenames.

Bash 4+ associative arrays: `declare -A users; users[alice]=admin; users[bob]=user`. Access: `${users[alice]}`. Keys: `${!users[@]}`. Values: `${users[@]}`. Length: `${#users[@]}`. macOS ships bash 3.2 — install bash 5 (`brew install bash`) for these. Indexed arrays: `arr=(a b c)`, `${arr[1]}`, `${arr[@]}` all, `${#arr[@]}` length.

Parameter expansion: `${var:-default}` use default if unset/empty, `${var:=default}` set var to default if unset, `${var:?err}` error out if unset, `${var:+alt}` alt if SET, `${var:offset:length}` substring, `${#var}` length, `${var#prefix}` shortest leading match, `${var##prefix}` longest, `${var%suffix}`/`${var%%suffix}` trailing, `${var/find/replace}`/`${var//find/replace}` substitution, `${var^}`/`${var^^}`/`${var,}`/`${var,,}` case.

Arithmetic expansion `$(( expr ))` evaluates integer expressions: `n=$(( i + 1 ))`. C-like operators: `+ - * / % ** == != < > && || ?:`. No floats — use `bc -l` or `awk` or python. `((expr))` runs an arithmetic command — exits zero if result is non-zero (yes, that's reversed). `let i++` is older syntax.

Globs: `*` any chars (not `/`), `?` one char, `[abc]` class, `[!abc]` negated. `shopt -s globstar` enables `**` for recursive matches. `shopt -s extglob` adds `?(p)` 0-or-1, `*(p)` 0+, `+(p)` 1+, `@(p)` exactly one, `!(p)` not. `shopt -s nullglob` makes non-matching globs expand to nothing (default: literal). `shopt -s nocaseglob` case-insensitive.

`trap 'cmd' SIG`: run cmd on signal. Common: `trap cleanup EXIT` (always runs, including normal exit), `trap 'echo line $LINENO' ERR` (on any failure under `set -e`), `INT` (Ctrl-C), `TERM`. `trap - SIG` removes. `trap '' SIG` ignores. Define cleanup early; pair with mktemp for safe temp files. `kill -l` lists signals.

Command substitution: prefer `$(cmd)` over backticks. Easier to nest (`$(echo $(date))`), works inside double quotes cleanly, and doesn't surprise with backslash handling. Backticks are POSIX-compatible (older sh). Trailing newlines of cmd output are stripped — use `IFS= read -rd ''` if you need to preserve them.

Here-doc: `cmd <<EOF\nline\nEOF` feeds multi-line stdin. Quote the delimiter (`<<'EOF'`) to disable variable expansion. Indent allowed with `<<-EOF` (strips leading tabs). Here-string: `cmd <<<"$var"` feeds a single string as stdin. Cleaner than `echo "$var" | cmd` (no subshell, preserves trailing whitespace better).

`cmd1 && cmd2` runs cmd2 only if cmd1 succeeded. `cmd1 || cmd2` runs cmd2 only if cmd1 failed. `cmd1; cmd2` runs both regardless. `cmd1 & cmd2` runs cmd1 in background then cmd2. Common idiom: `cd /path && rm *` — avoids deleting wrong dir if cd fails. `set -e` does NOT make scripts skip lines inside `&&` chains.

`local var` inside a function scopes `var` to that function and its callees. Without `local`, all variables are global — easy to clobber caller state. Always declare loop variables and helpers as `local`. Combine with assignment: `local count=0`. `local -r` makes it readonly within the function.

`readonly VAR=value` (or `declare -r VAR`) makes a variable immutable for the rest of the shell. Attempting to reassign or unset raises an error. Useful for script constants, environment guards. Note: in a function, use `local -r` to scope the readonly. Once readonly, a regular shell can only clear it by exiting.

`export VAR=value` (or `declare -x VAR=value`) marks VAR for export to child processes. Without export, the variable is local to the current shell — child processes won't see it. `env` lists exported variables. `export -p` shows export decls. `unset VAR` removes. To export only for one command: `VAR=value cmd`.

`type cmd` shows whether cmd is a builtin, alias, function, or external file. Builtins (cd, echo, printf, read, test, [, exit) run in-shell — no fork. External commands (ls, grep, find) live on PATH. `command cmd` bypasses functions/aliases to call the builtin/external. `builtin cmd` forces the builtin specifically. Builtins are faster; use `printf` over `/usr/bin/echo` in tight loops.

`cmd &` runs in background, prints PID into `$!`. `wait` blocks for all background jobs. `wait PID` for one. `wait -n` waits for any one to finish (4.3+). Common pattern: fire N jobs in parallel, then `wait`. Capture exit codes: `wait $pid; echo $?` (only valid for one pid at a time).

`coproc NAME { commands; }` starts a background pipeline whose stdin/stdout are bidirectional through `${NAME[1]}` (write) and `${NAME[0]}` (read). Lets a script chat with a long-running process — useful for streaming JSON over a tool's REPL. Rare; usually a named pipe (mkfifo) or a python helper is clearer.

Exit codes: 0 success, 1-255 failure. Conventions: 1 generic error, 2 misuse of builtins, 126 not executable, 127 command not found, 128+N killed by signal N (SIGTERM=15 -> 143, SIGINT=2 -> 130). Custom scripts: pick 2+, document them. `$?` holds the most recent exit. Inside `set -e`, a failing pipeline exits with the rightmost failure's code (or last if no pipefail).

POSIX sh (often dash on Debian/Ubuntu's /bin/sh) is the lowest-common-denominator. Bash-only features that DON'T work in sh: arrays, `[[ ]]` test (use `[ ]`), `==` (use `=`), `function` keyword (use `name() {}`), `local`, brace expansion, process substitution `<(...)`, `$'...'`, `${var^^}` case. Shebang `#!/bin/sh` means stick to POSIX; `#!/usr/bin/env bash` for bash.

fish: focuses on interactive UX — autosuggestions from history, syntax highlighting, sensible defaults. Not POSIX-compatible — its scripting syntax differs (no `$(...)` capture, `set` instead of `=`). Many users keep bash/zsh for scripts and fish for interactive. Plugin manager: fisher. Built-in `funced`/`funcsave` for fast function editing.

zsh: bash-compatible-ish with more features — globbing extensions (`**`, `(D)` for dotfiles, qualifiers), better completion, prompt themes (powerlevel10k, starship), associative arrays, floating-point arithmetic. Default shell on macOS since Catalina. oh-my-zsh: framework adding themes + plugins (git, autosuggestions, syntax-highlighting). Lighter alt: zinit, antidote.

`PS1` is the primary prompt string. Escapes: `\u` user, `\h` host, `\w` cwd, `\W` cwd basename, `\$` $ or # for root, `\n` newline, `\[`/`\]` non-printing markers (essential for colors — without them readline miscounts line width). Colors via `\[\033[31m\]...\[\033[0m\]`. `PROMPT_COMMAND` runs before each prompt — used for git status, dirty-tree indicators.

Bash history file: `~/.bash_history` (`$HISTFILE`). Size: `HISTSIZE` (in-memory), `HISTFILESIZE` (on-disk). Control: `HISTCONTROL=ignoredups:erasedups` dedups, `ignorespace` skips lines starting with space (handy for secrets). `shopt -s histappend` appends instead of overwriting on exit. `!!` re-run last, `!$` last arg, `^old^new` quick substitute. Ctrl-R reverse-search.

`shellcheck script.sh` is the de facto shell linter — catches unquoted vars, useless cats, broken comparisons, IFS bugs, here-doc indentation, command-substitution-loses-newlines. Has IDs (SC1234) you can suppress with `# shellcheck disable=SC1234`. Strongly recommended for any bash file longer than a one-liner. CI integration is one line.

`shfmt` is a shell parser + formatter (and minifier). `shfmt -i 2 -w file.sh` formats in place with 2-space indent. `-s` simplify, `-d` diff (good for CI). Supports bash, mksh, and POSIX sh modes. Pairs naturally with shellcheck.

`/etc/sudoers` controls who can sudo and how. Edit with `visudo` — locks the file and validates syntax (a broken sudoers locks you out of sudo). Drop-ins in `/etc/sudoers.d/`. Format: `user host = (runas) commands` — e.g. `deploy ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/systemctl restart app`. `%group` for group membership. Defaults: `Defaults env_reset, secure_path=...`.

systemd unit file `/etc/systemd/system/myapp.service`: `[Unit] Description=...
After=network.target
[Service]
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/myapp
Restart=on-failure
User=app
[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target`. `systemctl daemon-reload` after edits, `systemctl enable --now myapp`. `journalctl -u myapp -f` for logs. Type=simple (default), forking (for daemons that double-fork), notify (sd_notify).

systemd timers replace cron with better logging, dependencies, and missed-run handling (`Persistent=true` runs at boot if the time was missed). Pair: `myjob.service` + `myjob.timer`. Timer: `OnCalendar=*-*-* 03:00:00`, `OnBootSec=5min`, `OnUnitActiveSec=1h`. `systemctl list-timers` shows next runs. Cron is still everywhere and simpler for casual use.

Both detach/attach long-running terminals across SSH sessions. tmux: modern, scriptable, panes, vertical splits, prefix C-b (rebindable), better config, copy-mode like vim/emacs. screen: older, ubiquitous (often preinstalled), prefix C-a. tmux is the standard now — config in `~/.tmux.conf`. Both: detach with prefix-d, reattach with `tmux a` / `screen -r`.

The reflog records every move of HEAD (and named refs) — `git reflog` shows them. Entries expire (90 days unreachable, 30 days for refs/stash by default). Recover lost commits after `reset --hard` or bad rebase: `git reflog`, find the SHA before the screwup, `git reset --hard SHA` or `git checkout -b recover SHA`. Local-only — not pushed.

Git stores four object types in `.git/objects/`: blob (file contents, no name), tree (directory listing — names + modes + blob/tree SHAs), commit (tree SHA + parent(s) + author + message), tag (annotated tag — points at any object). Everything is SHA-1 (or SHA-256 in newer repos). Identical content = same blob = single storage. `git cat-file -p SHA` to inspect.

The index (`.git/index`) is a binary file listing tracked paths -> blob SHAs -> file modes. `git add` writes a new blob and updates the index entry. `git status` compares: working tree vs index (unstaged), index vs HEAD (staged). `git ls-files --stage` shows the index. Three-way during merges: stages 1/2/3 hold base/ours/theirs.

Loose objects (`.git/objects/xx/yy...`) get compressed into pack files (`.git/objects/pack/pack-*.pack` + `.idx`) by `git gc` or `git repack`. Packs store delta chains: similar objects encoded as diffs from a base, then zlib-compressed. Cloned repos arrive as packs (smart HTTP/SSH). `git verify-pack -v` to inspect.

`git gc` packs loose objects, expires reflogs (default >90d), prunes unreachable objects (>2 weeks, configurable). `git gc --auto` runs heuristically after some commands. `git gc --aggressive` recomputes deltas more thoroughly (slow). `git prune --expire=now` aggressively removes unreachable objects — risky if you have stash or detached work.

`git filter-repo` is the modern history rewriter, replacing `git filter-branch` (which is slow and footgun-laden). Use cases: remove a leaked secret/large file from history, extract a subdirectory into its own repo, rename emails. Always run on a fresh clone, then force-push to a new remote. Coordinate with the team — every clone is invalidated.

Submodule: a pointer to another repo at a specific commit, stored in `.gitmodules`. Lightweight but adds workflow friction — needs `git submodule update --init --recursive`, can drift, hard for newcomers. Subtree: merge another repo's history INTO yours under a path. Self-contained clone, no special commands. Subtrees grow your repo size; submodules don't. Most teams now avoid both in favor of monorepos or proper packages.

Git LFS stores large binary files outside the main repo (server-side blob store), keeping pointers in git. `git lfs install` once per machine, `git lfs track '*.psd'` writes `.gitattributes`. On clone/checkout, the LFS client fetches the actual bytes. Watch hosting limits (GitHub LFS bandwidth costs money). Alternatives: git-annex, DVC.

Git hooks live in `.git/hooks/` (client) or repo's `hooks/` (server). Client: applypatch-msg, pre-applypatch, post-applypatch, pre-commit (lint), prepare-commit-msg, commit-msg, post-commit, pre-rebase, post-checkout, post-merge, pre-push, pre-auto-gc. Server: pre-receive, update, post-receive, post-update. Make executable and they fire automatically. `pre-commit` framework manages these for you.

Config scopes (later overrides earlier): system (`/etc/gitconfig`, `--system`), global (`~/.gitconfig` or `~/.config/git/config`, `--global`), local (per-repo `.git/config`, default), worktree (`.git/config.worktree`, `--worktree`). `git config --list --show-origin` to see who set what. `git config --global core.editor vim`.

Define in `~/.gitconfig` under `[alias]` — or `git config --global alias.X 'cmd'`. Classics: `lg = log --oneline --graph --decorate --all`, `st = status -sb`, `co = checkout`, `br = branch`, `last = log -1 HEAD`, `unstage = reset HEAD --`, `amend = commit --amend --no-edit`. Shell aliases starting with `!`: `!git diff --cached`.
