`git --no-pager log` (note: before subcommand) skips the pager — useful for scripts and piping. `core.pager` config sets the pager (default `less`). `LESS='FRX'` is git's default less flags (quit if one screen, raw control chars, no init). To disable globally: `git config --global core.pager cat`.

`git diff` modes: no args (working tree vs index), `--staged`/`--cached` (index vs HEAD), `<rev>` (working tree vs rev), `<a>..<b>` (b vs a), `<a>...<b>` (b vs merge-base(a,b)). Display: `--word-diff` highlights changed words, `--color-moved=zebra` colors moved blocks differently from added/removed, `--stat`/`--shortstat`, `--name-only`, `-w` ignore whitespace.

SemVer: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. MAJOR bump = breaking change. MINOR = new backwards-compatible feature. PATCH = backwards-compatible fix. 0.x.y is 'anything goes'. Pre-release: `1.0.0-alpha.1`. Build metadata: `1.0.0+sha`. npm ranges: `^1.2.3` = 1.x.x compat, `~1.2.3` = 1.2.x. Pair with conventional commits + automated release tooling (semantic-release, changesets).

Monorepo benefits: atomic cross-package changes, single source of truth, shared tooling. Pains: clone size, slow git operations, build/test scope, access control. Tools to help: sparse-checkout (only fetch some paths), partial clones (`--filter=blob:none`), Bazel/Nx/Turborepo (task graph + caching), Buildkite/CircleCI dynamic pipelines. Examples: Google/Meta/Microsoft run massive monorepos with custom VCS layers.

GitHub: largest community, Actions CI, Copilot, free private repos, Codespaces. GitLab: self-hostable Community Edition, integrated DevOps platform (CI, registry, monitoring), strong MR workflow. Bitbucket: Atlassian — tight Jira/Confluence integration, Pipelines CI, free private repos for small teams. Gitea/Forgejo: lightweight self-hosted. Codeberg: nonprofit Forgejo instance.

Reusable workflows in GitHub Actions: a workflow with `on: workflow_call:` (defines inputs/secrets/outputs) can be called from another workflow's job via `uses: org/repo/.github/workflows/file.yml@ref`. Cleaner than composite actions for whole-job orchestration. Can be called recursively up to 4 levels deep. Use to standardize CI across repos.

`git fetch` updates remote-tracking branches (`origin/main`) without touching your working tree. `git pull` = `git fetch` + `git merge` (or `--rebase`). Many teams set `pull.rebase = true` globally to avoid 'merge of origin/main into local main' commits. Always fetch before reviewing local state — cheap, no risk.

`git cherry-pick SHA` replays one commit onto your current branch (creates a NEW commit with a new SHA). Range: `git cherry-pick A..B` (A exclusive..B inclusive). `-x` adds a `(cherry picked from commit ...)` note. Conflicts: resolve and `git cherry-pick --continue` (or `--abort`/`--skip`). Beware of cherry-picking from feature branches into main — usually you want merge/rebase.

`git rebase -i HEAD~5` opens an editor listing the last 5 commits with actions: pick, reword, edit, squash (merge into prior, edit message), fixup (squash with prior message), drop, break, exec (run a shell command). Reorder lines to reorder commits. Powerful but destructive — never rebase shared history. `git rebase --abort` to bail out.

Useful pytest plugins: `pytest-xdist` parallel run (`-n auto`), `pytest-cov` coverage (`--cov=pkg`), `pytest-mock` (`mocker` fixture wrapping `unittest.mock`), `pytest-asyncio` (async test support — `@pytest.mark.asyncio` or `asyncio_mode=auto`), `pytest-randomly` shuffles test order, `pytest-sugar` prettier output, `pytest-benchmark` perf, `pytest-snapshot`/`syrupy` snapshots.

Jest matchers: `.toBe` (===), `.toEqual` (deep equal), `.toStrictEqual` (strict deep), `.toMatchObject` (subset), `.toContain`, `.toHaveLength`, `.toThrow`, `.toHaveBeenCalled`/`.toHaveBeenCalledWith`/`.toHaveBeenCalledTimes`, `.toMatchSnapshot`, `.toMatchInlineSnapshot`. Negate any: `.not.toBe(x)`. Async: `await expect(promise).resolves.toBe(x)` / `.rejects.toThrow(...)`.

Jest mocks: `jest.fn()` creates a mock function with `.mock.calls`/`.mock.results`. `jest.spyOn(obj, 'method')` wraps an existing method. `jest.mock('module')` auto-mocks; `jest.mock('mod', () => ({ default: ... }))` for factories. `mockResolvedValue`, `mockReturnValue`, `mockImplementation`. Reset between tests with `jest.clearAllMocks()` (cheap) / `resetAllMocks()` (also drops impls) / `restoreAllMocks()` (un-spies).

Vitest features: native ESM/TS, Vite config sharing, browser mode (run tests in real browser via Playwright), `expect.poll`, `vi.fn`/`vi.spyOn`/`vi.mock` mirror Jest, in-source testing (write tests inside source under `if (import.meta.vitest)`), snapshot serializers, `--ui` browser dashboard, smarter watch mode. Compatible enough that most Jest suites migrate cleanly.

Playwright (Microsoft) runs Chromium, Firefox, WebKit. Auto-wait baked into actions (no flaky sleeps). `page.locator(...)` is the recommended API — re-evaluates on retries. `expect(locator).toBeVisible()` web-first assertions. Codegen: `npx playwright codegen <url>` records interactions. Trace viewer (`trace.zip`) lets you scrub through a failed run with DOM snapshots. Parallel by default.

Cypress runs in the browser alongside the app (not via WebDriver) — visual time-travel debugger is a killer feature. Limitations: historically one tab/origin per test (multi-origin and component testing have matured), no multi-tab, no native iframe access without workarounds. Component testing mode for React/Vue. Playwright tends to be the choice for cross-browser; Cypress for DX on a single Chromium target.

Selenium is the original cross-browser WebDriver — still the lingua franca for cross-language test suites (Java, Python, Ruby, C#, JS). Cons: flakiness without explicit waits, no built-in auto-wait, slower, weaker dev tools integration. Modern alternatives (Playwright, Cypress, WebdriverIO) usually feel sharper for a new project. Selenium still wins for cross-platform legacy and BrowserStack/Sauce-style farms.

Test pyramid (Mike Cohn): lots of fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, fewest end-to-end tests. Rationale: unit tests are fast/stable/isolating; e2e tests are slow/flaky/expensive. Variants: 'testing trophy' (Kent C. Dodds) elevates integration; 'honeycomb' inverts for service architectures. Real shape depends on the system — heed the principle, ignore the exact ratio.

Test doubles (Meszaros): Dummy — placeholder, never used. Fake — working but simplified (in-memory DB). Stub — pre-programmed answers to specific calls. Spy — stub that also records calls for inspection. Mock — pre-programmed AND has expectations verified at end. The mocking-library term 'mock' covers spies/stubs too. Prefer fakes for collaborators with behavior; stubs/mocks for boundaries.

Property-based testing generates many random inputs to check that a property holds, then shrinks failing inputs to a minimal counter-example. Python: `Hypothesis` (`@given(integers())`). JS/TS: `fast-check`. Ruby: `propcheck`. Strengths: finds edge cases (empty, unicode, max int) you wouldn't write by hand. Watch: properties are harder to write than examples — invariants, round-trips, oracle comparisons.

Snapshot testing captures output and asserts it stays the same. Strengths: low-effort regression coverage on rendered HTML, API responses. Pitfalls: 'all green, just update the snapshot' becomes muscle memory and the test loses meaning; large snapshots hide diffs; non-determinism (dates, ids) causes churn. Prefer focused inline snapshots (`toMatchInlineSnapshot`) and serialize stably.

Mutation testing measures test SUITE quality: a mutator changes your source (flip operators, drop branches), reruns tests — if no test fails, the mutant 'survived' and your tests missed that change. Tools: `mutmut`/`mutpy` (Python), `Stryker` (JS/TS/.NET), `PIT` (Java). Slow — typically run on PRs for changed files only. Aim for >80% mutation score on critical code.

BDD: write tests in a natural-language DSL (Gherkin: Given/When/Then) so non-developers can author them. Tools: Cucumber (Ruby/Java), Behave (Python), Cucumber.js, SpecFlow (.NET). Strengths: shared vocabulary with product, executable specs. Cost: lots of glue code between Gherkin steps and assertions — usually only worth it when non-devs actively author tests.

Line/branch coverage measures executed code, NOT tested behavior. 100% coverage doesn't mean correct (assertions could be missing). Watch for: covered-but-not-asserted code, generated code inflating numbers, dead code excluded. Useful as a floor (`<80% PR fails`) and trend; bad as a target (Goodhart's law). Pair with mutation testing to measure assertion quality.

Flaky tests: pass sometimes, fail sometimes. Causes: time/clock dependence, network, shared state, ordering, timeouts too tight, real concurrency. Strategies: detect via repeated runs (`pytest-flakefinder`, `jest --runInBand --testFailureExitCode 1` x N), quarantine (skip in CI but track), fix at the source (mock the clock, isolate state, increase timeout WITH justification). Never accept 'just retry it' as a long-term fix.

GHA matrix: `strategy.matrix.os: [ubuntu-latest, macos-latest, windows-latest]` runs the job once per combo. Multiple keys cartesian-product. `include` adds extras, `exclude` drops combos, `fail-fast: false` lets failures continue. `max-parallel` throttles. Reference in steps as `${{ matrix.os }}`. Common: test Python/Node versions x OSes.

`actions/cache@v4`: `path`, `key`, `restore-keys` (fallback prefixes). Cache pip/poetry/npm/pnpm/yarn — package managers' own setup actions (`setup-python`, `setup-node`) have a `cache` shortcut. Cache key SHOULD include lockfile hash. Caches are scoped per branch with fallback to default branch. 10GB org limit, evicted LRU after 7 days unused.

Secrets in GitHub Actions: repo, environment, or org level. Reference via `${{ secrets.NAME }}`. Auto-masked in logs (but you can leak them via base64). Not passed to PR workflows from forks by default (`pull_request_target` is the dangerous escape — only use for vetted cases). Use environment protection rules for prod deploy gates. Rotate regularly.

`concurrency: { group: ${{ github.ref }}, cancel-in-progress: true }` cancels older runs of the same group when a new one starts — perfect for PR CI to cancel obsolete pushes. For deploys, use a serial-only group (no cancel) so two deploys to prod can't race. Group key is a string you design.

GitLab CI config in `.gitlab-ci.yml`. Pipelines have stages, each stage has jobs (parallel). Job: `script`, `image`, `services` (sidecar containers like postgres), `rules` (conditional running, replaces deprecated `only/except`), `artifacts`/`cache`. Runners: shared, group-level, or self-hosted. `needs:` builds a DAG of jobs across stages. Strong integration with merge requests and review apps.

CircleCI config in `.circleci/config.yml`. Jobs run in Docker/Linux/macOS/Windows executors. Workflows orchestrate jobs (parallel, fan-in, manual approval). Orbs: shareable config packages. Caching: `restore_cache`/`save_cache` with key templating; workspaces pass artifacts between jobs. Strong Apple Silicon / iOS support. Concurrency control via `parallelism` and named contexts for secrets.

Multi-stage Dockerfile: `FROM image AS stage1`, ..., `FROM image AS final` then `COPY --from=stage1 /artifact /`. Lets you compile in a fat image (with gcc/node toolchain) and copy only the final binary into a slim runtime image. Smaller, fewer CVEs, faster pulls. Common pattern: `builder` stage builds, `runtime` stage runs.

BuildKit is Docker's modern build backend (default in recent versions, `DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1` in older). Features: parallel build of independent stages, build cache mounts (`RUN --mount=type=cache`), secret mounts (`--mount=type=secret`), SSH agent forwarding (`--mount=type=ssh`), remote cache (`--cache-to`/`--cache-from`), better output. `docker buildx` exposes BuildKit features.

Distroless images (gcr.io/distroless/*) contain only your app and its runtime deps — no shell, no package manager, no busybox. Smaller, drastically reduced attack surface. Variants: `static` (for Go binaries), `cc` (C/C++), `java`, `nodejs`, `python`, plus `:debug` versions with busybox for emergency shells. Trade-off: no `exec` for debugging in production.

`direnv` loads/unloads env vars per-directory from `.envrc` (run `direnv allow` once). `asdf` is a polyglot version manager (Python, Node, Ruby, ...) — `.tool-versions` file pins versions. `mise` (formerly rtx) is a Rust rewrite of asdf, much faster, drop-in compatible, also handles env vars (direnv-like). Many teams pair: mise for tool versions, direnv for secrets/env.

`pre-commit` (`pre-commit.com`) runs configurable hooks before git commits — `.pre-commit-config.yaml` lists repos and hooks (ruff, black, prettier, shellcheck, eof-fixer). `pre-commit install` writes a `.git/hooks/pre-commit`. `pre-commit run --all-files` to lint everything. Pins hook versions, caches their tool envs. Skip in emergencies: `git commit --no-verify` (rare).

`.editorconfig` at the project root sets per-editor defaults: `indent_style = space|tab`, `indent_size`, `end_of_line`, `charset`, `trim_trailing_whitespace`, `insert_final_newline`. Sections by glob: `[*.py]` / `[*.{js,ts}]`. Supported natively by VS Code, IntelliJ, and via plugin elsewhere. Pair with prettier/ruff for actual code formatting — editorconfig sets editor behavior, not source style.

VS Code debug config in `.vscode/launch.json`. `configurations` is a list; each has `type` (node, python, chrome, ...), `request` (launch or attach), `program`/`url`, `args`, `env`, `cwd`, `console` (integratedTerminal preserves stdin). `compounds` to run several at once. `preLaunchTask` runs a tasks.json task first (build, dev server). Use variables like `${workspaceFolder}`, `${file}`.

Renovate (Mend): highly configurable, supports many ecosystems and registries, schedules, dashboard, group rules, auto-merge for safe ranges. Dependabot (GitHub-native): simpler config in `.github/dependabot.yml`, also covers GitHub Actions versions, security alerts. Pair either with CI + auto-merge to keep deps fresh without manual toil. Renovate is more powerful; Dependabot is closer at hand on GitHub.

`pip-audit` scans installed packages or `requirements.txt` against PyPI advisory DB (OSV/PyPA). `pip-audit -r requirements.txt`. CI-friendly (`--strict` non-zero on findings). Similar tools: `safety` (PyUp DB, requires login for full), `osv-scanner` (Google's polyglot). Also: `bandit` for code-level Python security smells (eval, subprocess shell=True).

SAST (Static): analyze source/binary without running — Semgrep, CodeQL, Snyk Code, SonarQube. Catches injection patterns, secrets, broken crypto. DAST (Dynamic): probe a running app — OWASP ZAP, Burp Suite. Catches what only happens in production-shape requests. IAST instruments running code (mixes both). SCA (Composition Analysis) scans dependencies — Dependabot/Renovate/pip-audit are SCA.

Big-O describes worst-case asymptotic time/space growth. Common classes (small to large): O(1) constant, O(log n) logarithmic (binary search), O(n) linear (scan), O(n log n) linearithmic (good sorts), O(n^2) quadratic (nested scan, naive sort), O(2^n) exponential (subsets), O(n!) factorial (permutations). Drop constants and lower-order terms. Big-Theta (tight), Big-Omega (lower bound). Real perf also depends on constants, cache, branch prediction.

Binary search: O(log n) lookup in a sorted array. Repeatedly halve the search range based on the middle element. Tricky to write correctly: integer overflow in `(lo+hi)/2` (use `lo + (hi-lo)/2`), off-by-one on `hi` (inclusive vs exclusive), termination (`lo < hi` vs `lo <= hi`). Variants: lower_bound (first >= x), upper_bound (first > x). `bisect` in Python, `lower_bound` in C++.

Merge sort: divide & conquer, O(n log n) worst-case, stable, NOT in-place (needs O(n) aux). Recursively split array in half, sort each, merge. Strong for linked lists (no random access needed), external sorts (data > RAM), and when stability matters. Python's Timsort is a hybrid of merge sort + insertion sort optimized for real-world (partially sorted) data.

Quicksort: divide & conquer with partition around a pivot. Average O(n log n), worst O(n^2) (sorted input + bad pivot). In-place, NOT stable. Critical: pivot selection (median-of-three, random) and small-array switch to insertion sort. Introsort (C++ std::sort) is quicksort with a heapsort fallback when recursion gets too deep, guaranteeing O(n log n).

Dijkstra: shortest path from a source to all nodes in a graph with NON-NEGATIVE edge weights. O((V+E) log V) with a binary heap. Greedy: extract the unvisited node with smallest distance, relax its edges. Fails on negative edges — use Bellman-Ford (O(VE), detects negative cycles) or for DAGs, topological order. A* generalizes Dijkstra with a heuristic for goal-directed search.

Hash table: O(1) average insert/lookup/delete by hashing keys to bucket indices. Collision handling: chaining (linked lists per bucket) or open addressing (probe sequence — linear, quadratic, double-hashing). Load factor (entries/buckets) — resize/rehash above ~0.75 (chained) or ~0.5 (open). Worst case degrades to O(n) with adversarial keys (hashDoS); some langs randomize the hash seed.

B-tree: balanced multi-way tree with high fan-out — each node holds many keys, branches go to many children. Disk- and SSD-friendly: one node = one page = one IO. Variant B+ tree: data only at leaves, leaves linked for range scans — used by most relational DB indexes (PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB) and many filesystems. LSM trees (used by RocksDB, Cassandra) are the write-optimized alternative.

Trie (prefix tree): each node holds one character; paths spell strings. Lookup O(L) where L is key length. Strong for prefix queries (autocomplete, IP routing), longest-prefix-match, dictionary lookup. Space-hungry — compressed variants (radix tree, Patricia trie) merge single-child chains. Used in Linux kernel routing tables, network namespaces, regex engines.

Binary heap: complete binary tree with heap property (max-heap: parent >= children; min-heap reverse). Stored in an array — children of index i at 2i+1, 2i+2. O(log n) push/pop, O(1) peek. Used by priority queues, Dijkstra, top-K selection. Python `heapq` is a min-heap (push -x for max-heap). Heap sort: O(n log n), in-place, not stable.

Graph representations: adjacency list (each vertex -> list/set of neighbors) — O(V+E) space, fast iterate. Adjacency matrix (V x V boolean/weight) — O(V^2) space, O(1) edge query, good for dense graphs. Edge list — just pairs/triples. Choice: list for sparse, matrix for dense or when you query edges constantly. Traversals: BFS (queue, shortest unweighted path), DFS (stack/recursion, topo sort, cycles).

Linked list: nodes carry data + next pointer (doubly linked: + prev). O(1) insert/delete given a node reference, O(n) random access. Trade-offs vs arrays: poor cache locality, pointer overhead per node, no contiguous memory. Real world: rarely your first choice — arrays/vectors usually beat them due to cache. Useful for splice operations, intrusive containers (Linux kernel), LRU caches.

Recursion: function calls itself; clearer for tree/graph problems, divide & conquer. Iteration: explicit loop; lower overhead. Conversion: use an explicit stack data structure to iterate when recursion depth would blow the call stack. Tail-call optimization (TCO) makes tail-recursive calls O(1) stack — supported by Scheme/Scala/some Lisps. NOT by Python (intentional — Guido prefers visible stacks) or default JS.

A monad wraps a value with a context and provides `bind` (`flatMap`, `>>=`) to chain operations that produce wrapped values, plus `return`/`unit` to wrap a plain value. Examples: Maybe/Option (null safety), Either/Result (error channel), List (non-determinism), Promise/Future (async), IO (effects). The 'aha' is that `bind` lets you compose context-aware operations without unwrapping repeatedly — like `?.` for nullables, generalized.

A closure is a function bundled with the environment of free variables captured from its enclosing scope. Lets functions remember state between calls without globals or classes. Power: data hiding (the environment is private), partial application, callbacks that 'remember' context, memoization, the entire functional toolkit. Costs: GC keeps captured variables alive as long as the closure exists — beware leaks in long-lived event handlers.

A Promise/Future represents a value that may not exist yet (pending), eventually settling to fulfilled (with a value) or rejected (with an error). Composable: `.then`/`map`/`flatMap` chain transformations without blocking. Three states are terminal once entered. Models async work as values, replacing callback pyramids. Async/await is syntax sugar over promises in most languages. Hot vs cold: JS promises are hot (start immediately); Rust Futures are cold (must be polled/awaited).

Event-driven architecture: services communicate by emitting/consuming events (asynchronous, typically through a message broker — Kafka, RabbitMQ, NATS, AWS SNS/SQS). Decouples producers from consumers, scales horizontally, naturally audit-loggable. Trade-offs: eventual consistency, harder debugging across services, ordering and exactly-once semantics are subtle. Patterns: event notification, event-carried state transfer, event sourcing.

Message queue: one producer, one consumer pulls each message — load balances work (Celery, RabbitMQ queue, SQS). Pub/sub: one publisher, many subscribers each receive every message — fan-out (Kafka topics with consumer groups simulate both, Redis pub/sub, SNS, NATS). Hybrids: Kafka consumer groups (queue across instances, pub/sub across groups). Pick by access pattern: 'every interested party gets it' vs 'one worker handles it'.

ACID: Atomicity (all-or-nothing), Consistency (invariants preserved), Isolation (concurrent txns appear serial — usually relaxed to a level: read-uncommitted, read-committed, repeatable-read, serializable), Durability (committed data survives crash). Most relational DBs offer ACID. NoSQL often relaxes for scale (BASE — eventual consistency). Isolation levels trade correctness for throughput; pick deliberately.

Two-phase commit (2PC): coordinator asks each participant to PREPARE (vote yes/no, durably log). If all vote yes, COMMIT; otherwise ABORT. Provides atomicity across nodes — at the cost of blocking on coordinator failure mid-protocol (participants stuck holding locks). 3PC reduces blocking but assumes synchronous network. Modern alternatives: Sagas (per-step compensations), TCC (Try/Confirm/Cancel), or designing around it (idempotency + outbox pattern).

Monolith: one deployable, one codebase, one DB. Simpler to develop, deploy, debug; harder to scale teams independently. Microservices: many deployables, independent teams, polyglot, scale parts independently — but network failures, distributed tracing, schema versioning, eventual consistency, ops overhead. Sam Newman / Martin Fowler advice: monolith first, extract services when you have a clear seam AND organizational pain. 'Distributed monolith' is the worst of both worlds.

Bun (Jarred Sumner, 2021) is a JavaScript/TypeScript runtime written in Zig, designed as a faster Node.js replacement. Built on JavaScriptCore (Safari's engine) rather than V8. Includes a package manager, bundler, transpiler, and test runner in one binary. Notable: `bun install` is ~10-100x faster than npm; native TypeScript and JSX execution without a build step; `Bun.serve()` HTTP server competitive with frameworks like Hono. Released 1.0 in September 2023.

`bun install` is a drop-in npm replacement that reads package.json and writes a binary `bun.lockb` lockfile. It uses a global cache and hardlinks (or copies on filesystems that don't support them) to avoid duplicating files across projects. Common commands: `bun add react`, `bun add -d typescript`, `bun remove lodash`, `bun update`. The `--frozen-lockfile` flag enforces CI reproducibility.

`bun test` is a Jest-compatible test runner built into Bun. It supports `describe`, `test`, `expect`, snapshots, mocks, and lifecycle hooks (`beforeAll`/`afterEach`). Runs TypeScript and JSX natively with no config. Typically 10-30x faster than Jest because there's no transpile step and no spawn overhead per test file. Filter tests with `bun test --watch` or `bun test name-pattern`.

Deno 2.0 (October 2024) added full npm compatibility — you can `import express from 'npm:express'` directly and most npm packages just work. It also introduced workspaces, long-term backward compatibility guarantees, and stable `deno install`/`deno add` package commands. Deno 2 reads package.json and node_modules when present, removing the biggest friction with the Node ecosystem. The default permission model (`--allow-read`, `--allow-net`) is unchanged.

JSR (jsr.io) is an open-source JavaScript registry launched in 2024 by the Deno team. Unlike npm, it's TypeScript-first — packages publish source `.ts` files and JSR generates type declarations and JS bundles for every runtime (Node, Deno, Bun, browsers). Imports look like `import { foo } from 'jsr:@scope/pkg'`. Scores packages on docs coverage, runtime compatibility, and provenance. Works alongside npm; many packages dual-publish.

Biome is a Rust-based formatter and linter for JavaScript/TypeScript/JSON, forked from Rome in 2023. One tool replaces both Prettier and ESLint with ~25x faster performance — formats and lints a typical project in under a second. `biome.json` config; `biome check --write .` formats and fixes in one pass. Doesn't yet support every ESLint plugin (e.g. some React-specific rules), but covers most common rules out of the box.

Oxlint is a Rust-based JavaScript/TypeScript linter from the Oxc (Oxidation Compiler) project, designed as a fast ESLint alternative. Roughly 50-100x faster than ESLint because it parses with its own SWC-style parser and avoids the plugin VM. Ships with ~500 rules ported from ESLint, typescript-eslint, and eslint-plugin-react. Often used as a pre-commit gate alongside ESLint for slower deep rules.

Turbopack is Vercel's Rust-based incremental bundler, built as the successor to Webpack. Powers `next dev --turbo` in Next.js 13+ and became default for `next dev` in Next.js 15 (October 2024). Uses function-level caching so a tiny edit only recomputes affected modules. Production `next build --turbo` is still in beta as of late 2024 but rapidly approaching stable.

uv (Astral, 2024) is a Rust-based Python package and project manager. Replaces pip, pip-tools, pipx, poetry, pyenv, and virtualenv with one binary. `uv pip install` is ~10-100x faster than pip due to parallel downloads and a global cache. `uv add requests` updates pyproject.toml and uv.lock; `uv run script.py` auto-creates and activates a venv. Can also manage Python interpreter installs with `uv python install 3.12`.

Ruff (Astral, 2022) is a Rust-based Python linter and formatter that replaces Flake8, isort, pyupgrade, and (since 2024) Black. Implements 800+ rules from popular plugins, runs ~100x faster than Flake8. `ruff check .` lints, `ruff format .` formats. Config in pyproject.toml under `[tool.ruff]`. Now the default linter in most new Python projects and shipped by tools like Hatch.

Mise (formerly rtx) is a polyglot runtime version manager that replaces asdf, nvm, pyenv, and rbenv. Reads a `.mise.toml` or `.tool-versions` file and auto-switches Node/Python/Ruby/Go/etc versions per directory. `mise install` grabs everything listed; `mise use node@20` pins a version. Faster than asdf (written in Rust) and supports tasks, env vars, and hooks like direnv.

pnpm (Zoltan Kochan, 2017) is a Node package manager that uses a content-addressed global store at `~/.local/share/pnpm/store`. Each package version is stored exactly once on disk; `node_modules` contains hardlinks (or reflinks on APFS/btrfs) pointing into the store. Saves gigabytes across projects and installs ~2x faster than npm. Strict by default: a package can only import dependencies it declares, catching phantom dependency bugs.

esbuild (Evan Wallace, 2020) is a JavaScript/TypeScript bundler and minifier written in Go. Famous for being 10-100x faster than Webpack or Rollup — bundles the entire Three.js library in ~50ms. Uses Go's goroutines for parallel parsing and aggressive bytewise optimization. Lacks some Webpack features (HMR, complex plugin ecosystem) so often used inside larger tools like Vite, Snowpack, or for pure production builds.

Rspack (ByteDance, 2023) is a Rust-based bundler that's API-compatible with Webpack — most webpack configs work with minor changes. 5-10x faster than Webpack on large projects, with full support for loaders, plugins (most), code splitting, and HMR. Used in production by ByteDance for apps like Lark and Douyin. Pairs with Rsbuild (an opinionated wrapper) similar to how Webpack pairs with Next.js.

Vite (Evan You, 2020) is a frontend build tool that combines esbuild for dev (instant cold start via native ES modules) and Rollup for production builds. The dev server serves source files unbundled — the browser fetches modules as needed, with HMR updates in <50ms regardless of project size. `npm create vite@latest` scaffolds React/Vue/Svelte/Solid/Preact templates. Now the default for most modern frontend frameworks.

Vitest is a Vite-native test runner with a Jest-compatible API. Reuses your Vite config and plugins, so TS/JSX/CSS handling Just Works without separate setup. Features: watch mode that only reruns affected tests via the dev server's module graph, built-in coverage (c8 or istanbul), in-source testing, and snapshot testing. Typically 2-5x faster than Jest on Vite projects.

Astro (Fred K. Schott, 2021) is a static-site framework using the islands architecture: pages ship as zero-JS HTML by default, with interactive components (React/Vue/Svelte/Solid) hydrated as isolated 'islands'. Result is dramatically smaller bundles than SPA frameworks. `client:load`/`client:idle`/`client:visible` directives control when each island hydrates. Astro 4 (2024) added view transitions and a Dev Toolbar.

Tauri is a framework for building desktop apps with a web frontend and a Rust backend. Unlike Electron (which bundles Chromium ~120MB), Tauri uses the OS's native webview (WebKit on macOS, WebView2 on Windows, WebKitGTK on Linux) — final app sizes are typically 3-10MB. Frontend can be any JS framework; backend invokable from JS via `invoke('command_name', args)`. Tauri 2.0 (October 2024) added mobile (iOS/Android) support.

SST (Serverless Stack) is a TypeScript framework for deploying full-stack apps to AWS. v3 (2024, codename Ion) rewrote on top of Pulumi instead of CDK, dropping the CloudFormation dependency for faster deploys. Define infrastructure as code in `sst.config.ts`: `new sst.aws.Function('api', { handler: 'index.handler' })`. Includes live Lambda development that proxies invocations to your local machine for instant iteration.

OpenTofu is a Linux Foundation fork of Terraform created in 2023 after HashiCorp relicensed Terraform under the BUSL (Business Source License). State files and HCL syntax are compatible — most projects can swap `terraform` for `tofu` with no changes. Adds state encryption and dynamic provider functions ahead of Terraform. Maintained by an independent steering committee with contributors from Spacelift, Harness, and others.

Pulumi is an infrastructure-as-code tool that lets you define cloud resources in TypeScript, Python, Go, C#, or Java instead of a DSL like HCL. Same providers as Terraform (AWS/Azure/GCP/K8s) but with real programming language features: loops, conditionals, classes, npm packages. State stored in Pulumi Cloud by default; can self-host with S3 backend. Trade-off vs Terraform: more flexibility, but easier to write convoluted code.

Bazel is Google's open-source build system, designed for huge monorepos. Builds are hermetic (no system dependencies leak in) and incremental — a rebuild only redoes work whose inputs changed. Uses BUILD files with Starlark (a Python subset) to declare targets. Famous for its remote cache: a CI build can complete in seconds if another machine already built the same inputs. Used at Google, Uber, Stripe, Pinterest.

Parcel is a zero-configuration web bundler — point it at an HTML file and it figures out the rest (TypeScript, Sass, images, asset hashing). Parcel 2 (2021) rewrote the core in Rust for ~10x speedups. Less popular than Vite for modern apps but still excellent for quick prototypes, multi-page sites, or browser extensions where its file-detection magic shines.

Wrangler is Cloudflare's CLI for developing and deploying Workers (edge functions). `wrangler dev` runs your worker locally on the workerd runtime (the same one Cloudflare uses in production). `wrangler deploy` ships it. Config in `wrangler.toml` declares routes, KV namespaces, R2 buckets, D1 databases, and Durable Objects. v3 (2023) made local mode the default and added Miniflare 3 for accurate emulation.

`bun build` is Bun's built-in bundler, competitive with esbuild on speed and bundle size. Supports tree shaking, code splitting, JSX, TypeScript, CSS imports, and the `--compile` flag which produces a single executable embedding the Bun runtime + your app (~50MB). Useful for shipping CLIs without requiring users to install Node or Bun. API also exposed as `Bun.build({ entrypoints, outdir })`.

SWC (Speedy Web Compiler) is a Rust-based JS/TS compiler that replaces Babel. ~20x faster than Babel on single-thread, ~70x on multi-core because Rust has no GIL. Used by Next.js (since v12), Parcel 2, Deno (originally), and Vercel's bundler. Implements TypeScript stripping, JSX transform, modern JS down-leveling, and a Babel-compatible plugin system (Wasm-based).

Nx is a monorepo build system from Nrwl, focused on JavaScript ecosystems (with plugins for Go, Rust, .NET). Provides `nx affected -- test` which only runs tasks for projects affected by your git diff — saves huge time on CI. Includes generators (`nx g app my-app`), a task graph, distributed caching (Nx Cloud), and integrations for React/Angular/Vue/Next/Express/NestJS. Competes with Turborepo and Bazel.

Turborepo is a JavaScript monorepo build orchestrator from Vercel. Uses a `turbo.json` task pipeline definition and content-hashes inputs to skip re-running unchanged tasks. Remote cache (free with Vercel account) lets a teammate's CI build populate your local cache. Lighter than Nx — orchestrates existing tools (npm scripts, tsc, vitest) rather than wrapping them. Pairs naturally with pnpm workspaces.

Zod is a TypeScript-first schema validation library. `z.object({ name: z.string(), age: z.number().min(0) })` validates at runtime AND produces a TypeScript type via `z.infer<typeof Schema>`. Used heavily in tRPC, Next.js server actions, and form libraries. Common pattern: parse `process.env` through a Zod schema at startup so missing env vars fail loudly instead of becoming `undefined` deep in your code.

Drizzle is a TypeScript ORM with a SQL-like query builder — you write `db.select().from(users).where(eq(users.id, 1))` instead of finding the right method name. Generates type-safe results from your schema definitions. Migrations via `drizzle-kit generate` produce plain SQL files you can review. Lighter and faster than Prisma (no Rust query engine binary), with first-class support for Postgres, MySQL, SQLite, and edge runtimes.

Transformer attention lets each token in a sequence look at every other token and decide which ones matter. For each token, the model computes three vectors: Query (what am I looking for?), Key (what do I have?), Value (what do I give if matched?). The attention score is softmax(Q·Kᵀ / √d), which weights how much each token's Value contributes to the output. This replaces the strict left-to-right pass of RNNs with a fully parallel operation — the breakthrough that made GPT possible.

Multi-head attention runs the Q/K/V attention mechanism several times in parallel with different learned projections, then concatenates the results. GPT-3 uses 96 heads per layer; each head can specialize in a different pattern (one might track syntactic agreement, another long-range coreference). Splitting into heads means each head operates on a smaller dimension (e.g. 128) which is cheaper than one giant attention. Output is `Concat(head_1, ..., head_n) · W_O`.

Backpropagation trains neural networks by computing the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight, layer by layer, working backwards from the output. Forward pass: input → predicted output → loss. Backward pass: apply the chain rule to push gradients back through each layer (∂loss/∂w = ∂loss/∂y · ∂y/∂w). Then the optimizer (SGD, Adam) nudges each weight in the direction that lowers the loss. Modern frameworks (PyTorch, JAX) build a computation graph and run backprop automatically.

GPUs beat CPUs at neural network math because matrix multiplication is embarrassingly parallel — every output cell can be computed independently. A modern CPU has ~32 high-clock cores; an H100 GPU has ~17,000 CUDA cores plus dedicated tensor cores doing 4x4 matrix mults per cycle. GPUs also have ~10x the memory bandwidth (3 TB/s on H100 vs 100 GB/s on a desktop CPU) which matters because matrix mult is bandwidth-bound. CPUs win on branchy single-thread code; GPUs win on uniform dense math.

Quantization shrinks model weights from FP32 (32-bit float) to lower precision: FP16/BF16 (half memory, near-zero accuracy loss), INT8 (quarter memory, small loss), INT4 (eighth memory, larger loss). A 70B-parameter model needs 280GB at FP32 but only 35GB at INT4 — fitting on a single consumer GPU. Modern formats like GPTQ, AWQ, and GGUF (used by llama.cpp) use clever per-group scaling to minimize accuracy drop. Inference is also faster because more weights fit in cache.

LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation, Hu et al. 2021) fine-tunes a large model by freezing the original weights and training small rank-decomposed update matrices alongside them. Instead of updating a 4096×4096 weight matrix (16M params), LoRA trains A (4096×8) and B (8×4096) totaling 64K params — a 250x reduction. At inference you compute `W·x + B·A·x`. Multiple LoRA adapters can be swapped at runtime, enabling per-user personalization without storing copies of the base model.

RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) feeds relevant documents into an LLM's context so it can answer using your data without fine-tuning. Pipeline: (1) chunk your docs into 200-1000 token passages, (2) embed each chunk with a model like text-embedding-3-small, (3) store vectors in a database (Pinecone, pgvector, Qdrant), (4) at query time, embed the question and find top-k similar chunks via cosine similarity, (5) stuff those chunks into the prompt before the question. Cheaper than fine-tuning and lets you cite sources.

Vector similarity measures how 'close' two embeddings are. Cosine similarity (1 - cos angle, range -1 to 1) ignores magnitude and is the default for text embeddings. Dot product is faster but biased toward longer vectors. Euclidean (L2) distance treats embeddings as points in space. Most production embedding models (OpenAI, Cohere) normalize outputs to unit length, which makes cosine and dot product equivalent.

Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) search finds similar vectors fast without scanning the entire dataset. HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) builds a multi-layer graph where upper layers have fewer long-range links; queries greedy-walk down for ~log N lookups. IVF (Inverted File Index) clusters vectors with k-means and only searches the nearest clusters. Used by FAISS, Qdrant, Pinecone, pgvector's `vector_cosine_ops`. Trades a small accuracy hit (recall@10 ~99%) for huge speedups vs brute force.

Embeddings are dense numerical vectors that represent the meaning of text (or images, audio) so semantically similar items have similar vectors. OpenAI's text-embedding-3-small outputs 1536 dimensions; text-embedding-3-large outputs 3072. Sentence-BERT and Cohere embeddings are alternatives. The model learns these during training so 'dog' and 'puppy' end up close in vector space while 'dog' and 'algorithm' end up far apart. Used for search, clustering, classification, and RAG retrieval.

Tokenization splits text into the units an LLM actually sees. Modern models use Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) or SentencePiece, which build a vocabulary of common subword pieces. 'tokenization' might become ['token', 'ization']; 'gpt' might be ['g', 'pt'] if 'gpt' isn't common in training data. GPT-4 uses a ~100K token vocab. Why subwords? They handle unseen words ('un' + 'fudg' + 'able') without an out-of-vocabulary problem, and keep the embedding table manageable.

Three common subword tokenizers: BPE (GPT, Llama) merges the most frequent adjacent pairs iteratively. WordPiece (BERT) is similar but picks merges that maximize likelihood, not just frequency. SentencePiece (T5, Llama, Mistral) treats input as raw bytes and learns merges without pre-splitting on whitespace, so it handles Chinese/Japanese cleanly. All three produce a fixed-size vocabulary (~30K-256K tokens) that balances coverage with embedding table size.

When an LLM generates text, the final layer produces a probability for every token in the vocabulary. Temperature scales the logits before softmax: T<1 sharpens (more deterministic), T>1 flattens (more random), T=0 is greedy. Top-k samples only from the k highest-probability tokens (typically k=40). Top-p (nucleus) samples from the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities sum to p (typically p=0.9). Top-p adapts to the distribution shape; top-k is fixed.

Beam search keeps the top-k most likely sequences at each step instead of just one (greedy) — at the end it returns the highest-scoring complete sequence. Used in translation and summarization where you want the best output. Drawback: produces bland, repetitive text for open-ended generation because the highest-probability sequences are often generic ('I don't know, I don't know...'). Chatbots use sampling (top-p + temperature) for diversity; structured tasks use beam search.

Self-attention has Q, K, V all coming from the same sequence — a token attends to other tokens in its own sequence. Cross-attention has Q from one sequence and K, V from another — used in encoder-decoder models (T5, original Transformer) where the decoder attends to the encoder's output. In vision-language models like LLaVA, cross-attention lets text tokens attend to image patch features. Standard decoder-only LLMs (GPT, Llama) use only self-attention.

Layer Normalization (Ba et al. 2016) normalizes activations across the feature dimension within a single example: subtract the example's mean, divide by its standard deviation, then apply learned scale and shift. Batch Norm normalizes across the batch dimension. Transformers use LayerNorm (or its variant RMSNorm in Llama) because it works with any batch size and any sequence length, and doesn't break in inference when batch size = 1. RMSNorm skips the mean subtraction for ~10% speedup.

Adam (Kingma & Ba, 2014) maintains a running average of past gradients (momentum) and past squared gradients (adaptive learning rate per parameter). Each weight gets its own effective learning rate scaled by 1/√(avg squared gradient). Converges faster than plain SGD on most deep nets and is far less sensitive to learning rate choice. AdamW (Loshchilov, 2017) fixes Adam's weight decay to behave like true L2 regularization — the standard for training transformers.

Cross-entropy loss measures how far a predicted probability distribution is from the true distribution: -Σ y·log(ŷ). For a classifier predicting class probabilities, only the true class's log probability contributes, so the loss is -log(p_true). It's the standard loss for LLMs (next-token prediction = classification over the vocabulary) and image classifiers. Pairs naturally with softmax outputs because the gradients simplify to (predicted - true).

Mixture of Experts (MoE) replaces each feedforward layer with N parallel 'experts' (each a smaller FFN) and a router that picks the top-k experts (usually k=1 or 2) per token. A model can have 100B total parameters but only activate ~10B per token — combining the capacity of a huge model with the inference cost of a small one. Used in Mixtral 8x7B (8 experts, top-2), DeepSeek V3, and rumored in GPT-4. Trade-off: more memory bandwidth and tricky load balancing during training.

KV cache stores the Key and Value vectors computed for previous tokens during LLM inference, so generating each new token only requires computing K/V for that one token instead of the entire sequence. Without it, generating the 1000th token would redo work for the first 999 every step — quadratic cost. With it, generation is linear per token. Memory cost is significant: ~2 · layers · hidden_dim · seq_len · bytes per request, which is why long-context inference needs lots of GPU memory.

Flash Attention (Tri Dao, 2022) computes attention without materializing the full N×N attention matrix in memory. It tiles Q, K, V into blocks that fit in fast SRAM and computes attention block by block, recomputing during the backward pass instead of storing. Memory drops from O(N²) to O(N), enabling much longer context windows. Standard since 2023; Flash Attention 2 added better parallelism, Flash Attention 3 (2024) added FP8 support on H100.

Context window is the maximum number of tokens (prompt + response) an LLM can process at once. GPT-4o has 128K tokens (~96K English words), Claude 3.5 Sonnet has 200K, Gemini 1.5 Pro has up to 2M. Cost and latency scale with context length: doubling context doubles KV cache memory and (with standard attention) quadruples compute. Long-context retrieval accuracy isn't uniform — middle-of-context information is often recalled worse than start/end ('lost in the middle' effect).

A hallucination is when an LLM produces fluent but factually wrong output — invented citations, made-up function signatures, wrong historical dates. Caused by the model interpolating from training patterns when it lacks specific knowledge. Grounding techniques reduce it: RAG (retrieve real documents), tool use (call a calculator/search/database), structured output with validation, and chain-of-thought + verification steps. Fundamentally an LLM has no built-in notion of 'I don't know'.

Prompt engineering means crafting the input to an LLM to get reliable, useful output. Reliable patterns: (1) specify the role ('You are an expert Python reviewer'), (2) give examples (few-shot), (3) ask for step-by-step reasoning before the final answer (chain-of-thought), (4) constrain output format ('respond in JSON matching this schema'), (5) put critical info at the start or end of long prompts (the middle is often skimmed). Modern reasoning models (o1, o3) reduce the need for explicit CoT prompting.

Fine-tuning adjusts model weights on your data — best for teaching style, format, or new tasks. RAG injects retrieved data into the prompt — best for facts, recent info, or large knowledge bases. Rule of thumb: if you'd want the model to memorize it, fine-tune. If you'd want the model to look it up, RAG. They combine well: fine-tune for output style and tone, RAG for the underlying facts. Fine-tuning costs $$ upfront; RAG costs $$ at inference (longer prompts).

Hugging Face Transformers is the de facto Python library for using and fine-tuning open LLMs. `from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer; model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained('meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B')` downloads and loads a model from the HF Hub. Wraps PyTorch (default), TensorFlow, and JAX. Companion libraries: Datasets (data loading), Accelerate (multi-GPU), PEFT (LoRA), TRL (RLHF/DPO training), Tokenizers (Rust tokenizer impls).

llama.cpp (Georgi Gerganov, 2023) runs Llama-family models on CPU (and GPU) using highly-optimized C++ with AVX/AVX-512/ARM NEON SIMD. Uses the GGUF format which packs quantized weights + tokenizer + chat template into one file. Q4_K_M quantization is the popular sweet spot (~4.5 bits/param, ~5% perplexity hit). Powers Ollama, LM Studio, and most local-LLM apps. Makes a 7B model run at ~20 tokens/sec on a MacBook.

ONNX (Open Neural Network Exchange) is a model file format that lets you train in one framework (PyTorch) and run in another runtime (ONNX Runtime, TensorRT, CoreML, web). `torch.onnx.export()` converts a PyTorch model to .onnx. ONNX Runtime then runs it on CPU/GPU/NPU with framework-independent optimizations. Common pipeline: train in PyTorch → export to ONNX → run on mobile via ONNX Runtime Mobile or in-browser via onnxruntime-web.

Diffusion models generate images by learning to reverse a noising process. Training: take an image, add Gaussian noise in T steps until it's pure noise, train a U-Net to predict the noise at each step. Generation: start from pure noise, predict and subtract noise iteratively to recover an image. Text-to-image (Stable Diffusion, DALL·E 3) conditions the denoiser on a text embedding from CLIP or T5. Latent diffusion (Stable Diffusion) operates in a compressed VAE latent space for speed.

Chain-of-Thought prompting (Wei et al. 2022) asks an LLM to reason step-by-step before answering. Adding 'Let's think step by step' or showing few-shot examples with reasoning steps dramatically improves math, logic, and multi-step questions. Reasoning models like o1/o3 internalize this — they generate hidden 'thinking tokens' before the visible answer. CoT trades latency and tokens for accuracy: a problem that takes 50 tokens with direct answering might take 2000 with CoT.

Linux's default scheduler is CFS (Completely Fair Scheduler), introduced in 2.6.23 (2007). It tracks each task's 'vruntime' (virtual runtime) and always runs the task with the smallest vruntime, stored in a red-black tree for O(log N) lookups. Nice values (-20 to 19) weight vruntime — niceness 19 accumulates vruntime 1024x faster than -20. In kernel 6.6 (late 2023), EEVDF (Earliest Eligible Virtual Deadline First) replaced CFS as the default.

A context switch — saving one process's state and loading another's — takes ~1-10 microseconds of direct kernel work. The hidden cost is cache pollution: the new process's working set isn't in L1/L2 cache, so it stalls on memory until caches warm up. Total real-world cost can hit ~50 μs on heavily multitasked systems. Why threading-heavy workloads spend time profiling shows `sched_switch` overhead, and why async I/O (one thread, many sockets) often beats thread-per-connection.

TCP congestion control prevents a sender from overwhelming the network. Slow start: start with a small congestion window (cwnd), double it each RTT until packet loss. AIMD (Additive Increase Multiplicative Decrease): grow cwnd by 1 MSS per RTT, halve it on loss — the classic 'sawtooth' pattern. Modern variants: CUBIC (default on Linux, cubic function for faster recovery), BBR (Google, models bandwidth-delay product instead of reacting to loss, much better on lossy links).

DNS resolution converts a hostname like example.com to an IP. (1) App asks the OS resolver, which checks `/etc/hosts` and the local cache. (2) Miss → query the configured recursive resolver (e.g. 1.1.1.1). (3) Recursive resolver checks its cache, otherwise asks a root server (a.root-servers.net) for .com's TLD servers. (4) Asks the .com TLD server for example.com's authoritative servers. (5) Asks the authoritative server for the A record. Results are cached at every hop based on TTL.

TLS handshake (TLS 1.3): (1) ClientHello — client sends supported cipher suites, random bytes, and key share. (2) ServerHello — server picks a cipher, sends its key share, certificate, and a 'Finished' message, all encrypted from this point. (3) Client verifies the cert against trusted CAs, derives the shared session key via ECDHE, sends its 'Finished'. Total: 1 round trip (vs 2 for TLS 1.2). With 0-RTT resumption, repeat connections send application data in the first packet.

HTTP/2 (2015) runs multiple requests over one TCP connection (multiplexing), eliminating head-of-line blocking at the HTTP layer — but a single lost TCP packet still stalls all streams. HTTP/3 (2022) replaces TCP with QUIC, which runs over UDP and handles streams independently — one lost packet only stalls its own stream. QUIC also integrates TLS 1.3 (0-RTT handshake) and supports connection migration (your mobile keeps the connection when switching from WiFi to LTE).

A file descriptor (fd) is a small integer the kernel gives a process to identify an open file/socket/pipe. 0=stdin, 1=stdout, 2=stderr; the next `open()` returns 3. Each process has its own fd table. An inode is the on-disk structure that stores a file's metadata (permissions, size, timestamps, block pointers) — distinct from the filename, which lives in a directory entry. `stat` shows the inode number; hard links share an inode.

mmap maps a file into a process's virtual address space — you read/write memory and the kernel handles disk I/O on demand via page faults. Benefits: no read()/write() syscall overhead, automatic page cache sharing between processes, lazy loading (only touched pages get read). Used by databases (SQLite, LMDB), language runtimes for loading shared libraries, and tools like `ripgrep`. Downsides: page faults can be unpredictable latency, and writes don't sync until `msync()` or unmap.

select/poll/epoll let one thread monitor many file descriptors for I/O readiness. select (1983) takes a fixed-size bitmap (max 1024 fds) and scans all of them — O(N) per call. poll (1986) uses an array, no fd limit, still O(N). epoll (Linux 2.5, 2002) registers fds once via `epoll_ctl` and returns only the ready ones — O(1) per ready fd. epoll is what makes nginx/Node/Redis handle 100K+ concurrent connections per process. macOS/BSD use kqueue, which is equivalent.

io_uring (Jens Axboe, Linux 5.1 in 2019) is a shared-memory ring buffer interface for async I/O. Userspace puts requests in the submission queue; the kernel processes them and posts results in the completion queue — both visible to both sides without syscalls. Supports almost every syscall (read, write, accept, recv, fsync, openat). Massively faster than epoll + threads for high-throughput I/O — used by ScyllaDB, modern Postgres, and increasingly in Rust async runtimes.

Containers are built from two Linux kernel features. Namespaces isolate what a process can see: PID namespace (own process tree), mount (own filesystem view), network (own interfaces/IP), UTS (hostname), user (own UIDs), IPC. cgroups limit what a process can use: CPU shares, memory limits, block I/O bandwidth, PIDs count. Docker/podman/containerd combine these with an overlay filesystem and an OCI image to give the 'container' abstraction.

OCI (Open Container Initiative) standardized container image format and runtime spec in 2017, derived from Docker's original formats. An OCI image is a tarball-of-tarballs: a manifest pointing to a config JSON and a list of layer tarballs. Each layer represents filesystem changes (overlayfs-style). The runtime spec (runc, crun) describes how to launch a container from an unpacked image. Means images built by Docker run on podman, containerd, CRI-O, Kubernetes, etc.

systemd is the init system on most Linux distros (since ~2015). Manages services (called 'units') defined by `.service` files in `/etc/systemd/system/`. Common commands: `systemctl start nginx`, `systemctl enable nginx` (start on boot), `systemctl status nginx`. Logs go to the journal — view with `journalctl -u nginx -f`. Other unit types: `.timer` (cron replacement), `.socket` (socket activation), `.mount`, `.target` (groups, like runlevels).

Unix creates new processes via fork + exec. `fork()` clones the current process — child gets a copy of the parent's memory (copy-on-write so it's cheap) and a return value of 0; parent gets the child's PID. The child usually then calls `exec()` to replace its memory with a new program. Shell command execution is fork-then-exec. Modern alternative: `posix_spawn()` combines them and avoids the COW setup, useful when forking a huge process.

A pipe is a kernel buffer connecting two file descriptors — written bytes appear on the read end. Created with `pipe()` syscall, returning [read_fd, write_fd]. Anonymous pipes only work between related processes (parent/child) — the shell's `|` operator creates one and forks both sides. A FIFO (named pipe) is a pipe with a filesystem name (created with `mkfifo foo`); any process that opens it can read or write. Pipes typically buffer 64KB before blocking.

Shared memory IPC lets multiple processes map the same physical pages into their address spaces — the fastest IPC because no kernel copy is involved. POSIX API: `shm_open()` + `mmap()`. System V API: `shmget()` + `shmat()`. Used by Postgres (shared buffers), Chrome (renderer-GPU process), and any high-throughput app. Needs explicit synchronization (mutexes, atomics) since multiple processes write concurrently. /dev/shm is a tmpfs convention on Linux for backing files.

Signals are short messages the kernel delivers to processes. Common ones: SIGINT (Ctrl-C, polite stop), SIGTERM (default `kill`, request shutdown — process can clean up), SIGKILL (force kill, cannot be caught or ignored), SIGHUP (terminal closed, often used as 'reload config'), SIGSEGV (invalid memory access), SIGCHLD (child exited). Handle with `signal()` or `sigaction()` in C, or `signal` module in Python. Always run cleanup in a SIGTERM handler so containers shut down cleanly.

The GIL (Global Interpreter Lock) is a CPython lock that allows only one thread to execute Python bytecode at a time. Threading still helps for I/O-bound work (the lock is released during blocking syscalls) but not for CPU-bound work — two threads doing math run no faster than one. Workarounds: multiprocessing (real processes, no shared GIL but expensive IPC), or use C extensions (NumPy, Polars) that release the GIL during heavy computation. Python 3.13 (October 2024) added experimental free-threaded build (--disable-gil).

Stack memory is fast LIFO storage allocated per function call — local variables, function args, return addresses. Auto-freed when the function returns. Limited size (~8MB default per thread on Linux); deep recursion causes stack overflow. Heap is general-purpose memory allocated explicitly (malloc/new) and freed explicitly or by GC. Slower allocation but flexible lifetimes. In Rust, the borrow checker tracks which references point into the stack to prevent dangling pointers when functions return.

A cache line is the unit of transfer between CPU cache and RAM, typically 64 bytes. When you read one byte, the CPU pulls the surrounding 64. False sharing happens when two CPU cores write to different variables that happen to share a cache line — each write forces the other core to invalidate its cache, killing performance even though nothing is logically shared. Fix: pad hot per-thread data to 64+ bytes, or use thread-local storage.

Modern memory hierarchy, from fastest to slowest: CPU registers (~1 cycle), L1 cache (~4 cycles, ~32KB), L2 cache (~12 cycles, ~256KB), L3 cache (~40 cycles, ~16MB shared), RAM (~100 cycles, ~64ns), NVMe SSD (~100 μs), spinning disk (~10 ms), network (variable, ms). Each level is ~10-100x slower than the one above and 10x larger. Cache-friendly code (sequential access, small working set) can be 10-100x faster than cache-hostile code doing the same work.

x86 (Intel/AMD) is a CISC architecture with variable-length instructions, hundreds of opcodes, and rich addressing modes — designed when memory was scarce and instruction density mattered. ARM is RISC: fixed 32-bit instructions (or 16-bit Thumb), a smaller orthogonal instruction set, load/store separated from arithmetic. ARM's simpler decoder uses less power per op — why phones run ARM and Apple's M-series laptops get great battery life. Modern x86 chips internally translate to micro-ops, blurring the distinction at the execution level.

BIOS (Basic Input/Output System) was the original IBM PC firmware — 16-bit real mode, loads the first 512 bytes of the boot disk (MBR) and jumps to it. UEFI (Unified Extensible Firmware Interface) is the modern replacement: 64-bit, loads .efi executables from a FAT32 EFI System Partition, supports disks >2TB via GPT, includes Secure Boot (signed bootloaders), and has a built-in shell. All x86 machines since ~2012 ship UEFI, with optional BIOS compatibility ('CSM').

Linux boot stages with GRUB: (1) Firmware (UEFI/BIOS) loads GRUB from the boot partition. (2) GRUB shows the menu, loads the selected kernel + initramfs into memory. (3) Kernel decompresses itself and mounts initramfs as a temporary root, runs early userspace. (4) initramfs loads filesystem/storage drivers, finds the real root partition, switches root with `switch_root`. (5) PID 1 (systemd) starts, brings up services. Each stage is debuggable: `dmesg` for kernel messages, `journalctl -b` for systemd's boot log.

A B-tree is a balanced multi-way search tree used by almost every relational database (Postgres, MySQL, SQLite) for indexes. Each node holds many keys (hundreds, sized to fit a disk page ~8KB) and pointers to child nodes. Lookups are O(log_n N) where n is the branching factor — finding a row in a billion-row table takes ~4 disk reads. B+ trees (the actual variant used) keep all data in leaf nodes and link leaves for fast range scans.

Postgres uses MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control): every UPDATE creates a new row version instead of overwriting, and every transaction sees a snapshot of the database at its start time. Readers never block writers, writers never block readers. Cost: old row versions ('dead tuples') accumulate until VACUUM removes them. Each row has xmin/xmax columns (transaction IDs that created/deleted it) used to determine visibility for each snapshot.

Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) durability strategy: before modifying data pages, append the change to a sequential log file and fsync it. On crash recovery, replay the log to restore consistency. Used by Postgres (`pg_wal/`), SQLite (`-wal` file), MySQL (binlog + redo log), and most NoSQL stores. Bonus: streaming the WAL to a replica provides asynchronous replication for free. Sequential WAL writes are way faster than random data page writes.

PgBouncer is a lightweight Postgres connection pooler. Why it matters: Postgres allocates ~10MB per connection and uses a backend process per session, so 1000 idle connections cost ~10GB RAM. PgBouncer accepts many client connections and multiplexes them onto a small pool of real Postgres connections (often <100). Three modes: session (1:1, only the auth differs), transaction (clients share a backend between transactions — most common), statement (per query, breaks prepared statements). Critical for serverless apps that spawn many short-lived clients.

Postgres VACUUM reclaims space from dead tuples (rows left behind by UPDATE/DELETE in MVCC) and updates the visibility map. Autovacuum runs automatically when ~20% of a table's rows are dead. VACUUM ANALYZE also updates statistics for the query planner. VACUUM FULL rewrites the table to compact it but takes an exclusive lock — use `pg_repack` for online equivalent. Skipping vacuum eventually causes transaction ID wraparound, which forces emergency vacuum and can stall writes.

WiredTiger has been MongoDB's default storage engine since 3.2 (2015). It supports both B-tree and LSM-tree formats per collection (B-tree by default). Provides document-level locking (vs the original MMAPv1's collection-level lock), per-collection compression (snappy/zstd/zlib), and a journaling write-ahead log. Uses MVCC internally for snapshot isolation. Acquired by MongoDB Inc in 2014; originally built by the BerkeleyDB team.

LSM (Log-Structured Merge) trees optimize for write throughput. Writes go to an in-memory sorted buffer (memtable) and an append-only commit log. When memtable fills, it's flushed to disk as an immutable sorted file (SSTable). Background compaction merges SSTables into larger ones to maintain read performance. Used by RocksDB, Cassandra, ScyllaDB, LevelDB, BigTable, ClickHouse. Trade-off vs B-trees: faster writes but read amplification (may need to check several SSTables for a key).

Hash indexes provide O(1) point lookup by hashing the key to a bucket location. Used by Postgres's HASH index type, MySQL's MEMORY engine, and dict/map structures in memory. Trade-off vs B-trees: faster equality lookup, but no support for range scans (BETWEEN, <, >) or ordered iteration because the hash scrambles natural order. In Postgres, hash indexes only beat B-trees for very large tables where collision cost is worth it — usually B-tree is the safe default.

A covering index includes all the columns a query needs, so the database can answer the query from the index alone without touching the heap (the actual table data). In Postgres: `CREATE INDEX idx ON users(email) INCLUDE (name, created_at)`. Triggers an 'Index Only Scan' in EXPLAIN. Saves random I/O — instead of 'find row via index, then fetch row from heap', it's just 'walk index'. Worth it for hot read paths; costs more disk and slower writes.

A composite index on (a, b, c) can serve queries filtering on a, on (a, b), or on (a, b, c) — but NOT on b alone or c alone. The leftmost prefix rule: the index is sorted by a first, then b within each a, then c. So `WHERE a = 1 AND b > 5` uses the index efficiently; `WHERE b = 5` requires a full scan. Order columns by: equality filters first, then range filters, then sort columns. Selectivity matters — most-selective equality column first.

The query planner estimates the cheapest way to execute a SQL query using table statistics. `EXPLAIN` shows the plan; `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` actually runs the query and shows real times. Read the plan bottom-up: leaf nodes (scans) feed into joins, which feed into aggregates, etc. Look for: 'Seq Scan' on large tables (might want an index), bad row estimates (stats are stale — run ANALYZE), nested loops over large result sets (a hash join might be faster). `pg_stat_statements` shows the slowest queries over time.

A sequential scan reads every row in a table; an index scan walks an index to find specific rows. Indexes aren't always faster — if a query touches more than ~10% of the table, the random I/O of index lookups can be slower than a streaming sequential read. The planner uses statistics (pg_stats) to estimate row counts and decide. This is why a query can suddenly switch plans as table size grows or data distribution changes, and why outdated stats cause performance cliffs.

ACID describes the guarantees of a database transaction. Atomicity: all-or-nothing — partial updates never persist. Consistency: transactions move the DB from one valid state to another (constraints, foreign keys hold). Isolation: concurrent transactions don't see each other's intermediate state (isolation levels: read committed, repeatable read, serializable). Durability: once committed, data survives crashes (usually via WAL + fsync). Most relational DBs offer ACID; many NoSQL stores trade some of these for scale.

BASE (Basically Available, Soft state, Eventually consistent) is the consistency model of many distributed NoSQL systems (DynamoDB, Cassandra, S3). Instead of immediate consistency, replicas converge over time — a read right after a write might return stale data. Trade-off: massive scale and availability vs strict consistency. Modern systems offer tunable consistency: DynamoDB has 'eventually consistent reads' (cheaper, faster) and 'strongly consistent reads' (more expensive, may not work cross-region).

Two-phase commit coordinates a transaction across multiple databases/services. Phase 1 (prepare): coordinator asks each participant 'can you commit?' — each participant writes the transaction to durable storage and replies yes/no. Phase 2 (commit): if all said yes, coordinator tells everyone to commit; if any said no, tells everyone to abort. Problem: if the coordinator crashes mid-phase-2, participants are stuck holding locks. Used in XA transactions; modern distributed systems often prefer sagas (compensating actions) for this reason.

Sharding splits a large table across multiple databases by some key (the shard key). Range sharding: rows 1-1M on shard A, 1M-2M on B — easy range scans, but hot shards if traffic isn't even. Hash sharding: hash(key) % N picks the shard — evenly distributed but hard to range scan. Directory sharding: a lookup service maps keys to shards — flexible but adds a hop. Choose the shard key to colocate related data (e.g. user_id) so common queries hit one shard.

Replication keeps copies of data on multiple servers for availability and read scaling. Primary/replica (most common): writes go to one primary, replicate to read-only replicas. Synchronous replication waits for replica ack before confirming write — durable, but slow if a replica is laggy. Asynchronous: primary commits immediately, replicates in the background — fast but can lose recent writes on primary failure. Multi-primary (Galera, CockroachDB): writes accepted at any node, requires conflict resolution.

Read replicas serve SELECT queries to offload work from the primary, but they lag by milliseconds-to-seconds behind. Common gotcha: user writes a comment, page reloads from a replica, comment isn't there yet. Fixes: route writes-followed-by-reads to the primary ('read your writes'), use causal consistency tokens (Postgres LSN, DynamoDB), or wait for replica catch-up. Modern Postgres can be queried `synchronous_commit = remote_apply` to wait for replica apply at write time.

A materialized view stores the result of a query as a real table that can be queried like any other. Unlike a regular view (always re-evaluated), it's pre-computed — great for expensive aggregations. Trade-off: data goes stale. Refresh manually with `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW name` or `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY name` (no exclusive lock, requires a unique index). Common pattern: nightly refresh for analytics dashboards.

A CTE (Common Table Expression) is a named temporary result you can reference within a single query: `WITH active_users AS (SELECT * FROM users WHERE active) SELECT * FROM active_users JOIN orders ON ...`. Improves readability and lets you reuse a subquery multiple times. Recursive CTEs (`WITH RECURSIVE`) traverse hierarchies — perfect for org charts, comment trees, graph walks. In Postgres 12+, CTEs are inlined by default (faster); pre-12 they were always optimization fences.

Window functions compute values across a 'window' of related rows without collapsing them like GROUP BY does. `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY created_at)` numbers each user's rows by date. Common functions: ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK, LAG/LEAD (previous/next row), SUM/AVG OVER (running totals). Used for top-N-per-group, gaps-and-islands, deduplication, time-series differencing. Available in Postgres, MySQL 8+, SQL Server, BigQuery, Snowflake, SQLite.

Postgres jsonb stores JSON as a parsed binary format — faster to query than text JSON, supports indexing. Operators: `->` extracts as jsonb (`data->'name'`), `->>` extracts as text (`data->>'name'`), `@>` 'contains' (`data @> '{"active": true}'`). GIN index speeds up containment queries: `CREATE INDEX ON users USING GIN (data jsonb_path_ops)`. Good for flexible/sparse fields; bad as a substitute for proper relational columns (no foreign keys, harder constraints).

Postgres full-text search via tsvector (parsed document) and tsquery (parsed query). `to_tsvector('english', body)` converts text into normalized lexemes (stemmed, stopwords removed). Match with `@@`: `body_tsv @@ to_tsquery('english', 'cat & dog')`. Index with GIN for fast search. Rank results with `ts_rank()`. Solid for small-to-medium datasets; switch to dedicated search (Elasticsearch, Meilisearch, Typesense) when you need typo tolerance, faceting, or huge corpora.

pg_stat_statements is a Postgres extension that tracks execution stats for every normalized query — total time, call count, mean time, rows returned. Enable in `postgresql.conf` (`shared_preload_libraries = 'pg_stat_statements'`) and `CREATE EXTENSION pg_stat_statements`. Query `SELECT query, mean_exec_time, calls FROM pg_stat_statements ORDER BY mean_exec_time DESC LIMIT 10` to find slow queries. Essential for production performance debugging.

ClickHouse (Yandex, 2016) is an open-source columnar OLAP database optimized for analytical queries over huge tables (billions of rows). Stores each column separately and compresses heavily — analytical queries that touch a few columns out of hundreds run very fast. Uses LSM-style 'parts' for writes, merged in background. SQL-compatible with some extensions. Outperforms row-oriented databases on aggregations by 10-1000x; not designed for high-concurrency point updates.

Snowflake and BigQuery are cloud data warehouses that separate storage from compute — store data in cheap object storage (S3/GCS), spin up compute on demand for queries. Both use columnar storage, automatic partitioning, and SQL. Snowflake's 'virtual warehouses' let teams isolate workloads at different sizes; BigQuery is serverless with pay-per-byte-scanned pricing. Common use: stream operational data via Fivetran/Airbyte → transform with dbt → expose via BI tools.

The Strangler Fig pattern (Martin Fowler) gradually replaces a legacy system by routing more traffic to a new system over time, eventually 'strangling' the old one. Steps: (1) put a proxy/facade in front of the legacy system, (2) build the new system for one feature, (3) route that feature's traffic to the new system via the proxy, (4) repeat until the legacy is decommissioned. Named after the strangler fig tree which grows around a host tree, eventually outliving it. Lower-risk than a big-bang rewrite.

CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) separates the write model (commands that change state) from the read model (queries that read state). Writes go through domain logic into a normalized store; reads come from denormalized projections optimized for query shapes. Useful when read and write workloads differ massively (e.g. write a few events, read many dashboards). Overkill for most CRUD apps — adds complexity (two models to keep in sync). Often paired with Event Sourcing but not required.

Event sourcing stores every change as an immutable event (UserRegistered, OrderShipped) — current state is derived by replaying events. Benefits: full audit trail, time travel, easy projections, natural fit for CQRS. Pitfalls: events become a public API (renaming them is hard — need versioning + upcasters), replaying years of events is slow (use snapshots every N events), and most business logic is now 'apply this event' which is awkward for some domains. Not a default — use when audit/temporal queries justify the complexity.

The Outbox pattern reliably publishes events when updating a database, avoiding the dual-write problem (DB write succeeds but message publish fails or vice versa). Solution: in the same DB transaction that updates business data, INSERT an event row into an `outbox` table. A separate worker polls the outbox (or tails the DB log via CDC) and publishes events to Kafka/RabbitMQ/etc, marking them sent. Guarantees at-least-once delivery and exactly-once if you also use idempotent consumers.

A saga implements a long-running distributed transaction as a sequence of local transactions, each with a compensating action that undoes it. Order saga: reserve inventory → charge card → ship. If charge fails, run compensations (release inventory) instead of a 2PC rollback. Two flavors: orchestration (a central coordinator calls each step) and choreography (services react to each other's events). Trade-off: business logic must define compensations for every step, which can be tricky for irreversible actions (sending an email).

BFF (Backend For Frontend) is an architecture where each client type (mobile app, web app, partner API) has its own dedicated backend service that aggregates and shapes data from microservices. Avoids overloading one general-purpose API with conditionals for different clients. Mobile BFF can return smaller payloads optimized for cellular networks; web BFF can do server-side rendering. Trade-off: more services to maintain. GraphQL is sometimes used as a flexible alternative to a per-client BFF.

An API gateway is a single entry point in front of multiple backend services. Handles cross-cutting concerns: authentication, rate limiting, request routing, response aggregation, protocol translation (REST→gRPC), caching. Popular options: AWS API Gateway, Kong, Tyk, Envoy, Apigee. Pairs naturally with microservices to give clients one address. Risk: becomes a bottleneck or god-object if too much logic accretes there — keep it focused on infrastructure concerns, not business logic.

The Circuit Breaker pattern protects a system from cascading failures when a downstream dependency is slow or failing. Three states: Closed (normal — requests pass through), Open (failing — fail fast without calling the dependency), Half-Open (probe — try one request to see if recovered). After N consecutive failures, trip Open for a cooldown period. Originally popularized by Netflix Hystrix; now built into resilience libraries like Resilience4j, Polly (.NET), and service mesh sidecars.

The Bulkhead pattern isolates resources so a failure in one area can't sink the whole system — named after ship hull compartments. Concretely: separate thread pools or connection pools per downstream service, so when service A is slow, its threads block but service B's pool is unaffected. Kubernetes namespaces and resource quotas are a form of bulkhead. Applied at many layers: networking (separate egress per tenant), CPU (cgroups), memory (per-process limits).

Three common rate-limit algorithms. Token bucket: tokens refill at rate R up to capacity C; each request consumes one — allows bursts up to C, sustained R. Leaky bucket: requests fill a queue that drains at rate R — smooths output but doesn't allow bursts. Sliding window: count requests in the past N seconds — accurate but more memory. Redis is the typical state store. For APIs, return `429 Too Many Requests` with `Retry-After` and `X-RateLimit-Remaining` headers so clients can back off.

An idempotency key lets a client safely retry a request without causing duplicate side effects. Client generates a unique key (UUID) and sends it in a header (`Idempotency-Key`); server stores the key + response for ~24 hours. If the same key comes in again, server returns the cached response instead of re-processing. Stripe popularized this for payment APIs. Critical for any non-idempotent operation (charges, sends) that might be retried after a network timeout.

Request/response: client calls server, waits for answer — simple, tightly coupled, fails fast. Event-driven: producer publishes an event, any number of consumers react asynchronously — loosely coupled, scales independently, harder to debug (no straightforward call stack). Use request/response for synchronous needs (user-facing reads, transactional writes). Use events for fan-out, audit trails, integration with systems that should react but aren't on the critical path.

Message queue (RabbitMQ, SQS): one message goes to one consumer in a worker pool — load balancing. Pub/sub topic (Kafka, SNS, Redis pub/sub): one message goes to every subscriber — fan-out. Kafka blurs the line with consumer groups (each group gets the full stream; within a group, partitions distribute to consumers).
