Choose by your needs: queue for distributing work, pub/sub for notifying many systems of an event.

In distributed workflows: orchestration uses a central coordinator that calls each step in order (think workflow engine like Temporal, Step Functions). Choreography has each service react to events others publish — no central brain. Orchestration is easier to monitor and debug (one place sees the whole flow) but creates coupling to the coordinator. Choreography scales independently but the workflow is implicit, scattered across services — hard to understand at a glance.

A service mesh moves service-to-service concerns (mTLS, retries, observability, traffic splitting) out of app code and into a sidecar proxy (Envoy) deployed next to each service. The control plane (Istio, Linkerd) configures all sidecars. Benefits: language-agnostic, zero app code change for canary deploys or encryption. Costs: extra latency (~1ms), operational complexity, more infrastructure to manage. Linkerd is simpler; Istio is more featured.

Hexagonal architecture (Alistair Cockburn, 2005) — aka ports and adapters — puts business logic at the center with no dependency on infrastructure. The core defines 'ports' (interfaces) for what it needs; 'adapters' on the outside implement these for specific tech (Postgres adapter, REST adapter, RabbitMQ adapter). Swap a DB by swapping an adapter without touching domain code. Aligns with Clean Architecture and Onion Architecture; the diagram is a hexagon to emphasize multiple equivalent sides.

A bounded context (Eric Evans, DDD) is a boundary within which a domain model has consistent meaning. 'Customer' in Sales might mean a paying user; 'Customer' in Support might mean any contact — same word, different model, different code. Each bounded context owns its own database, language (ubiquitous language), and team. Maps roughly to microservice boundaries when done well. Without explicit contexts, models grow ambiguous and entangled — the hallmark of a 'big ball of mud'.

An Anti-Corruption Layer (ACL) translates between your domain model and a legacy or external system with a different model, preventing the foreign concepts from polluting your code. Implemented as a thin adapter that maps incoming data to your domain types and outgoing calls back to their format. Critical when integrating with vendor APIs, legacy mainframes, or another team's bounded context whose model you don't want to inherit. The translation layer absorbs the messiness.

Feature flags decouple deploy from release — ship code disabled, turn it on for a subset of users at runtime. Enables canary launches, A/B tests, kill switches, and trunk-based development with incomplete features. Common categories (Pete Hodgson): release toggles (temporary, remove after launch), experiment toggles (A/B), ops toggles (kill switches), permission toggles (per-user features). Tools: LaunchDarkly, Unleash, PostHog, Flagsmith, or a homegrown table. Discipline: clean up stale flags or your codebase becomes a maze.

Blue/green: run two identical environments (blue=current, green=new). Deploy to green, switch the load balancer when ready. Instant rollback by switching back. Doubles infrastructure cost during deploys. Canary: deploy new version to a small percentage of servers/users first (e.g. 5%), monitor metrics, gradually ramp up if healthy. Catches problems before full rollout but requires good metrics and traffic-splitting infra. Most modern setups use canary for big services and blue/green for stateless apps with database compatibility.

SQL injection happens when user input is concatenated into a SQL query: `"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name='" + name + "'"`. If `name` is `' OR '1'='1`, the query returns all users — or worse with `'; DROP TABLE users; --`. Defense: parameterized queries (prepared statements) where the driver sends SQL and values separately so values can never be interpreted as SQL. Every modern DB driver supports them (`?` or `$1` placeholders). String concatenation in queries is the single biggest source of SQL injection.

A timing attack exploits the fact that naive string/secret comparison short-circuits at the first mismatched byte — the function takes longer for inputs with more correct prefix bytes. Attackers measure microsecond differences over many requests to learn the secret byte by byte. Defense: constant-time comparison that always examines every byte. Use `crypto.timingSafeEqual` in Node, `hmac.compare_digest` in Python, `secrets_eq` in Rust. Critical for comparing API tokens, password hashes, HMAC signatures.

bcrypt is a password-hashing function that's deliberately slow — by design, you can't compute many hashes per second. The cost factor (rounds) controls slowness: each +1 doubles the time. Typical cost in 2025: 12-14 (~250ms-1s per hash on modern hardware). As hardware gets faster, bump the cost. bcrypt also salts automatically — the same password hashes differently every time. Resistant to GPU acceleration vs unsalted SHA-256, but modern best practice is Argon2id.

Argon2 (2015, winner of the Password Hashing Competition) is the current best password hash. Argon2id is the recommended variant — combines Argon2i (side-channel resistant) and Argon2d (GPU-resistant). Three tunables: memory (MB), iterations, parallelism. Memory-hard: forces attackers to spend RAM, not just compute — kills GPU/ASIC advantage. Recommended params: 19 MiB memory, 2 iterations, 1 thread (OWASP 2024). Use `argon2-cffi` in Python, `argon2` in Node, `argon2` crate in Rust.

scrypt (Colin Percival, 2009) is a memory-hard password hash designed before Argon2 — used by LiteCoin and some password systems. Like Argon2, makes GPU/ASIC attacks expensive by requiring lots of RAM. Tunables: N (cost), r (block size), p (parallelism). Recommended N=2^17, r=8, p=1 for interactive logins (~~100MB RAM, ~~100ms). Still solid, but Argon2id is preferred for new systems.

Certificate Transparency logs are public append-only records of every TLS certificate issued by participating CAs. Browsers (Chrome, Safari) require certs to appear in at least 2 logs or they're rejected. Lets anyone detect mis-issued or rogue certs for domains they own — Google originally built CT after rogue Symantec certs went undetected for years. Search public CT logs at crt.sh. As an operator: monitor for certs you didn't issue for your domain.

OAuth PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange, RFC 7636) protects the Authorization Code flow against code-interception attacks in public clients (mobile apps, SPAs). Client generates a random code_verifier and sends its SHA-256 hash (code_challenge) when starting auth. When exchanging the code for a token, client sends the original code_verifier — the auth server verifies the hash matches. If an attacker steals the auth code, they can't redeem it without the original verifier. Now required for all OAuth public clients (was optional).

CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is the browser mechanism that lets a server allow cross-origin requests, bypassing the same-origin policy. Simple requests (GET/POST with safe headers) include an `Origin` header; the server responds with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`. Complex requests (custom headers, PUT/DELETE, JSON content-type) trigger a preflight OPTIONS request first — the browser asks 'can I send this?' and only proceeds if the server allows. CORS is enforced by the browser, not the server — curl ignores it.

CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery) tricks a logged-in user's browser into making an unintended request to a site they're authenticated on — a malicious image tag could trigger a money transfer if cookies auto-attach. Defenses: (1) `SameSite=Lax` (default in modern browsers) — cookies only sent on top-level navigations to your site, (2) CSRF synchronizer tokens — server-generated random token submitted with each form, (3) custom request headers (CSRF can't set them cross-origin without preflight). SameSite=Lax mitigates most CSRF in modern browsers.

XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) injects attacker-controlled JavaScript into a page that other users view. Three types: stored (script saved in DB, served to every viewer), reflected (script in URL, executed when victim clicks the link), DOM-based (JS reads attacker-controlled input and inserts it unsafely). Defense: contextual output escaping (HTML, JS, CSS, URL all need different rules — frameworks like React do it automatically), avoid `innerHTML`/`eval`, set a strict Content Security Policy (CSP) to block inline scripts as defense in depth.

Session cookies: server stores session state, cookie holds just a session ID — easy to revoke (delete from DB), stateful (requires session store). JWTs: token contains user info, signed by server — stateless (no DB lookup), but can't revoke until it expires unless you maintain a denylist (which defeats the statelessness). Use sessions for typical web apps (revocation matters); use JWTs for short-lived tokens between services or as access tokens paired with a separate revocable refresh token.

HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security) is a response header (`Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains; preload`) that tells browsers to always use HTTPS for your site, even if a user types http:// or clicks an http link. Prevents downgrade attacks where a network adversary strips TLS. The `preload` flag lets you submit your domain to a list baked into Chrome/Firefox/Safari, so browsers never connect over HTTP even on first visit. Once preloaded, hard to undo — be sure HTTPS works.

Subresource Integrity (SRI) lets you specify a hash of a script or stylesheet you load from a CDN: `<script src="https://cdn.com/lib.js" integrity="sha384-..." crossorigin="anonymous">`. The browser refuses to execute the file if its hash doesn't match. Protects against compromised CDNs serving tampered code — a real risk after several CDN supply-chain attacks. Generate hashes with `openssl dgst -sha384 -binary file.js | openssl base64 -A`.

Same-Origin Policy is the foundational browser security rule: a document from one origin (scheme + host + port) can't read responses from another origin by default. Origin = `https://example.com:443`; `https://api.example.com` is a different origin. Without SOP, any site you visit could read your Gmail. Exceptions exist: scripts, images, and CSS can load cross-origin (but not be read), and CORS lets servers explicitly opt in to letting other origins read responses.

Asymmetric (public-key) cryptography uses a key pair: the public key encrypts/verifies, the private key decrypts/signs. You can share the public key freely. RSA (1977) bases security on factoring large primes — keys are 2048-4096 bits. ECDSA / Ed25519 use elliptic curves — equivalent security at much smaller key sizes (256 bits ≈ 3072-bit RSA), faster operations. Modern systems prefer Ed25519 for new keys (SSH, signing); RSA still common for compatibility.

Diffie-Hellman key exchange lets two parties agree on a shared secret over an open channel without ever transmitting it. Plain version: both agree on public numbers g and p. Alice picks secret a, sends g^a mod p. Bob picks secret b, sends g^b mod p. Both compute g^(ab) mod p as the shared key — an eavesdropper sees g, p, g^a, g^b but can't easily derive g^(ab) (the discrete log problem). Modern TLS uses Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDHE) for performance and forward secrecy.

WebSocket (RFC 6455) is a bidirectional, persistent connection over TCP, upgraded from a normal HTTP request. The client sends `Upgrade: websocket`; the server responds with 101 Switching Protocols, after which both sides exchange frames freely with no per-message overhead. Used for chat, live dashboards, multiplayer games, collaborative editing. Browser API: `new WebSocket('wss://...')`. Server libraries: `ws` (Node), `websockets` (Python), Tokio Tungstenite (Rust). Use wss:// (TLS) in production.

Server-Sent Events (SSE) is a one-way streaming protocol over plain HTTP — server pushes text events to the client. Browser API: `new EventSource('/stream')`. Much simpler than WebSockets when you only need server-to-client streaming (notifications, log tails, LLM token streaming). Built-in reconnection with `Last-Event-ID` header. Works through proxies and CDNs that don't understand WebSocket. OpenAI/Anthropic streaming APIs use SSE.

gRPC (Google, 2015) is an RPC framework using HTTP/2 for transport and Protocol Buffers for messages. Define services in `.proto` files; the compiler generates client+server stubs in Go, Java, Python, Rust, etc. Supports unary calls plus three streaming flavors (client-streaming, server-streaming, bidirectional). Much faster than JSON REST (binary, smaller payloads, HTTP/2 multiplexing) and strongly typed. Common for service-to-service inside data centers; less ideal for browsers (needs gRPC-Web).

WebAssembly (Wasm) is a portable binary instruction format that runs in browsers and standalone runtimes (Wasmtime, Wasmer). Compile from C/C++/Rust/Go/AssemblyScript. Loads faster than JS (already parsed), runs at near-native speed for CPU-heavy work (codecs, image processing, games, crypto). In browsers: complements JS, not replaces it. Outside browsers: emerging as a fast, sandboxed plugin format — Envoy filters, Shopify Functions, Fastly Compute@Edge, eBPF userland.

A service worker is a background JS script in the browser that can intercept network requests, cache responses, and run when the page is closed — enabling offline-first behavior. Registered with `navigator.serviceWorker.register('/sw.js')`. PWAs (Progressive Web Apps) combine a service worker + a Web App Manifest (icons, name, display mode) so the browser offers 'Install' and the app launches in a standalone window. Push notifications also flow through service workers.

Web Components are a set of browser APIs for building reusable custom HTML elements. Three pieces: Custom Elements (`class MyEl extends HTMLElement; customElements.define('my-el', MyEl)`), Shadow DOM (encapsulated subtree with scoped CSS), and HTML Templates (`<template>` tag for inert markup). Used to build framework-agnostic UI libraries (Lit, Stencil, Ionic, GitHub's custom elements). Less popular than React/Vue but useful for design systems shared across apps with different frameworks.

Two HTTP caching mechanisms work together. `Cache-Control: max-age=3600` says 'fresh for an hour, no revalidation needed' — fastest, no network for cached resources. ETag is a content fingerprint; the client sends `If-None-Match: "abc123"` and the server returns 304 Not Modified if unchanged (saves bandwidth, not the roundtrip). Combine for assets: hash-named files (`/app.a1b2c3.js`) with `Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable`; HTML with short max-age + ETag.

Three common compression algorithms for web/storage. gzip (1992): ubiquitous, ~3x compression, fast. Brotli (Google, 2015): ~20% smaller than gzip for text, slightly slower to compress but same speed to decompress — supported by all modern browsers via `Content-Encoding: br`. Zstd (Facebook, 2016): similar ratio to gzip with 3-5x speed, or matches brotli's ratio with a tunable level. Use brotli for HTTP text (HTML/JS/CSS), zstd for general-purpose storage and inter-service compression.

Git stores everything as objects in `.git/objects/`, each identified by the SHA-1 of its contents. Four types: blob (file content), tree (directory listing — names + permissions + child object IDs), commit (tree ID + parent commit IDs + author + message), tag (annotated tag). A commit isn't a diff — it's a snapshot pointing to a complete tree. Branches and tags are just files in `.git/refs/` containing a commit SHA. `git cat-file -p <sha>` shows any object's contents.

Git starts with loose objects (one file per object in `.git/objects/ab/cdef...`). `git gc` repacks them into packfiles: zlib-compressed and delta-compressed (similar files stored as differences). A packfile pairs with an index for fast lookups. Massively reduces repo size — the Linux kernel is ~5GB loose but ~2GB packed. Happens automatically; `git gc --aggressive` does deeper delta search (slow but smaller).

Docker images are stacks of read-only layers, each representing one Dockerfile instruction (FROM, RUN, COPY, etc). At runtime, a thin writable layer is added on top using a copy-on-write filesystem (overlayfs on Linux). Files unchanged from layers below are read directly; writes copy the file to the writable layer first. Layers are shared between images and containers — pulling an image only downloads layers you don't have. Order Dockerfile instructions least-changing-first to maximize cache hits.

Key Dockerfile patterns. Multi-stage builds: `FROM node:20 AS build` for compilation, then `FROM nginx:alpine` for runtime — copy only the build output across, drop the build toolchain. Order COPY by change frequency: package.json before source code so dependency install is cached. Use specific tags, not `latest`. Pin base image digests for reproducibility (`FROM node@sha256:...`). Run as non-root user (`USER node`). One process per container — let the orchestrator handle restarts and supervision.

HTTP status codes by class: 2xx success (200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content), 3xx redirect (301 permanent, 302/307 temporary, 304 Not Modified), 4xx client error (400 Bad Request, 401 needs auth, 403 forbidden even when authed, 404 not found, 409 conflict, 422 unprocessable, 429 too many requests), 5xx server error (500 internal, 502 bad gateway, 503 unavailable, 504 gateway timeout). Use 401 vs 403 correctly: 401 = 'I don't know who you are', 403 = 'I know who you are, you can't do this'.

REST: one URL per resource, standard HTTP verbs, multiple endpoints often needed for a single page (n+1 over the network). Easy to cache via HTTP, easy to debug. GraphQL: one endpoint, client specifies exact data shape, one round trip per page. Stronger typing via schema. Trade-offs: harder to cache (one URL for everything), N+1 query problem moves into your resolvers (need DataLoader), harder rate limiting. Many projects use REST for public APIs and GraphQL for in-house BFFs.

tRPC is a TypeScript-first RPC framework where the client gets full type inference from the server — no codegen step, no schema file. Define procedures on the server with Zod input schemas, call them from the client like local functions, with autocomplete and type errors at compile time. Best for full-stack TS apps (Next.js, Remix) where client and server are in the same monorepo. Not appropriate when clients aren't TypeScript or when you need a stable cross-language schema.

OpenAPI (formerly Swagger) is a YAML/JSON spec format for REST APIs — describes endpoints, parameters, request/response schemas, auth. Tooling generates client SDKs (multiple languages), server stubs, documentation sites (Swagger UI, Redoc), and validation middleware. OpenAPI 3.1 (2021) aligned with JSON Schema. Annotate endpoints in code (FastAPI generates OpenAPI automatically; Express needs `swagger-jsdoc`) or write the spec first and code against it.

JSON Schema is a vocabulary for describing the structure of JSON documents — types, required fields, regex patterns, enums, nested schemas. Used by OpenAPI, JSON-RPC, configuration validators (Ajv in JS, jsonschema in Python). Draft 2020-12 is the latest version. Common keywords: `type`, `properties`, `required`, `enum`, `pattern`, `minimum`, `oneOf`/`anyOf`/`allOf`. Many TypeScript schema libraries (Zod, Valibot) can export to JSON Schema for interop.

Protocol Buffers (protobuf, Google) is a language-neutral binary serialization format defined by `.proto` schemas. `protoc` generates encoder/decoder code in Go/Java/Python/Rust/etc. Wire format uses tag numbers (not field names) so messages are small and forward-compatible — add new optional fields without breaking old clients. Used by gRPC by default. Trade-off vs JSON: smaller and faster but requires the schema to decode.

TypeScript generics let functions and types operate on any type while preserving type info: `function identity<T>(x: T): T { return x }` — calling `identity(5)` returns a `number`, not `unknown`. Constraints with `extends`: `<T extends { id: string }>`. Common in collection types (`Array<T>`, `Map<K, V>`), API response types (`Response<UserData>`), and utility types (`Partial<T>`, `Pick<T, K>`). The compiler infers most type arguments — explicit `<T>` only when inference fails.

Built-in TS utility types for transforming existing types. `Partial<T>` makes all properties optional. `Required<T>` makes them required. `Readonly<T>` marks all readonly. `Pick<T, K>` keeps only listed keys; `Omit<T, K>` excludes them. `Record<K, V>` builds an object type. `ReturnType<F>` extracts a function's return type; `Parameters<F>` extracts its argument tuple. `Awaited<T>` unwraps a Promise. Reach for these instead of writing parallel type definitions by hand.

React Server Components (RSC) run on the server, can directly access databases and the filesystem, and stream serialized output to the client — no client JS for that component. Marked with `'use server'` (server actions) or by default in Next.js app router. Client Components opt in with `'use client'`. RSCs can pass serializable props (not functions) to client components. Major benefit: tiny JS bundle for content-heavy pages while still using React's component model on the server.

Edge runtimes (Cloudflare Workers, Vercel Edge, Deno Deploy) run serverless functions inside V8 isolates instead of Node containers — startup in ~5ms vs ~100-1000ms, geographically distributed to ~200+ cities. Trade-offs: no access to Node APIs (no `fs`, limited `net`), limited memory (~128MB) and CPU time. Best for short-lived JSON APIs, auth, redirects, A/B routing, geo-aware logic. Use a regular server for long compute or filesystem access.

htmx is a small JS library (~14KB) that adds HTMX attributes to HTML so the server returns HTML fragments that swap into the page — no client framework, no virtual DOM, no JSON API. `<button hx-post="/cart" hx-target="#count">Add</button>` posts to /cart and replaces #count with the response HTML. Pairs well with server-rendered apps (Django, Rails, Phoenix, Go html/template). Best for traditional CRUD apps; less suited for highly interactive UIs.

SolidJS (Ryan Carniato) is a reactive UI framework that looks like React (JSX, components) but compiles to fine-grained DOM updates with no virtual DOM. Signals (`const [count, setCount] = createSignal(0)`) track exactly which DOM nodes depend on which values, so setCount(1) only updates the one text node showing count. Result: top performer in framework benchmarks, tiny runtime (~7KB). SolidStart is its full-stack meta-framework like Next.js.

Svelte is a UI framework that compiles components to vanilla JS at build time — no virtual DOM, minimal runtime. Svelte 5 (October 2024) introduced 'runes' (`$state`, `$derived`, `$effect`) replacing the reactive `$:` syntax with explicit fine-grained signals (similar to Solid). SvelteKit is the full-stack meta-framework with file-based routing, server actions, and adapter-based deploys (Vercel, Cloudflare, Node).

TanStack Query (formerly React Query) handles async data fetching, caching, and revalidation for React/Solid/Vue/Svelte. `useQuery({ queryKey: ['user', id], queryFn: () => fetchUser(id) })` returns data + loading/error state, dedupes parallel calls, caches by key, and refetches on window focus. Mutations (`useMutation`) update the server and invalidate affected queries. Replaces hand-rolled `useEffect + setState` data fetching with predictable behavior — the de-facto standard for client-side data.

Zustand is a tiny (~1KB) state management library for React. Define a store with `create((set) => ({ count: 0, inc: () => set((s) => ({ count: s.count + 1 })) }))`. Components subscribe with selectors: `const count = useStore((s) => s.count)` — only re-render when their slice changes. No providers needed, works outside React, supports middleware (persist, devtools, immer). Simpler than Redux for most apps; less ceremony than Context for cross-component state.

Valkey is a Linux Foundation fork of Redis created in March 2024 after Redis Inc relicensed Redis under SSPL/RSAL. Maintained by AWS, Google Cloud, Oracle, Ericsson, and others. Wire-protocol compatible with Redis 7.2 — existing clients work unchanged. As of Valkey 8.0 (September 2024), it adds multi-threading improvements and dictionary memory optimizations that make it slightly faster than Redis on the same hardware. Most managed cache services (ElastiCache, MemoryDB) have switched to Valkey by default.

Redis is an in-memory key-value store with rich data types beyond strings: lists, sets, sorted sets (ordered by score, used for leaderboards), hashes (field-value within a key), streams (append-only logs like a lightweight Kafka), HyperLogLog (cardinality estimator), geospatial. Single-threaded for commands (atomic by design), persists to disk via snapshots (RDB) or append-only log (AOF). Common uses: cache, rate limiting, job queue (lists or streams), pub/sub, session store.

Python's asyncio runs concurrent I/O in a single thread via cooperative multitasking. `async def fetch(url)` defines a coroutine; `await` yields control back to the event loop while waiting on I/O. Run with `asyncio.run(main())`; combine with `asyncio.gather(*tasks)` for concurrent execution. Despite the GIL, async is great for I/O-bound code — handling thousands of network connections per process. Not for CPU-bound work (use multiprocessing or release the GIL via C extensions).

Python type hints (PEP 484, 2014) add optional static types: `def greet(name: str) -> str: return f'hi {name}'`. Checked with mypy, pyright (used by VS Code's Pylance), or ruff's type-check rules. Generic types via `list[int]`, `dict[str, User]` (3.9+). `Optional[X]` or `X | None` for nullable. `Protocol` for structural typing. Runtime is unaffected — Python ignores annotations at execution. Used heavily in modern libs (FastAPI, Pydantic, SQLAlchemy 2.0).

Pydantic is a Python data validation library based on type hints. Define a model: `class User(BaseModel): name: str; age: int`. `User.model_validate({'name': 'Alice', 'age': 30})` validates and coerces. v2 (2023) rewrote the core in Rust for ~10x speedup. Used by FastAPI for request validation, by AWS Lambda Powertools, and as a settings manager (BaseSettings reads from env vars). Replaces dataclasses when you need validation, JSON serialization, or coercion.

Polars is a Rust-based DataFrame library, with Python and Node bindings. Lazy evaluation by default — `pl.scan_csv('big.csv').filter(...).group_by(...).collect()` builds a query plan and executes it in parallel. Often 5-30x faster than pandas on large data, uses 2-5x less memory. API is more consistent (no `inplace=True` traps). Pandas still has a larger ecosystem (scikit-learn, statsmodels, plotting); Polars wins for ETL and analytics pipelines.

DuckDB is an embedded analytical (OLAP) database — think SQLite for data science. Single file, no server, runs in-process from Python/R/Node/CLI. Columnar storage with vectorized execution; SQL queries on CSV/Parquet/Arrow files directly: `duckdb.sql("SELECT * FROM 'data.csv' WHERE x > 10")`. Often faster than pandas for analytical SQL. Reached 1.0 in June 2024 (stable storage format guarantee).

PyO3 is a Rust library for writing Python extension modules in Rust. Build with maturin: `pip install maturin; maturin develop`. Annotate Rust functions with `#[pyfunction]` and modules with `#[pymodule]` — PyO3 generates the CPython glue. Used by Ruff, Polars, Pydantic core, Tokenizers, and many other 'fast Python library written in Rust' projects. Trade-off: distribute wheels for every platform you support (manylinux + macOS arm64/x64 + Windows).

FastAPI is a modern Python web framework built on Starlette (ASGI) and Pydantic. Use type hints for request/response validation: `def create(item: Item) -> Item:` — FastAPI parses the body, validates against Item, and generates OpenAPI docs at /docs. Native async support. Auto-completion in editors via the type info. Performance is in the same league as Node.js for I/O-bound APIs. Replaced Flask as the default choice for new Python APIs.

Uvicorn is a fast ASGI server for Python (async-capable, the successor to WSGI). Runs FastAPI, Starlette, Django Channels, Quart. `uvicorn main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 --workers 4`. Production deploys often pair it with Gunicorn as a process manager: `gunicorn -k uvicorn.workers.UvicornWorker main:app`. Hypercorn and Granian are alternative ASGI servers; Granian (Rust) is the current speed leader.

Goroutines are Go's lightweight concurrent functions — `go fetch(url)` schedules fetch to run concurrently. Stack starts at 2KB and grows on demand (vs ~1MB for OS threads), so spawning millions is feasible. Go's runtime multiplexes goroutines onto OS threads via the M:N scheduler. Communicate via channels (`ch := make(chan int); ch <- 1; v := <-ch`) — 'don't communicate by sharing memory; share memory by communicating'. For bounded concurrency, use a buffered channel as a semaphore.

Go's `context.Context` carries deadlines, cancellation signals, and request-scoped values across API boundaries. `ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(parent, 5*time.Second); defer cancel()`. Pass `ctx` as the first argument to every function that does I/O. Functions check `ctx.Done()` channel or use context-aware APIs (`http.NewRequestWithContext`) that return early when the context is cancelled. Critical for cleaning up resources when a client disconnects mid-request.

Rust's ownership model: each value has one owner, and when the owner goes out of scope the value is dropped. Move semantics by default (`let b = a` makes b the owner, a is invalid). Borrow with references: `&x` (immutable, multiple OK) or `&mut x` (mutable, exclusive). The borrow checker enforces at compile time: no dangling pointers, no data races, no use-after-free — without a garbage collector. The cost is the famous learning curve.

Rust's async/await is futures-based — `async fn` returns a `Future` that's lazy (doesn't run until polled). The standard library provides the language features but not the runtime. Tokio is the dominant async runtime (multi-threaded scheduler, built-in TCP/UDP/timers, ecosystem of crates: hyper, tonic, axum). Alternatives: smol (minimal), async-std (deprecated), Glommio (thread-per-core). Choose the runtime once per binary; libraries should stay runtime-agnostic.

Axum is a Rust web framework built on Tokio and Hyper, by the Tokio team. Routes are plain functions whose argument types implement an `Extractor` trait — pull JSON bodies, path params, query strings, state via just changing function signatures: `async fn create(Json(input): Json<NewUser>) -> Json<User>`. Composable middleware via the Tower service abstraction (shared with tonic, hyper). De-facto default for new Rust web services as of 2024.

Zig (Andrew Kelley, 2016) is a low-level systems language positioned as a 'better C'. Manual memory management with explicit allocators passed as arguments. Compile-time code execution (`comptime`) replaces both macros and generics with one mechanism. Errors are values: `!T` is 'returns T or an error'. C interop is first-class — `@cImport` brings in C headers directly. Used by Bun, TigerBeetle, and increasingly as a cross-compiler (`zig cc` is a drop-in C/C++ compiler that cross-compiles trivially).

Nix is a purely functional package manager — every package lives in `/nix/store/<hash>-name/` where the hash captures all build inputs. Installing a package doesn't disturb existing ones; multiple versions coexist. `nix-shell -p python312 ruby_3_3` drops you into a temporary shell with those tools. NixOS extends this to the whole OS — config in a single `configuration.nix`, atomic rollback to any previous generation. Steep learning curve but unmatched reproducibility.

Dev Containers (devcontainer.json spec) define a development environment as a Docker container — language version, system deps, VS Code extensions, settings. `code .` in a devcontainer-enabled repo prompts to reopen inside the container. Same env for every contributor and for CI. GitHub Codespaces builds on this spec. Common files: `.devcontainer/devcontainer.json` + optional `Dockerfile` or `docker-compose.yml`. Replaces 'works on my machine' debugging.

GitHub Actions runs CI/CD workflows defined in `.github/workflows/*.yml`. Triggers: `push`, `pull_request`, `schedule`, `workflow_dispatch`. A job runs on a `runs-on:` runner (ubuntu-latest, macos-latest, self-hosted). Steps either run shell commands or invoke reusable actions (`uses: actions/checkout@v4`). Matrix builds run the same job across versions: `strategy.matrix.node: [18, 20, 22]`. Cache deps with `actions/cache@v4` to speed up subsequent runs.

UTF-8 is the dominant Unicode encoding on the web (~98% of sites). Variable-length: ASCII chars are 1 byte, most Latin extended 2 bytes, CJK 3 bytes, emoji and rare scripts 4 bytes. Self-synchronizing — you can start reading mid-string and find the next code point boundary without a header. Backwards compatible with ASCII. Common bug: confusing 'characters' with code points (an emoji like 👨‍👩‍👧‍👦 is several code points joined with zero-width joiners) or with grapheme clusters.

Regex syntax basics: `.` any char, `*` 0+, `+` 1+, `?` 0-1, `{n,m}` n-to-m. Character classes: `[a-z]`, `\d` digit, `\w` word, `\s` whitespace. Anchors: `^` start, `$` end, `\b` word boundary. Groups: `(abc)` capture, `(?:abc)` non-capture, `(?<name>abc)` named. Lookarounds: `(?=...)` ahead, `(?!...)` not-ahead. Greedy by default — append `?` for lazy (`.*?`). Test with regex101.com. Different flavors (PCRE, ECMAScript, RE2) support different features.

Big-O describes how runtime/memory scales with input size n. O(1) constant — array index, hash lookup. O(log n) — binary search, balanced tree lookup. O(n) — linear scan. O(n log n) — efficient sorts (mergesort, quicksort average, heapsort). O(n²) — nested loops, bubble sort. O(2^n) — exponential, brute-force subsets. O(n!) — permutations, traveling salesman brute force. The constants matter at small n; algorithm class dominates at large n.

Common sorts. Quicksort: O(n log n) average, O(n²) worst, in-place, cache-friendly — the default for `qsort` in C, `sort.Slice` in Go. Mergesort: O(n log n) guaranteed, stable, needs O(n) extra space — used in Java's `Arrays.sort` for objects and Python's Timsort (a hybrid). Heapsort: O(n log n), in-place, not stable. Introsort (C++ STL): quicksort that falls back to heapsort if recursion gets too deep. For nearly-sorted data, Timsort is unbeatable (O(n) best case).

Dynamic programming solves problems by breaking them into overlapping subproblems and memoizing results. Two styles: top-down (recursive + cache) or bottom-up (build a table from base cases up). Classic problems: Fibonacci (O(2^n) naive → O(n) with memo), longest common subsequence, knapsack, edit distance (Levenshtein). The trick is recognizing the recurrence relation: `dp[i] = min(dp[i-1], dp[i-2]) + ...`. State design (what does dp[i] mean?) is the hard part.

BFS (Breadth-First Search): use a queue, visit all nodes at depth d before depth d+1 — finds the shortest path in unweighted graphs. DFS (Depth-First Search): use a stack (or recursion), go deep first — used for topological sort, cycle detection, connected components. Both O(V + E). For weighted graphs use Dijkstra (non-negative weights, priority queue) or Bellman-Ford (handles negative weights, detects negative cycles).

The testing pyramid: many unit tests (fast, isolated, test one function), fewer integration tests (test a few units together, real DB sometimes), few end-to-end tests (browser-driven, whole stack). Unit tests give fast feedback; e2e tests catch real-user bugs. Anti-pattern: ice-cream-cone shape (lots of slow flaky e2e tests). Modern adjustment: 'testing trophy' (Kent C. Dodds) emphasizes integration as the sweet spot for confidence vs speed.

Playwright (Microsoft, 2020) is a Node/Python/.NET/Java library for cross-browser end-to-end testing — drives Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit with one API. Auto-waits for elements to be actionable (no `sleep(500)` hacks). `await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Submit' }).click()`. Built-in trace viewer shows screenshots + DOM + network per step, making failures debuggable. Replaced Cypress as the most popular new e2e framework in 2023-2024.

Snapshot testing records a serialized form of an output (HTML, JSON, text) on first run, then compares future runs against it. `expect(component).toMatchSnapshot()` in Jest/Vitest. Great for catching unexpected changes in UI markup or large data structures. Pitfall: developers can blindly update snapshots without reviewing diffs, making them noise instead of safety. Best for outputs that change rarely and intentionally.

Property-based testing generates many random inputs and checks invariants instead of asserting specific outputs. Hypothesis (Python), fast-check (JS), proptest (Rust), Go's native fuzz support (`go test -fuzz`). Example: `forAll(strings, s => decode(encode(s)) === s)`. Frameworks shrink failing inputs to the smallest reproducing case. Catches edge cases (empty strings, unicode, huge numbers) that humans forget. Fuzzing is the security-flavored cousin — feed garbage and watch for crashes.

Test doubles (Gerard Meszaros): dummies (pass-through values), stubs (return canned responses), fakes (working implementations, e.g. in-memory DB), spies (record calls), mocks (verify expected calls). Modern frameworks blur these (`jest.fn()` is a spy + stub). Rule of thumb: mock external dependencies (network, time, randomness), not your own code — over-mocking creates tests that pass when the code is broken. For DB-dependent tests, prefer test containers or transaction rollback over mocking the DB.

Code coverage measures what fraction of lines/branches your tests execute. Useful for finding obvious gaps; misleading as a quality goal — 100% coverage with weak assertions catches nothing. Branch coverage is stronger than line coverage (forces both arms of every if). Set a floor (e.g. 80%) to prevent regression, not a goal. Tools: c8/istanbul (JS), coverage.py (Python), tarpaulin/llvm-cov (Rust). 'Mutation testing' is a stronger signal — modifies the code and checks if tests fail.

Observability is built on three pillars. Logs: timestamped text events — easy to grep, hard to query at scale (use structured JSON). Metrics: numeric time-series aggregates (request count, p99 latency) — cheap to store, great for dashboards/alerts but no individual-request detail. Traces: end-to-end record of a request across services with span timings — answers 'why was THIS request slow'. OpenTelemetry standardizes the data model and SDKs across vendors (Datadog, Honeycomb, Grafana stack, Jaeger).

OpenTelemetry (OTel) is a CNCF project providing vendor-neutral APIs, SDKs, and a collector for traces, metrics, and logs. Auto-instrumentation libraries exist for most languages (Java agent, Python opentelemetry-instrument, Node SDK). Instrument once, export anywhere — switch from Jaeger to Honeycomb by changing exporter config, no code change. Replaces older split tools (OpenTracing + OpenCensus merged in 2019). Now the de-facto standard for observability instrumentation.

Prometheus is the dominant open-source metrics system. Pull-based: Prometheus scrapes HTTP endpoints exposing metrics in its text format. Stores time-series in a custom TSDB on local disk. Four core metric types: counter (monotonic), gauge (up/down), histogram (distribution), summary (quantiles). PromQL is the query language: `rate(http_requests_total{job="api"}[5m])`. Pair with Grafana for dashboards, Alertmanager for alerts. Long-term storage via Thanos, Mimir, or VictoriaMetrics.

Kubernetes orchestrates containers across a cluster. Core objects: Pod (one+ containers sharing network and storage, the smallest deployable unit), Deployment (declares how many replica Pods of a template), Service (stable network endpoint that load-balances to a set of Pods), Ingress (routes external HTTP traffic to Services), ConfigMap/Secret (configuration). The control loop reconciles desired state (your YAML) to actual state — declarative, not imperative. `kubectl apply -f deploy.yaml`.

Helm is the Kubernetes package manager. A 'chart' is a templated bundle of K8s YAML manifests plus a `values.yaml` for parameters. `helm install postgres bitnami/postgresql --set auth.password=...` deploys an entire database stack. Tracks releases (you can `helm rollback` to a previous version). Templates use Go's text/template syntax — can get hard to read for complex charts. Alternatives: Kustomize (overlay-based, no templating), Pulumi/CDK8s (real code).

eBPF runs sandboxed programs in the Linux kernel without modifying kernel code or loading modules. Originally for packet filtering (BPF); now used for tracing (perf, bpftrace, BCC), networking (Cilium replaces kube-proxy), security (Falco), and observability (Pixie, Parca). Programs are verified at load time for safety (bounded loops, no random memory access). Hook into syscalls, network events, kprobes, tracepoints. Powerful: see what every process is doing, in production, with near-zero overhead.

WireGuard (Jason Donenfeld, 2016) is a modern VPN protocol — runs in the Linux kernel since 5.6, available as userspace daemon elsewhere. Tiny codebase (~4000 lines vs OpenVPN's ~100K), simple config (peer = public key + allowed IPs), uses modern cryptography (Curve25519, ChaCha20Poly1305, BLAKE2s). Faster and lower-latency than OpenVPN. Used by Tailscale (mesh on top of WireGuard) and Mullvad, NordVPN, etc.

SQLite is a single-file embedded relational database — the world's most deployed DB (every phone, browser, OS). Zero config, no server process, ACID via a journal or WAL file. Excellent for: app local storage, edge databases (Cloudflare D1, Turso), test fixtures, single-writer workloads. WAL mode (`PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL`) allows readers while one writer is active. Limits: one writer at a time, no network access (use a wrapper like LiteFS or rqlite for distribution).

NATS is a high-performance messaging system focused on simplicity — single Go binary, no Zookeeper-style coordination. Core NATS: at-most-once pub/sub and request/reply with subject-based routing (`orders.us.>` is a wildcard). JetStream adds persistence, exactly-once delivery, KV store, and object store on top. Lower operational complexity than Kafka; lower throughput at the extreme high end. Popular for IoT, edge, and microservice messaging.

Apache Kafka is a distributed log designed for high-throughput event streaming. Producers append messages to topics, partitioned across brokers for parallelism. Consumers read at their own pace via offset; messages are retained for days/weeks regardless of consumption. Consumer groups partition work among instances. Trade-offs: powerful (millions msgs/sec) but operationally heavy (Zookeeper historically, KRaft now). Pair with Schema Registry (Avro/Protobuf) for forward/backward compatibility.

Temporal is a durable execution framework — write workflow code that survives crashes, restarts, and process failures as if it were running on an infallible computer. The framework persists every function call's input and output to a database, so on resume it replays history and skips already-completed steps. Great for long-running business processes (order fulfillment, signup flows). SDKs in Go, Java, TypeScript, Python, .NET. Cadence is the Uber-originated predecessor.

Chrome DevTools panels worth knowing. Elements: inspect/edit DOM and CSS. Console: REPL with $0 (last selected element), monitorEvents(el). Sources: set breakpoints, conditional breakpoints, blackbox library code. Network: filter by type, throttle to 'Slow 3G', see waterfall. Performance: record CPU profile to find slow JS, frame drops. Memory: heap snapshots for leak hunting. Application: inspect localStorage/IndexedDB/cookies/service workers. Lighthouse: audit perf, accessibility, SEO. Coverage: see which CSS/JS is unused.

Lighthouse (Google) audits web pages on performance, accessibility, best practices, SEO, and PWA. Runs in Chrome DevTools or as a CLI / CI tool. Performance score weighs Core Web Vitals: LCP (Largest Contentful Paint, <2.5s good), CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift, <0.1), INP (Interaction to Next Paint, <200ms, replaced FID in 2024). Also flags accessibility issues (missing alt text, low contrast), unused CSS, and image format suggestions (use WebP/AVIF). CrUX data feeds the same metrics from real users.

Common DNS record types. A: hostname → IPv4. AAAA: hostname → IPv6. CNAME: alias one name to another (can't coexist with A on the same name; can't be at the apex except via flattening). MX: mail server for a domain (with priority). TXT: arbitrary text — used for SPF, DKIM, domain ownership verification. NS: nameservers for the zone. SOA: zone metadata (serial, refresh times). CAA: which CAs may issue certs for the domain.

Default arguments are evaluated once at function-definition time, not per call. `def f(a=[]): a.append(1)` reuses the same list across calls, so it grows. Use `def f(a=None): a = a or []` to get a fresh list each call.

`is` tests object identity; `==` tests value equality. `a is b` is true only if both names point to the same object. CPython caches small ints (-5..256) and some strings, so `256 is 256` is True but `1000 is 1000` may be False — never use `is` for value comparison.

In Python 3 the loop variable of a list/set/dict comprehension is scoped to the comprehension and doesn't leak into the enclosing namespace. In Python 2 it did leak. Generator expressions never leaked the variable in either version.

Closures capture variables by reference, not by value. `[lambda: i for i in range(3)]` all return 2 because they share the same `i`, read at call time. Bind it early with a default arg: `lambda i=i: i`.

`__slots__ = ('x','y')` replaces a class's per-instance `__dict__` with fixed storage, cutting memory and speeding attribute access. Trade-offs: you can't add new attributes not in the list, and subclasses without `__slots__` regain a `__dict__`.

A function with `yield` returns a generator: it computes values lazily, one per `next()` call, holding state between resumes. This streams huge or infinite sequences without building a list in memory. Calling the function doesn't run its body — iterating it does.

The walrus operator `:=` assigns inside an expression. `while (line := f.readline()):` reads and tests in one step; `if (n := len(data)) > 10:` reuses `n` after. Added in Python 3.8; it needs parentheses in most contexts.

f-strings embed expressions: `f"{x*2}"`. Use `f"{x:.2f}"` for formatting and the 3.8 `f"{x=}"` shorthand to print both name and value (`x=5`). They're evaluated at runtime and are the fastest string-formatting option.

Since Python 3.7 (and as a CPython 3.6 implementation detail) regular `dict` preserves insertion order as a language guarantee. `collections.OrderedDict` is now mostly only needed for its `move_to_end()` and order-sensitive `==`.

`list[:]`, `dict.copy()`, and `copy.copy()` are shallow — they copy the container but share the nested objects. Mutating a nested list shows through both copies. Use `copy.deepcopy()` to recursively clone everything.

Python chains comparisons: `1 < x < 10` means `1 < x and x < 10`, evaluating `x` once. This also makes `a == b == c` test all three equal, and surprising results like `False == False in [False]` parse as `(False==False) and (False in [False])`.

Empty containers (`[]`, `{}`, `()`, `''`), `0`, `0.0`, `None`, and `False` are falsy; almost everything else is truthy. Use `if not items:` to test emptiness, but use `if x is None:` when `0`/`''` are valid values you must distinguish from missing.
`first, *rest = seq` captures the middle/tail into a list: `a, *b, c = [1,2,3,4]` gives `b == [2,3]`. In calls, `*` splats an iterable into positional args and `**` splats a dict into keyword args.

The `with` block calls `__enter__` on entry and `__exit__` on exit even if an exception is raised — ideal for files, locks, connections. Write one quickly with `@contextlib.contextmanager` decorating a generator that `yield`s once.

A decorator wraps a function: `@dec` rebinds `f` to `dec(f)`. Always apply `@functools.wraps(func)` to the inner wrapper so the result keeps the original's `__name__`, `__doc__`, and signature metadata for introspection and debugging.

`except` clauses are tried top-to-bottom, so put specific exceptions before general ones or the broad one shadows them. Catch `Exception`, not bare `except:`, since bare except also swallows `KeyboardInterrupt` and `SystemExit`.

`//` is floor division and `%` is modulo, both rounding toward negative infinity: `-7 // 2 == -4` and `-7 % 2 == 1`. `divmod(a, b)` returns `(a // b, a % b)` in one call. Use `int(a / b)` if you want truncation toward zero instead.

Strings are immutable, so `s += x` in a loop creates a new string each time (O(n²) overall). Build a list and call `''.join(parts)` once, which is O(n). CPython sometimes optimizes in-place `+=` for refcount-1 strings, but don't rely on it.
`for i, x in enumerate(seq):` gives index and item together — prefer it over `for i in range(len(seq)):`. Pass `enumerate(seq, start=1)` to begin counting at 1 for human-facing output.

`d.get(k, default)` avoids a `KeyError` without inserting. `d.setdefault(k, []).append(x)` inserts the default only if missing and returns it. For accumulation prefer `collections.defaultdict(list)`, which auto-creates the value on first access.

`sorted(data, key=lambda x: x.age)` sorts by a derived key without mutating input; `list.sort()` sorts in place. Python's sort is stable, so sort by secondary key first then primary for multi-level ordering, or use a tuple key. `operator.itemgetter`/`attrgetter` are faster than lambdas.

Mutating a list while iterating skips elements; mutating a dict's size during iteration raises `RuntimeError: dictionary changed size`. Iterate over a copy (`for x in list(d):`) or build a new collection instead of editing in place.

Assigning to a name inside a function makes it local by default, so reading an outer variable then assigning it raises `UnboundLocalError`. Use `nonlocal x` to rebind an enclosing function's variable, or `global x` to rebind a module-level one.

`round()` uses banker's rounding (round-half-to-even): `round(0.5) == 0` and `round(2.5) == 2`. It also inherits float imprecision — `round(2.675, 2)` gives 2.67 because 2.675 isn't exactly representable. Use `decimal.Decimal` for exact money math.

`0.1 + 0.2 == 0.30000000000000004` because binary floats can't represent these decimals exactly. Compare with `math.isclose(a, b)` instead of `==`, and use `decimal.Decimal('0.1')` or `fractions.Fraction` when exactness matters.

`__str__` is the human-readable form used by `print()`/`str()`; `__repr__` is the unambiguous developer form used by the REPL, containers, and `repr()`. If you only define one, define `__repr__` — `str()` falls back to it but not vice versa. Aim for `repr` to look like valid constructor code.

An iterable has `__iter__` returning a fresh iterator; an iterator has `__next__` and raises `StopIteration` when exhausted. A generator is a one-shot iterator — once consumed it's empty, so you can't loop over it twice without recreating it.

`*args` collects extra positional args into a tuple; `**kwargs` collects extra keyword args into a dict. A bare `*` in a signature (`def f(a, *, b)`) forces everything after it to be keyword-only, which improves call-site readability.

`[[]] * 3` makes three references to the *same* inner list, so appending to one mutates all. Build independent rows with a comprehension: `[[] for _ in range(3)]`. The flat case `[0] * 3` is fine because ints are immutable.

CPython compiles modules to bytecode cached in `__pycache__/*.pyc`, keyed by source mtime (or hash with `--invalidation-mode`). It recompiles when source changes; the `.pyc` is just a startup optimization, not a faster runtime. Delete `__pycache__` to force recompilation.

Python resolves methods via the C3-linearized MRO, visible at `Cls.__mro__`. `super()` follows that order, not just the literal parent, so in diamond inheritance it can dispatch to a sibling class. Call `super().__init__(...)` in every class for cooperative multiple inheritance.

`str` is Unicode text; `bytes` is raw octets. Convert with `s.encode('utf-8')` and `b.decode('utf-8')` — mixing them raises `TypeError`. Always open binary files with mode `'rb'`/`'wb'` and specify encoding explicitly for text to avoid platform-dependent defaults.

Only hashable (effectively immutable) objects can be dict keys or set members. Lists and dicts are unhashable → `TypeError: unhashable type`. Use a `tuple` or `frozenset` as a key instead, and keep `__eq__`/`__hash__` consistent in custom classes.

`any(pred(x) for x in seq)` and `all(...)` short-circuit on the first decisive item, so pass a generator (not a list) to avoid evaluating everything. Note `all([])` is True and `any([])` is False — empty-sequence edge cases that often surprise.

`zip()` stops at the shortest iterable, silently dropping extras. Python 3.10+ adds `zip(a, b, strict=True)` to raise on length mismatch; use `itertools.zip_longest(fillvalue=...)` to pad the shorter ones instead.

A `return`/`break`/`continue` inside `finally` overrides any exception or return from the `try` block — silently swallowing errors. Use `finally` only for cleanup that doesn't change control flow, or you'll mask the real result.

`@functools.lru_cache(maxsize=None)` memoizes a function by its arguments, which must be hashable. Inspect hits with `.cache_info()` and clear with `.cache_clear()`. Python 3.9+ adds `@functools.cache` as an unbounded shorthand.

`assert` statements are stripped when Python runs with `-O` (optimized). Never use them for input validation or security checks, and never put side effects in them — raise explicit exceptions instead. They're for internal invariants only.

Sets support `&` (intersection), `|` (union), `-` (difference), `^` (symmetric difference), with `in` membership in O(1) average. `list(set(seq))` dedupes but loses order — use `list(dict.fromkeys(seq))` to dedupe while preserving insertion order.

Circular imports fail when module A needs a name from B at import time while B is still importing A — you get `ImportError: cannot import name ... (most likely due to a circular import)`. Fix by importing inside the function, importing the module (not the name), or restructuring shared code into a third module.

`==` runs the Abstract Equality algorithm: it coerces operands toward numbers. `null == undefined` is true but neither equals anything else. `[] == ![]` is true because `![]` is `false` → `0`, and `[]` becomes `''` → `0`. Use `===` to skip all coercion.

`Object.is(a, b)` is like `===` except for two cases: `Object.is(NaN, NaN)` is `true` (where `NaN === NaN` is false), and `Object.is(0, -0)` is `false` (where `0 === -0` is true). It implements the SameValue spec algorithm.

Arrow functions have no own `this`, `arguments`, `super`, or `new.target` — they close over the enclosing lexical scope. So you can't `bind`/`call` a new `this` onto them, you can't `new` them, and they make poor object methods but great callbacks.

All JS numbers are IEEE 754 doubles, so `0.1 + 0.2 === 0.30000000000000004`. Compare with a tolerance (`Math.abs(a-b) < Number.EPSILON`) or scale to integers. For exact decimals (money) use integer cents or a decimal library.

Doubles can only represent integers exactly up to `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` (2^53 − 1 = 9007199254740991). Beyond that, `9007199254740992 + 1 === 9007199254740992`. Use `BigInt` for larger exact integers; check with `Number.isSafeInteger(n)`.

Sparse arrays have holes: `[1,,3]` has length 3 but index 1 is empty. `forEach`/`map`/`filter` skip holes, but `for...of`, spread, and `Array.from` treat them as `undefined`. `new Array(3)` makes 3 holes; `Array(3).fill(0)` fills them.

`[].sort()` with no comparator converts elements to strings and sorts lexicographically, so `[10, 2, 1].sort()` gives `[1, 10, 2]`. Always pass a comparator for numbers: `.sort((a, b) => a - b)`. As of ES2019 `sort` is guaranteed stable.

`JSON.stringify` drops `undefined`, functions, and symbols in objects (turns them to `null` inside arrays). `NaN`/`Infinity` serialize to `null`. It calls a value's `toJSON()` method if present, which is why `new Date()` stringifies to an ISO string.

`JSON.stringify(value, replacer, space)`: the 3rd arg pretty-prints — a number is the indent width, a string is the indent unit. The 2nd arg is a function `(key, val) => val` to transform values, or an array of keys to whitelist which properties are kept.

`{...obj}` and `Object.assign({}, obj)` make a shallow copy — nested objects are still shared by reference. For a true deep clone of plain data use `structuredClone(obj)` (built into modern runtimes); it also handles `Map`, `Set`, `Date`, and cyclic references, but not functions.

Define accessors with `get`/`set` in object literals or classes: `get full() { return this.a + this.b }`. They look like properties but run code on access/assignment. `Object.defineProperty(o, 'x', {get, set, enumerable, configurable})` gives fine control over descriptors.
Since ES2019 you can omit the catch binding when you don't need the error: `try { risky() } catch { fallback() }`. Useful for probes like feature detection where the error object is irrelevant.

`Promise.allSettled(promises)` never rejects — it waits for all and returns objects `{status:'fulfilled', value}` or `{status:'rejected', reason}`. Use it when you want every result regardless of failures, unlike `Promise.all` which rejects on the first failure.

`Promise.any(promises)` resolves with the first *fulfilled* promise and ignores rejections; if all reject it throws an `AggregateError` whose `.errors` holds every reason. `Promise.race`, by contrast, settles with the first promise to settle — fulfilled *or* rejected.

A rejected promise with no `.catch`/await triggers the `unhandledrejection` event in browsers and `process.on('unhandledRejection')` in Node. Node may crash on it depending on `--unhandled-rejections` mode. Always handle or `await` promises so errors aren't silently lost.

`await` inside a `for` loop runs requests one at a time. To run them concurrently, kick them off first then await together: `await Promise.all(items.map(fetchOne))`. A `forEach` with an async callback does NOT wait — the loop returns before any promise settles.

`yield*` delegates to another iterable/generator, yielding all its values in place and forwarding `.next()` values to it. The expression `yield*` also evaluates to the delegated generator's `return` value, useful for composing sub-routines.

Make any object iterable by adding `[Symbol.iterator]()` returning an object with a `next()` that yields `{value, done}`. The easiest implementation is a generator method: `*[Symbol.iterator]() { yield* this.items }`. Then `for...of` and spread work on it.

`Map` allows any value as a key (including objects and `NaN`), preserves insertion order, has a `.size`, and isn't polluted by prototype keys. Plain objects coerce keys to strings/symbols. Use `Map` for dynamic dictionaries and frequent adds/deletes.

Object key iteration order is spec'd: integer-like keys come first in ascending numeric order, then string keys in insertion order, then symbols. That's why `{2:'b', 1:'a'}` iterates `1` before `2`. Use a `Map` if you need pure insertion order with numeric keys.

Concise method syntax `{ foo() {} }` differs from `{ foo: function(){} }`: the shorthand has an internal `[[HomeObject]]`, so it's the only object-method form where `super.method()` works. The shorthand method also can't be used as a constructor.

`void expr` evaluates `expr` and returns `undefined`. `void 0` is a safe way to get `undefined` (which used to be reassignable in old engines). `void` also forces a function statement into an expression: `void function(){}()` runs an IIFE.

The comma operator evaluates each operand left to right and returns the last: `(a = 1, b = 2, a + b)` is `3`. It's mostly seen in `for` loops with multiple counters: `for (let i=0, j=n; i<j; i++, j--)`.

ES2021 added logical assignment operators: `a ||= b` assigns only if `a` is falsy, `a &&= b` only if truthy, `a ??= b` only if `a` is null/undefined. They short-circuit, so `obj.x ??= compute()` skips `compute()` when `x` already has a value.

Numeric separators let you group digits with underscores for readability: `1_000_000`, `0xFF_FF`, `1_000.123_45`. They're purely cosmetic — the engine ignores them. You can't put one at the start/end or next to a decimal point.

`arr.flat(depth)` flattens nested arrays (default depth 1; use `Infinity` for fully flat). `arr.flatMap(fn)` maps then flattens one level — handy for one-to-many transforms or filtering by returning `[]`. Both are ES2019.
`arr.at(-1)` returns the last element using a negative index, avoiding `arr[arr.length-1]`. It works on strings and typed arrays too. Positive indices behave like bracket access. Added in ES2022.

`Object.fromEntries(entries)` is the inverse of `Object.entries`: it turns a list of `[key, value]` pairs (or a `Map`) into an object. Pair them to transform objects functionally: `Object.fromEntries(Object.entries(o).map(([k,v]) => [k, v*2]))`.

ES2022 added an error cause: `throw new Error('high level', { cause: originalError })`. The original is preserved on `err.cause`, so you can wrap a low-level failure in a meaningful message without losing the stack/context of the root error.

In TS, a discriminated union shares a literal 'tag' field across variants (`{kind:'circle', r} | {kind:'square', s}`). Switching on that tag narrows the type in each branch, so the compiler knows `r` exists only in the circle case. Add a `default: assertNever(x)` to catch missing cases.

`never` is TS's bottom type — no value is assignable to it. The classic use is exhaustiveness checking: a `default` branch with `const _x: never = value` fails to compile if a union case is unhandled. Functions that always throw or loop forever return `never`.

`unknown` is the type-safe `any`: you can assign anything to it, but you can't use it until you narrow it with a typeof/instanceof check or assertion. `any` silently turns off type checking and spreads through your code. Prefer `unknown` at API boundaries.

TS is structurally typed: types match if their shapes are compatible, regardless of declared names. A value with extra properties is assignable to a narrower type — except object *literals* get an excess-property check, which flags unknown keys to catch typos.

`readonly string[]` (or `ReadonlyArray<string>`) blocks `push`/`pop`/index assignment at compile time. A `readonly` modifier on properties prevents reassignment after construction. These are erased at runtime — they're compile-time-only guarantees, not `Object.freeze`.

`keyof T` gives a union of T's property names. `typeof value` (in a type position) gets the type of a runtime value. Combined: `type Keys = keyof typeof config` derives a string-literal union from an existing object — great for deriving types from a const config.

`interface` and `type` overlap heavily. Interfaces support declaration merging and `extends`; type aliases can express unions, tuples, mapped/conditional types, and primitives. Rule of thumb: interfaces for object shapes/public APIs, `type` for unions and computed types.

TS types are fully erased at compile time — there's no runtime type info, so you can't do `if (x instanceof MyInterface)` or branch on a generic `T`. Validate runtime data with checks or a schema library (zod, valibot). Enums and parameter properties are exceptions that emit code.

The `!` postfix is a non-null assertion: `value!` tells the compiler 'trust me, this isn't null/undefined' with no runtime check. `class { x!: number }` is definite-assignment, promising you'll set `x` before use. Overusing `!` defeats `strictNullChecks` — prefer real narrowing.

TS 5.0 added `const` type parameters: `function f<const T>(x: T)` infers the narrowest literal type for `T` without the caller writing `as const`. So `f(['a','b'])` infers `readonly ['a','b']` instead of `string[]`, preserving literal precision.

`satisfies` checks that a value matches a type WITHOUT widening it. `const cfg = {a:1} satisfies Record<string, number>` validates the shape but keeps the exact literal type so `cfg.a` stays `number` and autocomplete on keys still works — unlike a `: Type` annotation which widens.

Most relational indexes are B+trees: only leaf nodes hold keys (or row pointers), and leaves are linked for fast range scans. A clustered index (InnoDB primary key, SQL Server) stores the full row in the leaf, so the table *is* the index; a secondary index leaf holds the indexed columns plus the clustering key to look the row up.

SQL defines four isolation levels by which anomalies they forbid: READ UNCOMMITTED (dirty reads), READ COMMITTED (no dirty reads), REPEATABLE READ (no non-repeatable reads), SERIALIZABLE (no phantoms). Postgres defaults to READ COMMITTED and silently upgrades READ UNCOMMITTED to it; InnoDB defaults to REPEATABLE READ.

A phantom read happens when a re-run range query returns newly inserted rows matching the predicate, even under REPEATABLE READ. Preventing it requires locking the *range* (predicate/next-key locks) not just existing rows. InnoDB's gap and next-key locks block inserts into scanned gaps to stop phantoms.

Three core join algorithms: nested-loop (good for small outer + indexed inner), hash join (build a hash table on the smaller side, probe with the larger — best for big unsorted equijoins), and merge join (both inputs sorted on the key, then zipped — cheap if sorted order already exists). The optimizer chooses based on size and available indexes/sort order.

The planner relies on column statistics (row counts, distinct-value counts, and per-value histograms) gathered by `ANALYZE` (Postgres) or `UPDATE STATISTICS` (SQL Server). Stale stats cause cardinality misestimates and bad plans. Histograms model skewed distributions so the planner doesn't assume uniform value spread.

A deadlock is a cycle of transactions each waiting on a lock the other holds. The engine runs a deadlock detector (a wait-for graph cycle check) and aborts one transaction as the victim, returning an error you must retry. Reduce deadlocks by acquiring locks in a consistent order across all code paths.

Indexes pay off only when selective — returning a small fraction of rows. If a predicate matches a large share of the table, a sequential scan is cheaper than thousands of random index lookups plus heap fetches, so the planner ignores the index. A column with two distinct values rarely benefits from a plain B-tree index.

A foreign key enforces that the referenced row exists; it implicitly requires an index on the *parent* key (the PK/unique it points to) but NOT on the child column — and a missing child-side index makes parent deletes/updates do a full child scan. `ON DELETE CASCADE` propagates deletes; `ON DELETE SET NULL` nulls the child.

Normalization removes redundancy: 1NF (atomic columns), 2NF (no partial dependency on part of a composite key), 3NF (no transitive dependency on non-key columns). 3NF avoids update anomalies. Denormalization deliberately reintroduces redundancy (e.g. a cached count) to skip joins, trading write complexity for read speed.

SQL NULL means 'unknown', driving three-valued logic: `x = NULL` is never true (use `IS NULL`), and `NULL = NULL` is unknown. `WHERE` keeps only TRUE rows, so unknowns are dropped. `COUNT(col)` skips NULLs but `COUNT(*)` counts rows; most aggregates ignore NULLs.

Postgres transaction IDs are 32-bit and wrap around; tuples older than ~2 billion XIDs must be 'frozen' by VACUUM or the database shuts down to prevent data appearing to come from the future. Monitor `age(datfrozenxid)`; an under-vacuumed table is the classic cause of wraparound emergencies.

Partitioning splits one logical table into physical child tables by range/list/hash on a key. Its main win is partition pruning: the planner skips partitions that can't match the WHERE clause. It also makes bulk deletes cheap — `DROP` an old time partition instead of a slow `DELETE`.

Window functions compute across a set of rows related to the current row without collapsing them like GROUP BY. `SUM(x) OVER (PARTITION BY g ORDER BY t)` gives a running total per group; `ROW_NUMBER()`, `RANK()`, `LAG()`/`LEAD()` are window-only. The frame clause (`ROWS BETWEEN ...`) controls which rows feed the aggregate.

`WHERE` filters rows before grouping; `HAVING` filters groups after aggregation, so aggregate conditions like `HAVING COUNT(*) > 5` must go in HAVING. Every non-aggregated SELECT column must appear in GROUP BY (Postgres allows trailing functionally-dependent columns when grouping by a primary key).

A heap is an unordered table where rows live wherever there's free space; without a clustered index, row order on disk is arbitrary. Storage is page-based (Postgres 8KB, InnoDB 16KB); a row's physical address is a (page, slot) pair — Postgres calls it the `ctid`. Updates can move a row to a new page, invalidating its old location.

Optimistic locking avoids holding locks: read a row with its version/timestamp, then `UPDATE ... WHERE id=? AND version=?`. If zero rows update, someone else changed it first — you retry. It scales better than pessimistic `SELECT FOR UPDATE` when conflicts are rare, at the cost of occasional retries.

`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` takes a row-level write lock so concurrent transactions block until you commit — useful for read-modify-write. `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` instead skips already-locked rows, the standard pattern for a SQL-backed job queue where many workers each grab different rows.

Postgres `FILLFACTOR` leaves free space on each page so an UPDATE can place the new tuple on the same page as the old one — a HOT (heap-only tuple) update that skips updating every index. HOT updates require that no indexed column changed; they sharply cut index write amplification on hot rows.

A partial index (`CREATE INDEX ... WHERE active`) indexes only rows matching a predicate, making it smaller and faster and ideal for queries that always filter on that condition (e.g. only `status='pending'`). SQL Server calls the same thing a filtered index. Bonus: a partial unique index enforces uniqueness only among matching rows.

To cap lock-manager memory, SQL Server escalates many fine-grained row/page locks on one object into a single table lock once a threshold (~5000 locks) is hit — which can suddenly block other transactions. Postgres never escalates row locks (it stores lock info in the tuple itself), so it doesn't have this failure mode.

A random UUIDv4 as a clustered/primary key scatters inserts across the whole B-tree, causing page splits, cache misses, and bloat. Use a time-ordered ID — UUIDv7, ULID, or an auto-increment — so new rows append to the rightmost page. In InnoDB this matters doubly because every secondary index stores the PK value.

`EXISTS` and `IN` both express a semi-join and modern optimizers often plan them identically, but `IN (subquery)` has surprising NULL behavior: if the subquery returns any NULL, `NOT IN` yields no rows. `NOT EXISTS` is NULL-safe and usually the better default for anti-joins.

A transaction log keeps records until they're no longer needed for recovery/replication, then space is reclaimed. In SQL Server FULL recovery model, the log only truncates after a log backup — skip those and the log grows until the disk fills. A checkpoint flushes dirty pages so older log can be released.

Index Condition Pushdown lets the storage engine evaluate parts of the WHERE clause against the index before fetching the full row, cutting random row reads. In MySQL/InnoDB, a query like `WHERE last LIKE 'A%' AND first LIKE '%z%'` on index `(last, first)` can filter the `first` condition in the index rather than reading every matching row.

A CHECK constraint enforces a boolean condition on each row (`CHECK (price >= 0)`) at write time, pushing validation into the database where it can't be bypassed by a buggy app. Postgres also has DOMAINs (reusable named constrained types) and lets you add a constraint `NOT VALID` to skip checking existing rows, validating later.

When a query can use several indexes, Postgres builds an in-memory bitmap of matching tuple locations from each, combines them with AND/OR, then does a single bitmap heap scan visiting pages in physical order. This turns scattered random reads into a mostly sequential pass and lets multiple indexes cooperate on one query.

Sequences (`SERIAL`, `IDENTITY`, `AUTO_INCREMENT`) are non-transactional: a value consumed by a rolled-back transaction is not given back, so gaps in IDs are normal and expected. Don't treat them as a contiguous count. Sequences cache/allocate values for concurrency, which is also why InnoDB can leave gaps after a failed bulk insert.

To make `WHERE lower(email) = ?` use an index, build it on the expression: `CREATE INDEX ON users (lower(email))`. The indexed expression must match the query's expression exactly. SQL Server achieves the same with a persisted computed column plus an index on it.

Write skew is an anomaly that snapshot isolation/REPEATABLE READ allows: two transactions read an overlapping set, then each writes a disjoint row, together violating an invariant neither broke alone (e.g. both doctors going off-call). True SERIALIZABLE — Postgres's SSI tracks read/write dependencies — detects and aborts one to prevent it.

The buffer pool (InnoDB) / shared_buffers (Postgres) caches data pages in RAM so hot data avoids disk; reads and writes go through it, and dirty pages are flushed lazily at checkpoints. A high cache hit ratio is the single biggest performance lever. Postgres notably also leans on the OS page cache, so its shared_buffers is sized smaller than InnoDB's pool.

Redis sorted sets store members ranked by a float score. `ZADD board 100 alice` then `ZRANGE board 0 -1 WITHSCORES` reads ascending, `ZREVRANGE` descending. They make O(log N) leaderboards and time-window queues; `ZRANGEBYSCORE board 0 50` pulls a score range.

Set a per-key TTL with `EXPIRE key 60` (seconds) or atomically at write with `SET key val EX 60`. `TTL key` returns remaining seconds (-1 = no expiry, -2 = gone). Redis uses lazy + periodic sampling to evict expired keys, so memory isn't freed exactly on time.

When `maxmemory` is hit, `maxmemory-policy` decides eviction. `allkeys-lru` evicts least-recently-used across all keys; `volatile-ttl` evicts soon-to-expire keys first; `noeviction` (default) rejects writes with an error. Redis LRU is approximate — it samples N keys (`maxmemory-samples`) rather than scanning everything.

Redis offers RDB (point-in-time fork+dump snapshots, compact, can lose minutes of writes) and AOF (append-only log of every write, more durable). `appendfsync everysec` is the common AOF tradeoff: at most ~1s of data loss. Enabling both gives snapshot speed plus AOF recovery.

Pipelining sends many commands without waiting for each reply, collapsing N round trips into one. It's not transactional — commands just stream out and replies come back in order. For atomicity use `MULTI`/`EXEC`; for raw throughput on bulk writes, pipeline.

Redis hashes store field→value maps under one key: `HSET user:1 name alice age 30`, read with `HGET user:1 name` or `HGETALL user:1`. Small hashes are encoded as a compact listpack, so storing an object as a hash uses far less memory than many top-level keys.

MongoDB's aggregation pipeline chains stages: `[{$match:{status:'A'}}, {$group:{_id:'$cust', total:{$sum:'$amt'}}}]`. Put `$match` and `$limit` as early as possible so the engine filters before grouping/sorting. `$lookup` does left-outer joins; `$unwind` flattens arrays.

Create with `db.coll.createIndex({a:1, b:-1})`. Compound-index field order follows the ESR rule: Equality fields first, then Sort fields, then Range fields. A query can use a prefix of the index keys but not a non-prefix subset. `explain('executionStats')` shows whether an IXSCAN or a COLLSCAN ran.

Every MongoDB doc gets a 12-byte `_id`. The default ObjectId packs a 4-byte timestamp + 5 random bytes + 3-byte counter, so it's roughly time-ordered and you can extract creation time from it. You can supply your own `_id` of any type, but it's immutable once written.

Write concern controls how many replica-set members must ack a write. `{w:'majority'}` waits for a majority (durable across failover); `{w:1}` only the primary; `{j:true}` requires the journal flush. Lower w = faster but riskier on primary failure.

A replica set has one primary (takes writes) and secondaries that replicate its oplog. If the primary fails, an election picks a new one — needing a majority, so run an odd number of voting members (3+). Reads default to the primary; set `readPreference` to `secondaryPreferred` to offload reads.

Sharding splits a collection across shards by a shard key. Pick a high-cardinality, evenly-written key — a monotonically increasing key (timestamp) creates a hotspot since all new writes hit one shard. Hashed shard keys spread writes but kill range queries. The key is immutable per document (pre-5.0).

`updateOne(filter, update, {upsert:true})` updates a match or inserts if none exists. Use `$setOnInsert` for fields that should only be written on the insert path (e.g. createdAt) while `$set` applies on both. `findOneAndUpdate` returns the document; pass `returnDocument:'after'` to get the post-update version.

Embed sub-documents when they're read together and bounded in size; reference (store an _id) when data is large, shared, or grows unbounded. Mongo's 16MB document cap means an unbounded embedded array eventually breaks — that's the classic 'massive arrays' anti-pattern.

DynamoDB's primary key is a partition key (decides which physical partition) plus an optional sort key. Items sharing a partition key are stored together sorted by sort key, enabling range queries within a partition. Pick a high-cardinality partition key to avoid hot partitions.

`Query` targets one partition key and is efficient; `Scan` reads the entire table and filters after, burning RCUs on every item even those filtered out. Almost always design access patterns so you `Query`, never `Scan`, in production hot paths.

A Global Secondary Index (GSI) lets you query on a different partition/sort key; it's a separate replicated copy with its own throughput and is eventually consistent. A Local Secondary Index (LSI) shares the table's partition key, allows strongly-consistent reads, but must be created at table creation and shares the 10GB item-collection limit.

Single-table design stores multiple entity types in one table using generic `PK`/`SK` attributes (e.g. `USER#123` / `ORDER#456`) so related items live in the same partition and one query fetches them together. It trades query-time joins for upfront access-pattern modeling — you design the table around known queries.

Provisioned mode reserves RCUs/WCUs (one WCU = 1 write/s up to 1KB; one RCU = 1 strongly-consistent read/s up to 4KB, or 2 eventually-consistent). On-demand mode auto-scales and bills per request — better for spiky/unknown traffic, pricier per unit at steady high load.
