Conditional writes enforce atomic checks: `PutItem` with `ConditionExpression: attribute_not_exists(PK)` does insert-if-absent; a version attribute plus `version = :expected` gives optimistic locking. A failed condition throws `ConditionalCheckFailedException` and the write is rejected without consuming a full write.

Cassandra's PRIMARY KEY = partition key + clustering columns: `PRIMARY KEY ((user_id), ts)`. The partition key (first parenthesized group) hashes to a node; clustering columns sort rows within the partition on disk. You query by partition key; you generally can't filter on non-key columns without `ALLOW FILTERING` (a footgun).

Cassandra tunes consistency per query via consistency level. With replication factor 3, reading and writing at `QUORUM` (2 of 3) guarantees read-your-writes because R+W > RF. `ONE` is fastest/least consistent; `ALL` is strongest but a single down replica fails the op.

Cassandra deletes write a tombstone marker rather than removing data, since data is immutable on SSTables. Tombstones live until compaction past `gc_grace_seconds` (default 10 days). Querying a partition with thousands of tombstones (e.g. queue-as-table) blows up read latency and can throw `TombstoneOverwhelmingException`.

Cassandra is LSM-tree based: writes go to a commit log + in-memory memtable, then flush to immutable SSTables. Reads may merge several SSTables, so compaction periodically merges them and drops tombstones. This makes writes very fast (append-only, no read-before-write) but reads can touch multiple files.

Cassandra excels at time-series wide rows, but unbounded partitions hurt — keep a partition under ~100MB / ~100k rows. Bucket by time (`PRIMARY KEY ((sensor, day), ts)`) so partitions stay bounded and you avoid a single ever-growing hot partition.

CouchDB uses document-level MVCC: every doc has a `_rev`, and an update must send the current `_rev` or get a 409 conflict. Replication can create conflicting revisions on different nodes; CouchDB keeps both, picks a deterministic winner, and leaves the rest for your app to resolve.

Riak uses vector clocks (causal context) to track update causality across nodes. Concurrent writes that can't be ordered create siblings; with `allow_mult=true` the client must merge them (often via CRDTs). Always read-then-write passing the returned context so Riak can detect causality.

CRDTs are data types whose concurrent replicas merge deterministically without coordination, giving strong eventual consistency. Examples: G-Counter (grow-only, merge = per-node max then sum), PN-Counter (two G-Counters for inc/dec), OR-Set (add wins via unique tags). Riak and Redis (CRDT modules) ship some built-in.

HBase stores data by row key, sorted lexicographically, grouped into column families (each family is a separate store file, so keep families few). Tables auto-split into regions by row-key range served across RegionServers. Sequential row keys cause region hotspotting — salt or hash the prefix to spread writes.

ScyllaDB is a C++ rewrite of Cassandra (same CQL/wire protocol) on the Seastar framework, using a shard-per-core architecture that pins data to CPU cores and bypasses the page cache. It targets the same data model as Cassandra at lower latency and higher per-node throughput, often replacing Cassandra without app changes.

Neo4j is a native graph store queried in Cypher with ASCII-art patterns: `MATCH (a:Person)-[:FRIEND]->(b) WHERE a.name='Ann' RETURN b`. Relationships are first-class and stored as direct pointers, so traversals are index-free adjacency — hopping N relationships doesn't get costlier the way SQL JOINs do.

Redis Streams are append-only logs: `XADD s * field val` appends with an auto ID. Consumer groups (`XGROUP CREATE`, `XREADGROUP`) let multiple workers split a stream, and unacked messages sit in a Pending Entries List until `XACK`'d, so crashed consumers' work can be claimed with `XCLAIM`.

`EVAL` runs a Lua script atomically server-side — no other command interleaves while it runs — which is the clean way to do read-then-write logic (e.g. check-and-set, rate limiters). Pass keys via `KEYS[]` and args via `ARGV[]`; cache the script with `SCRIPT LOAD` + `EVALSHA` to avoid resending the body.

MongoDB supports multi-document ACID transactions (replica sets 4.0+, sharded 4.2+) via a session: `session.startTransaction()` … `commitTransaction()`. They carry overhead and have a default 60s `transactionLifetimeLimitSeconds` — favor a good schema that keeps related data in one document so you rarely need them.

Change streams (`db.coll.watch()`) tail the oplog to deliver real-time insert/update/delete events with a resumable `_id` token, so a consumer can restart from where it stopped. They require a replica set (or sharded cluster) and are the supported alternative to scraping the oplog directly for CDC.

MongoDB stores documents as BSON, a binary-encoded superset of JSON with length-prefixed fields for fast traversal and extra types JSON lacks: `Date`, `ObjectId`, `Decimal128`, binary, and 32/64-bit ints. Field names are repeated in every document, so short keys meaningfully cut storage at scale.

Consistent hashing maps keys and nodes onto a ring so adding/removing a node only reshuffles keys near it, not the whole keyspace (unlike `hash % N`). Virtual nodes (vnodes) — many ring positions per physical node — even out the load and smooth rebalancing. Used by DynamoDB, Cassandra, and Riak.

A Bloom filter is a bit-array + k hashes giving 'definitely not present' or 'maybe present' — false positives possible, false negatives never. LSM stores (Cassandra, RocksDB, HBase) attach one per SSTable so a read can skip files that definitely lack the key, avoiding disk seeks.

RocksDB is Facebook's embeddable LSM-tree key-value engine (a LevelDB fork) used as a storage layer under many systems. Tunables trade off the three amplifications: leveled compaction lowers space/read amplification at higher write amplification; universal compaction does the reverse.

etcd is a strongly-consistent distributed key-value store using the Raft consensus protocol; it backs Kubernetes' cluster state. It exposes watches (stream changes on a key/prefix), leases (TTL keys for service liveness), and compare-and-swap transactions for leader election and config coordination.

Redis Cluster shards keys across 16384 hash slots (slot = `CRC16(key) mod 16384`), each owned by a master with replicas. Multi-key commands only work if keys share a slot — wrap a substring in `{}` (hash tag) like `user:{42}:name` so related keys co-locate. Clients are redirected via `MOVED`/`ASK` responses.

Hash maps resolve collisions two main ways. Separate chaining stores a list (or tree) per bucket — Java's `HashMap` converts a bucket to a red-black tree once it holds 8+ entries. Open addressing (linear/quadratic probing) stores entries inline in the table and probes for the next free slot, which is cache-friendlier but degrades sharply as load factor approaches 1.

Load factor = entries / buckets. Java's `HashMap` resizes (doubles capacity and rehashes everything) when it exceeds 0.75. Keep it lower for fewer collisions at the cost of memory. Resizing is O(n), so if you know the size up front, pre-size with `new HashMap<>(expectedSize / 0.75 + 1)` to avoid repeated rehashes.

A binary search tree keeps `left < node < right`. An in-order traversal (left, node, right) visits keys in sorted order — that's the defining property. Lookup/insert/delete are O(h) where h is height, so O(log n) only if the tree stays balanced; insert sorted data into a plain BST and it degenerates into a linked list with O(n) ops.

A red-black tree guarantees O(log n) by enforcing: nodes are red or black, the root is black, red nodes can't have red children, and every root-to-null path has the same number of black nodes. This bounds the longest path to at most twice the shortest. C++ `std::map` and Java `TreeMap` are red-black trees under the hood.

An AVL tree keeps the balance factor (height of left subtree minus right) within {-1, 0, 1} at every node, rebalancing with rotations on insert/delete. It's more rigidly balanced than a red-black tree, so lookups are slightly faster, but it does more rotations on writes — prefer AVL for read-heavy workloads, red-black for write-heavy.

A rotation locally restructures a BST while preserving in-order ordering. A right rotation at node X makes X's left child the new subtree root and X its right child; a left rotation is the mirror. It's O(1) — just re-pointing a few references — and is the primitive that AVL and red-black trees use to restore balance.

A B+ tree stores all values only in the leaves and uses internal nodes purely as a routing index; the leaves are linked in a sequential list. That linked leaf layer makes range scans fast — find the start, then walk leaves — which is why most relational database indexes (e.g. InnoDB's clustered index) are B+ trees, not plain B-trees.

A binary heap is stored in a flat array with no pointers: for 0-based index `i`, the children are at `2i+1` and `2i+2` and the parent is at `(i-1)/2`. Because the tree is complete, the array has no gaps. This cache-friendly layout is why heaps are fast in practice and why `heapify` can build a heap bottom-up in O(n).

Building a heap by inserting n items one at a time is O(n log n), but bottom-up `heapify` is O(n): start at the last non-leaf node and sift-down each node toward the leaves. The reason it's linear is that most nodes are near the bottom and sift down only a short distance. C++ `std::make_heap` does exactly this.

Heapsort builds a max-heap in O(n), then repeatedly swaps the root to the end and sifts down the shrinking heap. It's O(n log n) worst case and in-place (O(1) extra space), but not stable, and its scattered memory access makes it usually slower than quicksort in practice despite the better worst case.

A Fibonacci heap gives O(1) amortized insert and decrease-key, with O(log n) amortized extract-min. That decrease-key cost is what improves Dijkstra's theoretical bound to O(E + V log V). In practice the large constant factors and pointer overhead mean a plain binary heap usually wins, so Fibonacci heaps are mostly of theoretical interest.

A trie stores strings by sharing common prefixes along the path from the root, so lookup/insert of a key of length k is O(k) and independent of how many keys are stored. It's the natural fit for autocomplete and prefix queries (all words under a node share its prefix), at the cost of high memory from one node per character per branch.

A radix tree (PATRICIA trie) compresses chains of single-child nodes in a trie into one edge labeled with a substring, cutting both depth and memory. The Linux kernel uses radix trees for page caches and IP routing tables. Use it over a plain trie when keys are long and sparse with few branch points.

Adjacency list: per-vertex list of neighbors — O(V+E) space, fast to iterate a vertex's edges, ideal for sparse graphs. Adjacency matrix: a V×V boolean/weight grid — O(V²) space, O(1) edge lookup, good for dense graphs or when you frequently ask 'is there an edge u→v?'. Most real-world graphs are sparse, so the list is the default.

Breadth-first search explores a graph level by level using a FIFO queue, marking nodes visited as it enqueues them. On an unweighted graph it finds the shortest path (fewest edges) from the source to every reachable node, in O(V+E). Mark visited at enqueue time, not dequeue, or you'll add the same node multiple times.

Depth-first search dives as deep as possible before backtracking, using a stack (or recursion). It's O(V+E) and underpins cycle detection, topological sort, and finding connected components. On deep graphs the recursive version can blow the call stack — use an explicit stack for large inputs.

Dijkstra finds shortest paths from one source on a graph with non-negative edge weights, greedily expanding the closest unsettled node via a min-priority-queue. With a binary heap it's O((V+E) log V). It breaks with negative edges — once a node is settled it's assumed final, which a later negative edge could violate; use Bellman-Ford instead.

Bellman-Ford computes single-source shortest paths and tolerates negative edge weights by relaxing every edge V-1 times, in O(V·E). A V-th pass that still relaxes an edge proves a reachable negative-weight cycle (meaning no finite shortest path exists). It's slower than Dijkstra but the go-to when weights can be negative.

A topological sort linearly orders a DAG so every edge u→v has u before v — the order to run tasks given dependencies. Kahn's algorithm repeatedly removes a node with in-degree 0 and decrements its neighbors; if nodes remain when the queue empties, the graph has a cycle. It's O(V+E).

A disjoint-set (union-find) tracks elements partitioned into sets with `find` (which set?) and `union` (merge). With both path compression and union by rank/size, the amortized cost per op is O(α(n)) — the inverse Ackermann function, effectively constant. It's the backbone of Kruskal's MST and connected-component queries.

Kruskal builds a minimum spanning tree by sorting all edges ascending by weight, then adding each edge whose endpoints are in different components (checked with union-find), skipping any that would form a cycle. It's O(E log E), dominated by the sort. Prefer it for sparse graphs; Prim's tends to win on dense ones.

A skip list is a stack of sorted linked lists where higher levels skip over many nodes, giving O(log n) expected search/insert/delete without rotations. Each node's height is chosen randomly (coin flips), so balance is probabilistic, not enforced. Redis sorted sets and LevelDB's memtable use skip lists because they're simple to make concurrent.

An O(1) LRU cache combines a hash map (key → node) with a doubly linked list ordered by recency. On access you move the node to the front; on insert past capacity you evict the tail. Both structures are needed: the map gives O(1) lookup, the list gives O(1) reordering and eviction. Java's `LinkedHashMap` with `accessOrder=true` does this for you.

A segment tree answers range queries (sum/min/max over [l,r]) and point updates in O(log n) each, by storing aggregates over recursively halved intervals in a tree (often a 2n-sized array). Add lazy propagation to also support O(log n) range updates. Use it when both queries and updates are frequent; a prefix-sum array beats it if the data is static.

A Fenwick tree (binary indexed tree) supports prefix-sum queries and point updates in O(log n) with far less code and memory than a segment tree. It exploits the low bit of an index: `i += i & -i` walks the update path, `i -= i & -i` walks the query path. It's 1-indexed and limited to invertible operations like sum.

A singly linked list node holds a value and a `next` pointer to the following node; the last node's `next` is null. Insert/delete at a known position is O(1) (just re-point), but random access is O(n) because you must walk from the head. Cache locality is poor versus an array, so prefer arrays/vectors unless you need cheap middle insertions.

Floyd's tortoise-and-hare detects a cycle in a linked list with two pointers, one moving one step and one moving two; if they ever meet, there's a loop, in O(n) time and O(1) space. To find the cycle's start, reset one pointer to the head and advance both one step at a time — they meet at the entry node.

A circular (ring) buffer is a fixed-size array with head and tail indices that wrap via modulo, giving O(1) enqueue/dequeue with no allocation after construction. It's the standard structure for streaming, audio, and producer/consumer pipelines. Keeping the capacity a power of two lets you wrap with a cheap `& (size-1)` mask instead of `%`.

A deque supports O(1) (amortized) insert/remove at both ends. It can act as both a stack and a queue. Python's `collections.deque` is a doubly linked list of fixed-size blocks (so indexing the middle is O(n)); C++ `std::deque` is a segmented array of chunks giving O(1) random access but non-contiguous storage.

A min-max heap supports O(1) access to both the minimum and the maximum and O(log n) extraction of either. Alternating tree levels are min-levels and max-levels, so the root is the global min and its children hold the global max. Use it for a double-ended priority queue; two separate heaps with cross-deletion is the simpler-but-clunkier alternative.

Robin Hood hashing is an open-addressing scheme that equalizes probe distances: on insert, if the existing entry is closer to its ideal slot than the new key is to its own, the new key steals the slot and the existing one keeps probing. This 'rob from the rich' rule cuts variance in probe length, making worst-case lookups much better than plain linear probing.

Cuckoo hashing uses two hash functions and two tables; each key lives in one of its two candidate slots, giving guaranteed O(1) worst-case lookups (check both spots). Inserts can cascade — kicking out an occupant that re-homes to its alternate slot — and a cycle forces a rehash. It trades insert complexity for fast, predictable reads.

A suffix tree indexes all suffixes of a string so any substring query runs in O(m) for a pattern of length m, and it solves longest-common-substring and repeated-substring problems. It's memory-heavy (Ukkonen's algorithm builds it in O(n)); a suffix array (sorted suffix start positions) does similar jobs in far less space and is what most production code uses.

Detect a cycle in a directed graph with DFS and three colors: white (unvisited), gray (on the current recursion path), black (fully done). Reaching a gray node means a back edge, i.e. a cycle. In an undirected graph you instead just look for a visited neighbor that isn't the parent. Both run in O(V+E).

Use a heap when you only ever need the single min or max repeatedly (priority queue, top-k, scheduling) — it gives O(1) peek and cheaper construction than a tree. Use a balanced BST when you need sorted iteration, range queries, predecessor/successor, or membership tests — a heap can't do those efficiently because it only maintains a partial order.

A polynomial rolling hash treats a string as a number in some base mod a large prime, e.g. `h = (h * base + c) mod p`. The 'rolling' part lets you slide a window and update the hash in O(1) by removing the leading char and adding the trailing one — that's the core of Rabin-Karp substring search. Use two different moduli to make collisions astronomically unlikely.

Storing each vertex's neighbors in a hash set instead of a list gives O(1) average 'is u adjacent to v?' checks while keeping O(V+E) space — a middle ground between an adjacency list (slow edge lookup) and a matrix (O(V²) space). Worth it when your algorithm repeatedly tests edge existence on a sparse graph.

When keys are small dense integers (e.g. 0..n), a plain array beats a hash map: O(1) with no hashing, no collisions, and contiguous memory that the CPU cache loves. Hash maps win for sparse, large, or non-integer keys. For tens of items, even linear scan of an array can outrun a hash map because of constant factors and cache effects.

A node's depth is its distance from the root; a tree's height is the longest root-to-leaf path. A binary tree of n nodes has height at least ⌊log₂ n⌋ (fully balanced) and at most n-1 (a degenerate chain). Because most BST operations cost O(height), keeping height ~log n is exactly why self-balancing trees exist.

Big-O describes how runtime or space grows as input size `n` grows, ignoring constants and lower-order terms. `O(n)` means roughly linear, `O(n^2)` quadratic, `O(1)` constant. It's an upper bound on the worst case, so `O(2n+5)` is just written `O(n)`.

Binary search finds a target in a sorted array in `O(log n)` by halving the range each step. Requires sorted input. Classic bug: `mid = (lo+hi)/2` can overflow in fixed-width ints; use `mid = lo + (hi-lo)/2`. Off-by-one in the `hi = mid-1` / `lo = mid+1` updates is the usual cause of infinite loops.

Mergesort is `O(n log n)` in all cases (best/avg/worst) and stable, but needs `O(n)` extra space for merging. Good for linked lists (no random access needed) and external sorting of data too big for RAM. The guaranteed worst case makes it preferable when you can't tolerate quicksort's `O(n^2)` blowup.

Timsort is the default sort in Python (`sorted`, `list.sort`) and Java for objects. It's a hybrid of mergesort and insertion sort that detects pre-sorted 'runs', giving `O(n)` on nearly-sorted data and `O(n log n)` worst case. It's stable, which is why Python's sort is.

Bubble, insertion, and selection sort are all `O(n^2)`. Insertion sort is the useful one: `O(n)` on nearly-sorted data and fast for tiny arrays (under ~10-50 elements), which is why real sorts switch to it for small subarrays. Bubble sort is essentially only a teaching tool.

Counting and radix sort beat the `O(n log n)` comparison-sort lower bound by not comparing elements. Counting sort is `O(n+k)` for integers in range `[0,k)`. Radix sort is `O(d·(n+k))` for `d`-digit keys. Both need bounded, integer-like keys; useless for arbitrary comparable objects.

Any comparison-based sort needs at least `O(n log n)` comparisons in the worst case. The proof: there are `n!` possible orderings, a binary decision tree distinguishing them needs depth `log2(n!) ≈ n log n`. You only beat this by exploiting key structure (counting/radix sort).

Amortized cost averages an expensive operation over many cheap ones. A dynamic array's `push` is amortized `O(1)`: doubling capacity on resize means `n` pushes cost `O(n)` total even though individual resizes are `O(n)`. Doubling (not adding a fixed amount) is what makes the geometric series collapse.

Greedy algorithms make the locally optimal choice at each step. They're fast and simple but only correct when the problem has the 'greedy choice property' (e.g. Dijkstra, Huffman coding, activity selection). For coin change they fail on arbitrary denominations — use DP there. Always prove correctness; greedy is easy to get wrong.

The two-pointer technique solves many array problems in `O(n)` time and `O(1)` space by moving indices inward or in tandem. Classic uses: find a pair summing to a target in a sorted array, reverse in place, remove duplicates. The sliding-window variant handles 'longest substring' style problems.

Sliding window turns an `O(n^2)` nested-loop over subarrays into `O(n)` by maintaining a moving range and incrementally updating its state as you slide. Fixed-size windows track a running sum; variable-size windows grow/shrink based on a condition (e.g. longest substring without repeating characters).

Space complexity counts extra memory beyond the input. 'In-place' means `O(1)` auxiliary space (input may be modified). Recursion costs `O(depth)` stack space even with no explicit allocation — easy to overlook. Time-space tradeoffs are common: a hash set turns an `O(n^2)` `O(1)`-space scan into `O(n)` time, `O(n)` space.

`O(n log n)` (linearithmic) is the typical cost of efficient comparison sorts and divide-and-conquer algorithms that do `O(n)` work across `log n` levels. It's only slightly worse than linear: for `n = 1,000,000`, `log2 n ≈ 20`, so it's ~20× linear, not 1,000,000× like `O(n^2)` would be.

`O(2^n)` and `O(n!)` are intractable beyond tiny inputs — naive subset enumeration is `2^n`, permutation generation is `n!`. At `n=20`, `2^n` is a million but `n!` is 2.4 quintillion. These signal you need DP, pruning (branch and bound), or an approximation rather than brute force.

NP-complete problems (SAT, traveling salesman, knapsack) have no known polynomial-time solution, but a proposed solution can be verified in polynomial time. If you find a poly algorithm for one, you've solved them all (and P=NP). In practice: use approximations, heuristics, or solvers — don't seek an exact fast algorithm.

Divide-and-conquer splits a problem into subproblems, solves recursively, and combines. The Master Theorem solves recurrences `T(n) = a·T(n/b) + O(n^d)`: compare `d` to `log_b a` to get the answer. Mergesort (`a=2, b=2, d=1`) hits the tie case → `O(n log n)`.

Backtracking explores a decision tree depth-first and abandons ('prunes') a branch as soon as it can't lead to a valid solution. Used for N-Queens, Sudoku, permutations, and subset generation. Worst case is exponential, but good pruning makes many instances fast in practice.

Kadane's algorithm finds the maximum-sum contiguous subarray in `O(n)`, `O(1)` space. Track a running sum; reset it to the current element whenever it goes negative, and keep the best seen. It's the canonical example of turning an obvious `O(n^2)` (or `O(n^3)`) brute force into linear time.

Quickselect finds the k-th smallest element in average `O(n)` (worst `O(n^2)`) without fully sorting — it's quicksort that only recurses into the partition containing k. C++ `std::nth_element` uses introselect (median-of-medians fallback) to guarantee `O(n)` worst case.

Binary search isn't just for arrays — if a problem has a monotonic yes/no predicate over a numeric answer, binary-search the answer itself in `O(log range)`. Classic for 'minimum capacity to ship in D days' or 'smallest max-load' problems. Define `feasible(x)` and find the boundary where it flips.

A prefix-sum array precomputes cumulative sums so any range sum `[i,j]` is answered in `O(1)` as `prefix[j+1] - prefix[i]`, after `O(n)` preprocessing. Turns repeated range queries from `O(n)` each into `O(1)`. The 2D version (integral image) does rectangle sums in `O(1)`.

Best/average/worst case describe different inputs of the same size; amortized is different — it's a guaranteed average over a sequence of operations on the same structure. Hash table lookup is average `O(1)` but worst `O(n)`; dynamic-array append is amortized `O(1)` (no probabilistic assumption needed).

Bit tricks run in `O(1)`: `x & (x-1)` clears the lowest set bit, `x & -x` isolates it, `x ^ y` swaps without a temp, `n & 1` tests odd, `n << 1` / `n >> 1` multiply/divide by 2. XOR-ing all elements finds the single unpaired number in `O(n)`, `O(1)` space.

Naive substring search is `O(nm)`. KMP (Knuth-Morris-Pratt) precomputes a failure table to skip re-checking and achieves `O(n+m)`. Boyer-Moore is often faster in practice by skipping ahead from the end. Most stdlib `indexOf`/`find` use a tuned hybrid, not naive scanning.

Big-O hides constant factors and lower-order terms, so a lower-complexity algorithm can lose on real inputs. Insertion sort beats quicksort for tiny arrays; a cache-friendly `O(n^2)` can outrun a pointer-chasing `O(n log n)`. Always measure: asymptotics tell you scaling, not which is faster at your actual `n`.

`fork()` doesn't physically copy the parent's memory — the kernel marks all pages copy-on-write (COW) and shares them read-only. A page is only duplicated when either process writes to it, triggering a page fault that copies that single page. This makes `fork()` cheap even for large processes, and `fork()`+`exec()` rarely copies anything since `exec` discards the address space.

`vfork()` suspends the parent and shares its address space until the child calls `exec` or `_exit`, avoiding even COW page-table setup — but writing anything other than the `exec` is undefined behavior. Modern code prefers `posix_spawn()`, which the kernel can implement efficiently (often via `clone`/`vfork` internally) without the footguns.

Threads in one process share the same address space, file descriptors, and signal handlers, but each has its own stack, registers, and program counter. Processes have fully isolated address spaces. On Linux both are created by `clone()` — a thread just passes `CLONE_VM | CLONE_FILES | CLONE_FS | CLONE_SIGHAND` to share those resources.

A zombie (`Z`/`<defunct>` in `ps`) is a child that exited but whose parent hasn't called `wait()`/`waitpid()` to reap its exit status. Zombies hold only a process-table slot, not memory, but leaking them exhausts PIDs. If the parent dies first the child is re-parented to `init`/`systemd` (PID 1), which reaps it automatically.

When a parent exits before its children, those orphans are re-parented to PID 1 (or the nearest subreaper). A process can register as a subreaper with `prctl(PR_SET_CHILD_SUBREAPER, 1)` so it inherits and reaps orphaned descendants instead — this is how container runtimes and process managers keep zombies from piling up on init.

Each process sees a private virtual address space; the MMU translates virtual to physical addresses via multi-level page tables (4 levels on x86-64, giving 48-bit addresses). This isolation means two processes can both use address `0x400000` mapped to different physical RAM. The kernel maintains one page table per process and switches the table base (`CR3` on x86) on context switch.

The TLB caches recent virtual-to-physical page translations so the CPU avoids walking the page table on every access. A TLB miss costs a page-table walk; a context switch flushes the TLB unless PCID/ASID tags let entries from different address spaces coexist. Huge pages (2 MB/1 GB) reduce TLB pressure by mapping more memory per entry.

A minor fault resolves without disk I/O (page is in memory but not yet mapped — e.g. COW or first touch of a zeroed page). A major fault requires reading the page from disk/swap and is far slower. Watch them with `ps -o min_flt,maj_flt` or `/usr/bin/time -v`; lots of major faults usually means thrashing or insufficient RAM.

`malloc`/`mmap` reserve virtual address space but Linux doesn't back it with physical RAM until you actually touch each page (demand paging / lazy allocation). That's why allocating a huge buffer succeeds instantly and RSS only grows as you write to it. Combined with memory overcommit, a process can map far more than physical RAM exists.

Because Linux overcommits memory, allocations rarely fail; instead when RAM+swap is exhausted the OOM killer picks a victim and SIGKILLs it. Selection is driven by `oom_score`, which you bias per-process via `/proc/<pid>/oom_score_adj` (-1000 to 1000; -1000 = never kill). Tune overcommit with `vm.overcommit_memory` sysctl.

VSZ is the total virtual address space a process has mapped (including unused reservations and shared libs); RSS is the physical RAM actually resident right now. RSS double-counts shared pages across processes — for a truer figure use PSS (proportional set size) from `/proc/<pid>/smaps`, which splits shared pages by how many processes map them.

Swap moves inactive anonymous pages to disk to free RAM for active pages and the page cache. `vm.swappiness` (0–100, default 60) tunes how aggressively the kernel reclaims anonymous pages vs dropping file-cache pages — lower keeps anonymous memory in RAM longer. Heavy continuous swapping (thrashing) shows as high major-fault rates and tanks performance.

A context switch saves the running thread's registers, switches kernel stacks, and (for a different process) swaps the page-table base, flushing TLB/cache locality. Direct cost is ~1–10µs but the indirect cost from cold caches is often larger. `pidstat -w` shows voluntary (blocked on I/O) vs involuntary (preempted) switches per process.

`nice` values range -20 (highest priority) to 19 (lowest); lower nice means a larger CFS weight and more CPU share. Start a process niced with `nice -n 10 cmd`; change a running one with `renice -n 5 -p <pid>`. Only root can lower (raise priority) below 0. Nice affects share, not hard guarantees — use real-time scheduling for that.

Real-time scheduling classes `SCHED_FIFO` and `SCHED_RR` outrank all normal (`SCHED_OTHER`) tasks; a runnable RT task preempts everything below it. `SCHED_FIFO` runs until it blocks or yields (can monopolize a CPU); `SCHED_RR` round-robins among equal-priority RT tasks. Set with `chrt -f 50 cmd`. Guard against runaway RT tasks via `sched_rt_runtime_us` throttling.

CPU affinity pins a process/thread to a subset of cores, preserving cache locality and avoiding cross-core migration. Set it at launch with `taskset -c 0,2 cmd` or at runtime with `taskset -cp 0-3 <pid>`; programmatically via `sched_setaffinity()`. Useful for latency-sensitive workloads, but over-pinning can hurt by preventing the scheduler from balancing load.

On NUMA systems memory is attached to specific CPU sockets; accessing a remote node's RAM is slower than local. Linux defaults to a first-touch policy — a page lands on the node of whichever CPU first writes it. Inspect topology with `numactl --hardware` and bind with `numactl --cpunodebind=0 --membind=0 cmd` to keep a workload's CPU and memory on the same node.

A mutex blocks (deschedules) the waiter, so the CPU does other work — best when the lock may be held a while. A spinlock busy-waits in a tight loop, wasting CPU but avoiding the context-switch cost — only worth it for very short critical sections, and never on a single core where the holder can't run while you spin. Kernel code must use spinlocks in interrupt context where sleeping is illegal.

A futex (fast userspace mutex) is how glibc implements mutexes/condvars: the lock state lives in a userspace integer, and an atomic compare-and-swap takes/releases it with zero syscalls when uncontended. Only on contention does it call `futex(FUTEX_WAIT/FUTEX_WAKE)` to sleep or wake threads via the kernel — making the common uncontended path extremely cheap.

Deadlock requires all four Coffman conditions simultaneously: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and circular wait. Break any one to prevent it — the most practical is eliminating circular wait by always acquiring locks in a fixed global order. `try_lock` with backoff breaks hold-and-wait; timeouts approximate preemption.

Priority inversion happens when a high-priority task waits on a lock held by a low-priority task that's itself preempted by a medium-priority task — stalling the high task indefinitely (famously the Mars Pathfinder reset bug). The fix is priority inheritance: the lock holder temporarily inherits the highest waiter's priority. Enable with `PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT` mutex protocol.

A mutex enforces ownership — only the locking thread may unlock — and protects a critical section. A semaphore is a counter (`sem_wait` decrements/blocks at 0, `sem_post` increments) with no ownership, used to limit N concurrent users of a resource or to signal between threads. Posting from one thread and waiting in another is fine for a semaphore but illegal for a mutex.

Always wait on a condition variable inside a `while` loop checking the predicate, never an `if` — wakeups can be spurious (the thread wakes with the condition still false). `pthread_cond_wait` atomically releases the mutex and sleeps, then re-acquires it on wake. Hold the mutex when calling `signal`/`broadcast` (or just after) to avoid lost-wakeup races.

Each thread gets its own stack (Linux default ~8 MB, set by `ulimit -s`), so spawning thousands of threads can reserve gigabytes of virtual memory. Deep recursion or huge local arrays overflow it, usually crashing with SIGSEGV at the guard page. Tune per-thread with `pthread_attr_setstacksize()` before `pthread_create`.

Thread-local storage gives each thread its own copy of a variable, declared `__thread`/`_Thread_local` in C or `thread_local` in C++. The compiler/runtime accesses it via a per-thread base register (`fs` on x86-64). Use it for things like errno or per-thread caches; it avoids locking but each thread sees only its own value.

`SIGTERM` (kill default) is catchable — a process can trap it to flush buffers and shut down cleanly. `SIGKILL` (`kill -9`) and `SIGSTOP` cannot be caught, blocked, or ignored; the kernel kills the process immediately with no cleanup. Always send SIGTERM first and give a grace period before escalating to -9.

The kernel sends `SIGCHLD` when a child stops or exits; the parent's handler typically loops `waitpid(-1, &status, WNOHANG)` to reap all available children (one signal can coalesce several exits). Alternatively set `SA_NOCLDWAIT` or ignore SIGCHLD explicitly to have the kernel auto-reap so no zombies are created.

`mmap` maps a file into the address space so you read/write it as memory, with the kernel paging blocks in on access and the page cache handling write-back. It avoids the copy and syscall overhead of `read`/`write` for random access over large files, and lets multiple processes share the same physical pages. Call `msync` to force dirty pages to disk.

An anonymous pipe (`pipe()`) is a unidirectional byte stream between related processes (parent/child via inherited fds); a named pipe/FIFO (`mkfifo`) lets unrelated processes connect by path. Writes up to `PIPE_BUF` (4096 bytes on Linux) are atomic. Unix domain sockets add bidirectional flow, datagrams, and fd-passing via `SCM_RIGHTS`.

The CPU runs user code in a restricted mode (ring 3 on x86) that can't touch hardware or other processes' memory directly; privileged operations require a transition to kernel mode (ring 0) via a syscall trap (`syscall`/`sysret` instruction). This crossing has real cost (hundreds of cycles), which is why batching syscalls or using `vDSO` for cheap calls like `gettimeofday` matters.

The vDSO (virtual dynamic shared object) is a small kernel page mapped into every process that lets certain syscalls — `gettimeofday`, `clock_gettime`, `getcpu` — run entirely in user space, reading kernel-maintained data without a mode switch. That's why timestamping in a hot loop is cheap; the libc wrapper transparently routes through the vDSO when available.

A periodic timer interrupt (historically `HZ` ticks/sec, e.g. 250 or 1000) lets the kernel preempt the running task and update accounting. Modern kernels can run tickless (`NO_HZ`) on idle or single-task CPUs, suppressing the timer interrupt to save power and reduce jitter — valuable for low-latency and battery-sensitive workloads.

A thread pool reuses a fixed set of worker threads to run queued tasks, amortizing the cost of thread creation/teardown (stack allocation, kernel `clone`) and capping concurrency so you don't spawn unbounded threads under load. Size it near the core count for CPU-bound work, but higher for I/O-bound work where threads spend time blocked.

cgroups (control groups) let the kernel limit, account, and isolate CPU, memory, and I/O for groups of processes — the resource-control half of containers (namespaces provide the isolation half). cgroup v2 uses a single unified hierarchy under `/sys/fs/cgroup`; e.g. write to `memory.max` to cap RAM (exceeding it triggers reclaim then OOM-kill within the group).

Namespaces virtualize global kernel resources so a process group sees its own isolated view — types include pid, net, mnt, uts, ipc, user, and cgroup. A PID namespace makes a process think it's PID 1 with no visibility of host processes; a net namespace gives it its own interfaces and routing table. Create them via `clone()` flags or `unshare`; this is the isolation primitive behind containers.

External fragmentation leaves free memory split into chunks too small to satisfy a large request; internal fragmentation wastes space inside an allocated block rounded up to a size class. The kernel's buddy allocator manages physical pages in power-of-two blocks to limit external fragmentation, and the slab/SLUB allocator carves pages into same-size object caches to avoid internal waste for frequent kernel objects.

TCP opens a connection with a 3-way handshake: client sends `SYN` (with its initial sequence number), server replies `SYN-ACK`, client sends `ACK`. Only after the final ACK is the connection ESTABLISHED. The handshake costs one full round-trip before any data flows, which is why connection reuse (keep-alive) matters for latency.

TCP closes with FIN/ACK in each direction (a 4-way handshake). The side that closes first lands in `TIME_WAIT` for 2*MSL (often ~60s on Linux) to absorb stray packets and confirm the peer's FIN was ACKed. A server with thousands of TIME_WAIT sockets usually means it is initiating closes — flip that so clients close instead.

TCP is connection-oriented, ordered, reliable, and flow/congestion-controlled. UDP is fire-and-forget: no handshake, no ordering, no retransmission, just datagrams with a checksum. Use UDP for DNS, VoIP, games, and QUIC where you handle reliability yourself and can't afford head-of-line blocking.

Nagle's algorithm batches small outgoing TCP writes until the previous data is ACKed, reducing tiny-packet overhead but adding latency. Disable it with the `TCP_NODELAY` socket option (`setsockopt`) for latency-sensitive request/response protocols. The classic stall is Nagle interacting badly with delayed ACKs, causing ~40ms hiccups.

TCP flow control uses the receive window: the receiver advertises how many bytes it can buffer, throttling the sender. The 16-bit window field caps at 65535 bytes, so the `TCP Window Scale` option (a handshake-time shift factor) is required for high-bandwidth-delay links. Distinct from congestion control, which reacts to network loss, not receiver capacity.

MTU is the largest L2 frame payload (1500 bytes on standard Ethernet); MSS is the largest TCP segment (MTU minus IP+TCP headers, ~1460). Path MTU Discovery finds the smallest MTU on the route by sending DF-marked packets and reading ICMP 'fragmentation needed'. Blocked ICMP causes black-hole stalls where large packets silently vanish.

A DNS lookup walks the hierarchy: your stub resolver asks a recursive resolver, which queries a root server (returns the TLD nameserver for e.g. `.com`), then the TLD server (returns the domain's authoritative nameserver), then the authoritative server returns the record. Caching at each layer means most lookups never reach the root.

A DNS record's TTL is how long resolvers may cache it, in seconds. Lower it (e.g. to 300) a day before a planned IP change so the switch propagates fast; raise it afterward to cut query load. 'DNS propagation delay' is really just resolvers holding the old answer until its TTL expires — there is no global push.

`dig example.com A` queries a record; `dig +short example.com` prints just the answer. `dig @8.8.8.8 example.com` queries a specific resolver, bypassing your local cache. `dig +trace example.com` walks the delegation from the root down, and `dig -x 1.2.3.4` does a reverse PTR lookup.

Plain DNS (UDP/53) is unencrypted and trivially snoopable. DoH (DNS over HTTPS, port 443) and DoT (DNS over TLS, port 853) encrypt queries to the resolver. DoH hides DNS inside normal HTTPS traffic so it's hard to block selectively; DoT runs on a dedicated port that network operators can identify and filter.

TLS 1.3 0-RTT lets a returning client send 'early data' in its first flight using a pre-shared key from a prior session, saving a round-trip. The catch: 0-RTT data is replayable by an attacker, so it must only carry idempotent requests (e.g. GET, never a money transfer). Servers can disable it if replay risk is unacceptable.

A server presents its leaf cert plus intermediate certs; the client builds a chain up to a trusted root CA in its store. A common production bug is forgetting to bundle the intermediate — it works in browsers (which cache intermediates) but fails for stricter clients like curl or Java. Check with `openssl s_client -connect host:443 -showcerts`.

SNI puts the target hostname in the TLS ClientHello so one IP can host many HTTPS sites and serve the right certificate. SNI is sent in cleartext in classic TLS, leaking which site you visit; Encrypted Client Hello (ECH) encrypts it. Missing SNI is why old clients get the wrong cert on shared hosting.

A TCP server's socket lifecycle: `socket()` creates the fd, `bind()` attaches an address/port, `listen()` marks it passive with a backlog queue, `accept()` blocks and returns a new connected socket per client. A client just does `socket()` then `connect()`. Each accepted connection is its own fd, separate from the listening socket.

`SO_REUSEADDR` lets you re-bind a port still lingering in TIME_WAIT, avoiding 'Address already in use' on quick server restarts. `SO_REUSEPORT` (Linux) is different: it lets multiple processes bind the *same* port and kernel-load-balances connections across them — handy for multi-process servers without a shared listener.

A blocking socket's `read`/`write` waits until data is available or space frees up. Set `O_NONBLOCK` (via `fcntl` or `SOCK_NONBLOCK`) and the call returns immediately with `EAGAIN`/`EWOULDBLOCK` when it would block, letting an event loop juggle many sockets on one thread. Nonblocking + epoll is the foundation of async servers.

TCP keepalive probes a quiet connection to detect dead peers. On Linux it defaults to a 2-hour idle (`tcp_keepalive_time`) before the first probe — far too long for most apps. Tune per-socket with `TCP_KEEPIDLE`, `TCP_KEEPINTVL`, `TCP_KEEPCNT`. Without it, a peer that crashed or had its cable pulled leaves a 'half-open' connection your side never notices.

NAT lets many devices on private IPs (10.x, 172.16-31.x, 192.168.x) share one public IP by rewriting source address+port and tracking the mapping in a translation table. This breaks inbound connections (no public address to reach) and is why peer-to-peer needs hole punching or relays, and why servers behind NAT need explicit port forwarding.

IPv4 has ~4.3 billion 32-bit addresses (exhausted); IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses written in hex groups like `2001:db8::1`. IPv6 drops NAT-by-default (every device can be globally addressable) and removes header checksums for speed. Most networks run dual-stack, and 'happy eyeballs' races IPv4 vs IPv6 connections to use whichever responds first.

CIDR notation `/24` means the first 24 bits are the network prefix, leaving 8 host bits → 256 addresses (254 usable, minus network and broadcast). `10.0.0.0/8` is a huge block; `192.168.1.0/24` is a typical LAN. Smaller prefix number = larger network. A `/32` is a single host.

Outbound connections get a random source port from the ephemeral range (Linux default ~32768–60999, tunable via `net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range`). A 4-tuple (src ip, src port, dst ip, dst port) uniquely identifies a connection, so one client can open ~28k simultaneous connections to a single dst ip:port before exhausting ports.

HTTP keep-alive (default in HTTP/1.1) reuses one TCP connection for multiple requests, amortizing the handshake + TLS cost. Without it, every request pays a full setup round-trip. The server signals close with `Connection: close`; clients pool and reuse idle connections, which is why connection-pool sizing matters under load.

In HTTP/1.1 one slow response blocks every later request on the same connection (head-of-line blocking), so browsers open 6 parallel connections per host. HTTP/2 multiplexes many streams over one TCP connection — but a single lost TCP packet still stalls all streams. QUIC fixes this by moving multiplexing below the loss-recovery layer.

WebSocket upgrades an HTTP connection to a persistent full-duplex channel: the client sends `Upgrade: websocket` + `Sec-WebSocket-Key`, the server replies `101 Switching Protocols`. After that it's framed messages, not HTTP. Use `wss://` for TLS. Unlike SSE it allows client→server pushes, and unlike long-polling there's no per-message HTTP overhead.

`tcpdump` captures packets from the wire. `tcpdump -i any port 443` filters to HTTPS; `-n` skips DNS resolution; `-w file.pcap` writes a capture to open later in Wireshark. BPF filters like `tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-syn != 0` match only SYN packets. Capturing as non-root needs `CAP_NET_RAW`.

`ss -tlnp` (the modern replacement for `netstat`) lists TCP (`t`) listening (`l`) sockets with numeric (`n`) ports and the owning process (`p`). `ss -s` summarizes socket counts; `ss -tn state established` lists active connections. Use it to find what's holding a port: `ss -tlnp | grep :8080`.

`traceroute` maps the path to a host by sending packets with increasing TTL; each router that decrements TTL to 0 returns an ICMP 'time exceeded', revealing its hop. `*` means a hop didn't reply (often ICMP is rate-limited or filtered, not necessarily broken). `mtr` combines traceroute with continuous ping to spot which hop drops packets.

ARP maps an IPv4 address to a MAC address on the local subnet: a host broadcasts 'who has 192.168.1.1?' and the owner replies with its MAC. Results cache in the ARP table (`ip neigh` on Linux). It only works within one L2 segment — to reach another subnet you ARP for the gateway's MAC, not the remote host's.

DHCP auto-assigns IP config via the DORA exchange: client broadcasts `DISCOVER`, server `OFFER`s an address, client `REQUEST`s it, server `ACK`s. The lease has a duration; the client renews at ~50% elapsed. DHCP also hands out the gateway, subnet mask, and DNS servers, not just the IP.

`curl https://host` verifies the cert against the system CA bundle and fails on mismatch/expiry/untrusted issuer. `curl -k` (`--insecure`) skips verification — fine for debugging, dangerous in production. To trust a private CA properly use `curl --cacert ca.pem` instead of disabling checks. `curl -v` prints the negotiated TLS version and cipher.

`openssl s_client -connect host:443 -servername host` opens a raw TLS session showing the negotiated protocol, cipher, and full cert chain. Pipe to check expiry: `echo | openssl s_client -connect host:443 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -dates`. Add `-tls1_2` or `-tls1_3` to force a version and confirm what the server supports.

In mutual TLS both sides present certificates: the server authenticates the client, not just the reverse. Used for service-to-service auth in zero-trust networks and APIs. The server sends a CertificateRequest, the client responds with its cert + a signature proving it holds the private key. No passwords or tokens needed — identity is the cert itself.

A port is a 16-bit number (0–65535) identifying a service on a host. 0–1023 are well-known/privileged (HTTP 80, HTTPS 443, SSH 22, DNS 53) and on Unix need root to bind. TCP and UDP have *separate* port spaces, so DNS can use both UDP/53 and TCP/53 (the latter for large responses and zone transfers).

ICMP is the control/diagnostic protocol of IP: `ping` uses ICMP echo request/reply, traceroute reads 'time exceeded', and 'destination unreachable' / 'fragmentation needed' signal path problems. A host not responding to ping isn't necessarily down — many firewalls drop ICMP. But blocking ICMP entirely breaks Path MTU Discovery and causes mysterious large-packet hangs.

Two different layers carry the hostname: TLS SNI (in the encrypted-setup ClientHello) tells the server which cert to present, while the HTTP `Host:` header (inside the encrypted request) tells it which site to route to. A reverse proxy can route on SNI before decrypting, or on Host after — mismatched SNI and Host is a known request-smuggling vector.

The bandwidth-delay product (bandwidth × RTT) is how many bytes can be 'in flight' on a link. TCP throughput is capped at window/RTT, so on a high-latency fat pipe you need a large window (via window scaling and big socket buffers) to fill it. A 1 Gbps link at 100ms RTT needs ~12.5 MB of window to saturate.

`/etc/hosts` (or `C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts`) maps names to IPs locally, checked before DNS. Add `127.0.0.1 myapp.test` for local dev, or point a real domain at a staging IP to test before changing DNS. The lookup order is controlled by `/etc/nsswitch.conf` (`hosts: files dns`).

TCP detects loss two ways: a retransmission timeout (RTO, based on measured RTT) fires if no ACK arrives, or 3 duplicate ACKs trigger 'fast retransmit' without waiting for the timer. Selective ACK (SACK) lets the receiver tell the sender exactly which segments arrived so only the missing ones are resent, not the whole window.

Behind a load balancer the server sees the proxy's IP, not the client's. L7 proxies inject `X-Forwarded-For` (a comma-separated chain of IPs) and `X-Forwarded-Proto`; trust only the hop you control and append, never blindly believe a client-set header. For L4/TCP proxies that can't add HTTP headers, the PROXY protocol prepends the real client address before the byte stream.

Argon2id is the modern recommended password hash (PHC winner, OWASP-preferred). Being memory-hard it resists GPU/ASIC cracking better than bcrypt. Tune three knobs: memory cost (e.g. 19 MiB+), time cost (iterations), and parallelism. Use argon2id (the hybrid) over argon2i or argon2d for password storage.

PBKDF2 stretches a password by running an HMAC many times. It's not memory-hard, so it's the weakest of the recommended KDFs against GPUs — compensate with high iteration counts (OWASP suggests 600,000+ for PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256). It's still acceptable where FIPS compliance requires it.

A salt is a unique random value mixed into each password before hashing so identical passwords produce different hashes, defeating precomputed rainbow tables and revealing nothing from hash collisions across users. Salts don't need to be secret — store them alongside the hash. Modern KDFs (bcrypt/argon2/scrypt) generate and embed the salt for you.

A pepper is a secret value added to passwords that, unlike a salt, is NOT stored with the hash — it lives in app config or an HSM/KMS. It means a leaked database alone can't be cracked. Apply it by HMAC'ing the password with the pepper key before the KDF, so you can rotate the pepper without touching salts.

Two classic JWT verification flaws: the `alg: none` attack (a token claiming no signature is accepted if your lib trusts the header), and RS256→HS256 algorithm confusion (the attacker signs with the public key as if it were an HMAC secret). Defend by hard-coding the allowed algorithm in your verify call instead of reading it from the token header.

OAuth 2.0 is for authorization (delegated access via an access token); it does NOT prove who the user is. OpenID Connect layers identity on top of OAuth, adding an `id_token` (a JWT with user claims) and a `/userinfo` endpoint. Using a raw OAuth access token as a login signal is a common mistake — use OIDC for authentication.

TOTP (RFC 6238) is the 6-digit authenticator-app code: `HOTP(shared_secret, floor(unix_time / 30))`, truncated to 6 digits, valid for a 30-second window. The server stores the shared secret and computes the same value, allowing ±1 step for clock drift. Rate-limit verification attempts and store recovery codes hashed.

WebAuthn/passkeys replace passwords with public-key credentials. The private key never leaves the authenticator (TPM, Secure Enclave, security key); the server stores only the public key. It's phishing-resistant because the signed challenge is bound to the origin (relying-party ID), so a credential for `bank.com` won't work on `bank.evil.com`.

Session fixation lets an attacker set a victim's session ID before login, then ride it after. Fix: regenerate the session ID on every privilege change, especially right after authentication (`session.regenerate()` / `request.session.cycle_key()`). Also set session cookies `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, and `SameSite`.

AES-GCM is an AEAD cipher: it encrypts and authenticates in one pass, so tampering is detected on decrypt. Critical rule: never reuse a (key, nonce) pair — GCM nonce reuse is catastrophic, leaking the auth key and enabling forgery. Use a 96-bit random nonce or a counter, and rekey before you'd ever repeat one.

ECB mode encrypts each block independently, so identical plaintext blocks yield identical ciphertext blocks — patterns leak (the infamous 'ECB penguin'). Never use ECB. Prefer an authenticated mode like AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305; if you must use CBC, pair it with a separate MAC (encrypt-then-MAC).

An IV/nonce randomizes encryption so the same plaintext+key doesn't produce the same ciphertext. CBC needs an unpredictable (random) IV; CTR/GCM need a unique-per-key nonce (uniqueness matters more than unpredictability). IVs are not secret and are stored/sent with the ciphertext, but reusing them under one key breaks security.

Symmetric crypto (AES) uses one shared key and is fast; asymmetric crypto (RSA/ECC) uses a public/private keypair and is slow but solves key distribution. Real systems use hybrid encryption: asymmetric crypto encrypts a fresh random symmetric key, which then encrypts the bulk data. That's essentially what TLS does.

Diffie-Hellman lets two parties derive a shared secret over a public channel without ever transmitting it — each combines its private value with the other's public value. Ephemeral DH (DHE/ECDHE) generates a throwaway keypair per session, giving forward secrecy: stealing the long-term key later can't decrypt past recorded traffic.

Hashing is one-way (no key, can't be reversed) and is for integrity/verification; encryption is two-way (keyed, reversible) and is for confidentiality. So you hash passwords (and verify by re-hashing) but encrypt data you need to read back. And never use a fast hash like SHA-256 alone for passwords — use a slow KDF.

Never generate tokens, keys, or salts with a general-purpose PRNG like `Math.random()` or `rand()` — they're predictable. Use a CSPRNG: `crypto.randomBytes`/`crypto.getRandomValues` (JS), `secrets` (Python), `crypto/rand` (Go), `SecureRandom` (Java). For tokens, prefer a high-level helper like `secrets.token_urlsafe(32)`.

Path traversal uses `../` (or encoded `%2e%2e%2f`) in a filename to escape the intended directory and read arbitrary files like `/etc/passwd`. Don't sanitize by stripping `../`; instead resolve the canonical absolute path and verify it still starts with your base directory (`os.path.realpath` / `path.resolve` then prefix-check).

Command injection happens when user input reaches a shell (`os.system`, `exec`, backticks, `subprocess` with `shell=True`). Avoid the shell entirely: pass an argument array so the OS doesn't re-parse metacharacters (`subprocess.run(['ping', host])`, never `f'ping {host}'`). If you must shell out, there's no safe escaping shortcut — use the arg-list API.

Deserializing untrusted data can execute attacker code: Python `pickle`, Java `ObjectInputStream`, Ruby Marshal, and PHP `unserialize` can instantiate arbitrary objects and trigger gadget chains for RCE. Never deserialize untrusted input with these. Use a data-only format like JSON, and validate the parsed structure against a schema.

Build secure password resets with a single-use, high-entropy token (CSPRNG, 128+ bits) that expires quickly (15–60 min) and is invalidated on use or on a new request. Store only a HASH of the token server-side (it's a credential). Always respond identically whether or not the email exists, to prevent account enumeration.

Clickjacking loads your site in a transparent iframe over a decoy so users click hidden buttons. Block framing with the CSP directive `frame-ancestors 'none'` (or `'self'`), which supersedes the older `X-Frame-Options: DENY` header. Send one of these on every sensitive page.

Open redirects send users to an attacker URL via a parameter like `?next=https://evil.com`, lending your domain's trust to phishing and sometimes leaking OAuth tokens. Don't redirect to arbitrary user-supplied URLs: allowlist destinations, or accept only relative paths and reject anything with a scheme or `//` host prefix.

Mass assignment auto-binds request fields to model attributes, letting an attacker set fields you never exposed (e.g. POST `is_admin=true`). Defend with an explicit allowlist of bindable fields — Rails strong params, a DTO/whitelist, or a schema — never blindly `Model(**request.json)`.

Grant every user, service, token, and DB account only the permissions it needs, nothing more, so a compromise has minimal blast radius. Practically: separate read vs write DB roles, scope API tokens to specific actions, avoid wildcard IAM policies, and prefer short-lived, narrowly-scoped credentials over long-lived admin keys.

Prefer allowlisting (accept only known-good patterns) over denylisting (block known-bad), because attackers find encodings and cases your blocklist missed. Validate type, length, range, and format server-side — client-side validation is UX only, never a security control. Validate on input, but encode/escape on OUTPUT for the destination context.

HMAC = a keyed hash (`HMAC(key, message)`) that proves both integrity AND authenticity — only someone with the secret key can produce a valid tag, unlike a plain hash anyone can recompute. Use it to sign webhooks, API requests, and cookies, then verify with a constant-time compare. Don't roll your own MAC by concatenating key+message (length-extension attacks).

`docker exec -it <container> sh` (or `bash`) opens an interactive shell in a running container. `-i` keeps stdin open, `-t` allocates a TTY. Run a one-off command without a shell: `docker exec <container> ls /app`. For images without a shell (distroless/scratch), exec won't work — debug with `docker debug` or a sidecar instead.

`docker logs <container>` shows stdout/stderr the container has written. `-f` follows live, `--tail 100` shows the last 100 lines, `--since 10m` filters by time. This only works if your app logs to stdout/stderr (the container convention) — apps that write to a log file inside the container show nothing here.

`docker system prune` removes stopped containers, dangling images, unused networks, and build cache. Add `-a` to also remove all unused images (not just dangling) and `--volumes` to drop unused volumes. Check usage first with `docker system df`. Build cache alone can eat tens of GB — `docker builder prune` targets just that.

`.dockerignore` excludes files from the build context sent to the daemon, like `.gitignore` for builds. Always exclude `node_modules`, `.git`, build artifacts, and secrets — a bloated context slows `docker build` and risks `COPY . .` baking secrets into a layer. Patterns are matched against the context root, not per-directory.

`ENTRYPOINT` sets the executable; `CMD` provides default arguments to it. With both, `CMD` args append to `ENTRYPOINT`, and `docker run <image> foo` overrides `CMD` (not `ENTRYPOINT`). Use exec form `ENTRYPOINT ["app"]` not shell form so signals reach your process. Common pattern: `ENTRYPOINT ["python","app.py"]` + `CMD ["--port","8000"]`.

Your container's main process runs as PID 1, which doesn't reap zombie child processes or forward signals by default — so `docker stop` may hang then SIGKILL after 10s. Fix with `docker run --init` (injects tini) or `ENTRYPOINT ["tini","--"]`. The shell form of CMD/ENTRYPOINT wraps in `/bin/sh -c`, which also swallows signals — use exec form.

`HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s CMD curl -f http://localhost:8000/health || exit 1` makes Docker probe the container; status shows as `healthy`/`unhealthy` in `docker ps`. Compose `depends_on` with `condition: service_healthy` waits for it. Exit 0 = healthy, exit 1 = unhealthy; the command runs inside the container so the tool must be installed.

`ARG` is a build-time variable (`docker build --build-arg VER=1.2`), available only during the build and not in the running container. `ENV` persists into the running container's environment. `ARG` before `FROM` is only usable in `FROM` lines. Never pass secrets via `ARG` — they're visible in image history; use BuildKit `--mount=type=secret`.

Image names are `registry/namespace/repo:tag` — e.g. `ghcr.io/user/app:1.2`. `docker tag local:latest ghcr.io/user/app:1.2` then `docker push ghcr.io/user/app:1.2`. With no registry prefix Docker defaults to Docker Hub. `:latest` is just a default tag, not 'newest' — it's whatever was last tagged latest, so pin real versions in production.

`FROM scratch` is an empty image with zero files — ideal for statically-linked binaries (Go with `CGO_ENABLED=0`, Rust musl). Image is just your binary, so attack surface is tiny and pulls are fast. Caveats: no shell, no `ca-certificates` (copy them in for TLS), no `/etc/passwd`, no timezone data — add what you actually need explicitly.

Docker caches each layer; a changed instruction invalidates that layer and everything after it. Copy dependency manifests and install deps BEFORE copying source: `COPY package*.json ./` + `RUN npm ci` + `COPY . .` — editing source then reuses the cached install layer. `RUN apt-get update` paired with install in the same RUN avoids a stale-cache 'update' layer.

`docker run --restart unless-stopped` restarts a container on crash and on daemon/host reboot, but not after a manual `docker stop`. Other policies: `no` (default), `on-failure[:max]` (only non-zero exits), `always` (even after manual stop, on reboot). In Compose use `restart: unless-stopped`. Kubernetes ignores this — it uses pod `restartPolicy` instead.

`docker cp <container>:/app/log.txt ./` copies a file out of a container to the host; reverse the order to copy in. Works on stopped containers too. For ongoing host-container file sharing use a bind mount instead — `docker cp` is for one-off extraction of logs, configs, or generated artifacts.

Common `docker run` flags: `-d` detached (background), `--rm` auto-remove on exit (great for one-offs), `-p 8080:80` publish host:container port, `-e KEY=val` set env var, `--env-file .env` load many, `-v vol:/path` mount volume, `--name x` name it, `-it` interactive shell. Combine: `docker run --rm -it -p 8080:80 nginx`.

`-p 8080:80` maps host port 8080 to container port 80; the host port comes first. `-p 80` (one number) picks a random host port — see it with `docker port <c>`. `EXPOSE` in a Dockerfile only documents intent and enables `-P` (publish all exposed to random ports) — it does NOT actually open a port. Bind to one interface with `-p 127.0.0.1:8080:80`.

By default containers run as root, so a container escape is root on the host. Add `RUN adduser -D app && USER app` in the Dockerfile to drop privileges. Files copied before `USER` are root-owned — use `COPY --chown=app:app`. At runtime enforce it with `docker run --user 1000:1000` or Kubernetes `securityContext.runAsNonRoot: true`.

`docker stats` streams live CPU %, memory usage/limit, network and block I/O per container. `docker stats --no-stream` prints one snapshot for scripts. Memory shown respects the container's limit, not the host total. For historical metrics use cAdvisor + Prometheus — `docker stats` is real-time only.

`docker run --memory 512m --cpus 1.5` caps a container's RAM and CPU. Exceeding the memory limit gets the process OOM-killed (exit code 137) — check with `docker inspect --format '{{.State.OOMKilled}}'`. JVM and Node need their own heap flags to respect container limits on older runtimes; modern versions read cgroup limits automatically.

Three mount types: bind mounts map a host path (great for dev hot-reload, but tie you to host layout), named volumes are Docker-managed storage (best for prod data, portable, backupable), and tmpfs lives in RAM only (secrets, scratch). The modern `--mount type=volume,source=x,target=/data` syntax is more explicit than `-v` and fails loudly on typos.

`depends_on` only controls start ORDER, not readiness — the dependency's process may still be booting. To actually wait, give the dependency a `healthcheck` and use `depends_on: { db: { condition: service_healthy } }`. Alternatively bake a retry/wait-for loop into your app's startup — apps should tolerate a not-yet-ready dependency anyway.

`docker compose` auto-merges `compose.yaml` with `compose.override.yaml` if present — keep prod base in the first and local dev tweaks (bind mounts, debug ports) in the override. Combine explicitly with `-f base.yaml -f prod.yaml`. `profiles: [debug]` on a service keeps it off unless you run `--profile debug`.

`kubectl get pods` lists pods in the current namespace; add `-n <ns>` for another, `-A` for all namespaces, `-o wide` for node/IP columns, `-w` to watch. `kubectl get pods -l app=api` filters by label. `kubectl describe pod <name>` shows events and reasons a pod is stuck — usually your first debugging stop.

`kubectl logs <pod>` prints a pod's logs; `-f` follows, `-c <container>` picks a container in a multi-container pod, `--previous` shows the crashed prior instance (essential for CrashLoopBackOff). `kubectl logs -l app=api --tail=50` aggregates across pods by label. For richer multi-pod tailing, tools like `stern` help.

CrashLoopBackOff means the container keeps exiting and Kubernetes is backing off restarts (delays grow up to ~5min). Diagnose: `kubectl logs <pod> --previous` for the crash output, `kubectl describe pod` for events/exit codes. Common causes: bad command/entrypoint, missing env/config, failing liveness probe, OOMKill (exit 137), or app crash on startup.

ImagePullBackOff means Kubernetes can't fetch the image. `kubectl describe pod` shows why: wrong image name/tag, private registry without an `imagePullSecret`, or rate-limited Docker Hub pulls. Fix private registries with `kubectl create secret docker-registry` then reference it under `imagePullSecrets` in the pod spec. Verify the tag actually exists in the registry.

Liveness probe failure restarts the container (use for deadlock detection); readiness probe failure removes the pod from Service endpoints without restarting (use for 'not ready yet' / temporary overload). A too-aggressive liveness probe causes restart storms. Add a startupProbe for slow-booting apps so liveness doesn't kill them mid-startup.

A ConfigMap stores non-secret config as key/value pairs, decoupling it from the image. Consume it as env vars (`envFrom: configMapRef`) or mount it as files in a volume. Note: env-var values are captured at pod start and don't update live, but mounted ConfigMap files DO update (with a delay) — your app must re-read them to pick up changes.

A Secret looks like a ConfigMap but is meant for sensitive data. Critically, by default it's only base64-ENCODED, not encrypted — anyone with API/etcd read access can decode it. Enable encryption-at-rest in the API server (`EncryptionConfiguration`) and lock down RBAC. For real secret management use External Secrets Operator, Vault, or a cloud secrets store.

Namespaces partition a cluster into logical groups for RBAC, quotas, and naming scope — not hard isolation (pods can still talk across namespaces unless NetworkPolicies block them). Set a default to skip `-n`: `kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=dev`. Built-ins: `default`, `kube-system`, `kube-public`. Names must be unique within a namespace, not cluster-wide.

`kubectl apply -f` is declarative — it diffs your YAML against the live object and patches the difference, so re-applying is safe and tracks intended state in an annotation. `kubectl create` is imperative and errors if the object already exists. Prefer `apply` for GitOps-friendly, repeatable changes; avoid mixing it with manual `kubectl edit`, which causes drift.

`requests` are what the scheduler reserves to place a pod; `limits` are the hard ceiling. CPU over the limit is throttled; memory over the limit gets OOMKilled. Setting requests = limits gives the pod 'Guaranteed' QoS (last to be evicted). No requests = 'BestEffort' = first evicted under pressure. Right-size from real usage, don't guess.

The HorizontalPodAutoscaler adds/removes pod replicas based on metrics — `kubectl autoscale deployment api --min=2 --max=10 --cpu-percent=70`. It needs the metrics-server installed and CPU/memory `requests` set to compute percentages. For custom/external metrics (queue depth, RPS) wire in the custom-metrics API or KEDA. It scales pods; the Cluster Autoscaler scales nodes.

`kubectl port-forward svc/api 8080:80` tunnels a local port to a Service or pod inside the cluster — great for poking a database or internal API from your laptop without exposing it publicly. It's a single-connection debug tool, not for production traffic; it dies when the command stops and doesn't load-balance well.

A cluster has control-plane components (API server, etcd key-value store, scheduler, controller-manager) and worker nodes that actually run pods. Each node runs a kubelet (talks to the API server, manages pod lifecycle), a container runtime (containerd/CRI-O), and kube-proxy (Service networking). `kubectl get nodes` and `kubectl describe node` show capacity and pressure conditions.

A DaemonSet runs exactly one pod copy on every node (or a labeled subset), auto-adding pods as nodes join. Use it for per-node agents: log collectors (Fluent Bit), monitoring (node_exporter), CNI/network plugins, storage daemons. Unlike a Deployment, you don't set replica counts — the node set determines them.

Use a StatefulSet (not a Deployment) for stateful apps like databases: it gives stable, ordered pod names (`db-0`, `db-1`), stable per-pod persistent volumes via volumeClaimTemplates, and ordered, graceful rollout/scaling. Pair it with a headless Service (`clusterIP: None`) so each pod gets its own stable DNS record.

By default all pods can talk to all pods. A NetworkPolicy adds pod-level firewall rules by label selector — but it has no effect unless your CNI enforces them (Calico, Cilium; the default kubenet/flannel often don't). A common baseline is a default-deny ingress policy per namespace, then allow specific flows. Egress rules need `policyTypes: [Egress]`.

An Ingress object is just routing rules (host/path -> Service); it does nothing until an Ingress Controller (nginx, Traefik, cloud LB) is installed to actually fulfill it. Specify which with `ingressClassName`. It handles L7 HTTP/HTTPS routing and TLS termination. The newer Gateway API is positioned as Ingress's more expressive successor.

Kubernetes dropped the Docker shim in v1.24 — it now talks to runtimes via the CRI (Container Runtime Interface), commonly containerd or CRI-O. Docker images still run fine (they're OCI images); you just don't need the full Docker daemon on nodes. On a containerd node, debug with `crictl` instead of `docker`.

`docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 -t user/app:1.0 --push .` builds and pushes a multi-arch image behind one tag (a manifest list). Clients automatically pull the variant matching their CPU. Cross-arch builds use QEMU emulation (slower) or native build nodes. Essential when devs are on Apple Silicon but prod runs amd64.

`docker save myimage:1.0 -o image.tar` writes an image (all layers) to a tarball for air-gapped transfer; `docker load -i image.tar` imports it elsewhere. Don't confuse with `docker export`/`import`, which dump a container's flattened filesystem and LOSE history, layers, and metadata like ENTRYPOINT. Use save/load for images, export/import only for capturing a running container's filesystem.

A Job runs pods to completion (batch work, migrations) and tracks success with `completions`/`parallelism`; failed pods retry up to `backoffLimit`. A CronJob schedules Jobs on a cron expression (`schedule: "0 * * * *"`). Watch `concurrencyPolicy` (Forbid/Replace/Allow) so a slow run doesn't overlap, and set `ttlSecondsAfterFinished` to auto-clean finished Jobs.

`docker inspect <container|image>` dumps full JSON config — network settings, mounts, env, state, IP. Extract one field with a Go template: `docker inspect -f '{{.NetworkSettings.IPAddress}}' <c>` or `'{{json .State}}'`. Faster than scrolling the whole blob; useful in scripts to grab a container's IP, restart count, or health status.

Cache deps with `actions/cache@v4`: set a `key` (often `${{ runner.os }}-${{ hashFiles('**/package-lock.json') }}`) and `restore-keys` for partial fallback. A cache miss on the exact key but a hit on a restore-key still saves and reuses most of the cache. Caches are immutable once written and evicted after 7 days of no access or when the repo exceeds 10 GB.

A liveness probe failing makes Kubernetes restart the container; a readiness probe failing just pulls the pod out of Service load balancing without killing it. Use readiness for slow startup or dependency checks so traffic only arrives when the app can serve it, and keep liveness cheap to avoid restart loops.

Terraform records what it manages in a state file mapping config to real resource IDs. Keep it in a remote backend (S3 + DynamoDB lock, or Terraform Cloud) so teams share it and locking prevents concurrent `apply` from corrupting it. Never edit `terraform.tfstate` by hand — use `terraform state mv/rm/import`.

`terraform plan` diffs your config against state and shows the create/update/destroy actions without changing anything; `terraform apply` executes them. Save a plan with `terraform plan -out=tfplan` then `apply tfplan` to guarantee what you reviewed is exactly what runs. `terraform fmt` and `terraform validate` belong in CI.

`terraform import <address> <id>` brings an already-existing cloud resource under Terraform management by writing it into state — but it does NOT generate the config, so you must hand-write a matching resource block (or use `terraform plan -generate-config-out` in newer versions) or the next plan will try to destroy it.

Immutable infrastructure means you never SSH in to patch a running server — you bake a new image (e.g. with Packer), deploy fresh instances, and discard the old ones. This kills configuration drift and makes every deploy reproducible. The mantra is "cattle, not pets."

Push images to a registry (Docker Hub, GHCR, ECR) with `docker tag img registry/repo:tag` then `docker push`. Never rely on `:latest` in production — it's mutable and ambiguous; pin to an immutable tag like a git SHA or a digest (`repo@sha256:...`) so deploys are reproducible.

Expose a cheap `/healthz` (liveness — "am I running") and a `/readyz` (readiness — "can I serve, including DB/cache reachable"). Keep liveness from checking downstream deps, or a transient dependency outage triggers restart storms across your whole fleet. Return a 200 fast; don't run expensive queries.

On deploy, orchestrators send `SIGTERM` and wait a grace period before `SIGKILL`. Trap SIGTERM to stop accepting new requests, finish in-flight ones, and close DB pools. In Kubernetes the default grace is 30s (`terminationGracePeriodSeconds`); a `preStop` sleep helps endpoints deregister before the process exits, avoiding dropped requests.

An SLI is a measured signal (e.g. % of requests under 300ms); an SLO is the target (99.9%); the error budget is the allowed failure (0.1%). When the budget is spent you freeze risky launches and prioritize reliability. SLOs prevent both chasing impossible 100% uptime and shipping recklessly.

Emit logs as structured JSON (key/value fields) rather than free text so aggregators like Loki or Elasticsearch can index and filter them. Attach a request/trace ID to every line so you can stitch one request's path across services. Log to stdout/stderr in containers and let the platform ship them — don't write log files inside the container.

Trunk-based development has everyone commit to one main branch (or very short-lived branches merged within a day), behind feature flags for unfinished work. It avoids long-lived branch merge pain and keeps CI on a single integration point. It pairs with strong automated testing since main must stay releasable.

Continuous Integration = merge and auto-test frequently. Continuous Delivery = every passing build is releasable at the push of a button. Continuous Deployment goes further: every passing build ships to production automatically with no human gate. The acronym CD is ambiguous — clarify which you mean.

Pipeline-as-code defines CI/CD in a versioned file in the repo (`.github/workflows/*.yml`, `.gitlab-ci.yml`, `Jenkinsfile`) so the pipeline is reviewed, diffed, and rolled back like any code. It beats clicking config in a UI, which is invisible to history and hard to reproduce across projects.
