Horizontal scaling adds more instances; vertical scaling makes each bigger. Kubernetes' HPA adds/removes pod replicas based on CPU, memory, or custom metrics toward a target. Set a `minReplicas` floor and tune scale-down stabilization so traffic dips don't thrash your fleet up and down.

A serverless cold start is the latency to spin up a new function instance (container init + runtime + your init code) when none is warm — worst for large bundles and JVM/.NET runtimes. Mitigate with smaller deps, lazy-loading, keeping init code light, and AWS Lambda provisioned concurrency to pre-warm instances.

Drift is when real infrastructure diverges from your IaC definition — usually from a manual console change. Detect it by running `terraform plan` (it shows resources it would change back) on a schedule. Either re-apply to reconcile or import the manual change into config; ad-hoc console edits are the root cause to stamp out.

Containers run as root by default, so a breakout has host-root reach. Add a `USER` directive (e.g. `USER 1000`) in the Dockerfile, drop Linux capabilities, and set `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` plus `runAsNonRoot: true` in Kubernetes securityContext. Distroless or scratch base images shrink the attack surface further.

A webhook is an HTTP POST a system fires on an event (a git push, a merged PR) to a URL that kicks off a pipeline or deploy. Verify the payload's HMAC signature header (e.g. GitHub's `X-Hub-Signature-256`) so attackers can't forge triggers, and make handlers idempotent since providers retry on timeout.

GitOps makes a git repo the single source of truth for cluster state: an in-cluster agent (Argo CD, Flux) continuously reconciles the live state toward what's committed, so you deploy by merging a PR and revert by reverting the commit. Manual `kubectl` changes get auto-corrected back to the repo's declaration.

An idempotent operation produces the same result whether run once or many times — re-running a deploy/migration shouldn't double-apply changes. Tools like Ansible and Terraform converge toward a desired state rather than blindly executing steps, so a re-run after a partial failure is safe instead of compounding damage.

For zero-downtime schema changes use expand/contract: first deploy a migration that's backward-compatible (add a nullable column), deploy code that writes both old and new, backfill, then in a later release drop the old column. Never rename or drop a column in the same deploy that ships code depending on the new shape — old pods are still serving during a rollout.

Hosted CI runners are ephemeral VMs the provider manages — clean each run but with usage limits and no access to private networks. Self-hosted runners give you bigger machines, caching, GPUs, and VPC access, but you own patching and security; never run untrusted fork PRs on a self-hosted runner since the job can execute arbitrary code on your hardware.

A GitHub Actions `concurrency` group with `cancel-in-progress: true` cancels an older still-running workflow when a newer push to the same branch/PR arrives, saving runner minutes. Group by `${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}`. For deploy jobs, set `cancel-in-progress: false` so a release isn't aborted mid-flight.

An SBOM lists every component and version in your artifact so you can answer "are we affected by CVE-X" instantly. Generate one with Syft and scan images for known vulnerabilities with Trivy or Grype in CI, failing the build on criticals. Pin and verify base-image digests to defend against supply-chain tampering.

The four DORA metrics gauge delivery performance: deployment frequency, lead time for changes (commit to prod), change failure rate (% of deploys causing incidents), and time to restore service (MTTR). Elite teams deploy on demand with lead times under an hour; they're outcome signals, not targets to game by, say, splitting deploys.

Transformers have no built-in notion of order, so position info is injected. The original paper used fixed sinusoidal encodings of varying frequency added to token embeddings; many modern models instead learn position embeddings or use relative schemes like RoPE.

RoPE (rotary position embedding) encodes position by rotating query/key vectors by an angle proportional to their absolute position before the dot product. Because rotation is applied to Q and K, the attention score depends only on relative offset, and it extrapolates better than learned absolute embeddings.

RMSNorm normalizes by the root-mean-square of activations and skips the mean-subtraction step of LayerNorm, using only a learned scale. It is cheaper and works as well in practice, which is why LLaMA-style models adopted it over LayerNorm.

Each transformer block has an FFN applied per-token: two linear layers with a nonlinearity, expanding to ~4x the model dimension then back. This is where most of a model's parameters live, and it acts as a per-token key-value memory.

Softmax turns a vector of logits into a probability distribution: `exp(z_i) / sum(exp(z_j))`. Dividing logits by a temperature T before softmax sharpens (T<1) or flattens (T>1) the distribution. Numerically stable implementations subtract the max logit first to avoid `exp` overflow.

Top-k keeps only the k highest-probability tokens; top-p (nucleus) keeps the smallest set whose cumulative probability exceeds p (e.g. 0.9), then renormalizes and samples. Top-p adapts the candidate count to how peaked the distribution is, so it handles both confident and uncertain steps.

For English, one token averages roughly 4 characters or about 0.75 words, so ~100 tokens is ~75 words. Whitespace, code, and non-Latin scripts tokenize less efficiently. Always count tokens (e.g. with `tiktoken`) rather than words when budgeting context and cost.

RAG splits documents into chunks before embedding. Too large dilutes the embedding and wastes context; too small loses meaning. A common starting point is ~200-500 tokens with 10-20% overlap so facts spanning a boundary aren't cut in half. Split on semantic boundaries (headings, paragraphs) when possible.

QLoRA fine-tunes by loading the frozen base model in 4-bit (NF4 quantization) and training LoRA adapters in higher precision on top. It lets you fine-tune large models on a single consumer GPU. The base stays quantized; only the small adapters carry trainable params.

Mixed precision trains in 16-bit for speed and memory while keeping a master copy of weights in fp32. bf16 has the same exponent range as fp32 so it avoids the overflow/loss-scaling headaches of fp16. Use `torch.cuda.amp.autocast` plus a `GradScaler` for fp16.

Gradient accumulation runs several forward/backward passes, summing gradients before a single optimizer step, to simulate a large batch that won't fit in memory. Effective batch size = micro-batch x accumulation steps x num GPUs. Remember to scale the loss or it inflates the effective learning rate.

Gradient checkpointing trades compute for memory by discarding intermediate activations on the forward pass and recomputing them during backprop. It cuts activation memory roughly to O(sqrt(n)) layers at the cost of one extra forward pass. Enable with `model.gradient_checkpointing_enable()` in Transformers.

A decoder-only LM uses a causal mask: position i can attend only to positions <= i. It's implemented by setting the upper-triangular entries of the attention score matrix to -inf before softmax, so future tokens contribute zero. This is what enables parallel training on whole sequences while preserving autoregression.

LMs train with cross-entropy on next-token prediction: the negative log-likelihood the model assigns to the true next token. Perplexity is `exp(cross_entropy)` and reads as the effective branching factor; lower is better. Loss is typically computed over shifted labels, ignoring padding with an ignore index.

AdamW is the default LLM optimizer: Adam's adaptive per-parameter learning rates with weight decay applied directly to weights (decoupled) rather than folded into the gradient. Decoupling fixes Adam's broken L2 regularization. Typical betas are (0.9, 0.95) for large models.

LLM training warms the learning rate up linearly for the first few hundred-to-few-thousand steps, then decays it (commonly cosine) toward a small floor. Warmup avoids destabilizing the model while Adam's moment estimates are still noisy at the start. Skipping warmup often causes early loss spikes or divergence.

Gradient clipping rescales the gradient if its global norm exceeds a threshold (commonly 1.0), preventing rare huge updates from blowing up training. Use `torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0)` after `backward()` and before `optimizer.step()`.

RLHF aligns models in three stages: supervised fine-tuning on demonstrations, training a reward model on human preference comparisons, then optimizing the policy against that reward (classically with PPO) plus a KL penalty to stay near the SFT model. The KL term stops the policy from gaming the reward.

DPO skips the separate reward model and RL loop of RLHF: it optimizes the policy directly on chosen/rejected preference pairs with a simple classification-style loss derived from the RLHF objective. It's more stable and far simpler to implement than PPO while reaching comparable alignment quality.

Instruction tuning (SFT) fine-tunes a base model on (instruction, response) pairs so it follows directions instead of just continuing text. It's the step that turns a raw pretrained LM into a usable chat/assistant model, before any preference optimization.

Models recall information placed at the start or end of a long context far better than info buried in the middle, a U-shaped pattern called 'lost in the middle.' Put the most important instructions and retrieved context near the top or bottom of the prompt, not the center.

Greedy decoding picks the single highest-probability token each step; beam search keeps the top-b partial sequences and expands them, finding higher-probability full sequences. Beam search helps deterministic tasks like translation but tends to produce bland, repetitive text for open-ended generation, where sampling is preferred.

To curb loops, decoders penalize tokens already produced. Repetition/frequency penalty subtracts from logits proportional to how often a token appeared; presence penalty applies a flat penalty once it appears at all; `no_repeat_ngram_size` hard-bans repeating any n-gram. Overusing them degrades fluency.

Speculative decoding uses a small fast draft model to propose several tokens, then the large model verifies them in one parallel forward pass, accepting the longest correct prefix. It speeds up generation with identical output distribution because the big model still decides what's valid.

Continuous (in-flight) batching lets a serving engine add and evict requests at the token level instead of waiting for a whole batch to finish, keeping the GPU busy. vLLM pairs it with PagedAttention, which manages the KV cache in fixed pages like virtual memory to cut fragmentation and boost throughput.

Pretraining trains a model from scratch on a huge unlabeled corpus (next-token prediction) to learn general language; fine-tuning then adapts that base on a smaller task- or domain-specific dataset. Pretraining costs millions of GPU-hours; fine-tuning is comparatively cheap, which is the whole point of foundation models.

Scaling laws show loss falls predictably as a power law in model size, data, and compute. The Chinchilla finding is that for a fixed compute budget you should scale data and parameters together (~20 training tokens per parameter), and that many early large models were undertrained on too little data.

d_model (hidden size) is the width of the residual stream every token vector flows through; it sets the size of attention projections and FFN input/output. Larger d_model increases capacity and cost quadratically in the projection matrices. It must be divisible by the number of attention heads.

Function/tool calling has the model emit a structured (usually JSON) request naming a tool and arguments instead of prose; your code runs the tool and feeds the result back. Constrained or 'JSON mode' decoding guarantees parseable output. The model never runs the function itself, it only requests the call.

Each value in Rust has exactly one owner; when the owner goes out of scope the value is dropped. Assigning or passing a non-`Copy` value *moves* it, invalidating the original binding. After `let b = a;` on a `String`, using `a` is a compile error: "use of moved value".

Types that are `Copy` (all integers, `f32/f64`, `bool`, `char`, and tuples/arrays of `Copy` types) are duplicated bit-for-bit on assignment instead of moved, so the original stays usable. A type can't be `Copy` if it (or a field) implements `Drop`. `Copy` requires `Clone` as a supertrait.

`.clone()` makes an explicit, often heap-allocating, deep copy so both bindings own independent data. It's deliberately verbose because it can be expensive — the compiler never inserts it for you. Clippy's `clone_on_copy` lint flags `.clone()` on `Copy` types where it's pointless.

A shared borrow `&T` lets you read a value without taking ownership; the owner keeps it. You can have any number of `&T` borrows at once. Borrowing doesn't move, so the original is still usable after the borrow ends.

A `&mut T` is an *exclusive* borrow: while it's live you may have no other references (shared or mutable) to that value. This single-writer-XOR-many-readers rule is the core of Rust's aliasing model and is what prevents data races at compile time.

Since Rust 2018 (NLL), a borrow ends at its *last use*, not at the closing brace of its scope. So `let r = &v; println!("{r}"); v.push(1);` compiles — `r` is dead by the `push`. This made many previously-rejected programs valid.

You can't return a reference to a value created inside a function — the value drops at the end of the function and the reference would dangle. The compiler rejects it with "borrowed value does not live long enough". Return the owned value (or a `String`/`Box`) instead.

A lifetime like `'a` is a generic parameter naming a region of code over which a reference is valid; it constrains but never changes how long anything actually lives. `fn longest<'a>(x: &'a str, y: &'a str) -> &'a str` says the returned reference lives at least as long as both inputs.

The compiler infers lifetimes via three elision rules: each elided input ref gets its own lifetime; if there's exactly one input lifetime it's assigned to all outputs; and in methods, `&self`/`&mut self`'s lifetime is assigned to all outputs. That's why most `fn`s need no explicit annotations.

`'static` means a reference can be valid for the entire program duration. String literals are `&'static str` because they're baked into the binary. A `T: 'static` bound means `T` contains no non-static references — it does NOT mean the value lives forever.

A trait declares a set of method signatures a type can implement: `trait Summary { fn summarize(&self) -> String; }`. Implement it with `impl Summary for Article { ... }`. Traits are Rust's primary tool for shared behavior and generic bounds, similar to interfaces.

Trait methods can have default bodies; implementors override only what they need. A default method may call other (even non-default) methods of the same trait. `impl Summary for X {}` with an empty block uses all defaults.

Constrain a generic with a trait bound: `fn print<T: Display>(x: T)`. For many or complex bounds use a `where` clause: `where T: Clone + Debug, U: Iterator`. The bound is what lets the body call the trait's methods on `T`.

`fn f(x: impl Display)` is sugar for `fn f<T: Display>(x: T)` — an anonymous generic parameter. As a return type, `-> impl Iterator<...>` lets you return an unnameable concrete type (like a closure or chained iterator) without boxing.

`dyn Trait` is a trait object enabling dynamic dispatch via a vtable; use it behind a pointer like `Box<dyn Error>` or `&dyn Draw`. It lets a `Vec<Box<dyn Draw>>` hold mixed concrete types, trading a vtable indirection for runtime polymorphism.

Generics (`<T: Trait>`) use static dispatch: the compiler monomorphizes a specialized copy per concrete type, so calls inline with zero runtime cost but larger code. `dyn Trait` uses dynamic dispatch through a vtable: smaller code, one indirect call, no inlining.

keywords: cannot be made into an object
facts.answer: A trait is object-safe (usable as `dyn Trait`) only if its methods don't return `Self`, take no generic type parameters, and it has no `Sized` requirement on `Self`. Generic or `Self`-returning methods break it: "the trait cannot be made into an object". Mark such methods `where Self: Sized` to exclude them from the vtable.

An associated type is a placeholder type chosen by the implementor, e.g. `Iterator`'s `type Item;`, used as `Self::Item`. It keeps signatures clean versus a generic parameter and pins exactly one implementation per type — `impl Iterator for Counter { type Item = u32; ... }`.

The orphan rule lets you `impl` a trait for a type only if you own the trait or the type (locally defined). You can't `impl Display for Vec<T>` — both are foreign. Work around it with the newtype pattern: wrap it in a local `struct Wrapper(Vec<T>)` and impl on that.

A supertrait requires implementors to also implement another trait: `trait Printable: Display`. Inside `Printable`'s methods you can then call `Display` methods on `self`. It's a bound on the trait itself, not classical inheritance.

A blanket impl applies a trait to every type satisfying a bound: `impl<T: Display> ToString for T { ... }` — that's how the standard library gives every `Display` type a `.to_string()`. Blanket impls can interact with the orphan rule, so define them carefully in libraries.

`Deref` lets a smart pointer act like its target; deref coercion then auto-converts `&String → &str` and `&Box<T> → &T` at call sites. That's why a fn taking `&str` accepts `&my_string`. Never implement `Deref` for ordinary types just to fake inheritance — it surprises readers.

Implement `Drop::drop(&mut self)` to run cleanup when a value goes out of scope (RAII). You can't call `.drop()` manually — use `std::mem::drop(x)` to drop early. Within a scope, values drop in reverse declaration order; struct fields drop in declaration order.

`Box<T>` is the simplest owning smart pointer: it heap-allocates `T` and owns it, freeing on drop. Use it to give a recursive type a known size (`enum List { Cons(i32, Box<List>), Nil }`) or to move large values to the heap. It's a single pointer with no runtime overhead beyond the allocation.

`Rc<T>` enables multiple owners of the same heap value via reference counting; the value drops when the last `Rc` does. It's single-threaded only and gives shared (immutable) access. `Rc::clone(&a)` bumps the count cheaply — prefer it over `a.clone()` to signal intent.

`Arc<T>` is the thread-safe `Rc`: it uses atomic counter operations so it can be shared across threads (`T: Send + Sync` for `Arc<T>: Send + Sync`). The atomics make it slightly slower than `Rc`, so use `Rc` when you don't cross threads.

`RefCell<T>` moves borrow checking from compile time to runtime: `.borrow()`/`.borrow_mut()` hand out `Ref`/`RefMut`, and violating the aliasing rules panics with "already borrowed". It's `!Sync`, single-threaded, and the usual partner of `Rc` as `Rc<RefCell<T>>` for shared mutable graphs.

`Cell<T>` provides interior mutability for `Copy` types by moving values in/out with `.get()`/`.set()` — no references handed out, so no runtime borrow tracking and no panics. Use it for simple flags or counters behind a shared reference; for non-`Copy` types reach for `RefCell`.

`Mutex<T>` gives thread-safe interior mutability: `.lock()` returns a `Result<MutexGuard>` that derefs to `&mut T` and unlocks on drop. Combine with `Arc` as `Arc<Mutex<T>>` to share mutable state across threads. A thread panicking while holding the lock poisons it.

`Weak<T>` is a non-owning `Rc`/`Arc` reference that doesn't keep the value alive, used to break reference cycles (e.g. parent↔child). Create one with `Rc::downgrade(&rc)`; access it via `.upgrade()`, which returns `Option<Rc<T>>` — `None` if the value was already dropped.

`Rc`/`Arc` cycles leak memory: two nodes pointing at each other never reach count zero, so neither drops. Rust's safety guarantees don't prevent leaks (they're memory-safe). Break the cycle by making one direction a `Weak`.

`Send` marks types whose ownership is safe to transfer to another thread. Almost everything is `Send`; notable exceptions are `Rc<T>` and raw pointers. It's an auto trait: a struct is `Send` if all its fields are.

`Sync` marks types safe to share by reference across threads: `T: Sync` iff `&T: Send`. `Rc` and `Cell`/`RefCell` are `!Sync`; `Mutex` and atomics are `Sync`. Like `Send`, it's auto-derived from a type's fields.

`Sized` means a type's size is known at compile time; it's an implicit bound on every generic parameter. Opt out with `T: ?Sized` to also accept dynamically-sized types like `str` and `[T]`, which must then live behind a pointer (`&T`, `Box<T>`).

Implement `From<A> for B` to define an `A → B` conversion; you then get `Into<B> for A` for free via a blanket impl. Prefer implementing `From`. The `?` operator uses `From` to auto-convert error types when propagating.

`AsRef<T>` provides a cheap reference-to-reference conversion; a parameter `path: impl AsRef<Path>` accepts `&str`, `String`, `PathBuf`, etc. It's for borrowing flavors, while `From`/`Into` are for owned value conversions.

`PartialEq` provides `==`/`!=`; `Eq` is a marker (no methods) asserting total equality — reflexive, symmetric, transitive. `f64` is `PartialEq` but not `Eq` because `NaN != NaN`. `#[derive(PartialEq, Eq)]` compares all fields.

`Ord` gives a total order (`.cmp()` returns `Ordering`) and requires `Eq` + `PartialEq`; `PartialOrd` (`.partial_cmp() -> Option<Ordering>`) handles partial orders like floats. `Vec::sort` needs `Ord`; for floats use `sort_by(|a,b| a.partial_cmp(b).unwrap())` or `sort_by(f64::total_cmp)`.

Closures auto-implement `Fn` (borrows captures, callable repeatedly), `FnMut` (mutably borrows, repeatable), or `FnOnce` (consumes captures, callable once) based on how they use captured variables. `move` forces capture by value. A `Fn` is also `FnMut` and `FnOnce`.

Implement `Iterator` by defining one method — `fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item>` — and you inherit all 70+ adapters (`map`, `filter`, `collect`, …) for free. Iterators are lazy: adapters do nothing until a consuming method like `collect` or a `for` loop drives `next`.

`for x in collection` desugars to a call to `IntoIterator::into_iter`. `.into_iter()` yields owned items (consuming the collection), `.iter()` yields `&T`, and `.iter_mut()` yields `&mut T`. For `&vec` the loop borrows and yields references.

`PhantomData<T>` is a zero-sized marker that tells the compiler a type "owns" or uses a `T` it doesn't store, fixing unused-type-parameter and lifetime/variance/drop-check issues. Common in FFI and typed wrappers: `struct Id<T> { val: u64, _marker: PhantomData<T> }`.

A struct holding a reference must declare a lifetime: `struct Parser<'a> { input: &'a str }`. This ties the struct's validity to the borrowed data — the `Parser` can't outlive the `&str` it points into. Self-referential structs are not directly expressible because of this.

Referential transparency means an expression can be replaced by its value anywhere without changing the program. It's the property that makes equational reasoning work and is the practical payoff of purity — `f(2) + f(2)` is always `2 * f(2)`.

A higher-order function takes a function as an argument and/or returns a function. `map`, `filter`, `reduce`, and `sort(cmp)` are all HOFs. They let you parameterize behavior instead of data, which is the core of functional reuse.

`map` applies a function to every element, returning a new collection of the same shape — it never changes length. `[1,2,3].map(x => x*2)` → `[2,4,6]`. Use it instead of a `for` loop that builds a result array; the mapping function should be pure.

`filter` keeps only elements where a predicate returns truthy, producing a possibly shorter list. `nums.filter(n => n % 2 === 0)` keeps evens. The predicate must be a boolean-returning pure function; mutating inside it is a code smell.

`reduce`/`fold` collapses a collection to one value via an accumulator: `arr.reduce((acc, x) => acc + x, 0)`. Always pass an explicit initial value to avoid empty-array errors and ambiguous starting state. `map` and `filter` can both be expressed as folds.

Currying transforms `f(a, b, c)` into `f(a)(b)(c)` — a chain of single-argument functions. It enables partial application: fix some args now, supply the rest later. In Haskell every function is curried by default; in JS you curry manually or with a `curry` helper.

Partial application fixes some of a function's arguments to produce a new function taking the rest. JS `fn.bind(null, a)` or `(...rest) => fn(a, ...rest)`. Unlike currying it can fix multiple args at once and doesn't require one-arg-at-a-time.

Composition builds a new function by chaining others: `compose(f, g)(x) === f(g(x))`. `pipe` is the same left-to-right: `pipe(g, f)(x)`. Composing small pure functions instead of nesting calls keeps data flow readable top-to-bottom.

A tail call is a recursive call in the final position, with nothing left to do after it returns. TCO reuses the stack frame so deep recursion runs in constant stack space. Scheme/Lua/most ML guarantee it; JS specs it but only Safari/JavaScriptCore implements it — V8 does not.

A monad is a functor with `flatMap`/`bind` that lets you sequence operations returning wrapped values, flattening the nesting. It needs `of`/`return` to wrap a value and `flatMap` obeying left/right identity and associativity. Promises are monad-like: `.then` returning a promise auto-flattens.

The Maybe/Option type models a value that may be absent: `Some(x)` or `None` (Just/Nothing in Haskell). Chaining with `map`/`flatMap` short-circuits on `None`, so you replace nested null checks with a clean pipeline that can't NPE.

Either/Result models success-or-failure as data: `Right`/`Ok` carries the value, `Left`/`Err` carries an error. Operations chain on the success track and short-circuit on the first error — 'railway-oriented programming' — replacing exceptions with values you must handle.

An applicative functor adds `ap` (and `of`) so you can apply a wrapped function to wrapped arguments: combine several independent `Maybe`/`Validation` values without nesting. It's weaker than a monad (no dependency between steps) but lets you accumulate all errors instead of stopping at the first.

Lazy evaluation defers computing an expression until its value is actually needed, and (call-by-need) caches the result. Haskell is lazy by default, enabling infinite structures like `[1..]`. In strict languages you simulate it with thunks (`() => expr`) or generators.

Update immutable data by copying and overriding: `{...obj, count: obj.count + 1}` or `[...arr, x]`. Spread is shallow, so nested objects still share references — copy each level you change, or use a library like Immer that lets you 'mutate' a draft and produces a new tree.

Point-free (tacit) style defines functions by composing others without naming the data argument: `const sum = reduce(add, 0)` instead of `xs => xs.reduce(...)`. It can read cleanly but overuse hurts debuggability — there are no named values to inspect.

Imperative code describes step-by-step *how* (loops, mutable counters); declarative code describes *what* you want (`map`/`filter`/`reduce`, SQL, comprehensions). FP pushes you declarative, which removes incidental state and makes intent obvious at the cost of some control over execution order.

A pipeline threads data through a sequence of unary functions, each transforming the output of the last. Clojure has `->`/`->>`, Elixir/F# have `|>`, JS uses `pipe(...)` helpers (the `|>` proposal is stage 2). Result: linear top-down data flow with no temporary variables.

ADTs build types by combination: a product type bundles fields (a record/tuple — 'and'), a sum type is one of several variants (a tagged union — 'or', like `Shape = Circle | Square`). Sum types plus exhaustive pattern matching let the compiler prove you handled every case.

Pattern matching deconstructs a value by its shape and binds parts to names, dispatching on which variant of a sum type it is. Exhaustiveness checking (Rust `match`, Haskell `case`, Scala) warns when you miss a case. It replaces nested `if`/`instanceof` ladders.

A side effect is anything beyond returning a value: I/O, mutation, throwing, reading the clock or random. FP doesn't ban effects — it pushes them to the edges (a thin imperative shell) so the core stays pure, testable, and easy to reason about ('functional core, imperative shell').

A transducer is a composable transformation decoupled from its input/output collection. Composing `map`/`filter` transducers fuses them into a single pass with no intermediate arrays. Popularized by Clojure; the key is they abstract the 'reducing step' rather than the data source.

A lens is a first-class, composable getter+setter focused on a part of a structure. Composing lenses lets you read or immutably update deeply nested data without manual spread-copying at every level. Part of the broader 'optics' family (prisms, traversals).

Arity is how many arguments a function takes (unary=1, binary=2, n-ary=n). FP favors unary functions because they compose and curry cleanly. JS exposes it as `fn.length`, which counts params before the first default/rest parameter.

The identity function returns its argument unchanged: `const id = x => x`. It's a useful default (e.g. a no-op mapper or `keyFn`), the identity element for function composition, and appears in the functor law `map(id) === id`.

`map` and `filter` are both special cases of `reduce`: map collects `[...acc, f(x)]`, filter conditionally collects. Chaining `map().filter().reduce()` makes multiple passes and intermediate arrays; a single `reduce` does one pass if you need the performance, at the cost of readability.

A total function returns a valid result for every input in its type; a partial function is undefined for some (e.g. `head([])` or division by zero). FP prefers total functions, often by returning `Maybe`/`Option` instead of throwing, so the type signature tells the whole truth.

Persistent data structures make immutable updates cheap by sharing unchanged subtrees between old and new versions instead of deep-copying. Trie-based structures (HAMTs, RRB-trees) give ~O(log32 n) updates — effectively constant — which is why Clojure/Immutable.js immutability isn't slow.

`compose` runs right-to-left (`compose(f,g)(x) = f(g(x))`, matching math notation); `pipe` runs left-to-right, matching reading order. Composition is associative, so `compose(f, compose(g, h)) === compose(compose(f, g), h)` — grouping never changes the result.

A reducer is a pure function `(state, action) => newState` — the shape `reduce` wants. Redux/`useReducer` build on it: same inputs always give the same next state, so state changes are replayable, time-travel-debuggable, and trivially testable without mocks.

`zip` pairs elements of two lists positionally: `zip([1,2],[a,b]) -> [[1,a],[2,b]]`, stopping at the shorter one. `zipWith(f, xs, ys)` applies `f` to each pair instead of tupling — `zipWith(add, [1,2], [3,4]) -> [4,6]`. Useful for parallel iteration without index bookkeeping.

`flatMap` maps each element to a list, then concatenates the results one level deep: `[1,2].flatMap(n => [n, n*10]) -> [1,10,2,20]`. It's how you map a one-to-many function without nested arrays, and it's the list monad's `bind`.

The three monad laws: left identity `of(a).flatMap(f) === f(a)`; right identity `m.flatMap(of) === m`; associativity `m.flatMap(f).flatMap(g) === m.flatMap(x => f(x).flatMap(g))`. They guarantee chaining behaves predictably regardless of how you group it.

With immutable data you can often use cheap reference equality (`===`/`Object.is`) as a proxy for value equality: if the reference didn't change, the value didn't either. This is exactly what React leans on for `useMemo`/`memo` — a new object reference signals a real change.

Promises compose like a monad: `.then` chains and auto-flattens nested promises, so `p.then(f).then(g)` sequences async steps and short-circuits to `.catch` on rejection — the async analog of Either's error track. `async/await` is just sugar over this chaining.

Memoizing a function of object arguments needs a stable key strategy: a `WeakMap` keyed by the object reference works if callers reuse references; otherwise you serialize, which is slow and breaks on key order. And only memoize pure functions — caching an effectful or time-dependent function returns stale results.

FP's core wins come from purity + immutability: code is easier to test (no mocks for pure functions), to reason about (referential transparency), to parallelize (no shared mutable state means no data races), and to cache (memoization). The trade-off is indirection and sometimes performance overhead from copying.

A data race is two threads accessing the same memory concurrently where at least one is a write and there's no synchronization. It's undefined behavior in C/C++/Rust — the compiler may assume it never happens and optimize accordingly, so the bug isn't just "wrong value" but "anything." Fix with a mutex, atomic, or by not sharing the data.

A data race is the low-level memory hazard; a race condition is a logical bug where correctness depends on timing/ordering. You can have a race condition with zero data races — e.g. a TOCTOU bug where you `check` a file exists then `open` it, and it's deleted in between. Atomics fix data races but not all race conditions.

An atomic operation is indivisible — no other thread sees a half-completed state. `std::atomic<int>` counter increments via `fetch_add(1)` are safe without a mutex. Atomics are cheaper than locks for single-word updates but composing several atomics is not itself atomic.

CAS atomically does "if memory == expected, set it to new and return true; else load actual into expected and return false." It's the building block of lock-free algorithms: read value, compute update, `compare_exchange_weak` in a loop, retrying if another thread won. `_weak` may fail spuriously but is cheaper inside a loop.

The ABA problem: a CAS sees the value unchanged (A) and succeeds, but it actually went A→B→A in between, so the world changed underneath you. Common in lock-free stacks reusing freed nodes. Fix with a version tag/counter packed alongside the pointer (a "tagged" or "stamped" reference), or use hazard pointers / epoch reclamation.

C++ atomics take a memory order: `seq_cst` (default, total global order, strongest+slowest), `acquire`/`release` (pair a load with a store to publish data), and `relaxed` (atomicity only, no ordering — fine for counters you only read at the end). Use `release` on the store that publishes data and `acquire` on the load that reads it.

A release store followed by an acquire load of the same atomic establishes happens-before: everything the writer did before the release is visible to the reader after the acquire. This is how you publish a fully-initialized object via a flag without a mutex — set the data, then `flag.store(true, release)`; reader spins on `flag.load(acquire)`.

In C/C++ `volatile` only prevents the compiler from optimizing away accesses (for memory-mapped I/O); it gives NO atomicity and NO cross-thread ordering. Use `std::atomic` for threads. Note Java/C# `volatile` is different — there it does impose acquire/release ordering.

A spinlock busy-loops on an atomic flag instead of sleeping. Faster than a mutex when the critical section is nanoseconds and contention is low, because it avoids the syscall/context-switch. Terrible if held long or oversubscribed — you burn a whole core spinning. Add a `pause`/`yield` hint in the loop and consider a backoff.

A semaphore is a counter of available permits: `acquire` blocks if zero and decrements, `release` increments. A binary semaphore (count 1) acts like a lock but, unlike a mutex, can be released by a different thread than the one that acquired it — handy for signaling. C++20 has `std::counting_semaphore`.

In Python asyncio, `asyncio.create_task(coro())` returns a task you must keep a reference to — the event loop holds only a weak reference, so an unawaited task can be garbage-collected mid-flight and silently vanish. Store it in a set and discard in a done-callback, or `await` it / use a `TaskGroup`.

Calling an `async def` without `await` just creates a coroutine object and does nothing — the body never runs. Python warns "coroutine was never awaited." In JS, forgetting `await` returns a pending Promise, so a `try/catch` won't catch the rejection and you get an unhandled rejection. Lint rules like `no-floating-promises` catch this.

`Promise.all([...])` rejects as soon as any input rejects (others keep running, results lost); `Promise.allSettled` always resolves with an array of `{status, value/reason}` so you see every outcome. `Promise.race` settles with the first to settle (resolve OR reject); `Promise.any` resolves with the first fulfillment, ignoring rejections until all fail.

Rust encodes thread safety in the type system: `Send` means a type can be moved to another thread; `Sync` means `&T` can be shared across threads. The compiler refuses to share non-`Sync` data, so data races are a compile error. `Rc` is neither (not thread-safe); `Arc` is the atomic-refcount version that is `Send + Sync`.

The standard Rust pattern for shared mutable state across threads is `Arc<Mutex<T>>`: `Arc` shares ownership (atomic refcount), `Mutex` guards the data. `lock()` returns a guard; you can't touch the inner `T` without holding it, so forgetting to lock is a compile error. Use `RwLock` if reads vastly outnumber writes.

A read-write lock allows many concurrent readers OR one exclusive writer. Wins when reads dominate and the critical section is non-trivial; for tiny sections a plain mutex is often faster due to lower overhead. Watch for writer starvation under heavy read load, depending on the implementation's fairness policy.

A plain mutex deadlocks if the same thread locks it twice. A reentrant/recursive mutex tracks the owning thread and a count, so the holder can re-acquire it (unlocking N times to release). Convenient but often a code smell signaling tangled locking; prefer restructuring so a lock isn't taken recursively.

Thread-local storage gives each thread its own private instance of a variable — no synchronization needed because nothing is shared (C++ `thread_local`, Python `threading.local()`, Rust `thread_local!`). Great for per-thread caches/buffers and accumulators you merge at the end. Caveat: values don't carry over to thread-pool tasks the way you might expect, and async tasks may hop threads.

Double-checked locking lazily initializes once: check the flag without a lock, and only if unset take the lock and check again before initializing. Historically broken without proper memory ordering (the publish could be reordered). Modern fix: C++11 `std::call_once`/local `static` (thread-safe init guaranteed), or atomics with acquire/release.

Channels pass ownership of data between threads/goroutines instead of sharing memory — "don't communicate by sharing memory; share memory by communicating." An unbuffered channel synchronizes sender and receiver (rendezvous); a buffered one decouples them up to capacity. Eliminates many lock bugs by design. Go `chan`, Rust `mpsc`, Python `queue.Queue`.

Go's built-in race detector instruments memory accesses: `go run -race`, `go test -race`, `go build -race`. It reports data races at runtime with both stacks when they actually occur — so coverage depends on exercising the racy path. It adds significant CPU/memory overhead, so run it in CI/testing, not production.

ThreadSanitizer (`-fsanitize=thread` in Clang/GCC) detects data races, deadlocks, and some misuse at runtime by tracking the happens-before relation. Like Go's detector it only flags races on paths actually executed and adds ~5-15x slowdown plus heavy memory use, so it's a test/CI tool. Don't combine with `-fsanitize=address` in one build.

In a livelock threads aren't blocked — they keep changing state in response to each other but make no progress (two people stepping aside in a hallway in sync forever). Common with naive contention backoff or polite retry loops. Fix with randomized exponential backoff so the symmetry breaks.

For a shared counter, `atomic.fetch_add(1, memory_order_relaxed)` is the right tool: it's atomic so increments aren't lost, and `relaxed` is enough because you don't need ordering relative to other data — only the final total matters. `counter++` on a plain int from multiple threads loses increments (read-modify-write isn't atomic).

A latch is a one-shot countdown: threads `count_down` and others `wait` until it hits zero (C++20 `std::latch`, Java `CountDownLatch`) — great for "wait for N tasks to finish." A barrier is reusable: all participants block until everyone arrives, then all proceed, repeating each phase — ideal for lock-step parallel iterations.

Cancellation is cooperative: in asyncio `task.cancel()` raises `CancelledError` at the next `await`, so blocking-without-awaiting code can't be cancelled. Never swallow `CancelledError` — re-raise it. Use a `finally` block for cleanup. In Rust, dropping a future cancels it; in Go, you propagate a `context.Context` and check `ctx.Done()`.

To call blocking/CPU code from asyncio without freezing the loop, push it to a pool: `await asyncio.to_thread(blocking_fn, arg)` (3.9+) or `loop.run_in_executor(None, fn, arg)`. The default executor is a thread pool (good for blocking I/O); use a `ProcessPoolExecutor` to dodge the GIL for CPU-bound work.

Both the compiler and the CPU reorder memory operations for speed. A memory barrier/fence (`std::atomic_thread_fence`, CPU `mfence`/`dmb`) forbids reordering across it so other threads observe a consistent order. You rarely write bare fences by hand — atomic load/store with the right memory order inserts the needed barriers for you.

Lock contention is when threads pile up waiting on one hot lock, serializing your program — adding cores then makes it slower (per Amdahl). Reduce it by shrinking critical sections, sharding the lock (lock striping — e.g. one lock per hash bucket), using per-thread/local state merged later, or switching to lock-free/atomic structures.

A future is a read handle for a value that will be produced later; the promise (or async task) is the write side. C++ `std::promise`/`std::future` pair lets one thread `set_value` and another `get()` (which blocks until ready). `std::async` returns a future directly. Don't `get()` twice — a future is single-shot (use `shared_future` to read repeatedly).

JS is single-threaded with two queues: microtasks (resolved Promises, `queueMicrotask`) drain completely before the next macrotask (`setTimeout`, I/O callbacks). So an `await` continuation runs before a pending `setTimeout(...,0)`. A microtask that schedules more microtasks can starve macrotasks (and rendering) indefinitely.

"Function colors": once a function is `async`, callers must `await` it, so async spreads up the call stack. Bridging colors is where bugs live — blocking a thread inside async starves the loop, and calling `future.get()`/`.block_on()` from inside an async context can deadlock the single-threaded executor. Keep code consistently sync or async per layer.

A seqlock favors frequent reads of small data: the writer increments a sequence counter (odd = write in progress) around its update; the reader snapshots the counter before and after and retries if it changed or was odd. Readers never block writers and take no lock, but readers can spin under heavy writing, and the read data must be trivially copyable.

The lexer (a.k.a. scanner/tokenizer) is the first compiler phase: it turns raw source characters into a flat stream of tokens like `IDENT`, `NUMBER`, `LPAREN`. It usually runs a maximal-munch rule (longest match wins, so `>=` lexes as one token, not `>` then `=`) and discards whitespace/comments. Lexers are typically built from regular expressions / finite automata, which is why they can't match nested brackets — that's the parser's job.

A recursive-descent parser is a top-down parser where each grammar nonterminal becomes one function that calls other such functions, mirroring the grammar directly. It's the most common hand-written approach because it's easy to debug and gives great error messages. Plain recursive descent can't handle left recursion (`expr: expr '+' term`) — it infinite-loops — so you rewrite the grammar to be right-recursive or loop iteratively.

A Pratt parser (top-down operator-precedence) handles expressions by giving each operator a binding power and splitting tokens into prefix (`nud`) and infix (`led`) handlers. You loop calling infix handlers while the next operator's binding power exceeds the current minimum, which cleanly encodes precedence and associativity without a sprawling grammar. It's the go-to for expression grammars and is what most production languages use for the expression layer.

Left recursion (`A: A α | β`) breaks recursive-descent and LL parsers because the parser calls itself with no input consumed and loops forever. Eliminate it by rewriting to right recursion: `A: β A'` and `A': α A' | ε`, or just parse iteratively with a `while` loop accumulating operands. LR/bottom-up parsers handle left recursion natively and actually prefer it.

LL parsers read input Left-to-right and build a Leftmost derivation, top-down. LL(1) decides which production to use from just the next 1 token using FIRST/FOLLOW sets, so the grammar must have no left recursion and no common prefixes (needs left-factoring). LL(k) peeks k tokens; ANTLR's ALL(*) generalizes this to arbitrary lookahead chosen at runtime.

LR parsers are bottom-up: they shift tokens onto a stack and reduce them to nonterminals using a state machine plus a parsing table. LALR(1) (used by yacc/bison) merges LR(1) states with identical cores to shrink the table, at the cost of occasional spurious reduce-reduce conflicts. LR handles a strictly larger class of grammars than LL, including left recursion.

A shift/reduce conflict means the parser can't decide whether to consume another token or reduce what's on the stack (the classic dangling-`else` ambiguity); a reduce/reduce conflict means two rules could both apply. yacc/bison default to *shift* on shift/reduce, which usually does the right thing, and pick the earlier rule on reduce/reduce. Fix them with `%prec`/precedence declarations or by refactoring the grammar — don't just ignore the warnings.

Parser combinators build a parser by composing small parser functions with higher-order operators like `many`, `or`, `seq`, and `optional`, so the parser reads like the grammar in plain code (Haskell's Parsec, Rust's `nom`). They're recursive-descent under the hood, so they inherit the left-recursion problem. Naive backtracking combinators can blow up to exponential time, so libraries add committed choice or packrat memoization.

A PEG (parsing expression grammar) looks like a CFG but uses *ordered* choice: `a / b` always tries `a` first and only falls back to `b` if `a` fails, so PEGs are unambiguous by construction. A packrat parser runs a PEG in linear time by memoizing every (rule, position) result. The catch: ordered choice can silently hide alternatives, and PEGs can't express the longest-match preferences a human might expect.

A grammar is ambiguous if some input has more than one parse tree — the dangling-`else` (`if a if b x else y`) is the textbook case where the `else` could bind to either `if`. Ambiguity is undecidable in general, so tools surface it as parser conflicts you resolve by hand. Standard fixes: a precedence/associativity declaration, matched/unmatched-statement grammar rewrites, or PEG ordered choice.

A symbol table maps names to their declarations (type, scope, storage) and is built during semantic analysis after parsing. Lexical scoping is usually modeled as a stack/chain of tables: lookup walks from the innermost scope outward until it finds a binding, which is exactly how shadowing works. It's where you catch use-before-declaration and duplicate-declaration errors.

SSA (static single assignment) form requires every variable to be assigned exactly once, renaming `x = 1; x = 2` into `x1 = 1; x2 = 2`. Where control flow merges (a variable could come from multiple paths), a φ (phi) function picks the right version: `x3 = φ(x1, x2)`. SSA makes dataflow optimizations like constant propagation and dead-code elimination dramatically simpler, which is why LLVM IR is in SSA form.

An intermediate representation (IR) sits between the AST and machine code, decoupling the front end (parsing) from the back end (codegen) so N languages and M targets need N+M pieces, not N×M. Common forms: three-address code (`t1 = a + b`), SSA, and stack/bytecode. LLVM IR is the canonical example — typed, SSA-based, and the reason Clang, Rust, and Swift can share one optimizer and backend.

A tree-walking interpreter executes a program by recursively evaluating AST nodes directly (a `visit()`/`eval()` method per node). It's the simplest interpreter to write and great for prototyping a language, but it's slow because every step re-dispatches on node type and chases pointers through the tree. The usual speedup is to compile the AST to bytecode first and run that in a VM loop.

A JIT compiler translates bytecode to native machine code at runtime, after profiling shows which code is hot. Method JITs (HotSpot) compile whole hot methods; tracing JITs (early PyPy, LuaJIT) record and compile hot execution traces through loops. Tiered systems interpret first, then recompile hot paths at higher optimization levels, accepting slow startup for fast steady-state throughput.

Register allocation maps the unbounded virtual registers of the IR onto the CPU's finite physical registers. The classic approach models it as graph coloring: build an interference graph (two values that are live at the same time can't share a register) and color it with k colors for k registers. When it can't, the allocator *spills* a value to the stack — linear-scan allocation is a faster, lower-quality alternative used in JITs.

Constant folding evaluates constant expressions at compile time, so `60 * 60 * 24` becomes `86400` in the binary with no runtime cost. Constant propagation then substitutes known constant values forward through the code (`x = 5; y = x + 1` ⇒ `y = 6`), which often exposes more folding. Together they're among the cheapest, highest-value optimizations and run early in the pipeline.

Dead-code elimination removes computations whose results are never used and code that can never execute. It relies on liveness analysis (a value is dead if no later instruction reads it) and reachability over the control-flow graph. SSA form makes it easy: a definition with no uses is dead, and removing it can make its inputs dead too, so the pass iterates to a fixpoint.

A control-flow graph (CFG) models a function as basic blocks (straight-line instruction sequences with one entry and one exit) connected by edges representing possible jumps. Almost every back-end analysis — liveness, reachability, dominators, loop detection — runs over the CFG. A basic block ends at any branch, call that can't return, or label that's a jump target.

Inlining replaces a function call with the body of the callee, eliminating call/return overhead and — more importantly — exposing the caller and callee to each other's context for further optimization (constant folding across the boundary, DCE). The cost is code-size growth, so compilers use heuristics (callee size, call-site hotness) and won't inline recursive calls unboundedly. It's often called the 'mother of all optimizations' for what it unlocks.

AOT (ahead-of-time) compilation produces native machine code before the program runs, giving instant startup and predictable performance with no warm-up (GraalVM Native Image, Go, Rust). JIT trades slow startup for the ability to optimize using real runtime profiles, which can beat AOT on long-running workloads. AOT also can't speculate on runtime types, so it sometimes leaves dynamic-language performance on the table.

Error recovery lets a parser report multiple syntax errors in one run instead of dying at the first. Panic-mode recovery discards tokens until it reaches a synchronizing token (like `;` or `}`) and resumes; phrase-level recovery inserts/deletes a token to keep going. Good recovery is what lets compilers and IDEs show several real errors at once instead of one error plus a cascade of bogus ones.

FIRST(X) is the set of terminals that can begin a string derived from X; FOLLOW(X) is the set of terminals that can immediately follow X. An LL(1) parser builds its prediction table from these: for each production it knows which production to pick by the next token. If two productions for one nonterminal have overlapping FIRST sets, the grammar isn't LL(1) and you must left-factor it.

The 'lexer hack' is how C parsers resolve `A * B;` — it's a multiplication if `A` is a variable but a pointer declaration if `A` is a `typedef` name. The parser feeds type information back into the lexer so identifiers are tokenized as either `IDENTIFIER` or `TYPENAME`. It's a famous example of C not being context-free, forcing a feedback loop between phases that are 'supposed' to be independent.

BNF (Backus-Naur Form) describes grammars as rules like `<expr> ::= <expr> '+' <term> | <term>`. EBNF extends it with regex-style operators — `?` (optional), `*` (zero-or-more), `+` (one-or-more), and grouping `( )` — so you can write `args ::= expr (',' expr)*` instead of an explicit recursive rule. Most parser generators and language specs use an EBNF variant.

ANTLR is a parser generator: you write a `.g4` grammar with combined lexer/parser rules and it generates a recursive-descent parser plus a parse-tree walker (visitor or listener) in Java, Python, JS, Go, C#, etc. ANTLR4 uses the ALL(*) algorithm, which picks lookahead adaptively at runtime, so it handles most practical grammars including left recursion (it auto-rewrites direct left recursion). Run `antlr4 MyGrammar.g4` to generate the code.

The visitor pattern separates operations (type-check, codegen, pretty-print) from the AST node classes, so you add new passes without touching node definitions. It uses double dispatch: each node's `accept(visitor)` calls back `visitor.visitBinaryExpr(this)`, picking the method by both node type and visitor type. Trade-off: adding a new node type forces you to update every visitor — the dual of the expression-problem the visitor pattern is designed around.

Operator precedence decides grouping when operators of different rank meet (`*` binds tighter than `+`, so `1 + 2 * 3` is `1 + (2*3)`); associativity decides grouping among equal-rank operators. Left-associative `-` means `5 - 2 - 1` is `(5-2)-1`; right-associative `=` and `**` group rightward. Pratt parsers encode both with one number (binding power) per operator plus a left/right bias.

Lookahead is peeking at upcoming tokens without consuming them to decide which rule applies; backtracking is trying a rule, failing, and rewinding to try another. Predictive parsers (LL(1)) use fixed lookahead and never backtrack, so they're linear-time. Backtracking parsers are more flexible but can degrade to exponential time without memoization, which is exactly the problem packrat parsing solves.

Semantic analysis is the phase after parsing that checks meaning the grammar can't express: type compatibility, name resolution, definite assignment, breaking outside a loop, function arity. It annotates the AST (attaching resolved types and symbol references) so later phases don't re-derive them. The line is roughly: syntax errors come from the parser, type/scope errors come from here.

Peephole optimization slides a small window over the generated instruction stream and rewrites inefficient local patterns: deleting `mov eax, eax`, folding `push`/`pop` pairs, replacing `mul x, 2` with a shift, collapsing redundant loads. It's purely local and runs late in code generation, but cheap and surprisingly effective at cleaning up the mechanical output of earlier phases.

A macro transforms code (AST) before evaluation — Lisp `defmacro`, Rust `macro_rules!`, C's text-level `#define`. Hygienic macros automatically rename the identifiers they introduce so an expansion can't accidentally capture or be captured by names at the use site; Scheme and Rust macros are hygienic, C's preprocessor is not (hence the classic `#define SQUARE(x) x*x` bug with `SQUARE(a+b)`). Hygiene is what makes macros composable rather than a minefield.

Incremental parsing reparses only the part of the syntax tree affected by an edit instead of the whole file, which is what keeps editor syntax highlighting and folding instant on big files. Tree-sitter is the widely used GLR-based incremental parser (used by Neovim, GitHub, Zed): it produces a concrete syntax tree, recovers from errors gracefully, and reuses unchanged subtrees across edits.

A concrete syntax tree (CST) keeps every token including whitespace, comments, and punctuation, so it round-trips back to the exact source text. That losslessness is essential for tools that must preserve formatting — code formatters, linters with autofix, refactoring engines, and incremental parsers like tree-sitter. An AST throws that detail away, which is fine for compilation but useless if you need to re-emit the original source.

Sea-of-nodes is a graph IR that merges control flow and data flow into one graph of nodes, letting the scheduler place computations freely instead of fixing them to a basic-block order early. It enables aggressive global value numbering and code motion. It powers high-end JITs — HotSpot C2 and V8's TurboFan — though its complexity is why some projects (notably V8's later Maglev/Turboshaft) moved back toward a more conventional CFG-based IR.

A self-hosting compiler is written in the very language it compiles (the Go compiler is written in Go, rustc in Rust). You bootstrap it with a chicken-and-egg ladder: compile version N's compiler with version N-1's already-built binary, repeated each release. The deeper worry is Ken Thompson's 'Reflections on Trusting Trust' — a compiler binary could inject a backdoor that survives even though the source looks clean, which 'diverse double-compiling' is designed to detect.

By default quantifiers like `*` and `+` are greedy — they match as much as possible. Add `?` to make them lazy (match as little as possible): `<.+>` on `<a><b>` grabs the whole `<a><b>`, but `<.+?>` stops at the first `>` giving `<a>`. Lazy is great for tag/quote pairs, but a negated class like `<[^>]+>` is usually faster and clearer.

`^` matches the start of the string (or line in multiline mode), `$` matches the end. With the multiline flag `m`, `^`/`$` match at every line boundary instead of just the whole-string boundary. `\A` and `\z` (in PCRE/Python/Java) always mean absolute start/end regardless of `m`, and `\Z` matches end-of-string or before a final newline.

`\b` is a zero-width word boundary — the spot between a word char (`\w`) and a non-word char. `\bcat\b` matches `cat` but not `category` or `scatter`. `\B` is the negation (a non-boundary). Boundaries are based on `\w` = `[A-Za-z0-9_]`, so `\b` sits oddly around things like `don't` or hyphens; use explicit classes when that matters.

`(...)` creates a numbered capturing group you can recall later. Inside the pattern use a backreference `\1` (or `\k<name>`); in a replacement use `$1` (or `\1` in some tools). `\b(\w+)\s+\1\b` finds doubled words like `the the`. Groups are numbered by their opening paren, left to right, starting at 1.

`(?:...)` groups for alternation or quantifiers without creating a numbered capture. `(?:ab)+` repeats `ab` but doesn't store it. Use it to keep capture numbering clean and to avoid the small overhead of capturing — `(?:foo|bar)baz` is clearer than capturing when you don't need the group's text back.

Named groups make matches self-documenting. Python/PCRE use `(?P<year>\d{4})` and read it back as `m.group('year')`; JS/Java/.NET use `(?<year>\d{4})`. Reference in a replacement with `${year}` (JS/.NET), `\g<year>` (Python), or `$<year>` (some engines). Much safer than juggling `\1`, `\2`, `\3` when the pattern changes.

Lookbehind asserts what precedes the current spot: positive `(?<=...)`, negative `(?<!...)`. `(?<=\$)\d+` matches digits right after a `$` without including the `$`. JS gained lookbehind in ES2018 and allows variable length; many engines (Java, older Python) require fixed-length lookbehind, so `(?<=ab+)` may be rejected.

Common flags: `i` case-insensitive, `g` global (find all, JS), `m` multiline (`^`/`$` per line), `s` dotall (`.` matches newline). Inline form `(?i)` turns a flag on mid-pattern; `(?i:...)` scopes it to a group. In JS flags trail the literal: `/cat/gi`; in Python pass `re.IGNORECASE | re.MULTILINE` or prefix `(?im)`.

By default `.` matches any character except a newline. Enable the dotall/`s` flag (`/.../s`, `re.DOTALL`, or inline `(?s)`) to make `.` match newlines too — useful for matching across multiple lines. JS only added the `s` flag in ES2018; before that the idiom was `[\s\S]` to mean "truly any character."

`[...]` matches any one character inside it; `[a-z0-9]` allows ranges. Most metacharacters lose meaning inside a class — `.` is a literal dot there. A leading `^` negates: `[^0-9]` is any non-digit. To include `]`, `-`, or `^` literally, put `]` first, `-` first/last, and `^` not-first, or escape them.

`\d` = digit, `\w` = word char `[A-Za-z0-9_]`, `\s` = whitespace; uppercase versions `\D \W \S` are the negations. With Unicode mode, `\d`/`\w` may expand to all Unicode digits/letters depending on engine (e.g. Python 3 `\w` matches accented letters by default — use `re.ASCII` to restrict).

These need a backslash to match literally: `. ^ $ * + ? ( ) [ ] { } | \ /`. To build a pattern from arbitrary user text, escape it programmatically: `re.escape(s)` in Python, `RegExp.escape` (newer JS) or a `\\$&` replace, `Pattern.quote(s)` in Java. Skipping this is a common injection/bug source.

`|` means OR and has the lowest precedence, so `abc|def` is `abc` OR `def`, not `ab(c|d)ef`. Group it to scope: `gr(a|e)y` matches `gray`/`grey`. Order matters in some engines (leftmost alternative that works wins for the overall match position), so put longer/more-specific alternatives first when they share a prefix.

`*` = 0+, `+` = 1+, `?` = 0 or 1, and `{n,m}` = between n and m times (`{3}` exactly 3, `{2,}` 2 or more, `{,5}` up to 5 in some engines). `\d{3}-\d{4}` matches a phone-style chunk. Each can be made lazy with a trailing `?` or possessive with `+` (engine-dependent).

Nested or overlapping quantifiers like `(a+)+$` or `(a|a)*` can blow up exponentially on non-matching input — catastrophic backtracking, the basis of ReDoS attacks. Fixes: avoid ambiguous repetition, use atomic groups `(?>...)` or possessive quantifiers `a++`, anchor the pattern, or switch to a linear engine like RE2 / Rust `regex`.

Atomic groups `(?>...)` and possessive quantifiers (`a++`, `a*+`, `a?+`) match without giving back characters during backtracking. Once they commit, the engine won't retry them, which prevents catastrophic backtracking and speeds up failures. JS lacks both natively (added in some runtimes); PCRE, Java, Ruby, and Python 3.11+ support them.

RE2 (Go's `regexp`, used by Google) and Rust's `regex` crate guarantee linear-time matching by compiling to automata instead of backtracking. The tradeoff: they drop backreferences and lookaround, which need backtracking. Pick them for untrusted input or performance-critical scanning; pick PCRE/Python for backreferences and lookbehind.

In Python, `re.match` anchors at the start of the string (but not the end), `re.search` finds a match anywhere, and `re.fullmatch` requires the whole string to match. `re.match(r'\d+', 'abc123')` returns None; `re.search` finds `123`. JS `String.match`/`RegExp.test` are unanchored — add `^`/`$` yourself.

`re.findall` returns a list — of strings if there are no groups, of tuples if there are multiple groups (which trips people up). `re.finditer` yields match objects so you get `.start()`, `.end()`, and `.group(name)` — better for large input and when you need positions. To get full match strings with groups present, use `finditer` and `m.group(0)`.

Compile a pattern once if you reuse it: `pat = re.compile(r'\d+')` then `pat.findall(text)`. Python caches recent compiled patterns automatically, so the win is mostly readability and binding flags/methods. In tight loops or hot paths, an explicitly compiled object avoids repeated lookups and lets you call `pat.sub`, `pat.split`, etc.

`re.sub(pattern, repl, text)` replaces matches; `repl` can reference groups with `\1` or `\g<name>`, or be a function receiving the match object for dynamic replacement: `re.sub(r'\d+', lambda m: str(int(m[0])*2), s)`. Pass `count=` to cap replacements. `re.subn` returns `(result, num_replacements)`.

Always write Python regexes as raw strings `r'\d+'` so the backslashes reach the regex engine instead of being interpreted by Python's string parser. Without `r`, `'\d'` is fine but `'\b'` becomes a backspace char and `'\n'` becomes a newline — silent bugs. JS regex literals `/\d+/` avoid this; only `new RegExp('\\d+')` needs doubled backslashes.

`\p{...}` matches by Unicode property: `\p{L}` any letter, `\p{N}` any number, `\p{Lu}` uppercase letter, `\p{Script=Greek}` Greek letters, `\p{Emoji}` (engine-dependent). Negate with `\P{...}`. JS requires the `u` (or `v`) flag for `\p{}`; Python's stdlib `re` lacks it — use the third-party `regex` module.

Basic `grep` (BRE) makes `+ ? { } ( ) |` literal unless backslash-escaped. `grep -E` (ERE / `egrep`) treats them as metacharacters. `grep -P` enables PCRE — the only mode with `\d`, lookaround, and `\b` (on GNU grep). Quick rule: reach for `grep -E` for normal patterns and `-P` when you need Perl features.

`sed 's/old/new/'` replaces the first match per line; add the `g` flag for all (`s/old/new/g`), a number for the Nth, or `I` for case-insensitive (GNU). Use any delimiter to avoid escaping slashes: `s|/usr|/opt|`. `sed -i` edits files in place (`-i.bak` keeps a backup; BSD/macOS sed needs `-i ''` with an explicit empty suffix).

`awk` splits each line into fields `$1..$NF` on whitespace by default; `$0` is the whole line. Change the separator with `-F,` or `-F'\t'`. `awk -F: '{print $1}' /etc/passwd` prints usernames. `NR` is the line number, `NF` the field count, and you can filter with patterns: `awk '$3 > 100'` prints lines whose 3rd field exceeds 100.

`cut` extracts columns fast: `-d','` sets the delimiter, `-f1,3` picks fields 1 and 3, `-c5-10` picks character positions. `cut -d: -f1 /etc/passwd` lists usernames. Caveat: `cut` treats every delimiter as a separator (no merging of repeated spaces) and can't reorder fields — reach for `awk` when you need either.

`tr` transliterates by character set, not regex: `tr 'a-z' 'A-Z'` uppercases, `tr -d '\r'` strips carriage returns, `tr -s ' '` squeezes repeated spaces to one, `tr -cd '[:print:]'` keeps only printable chars. It reads stdin only (no filename arg), so pipe into it: `cat f | tr ...`.

`uniq` only collapses *adjacent* duplicate lines, so almost always `sort | uniq` first. The classic frequency count: `sort | uniq -c | sort -rn` gives counts descending. `uniq -d` shows only duplicated lines, `-u` only unique ones, and `-i` ignores case. For dedup without sorting, `awk '!seen[$0]++'` preserves first-seen order.

Handy `grep` flags: `-o` prints only the matched text (great for extraction), `-v` inverts (lines that don't match), `-i` ignores case, `-r`/`-R` recurses directories, `-n` adds line numbers, `-c` counts matches, `-l` lists only filenames, and `-A2 -B2 -C2` show lines after/before/around the match.

Splitting on a separator: Python `s.split(',')` (or `re.split(r'\s+', s)` for regex), JS `s.split(',')`, Java `s.split(",")` (note: the JS/Java arg is a *regex*, so split on `.` needs `\.`). Python's plain `s.split()` with no arg splits on any run of whitespace and drops empties — different from `split(' ')`.

Trim surrounding whitespace: Python `s.strip()` (and `lstrip`/`rstrip` for one side), JS `s.trim()` (`trimStart`/`trimEnd`), Java `s.strip()` (Unicode-aware, vs the older ASCII-only `trim()`). To collapse internal runs of whitespace too, use a regex: `re.sub(r'\s+', ' ', s).strip()`.

Membership test: Python `'cat' in s`, JS `s.includes('cat')`, Java `s.contains("cat")`. To get the position use `s.find('cat')` (Python, returns -1 if absent — vs `index()` which raises) or `s.indexOf('cat')` (JS/Java). For prefix/suffix checks use `startswith`/`endswith` (Python) or `startsWith`/`endsWith` (JS/Java).

There is no short, fully-correct email regex — the RFC 5322 grammar is enormous. For validation, a pragmatic `^[^@\s]+@[^@\s]+\.[^@\s]+$` catches typos, then send a confirmation email for the real check. Over-strict regexes reject valid addresses (plus-tags, new TLDs, quoted locals). Same lesson for phone numbers and URLs: validate loosely, verify out of band.

Normalize messy whitespace in one pass: `re.sub(r'\s+', ' ', text).strip()` collapses any run of spaces/tabs/newlines into a single space. To only collapse spaces and tabs but keep line breaks, use `[ \t]+`. Watch out — `\s` also matches non-breaking spaces and other Unicode whitespace depending on engine/flags.

Multiline mode (`m` flag / `re.MULTILINE`) makes `^` and `$` match at every line break, not just the string's ends. So `re.findall(r'^\w+', text, re.M)` grabs the first word of each line. It does NOT change `.` (that's the separate dotall `s` flag). Don't confuse the two — they're orthogonal.

To require the entire string to match (validation), anchor both ends with `^...$` or use a full-match API: Python `re.fullmatch`, Java `Pattern.matches`/`String.matches`, JS test against `^...$`. Forgetting anchors is a classic security/validation bug — `/\d+/` happily matches inside `abc123xyz`, so a partial match passes a check it shouldn't.

Patterns that can match the empty string (`a*`, `\b`, lookarounds) can match at every position, including between characters. Engines advance by one char after an empty match to avoid infinite loops, but it can yield surprising extra matches in global/replace operations. Anchor or require at least one char (`a+`) when you don't want zero-width hits.

In bash, a here-doc feeds multi-line text to a command's stdin: `cat <<EOF ... EOF`. Quote the delimiter (`<<'EOF'`) to disable `$variable`/backtick expansion inside. `<<-EOF` strips leading tabs for indentation. A here-string `<<<"$var"` feeds a single string: `grep foo <<<"$line"`.

Inline flags can be scoped to part of a pattern: `(?i:abc)def` matches `abc` case-insensitively but `def` case-sensitively. The bare form `(?i)` turns the flag on from that point to the end of the group. Some engines (PCRE) also support turning flags off mid-pattern with `(?-i:...)`. Handy when one section needs different rules than the rest.

GNU `sed` and Perl can change case in the replacement: `\U` uppercases following text until `\E`, `\L` lowercases, `\u`/`\l` affect just the next char. Example: `sed 's/\(\w\+\)/\u\1/g'` capitalizes each word's first letter. Standard `re.sub` has no such escapes — use a replacement function with `.upper()`/`.title()` instead.

`strace -f -e trace=open,read program` shows the syscalls a process makes — great for finding which file/config it actually opens. `-f` follows forked children, `-p PID` attaches to a running process, `-c` prints a summary table of syscall counts and time spent. On macOS the equivalent is `dtruss` (needs sudo / SIP disabled).

`ltrace program` traces dynamic library calls (e.g. `malloc`, `strcmp`) rather than kernel syscalls like strace does. Useful when a bug is in how your code calls libc/library functions. `ltrace -c` summarizes call counts and time per function.

`perf record -g ./prog` then `perf report` gives a sampling CPU profile with call graphs, no recompile needed. `perf stat ./prog` prints cycles, instructions, cache misses, and branch mispredictions. `perf top` is a live `top`-style view of hot functions across the whole system.

A flame graph visualizes sampled stacks: x-axis is sample population (NOT time), width = how often a frame was on-CPU, y-axis is stack depth. Read it by looking for wide plateaus at the top — those are where CPU time actually goes. Build from `perf script | stackcollapse-perf.pl | flamegraph.pl > out.svg`.

`valgrind --leak-check=full ./prog` detects memory leaks, use-after-free, and reads of uninitialized memory in C/C++. It runs code on a synthetic CPU so it's ~10-50x slower, but needs no recompile. 'definitely lost' = a real leak; 'still reachable' = memory held at exit (often fine).

Compile C/C++ with `-fsanitize=address -g` (gcc/clang) to catch heap/stack overflows, use-after-free, and double-free at runtime with ~2x slowdown — far faster than Valgrind. It prints the allocation and free stacks. Pair `-fsanitize=undefined` (UBSan) to also catch signed overflow and bad casts.

Compile with `-fsanitize=thread` to detect data races — two threads accessing the same memory without synchronization where at least one writes. It reports the two conflicting accesses with stacks. Go has it built in: `go test -race` and `go run -race`.

In gdb: `break file.c:42` sets a breakpoint, `run` starts, `bt` shows the backtrace, `print var` inspects, `next`/`step` advance. Conditional breakpoints stop only when needed: `break foo if x > 100`. `watch var` breaks when a variable changes value.

A core dump is a snapshot of a crashed process's memory. Enable with `ulimit -c unlimited`, then debug with `gdb ./prog core`. On systemd systems `coredumpctl list` and `coredumpctl gdb` find and open them. `bt` on the core shows exactly where it crashed.

`py-spy` profiles a running Python process without modifying or restarting it: `py-spy top --pid 1234` for a live view, `py-spy dump --pid 1234` for the current stack of every thread (great for hung processes), `py-spy record -o out.svg --pid 1234` for a flame graph. It reads memory externally, so near-zero overhead.

`python -m cProfile -s cumtime script.py` profiles a script and sorts by cumulative time. For finer control, save stats with `-o out.prof` and explore in `pstats` or visualize with `snakeviz out.prof`. cProfile is deterministic (instruments every call) so it adds overhead — use a sampling profiler like py-spy for production.

Python's stdlib `tracemalloc` tracks where memory is allocated. `tracemalloc.start()`, then `snapshot.statistics('lineno')` shows the lines holding the most memory. Diff two snapshots with `snapshot2.compare_to(snapshot1, 'lineno')` to find what grew — the standard way to hunt Python memory leaks.

Take a V8 heap snapshot to find Node memory leaks: in DevTools (via `--inspect`) use the Memory tab, or call `v8.writeHeapSnapshot()` in code. Take two snapshots and use 'Comparison' view to see which object types grew between them — the retained set that keeps growing is your leak.

Beyond `console.log`: `console.table(arr)` renders arrays/objects as a grid, `console.dir(obj, {depth:null})` shows full nested structure, `console.group()`/`groupEnd()` indent related logs, and `console.time('x')`/`timeEnd('x')` measure elapsed time. `console.trace()` prints a stack trace at the call site.

Standard log levels by severity: TRACE/DEBUG (developer detail, off in prod), INFO (normal milestones), WARN (unexpected but handled), ERROR (operation failed), FATAL/CRITICAL (process can't continue). Production typically runs at INFO; flipping to DEBUG temporarily is how you diagnose without redeploying.

Generate a unique correlation/request ID at the system edge and attach it to every log line and every downstream call (often via an `X-Request-ID` or `traceparent` header). It lets you reconstruct one request's full path across services by grepping a single ID — essential in microservices.

At high traffic, logging every event is expensive and noisy. Sample: log 100% of errors but only 1-in-N successful requests, or rate-limit a noisy line to once per second. Many loggers support this directly (e.g. zap's `Sampler`). Always log the full detail on errors regardless of sampling.

`curl -v https://api.example.com` shows the full request/response headers and TLS handshake. Add `-w '%{time_total} %{http_code}\n' -o /dev/null -s` to time a request and print just the status. `--trace-ascii out.txt` dumps the entire byte-level exchange for deep debugging.

`git bisect` binary-searches commit history to find the one that introduced a bug. `git bisect start`, `git bisect bad`, `git bisect good <old-sha>`, then test each commit it checks out and mark good/bad. With a test script you can automate it: `git bisect run ./test.sh` finds the culprit in log2(N) steps.

Golden-file (approval) testing records the output of code once into a checked-in file, then future test runs diff against it. Update intentionally (e.g. `go test -update`, or jest's `-u`). The risk: blindly regenerating goldens defeats the test, so review the diff like any other change.

Setup/teardown hooks run shared code around tests: `beforeEach`/`afterEach` (Jest/Vitest) run per test, `beforeAll`/`afterAll` once per suite. Prefer per-test setup for isolation — shared mutable state across tests is the #1 cause of order-dependent flakiness.

Structure each test as Arrange-Act-Assert (AAA): set up inputs/state, perform the one action under test, then assert the outcome. Keep it to one logical assertion concept per test so a failure points to exactly one cause. 'Given-When-Then' is the BDD phrasing of the same idea.

Tests must pass in any order and in isolation. Reset global state, use fresh DB transactions rolled back per test, and avoid relying on data another test created. Run with a random seed (`pytest -p no:randomly` off, or `--randomly-seed`) to surface hidden ordering dependencies.

Contract testing verifies a service and its consumers agree on the API shape without spinning up both. The consumer defines expectations (a 'pact'); the provider replays them in its own test suite. Tools like Pact catch breaking API changes before deploy, faster and more reliably than full end-to-end tests.

Go's built-in benchmarks: `func BenchmarkX(b *testing.B)` looping `b.N` times, run with `go test -bench=. -benchmem`. The framework auto-scales `b.N` until timing is stable and `-benchmem` reports allocations/op. Compare runs statistically with `benchstat` rather than eyeballing single numbers.

`hyperfine 'cmd1' 'cmd2'` benchmarks shell commands with statistical rigor — it runs warmup rounds, multiple samples, reports mean ± stddev, and flags outliers. Far better than `time cmd` for comparing two implementations. `--warmup 3` primes caches first.
