Bad assertions just say 'expected true, got false'. Include the actual values and context: `assert resp.status == 200, f"got {resp.status}: {resp.text}"`. Most frameworks already diff values for equality asserts — use the richest assert (`assertEqual`, `toEqual`) so failures show what differed.

A Heisenbug changes or vanishes when you try to observe it — adding a log, a debugger, or slowing execution alters timing and hides a race condition or uninitialized-memory bug. Fight it by capturing state non-intrusively (ring-buffer logs, post-crash dumps) rather than stepping through live.

SIGSEGV (segfault) means you touched memory you're not allowed to — usually a null/dangling pointer or out-of-bounds access. SIGBUS means the address is valid but unusable, e.g. misaligned access or an mmap'd file truncated under you. Run under a debugger or ASan to get the faulting line.

`bpftrace` (Linux, eBPF) and `dtrace` (BSD/macOS) let you probe a live kernel or process without recompiling: `bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:syscalls:sys_enter_openat { printf("%s\n", str(args->filename)); }'` prints every file opened system-wide. Production-safe because eBPF programs are verified before running.

`lsof -i :8080` shows which process holds a port (the cure for 'address already in use'). `lsof -p PID` lists every file/socket a process has open; `lsof +D /path` shows who's using files under a directory (e.g. why you can't unmount). On Linux `ss -ltnp` also maps ports to PIDs.

Fuzzing throws random/mutated inputs at code to find crashes and edge cases you didn't think of. Coverage-guided fuzzers (libFuzzer, AFL++, Go's `go test -fuzz`) mutate toward new code paths. Especially effective on parsers and anything handling untrusted input; pairs naturally with AddressSanitizer.

High line coverage doesn't mean well-tested — a line can execute without any assertion checking its result. Branch coverage is stricter (both sides of each `if`), but even 100% misses unconsidered inputs and integration bugs. Treat coverage as a floor for finding untested code, never as proof of correctness.

Log timestamps in UTC using ISO 8601 (`2026-05-28T14:03:22.481Z`) — local-time logs across servers in different zones are impossible to correlate. Include milliseconds; ordering events within the same second is exactly when you need that precision during an incident.

Sampling profilers periodically record the stack (low, fixed overhead; statistical) — good for production. Instrumenting profilers hook every function entry/exit (exact call counts, but high overhead that distorts timing, especially for many small functions). Use sampling to find hot paths, instrumenting to count exact calls.

`dmesg -T` shows the kernel ring buffer with human timestamps — check it when a process is killed mysteriously. The OOM killer logs 'Out of memory: Killed process' there; you'll also see hardware/driver errors and segfault traces. `journalctl -k` is the systemd equivalent.

Bugs that appear only in release builds usually come from optimizations (reordering, removing 'dead' code with undefined behavior) or `assert()` being compiled out by `-DNDEBUG`. Build with `-O0 -g` to debug, but also test with `-O2` since the optimizer can expose latent UB. Never put side effects inside `assert()`.

Factories build test objects with sane defaults so each test overrides only the field it cares about: `UserFactory(role='admin')`. This keeps tests readable and resilient to model changes versus hand-building full objects everywhere. Tools: factory_boy (Python), Faker for realistic field values, Fishery (JS).

Always profile before optimizing — developers are notoriously wrong about where time goes. Measure, find the actual hot path, optimize that one thing, then re-measure to confirm it helped. Amdahl's law: speeding up code that's only 5% of runtime can never give more than a 5% improvement.

The Strategy pattern encapsulates interchangeable algorithms behind a common interface so the caller swaps behavior at runtime without `if/else` chains. Classic use: a `PaymentStrategy` with `CreditCard`/`PayPal` implementations injected into a `Checkout`. In languages with first-class functions, a strategy is often just a function passed as an argument.

Observer lets subjects notify a list of observers when state changes, decoupling the source from consumers. It powers DOM event listeners, React state subscriptions, and reactive libraries (RxJS). Pub/sub is a variant that adds a broker so publishers and subscribers never reference each other directly.

Factory Method defers instantiation to a method so callers ask for an object by intent (`createButton()`) without naming a concrete class. It centralizes construction logic, making it easy to add new types or wrap creation with caching/pooling. Differs from Abstract Factory, which produces whole families of related objects.

Abstract Factory produces families of related objects (e.g. a `WindowsWidgetFactory` yielding matching `Button`+`Checkbox`+`Menu`) behind one interface, so the whole UI theme swaps by changing one factory. Use it when products must be used together; if you only vary one product, a plain Factory Method is simpler.

Singleton guarantees one instance with a global access point, common for config, logging, or connection pools. It's controversial: it's effectively global state, hides dependencies, and breaks unit tests (hard to mock/reset). Prefer dependency injection of a single shared instance over a hard-coded singleton.

Adapter wraps an incompatible interface so it matches what the client expects, like a power-plug converter. Use it to fit a third-party library into your own interface without changing either side. An object adapter holds the adaptee as a field; a class adapter inherits from it.

Decorator wraps an object to add behavior dynamically while keeping the same interface, so wrappers stack (e.g. `Buffered(Gzip(FileStream))`). Java's `java.io` streams and Python's `@decorator` syntax both embody it. Favor it over subclass explosion when you need composable, optional features.

Facade exposes one simple interface over a complex subsystem so callers don't wire up many classes themselves. It doesn't hide the subsystem (advanced callers can still reach in) but gives the 80% case a clean entry point. Many SDK client objects are facades over HTTP, auth, and serialization internals.

Proxy stands in for another object to control access: lazy-init (virtual proxy), permission checks (protection proxy), or remote calls (remote proxy/RPC stub). It shares the subject's interface so callers can't tell the difference. ORMs use proxies for lazy-loaded relations that hit the DB on first access.

Command turns a request into an object carrying its action and parameters, enabling queuing, logging, and undo/redo (each command stores how to reverse itself). It decouples the invoker (a button) from the receiver (the business logic). Task queues and CQRS write models are command-driven at scale.

Builder constructs complex objects step by step, often via a fluent chain (`new RequestBuilder().url(u).header(h).build()`), avoiding telescoping constructors with many optional args. It can enforce validity at `build()` time. In Rust and Kotlin, builders are common for optional-heavy config structs.

Template Method defines an algorithm's skeleton in a base method and lets subclasses override specific steps (hooks) without changing the overall flow. Inversion of the Strategy idea: structure is fixed by inheritance, steps vary. Test frameworks use it for `setUp`/`run`/`tearDown` lifecycles.

The State pattern lets an object change behavior when its internal state changes, by delegating to a state object instead of a giant `switch`. Each state class handles events and returns the next state, making transitions explicit and testable. It's the OO encoding of a finite state machine.

Chain of Responsibility passes a request along a chain of handlers until one handles it (or it falls through). Web middleware stacks (Express, ASP.NET) are this pattern: each handler can process the request, short-circuit, or call `next()`. Decouples sender from the specific handler.

Dependency Injection passes a class its collaborators from outside (constructor, setter, or interface) instead of constructing them internally, making code testable and loosely coupled. An IoC container automates wiring by resolving the dependency graph. Constructor injection is preferred: dependencies are explicit and the object is never half-built.

The Repository pattern abstracts data access behind a collection-like interface (`findById`, `save`) so domain code doesn't know about SQL, ORMs, or HTTP. It centralizes query logic and lets you swap or mock storage in tests. Don't make it a thin pass-through over an ORM that already is a repository, or you just add a layer.

Unit of Work tracks objects touched during a business transaction and commits all changes in one batch, coordinating writes and resolving concurrency. ORMs like Entity Framework and Hibernate implement it as the session/context: `SaveChanges()`/`flush()` issues the accumulated SQL in a single transaction.

MVVM puts a ViewModel between Model and View, exposing bindable state and commands; the View binds to it declaratively so there's little glue code. It shines with two-way data binding (WPF, Vue, SwiftUI). The ViewModel is UI-framework-agnostic and unit-testable without rendering.

Layered (n-tier) architecture stacks presentation, business logic, and data-access layers where each calls only the layer below. It's the default enterprise layout: easy to understand, but risks an anemic model and 'lasagna code' where a trivial change touches every layer. Keep dependencies pointing downward.

A DTO (Data Transfer Object) is a flat, behavior-free object used to move data across a boundary (API, service) in one shot, decoupling the wire format from your domain entities. Keeping DTOs separate from domain models lets the API contract stay stable while internals change. Map between them explicitly (or with a mapper).

A Value Object has no identity and is defined entirely by its attributes (e.g. `Money`, `DateRange`); two are equal if their values match. Make them immutable so they're safe to share and reason about. Pushing rules like currency validation into the value object keeps the domain model rich, not anemic.

In DDD, an Aggregate is a cluster of objects treated as one unit for consistency; the Aggregate Root is the only entry point and enforces invariants for the whole cluster. External code references the root by ID, never reaches inside. Keep aggregates small — one aggregate per transaction is the rule of thumb.

Dependency Inversion (the D in SOLID) says high-level modules and low-level modules should both depend on abstractions, not each other. In practice, the high-level policy defines an interface that the low-level detail implements, so the dependency arrow points away from the concrete code. It's what makes DI and hexagonal architecture work.

The Liskov Substitution Principle says objects of a subtype must be substitutable for their base type without breaking correctness. Violations: a subclass that throws on a method the base supports, strengthens preconditions, or weakens postconditions. The classic counterexample is `Square extends Rectangle`, where setting width also changes height.

'Favor composition over inheritance' means build behavior by combining objects (has-a) rather than deep class hierarchies (is-a). Inheritance is tight coupling: a subclass depends on its parent's internals and the fragile base-class problem bites on every parent change. Composition + interfaces is more flexible and is why patterns like Strategy and Decorator exist.

The Law of Demeter ('don't talk to strangers') says a method should only call methods on its own fields, parameters, and objects it creates — not reach through chains like `order.getCustomer().getAddress().getZip()`. Long chains ('train wrecks') couple you to the structure of distant objects. Tell, don't ask: let the object expose what you need.

The Null Object pattern replaces `null` with an object that implements the expected interface but does nothing (or returns neutral defaults), so callers skip repetitive null checks. Example: a `NoOpLogger` whose methods are empty. Use it when 'absence' has a sensible do-nothing behavior; don't use it where a missing value is genuinely an error.

pnpm builds a non-flat `node_modules` using symlinks so a package can only `require` deps it actually declared. This kills 'phantom dependencies' — code that imports a transitive dep that happens to be hoisted under npm/yarn. Set `node-linker=hoisted` in `.npmrc` to fall back to a flat layout if a tool breaks.

`npm ci` installs strictly from `package-lock.json`, deletes `node_modules` first, and errors if the lockfile and `package.json` disagree. It's faster and reproducible — use it in CI instead of `npm install`, which can mutate the lockfile.

`package-lock.json` pins the exact resolved version, integrity hash, and dependency tree for every package, including transitive ones. Commit it. `package.json` ranges (`^1.2.0`) describe what's acceptable; the lockfile records what was actually installed so installs are deterministic.

In a npm version range, `^1.2.3` allows any `1.x.x` >= 1.2.3 (minor + patch updates), while `~1.2.3` allows only `1.2.x` (patch updates). For `0.x` versions, `^0.2.3` is treated as locked to `0.2.x` since pre-1.0 minor bumps are considered breaking.

`npx <pkg>` runs a package's binary, fetching it temporarily if it isn't installed locally. It first checks `node_modules/.bin`, so `npx eslint` uses the project's pinned version. Use `npx -y create-vite@latest` to skip the install prompt in scripts.

npm/pnpm/yarn workspaces let one root `package.json` manage many packages via a `workspaces: ["packages/*"]` glob. Shared deps hoist to the root `node_modules`, and intra-repo packages link by symlink. Run a script in one with `npm run build --workspace=pkg-a` or all with `--workspaces`.

Tree-shaking removes unused exports, but it relies on static ES module `import`/`export` — CommonJS `require` can't be shaken reliably. Mark a package `"sideEffects": false` in `package.json` so bundlers know unused imports are safe to drop; list specific files (e.g. CSS) if some imports do have side effects.

In webpack, loaders transform individual files as they're imported (e.g. `babel-loader` for JS, `css-loader` for CSS), applied right-to-left in the `use` array. Plugins hook into the broader build lifecycle to do things loaders can't, like generating HTML or splitting chunks.

A dynamic `import('./module')` tells webpack/Rollup/Vite to split that module into a separate chunk loaded on demand, shrinking the initial bundle. The call returns a promise resolving to the module's namespace. This is the standard way to lazy-load routes or heavy components.

Rollup pioneered ES-module tree-shaking and is the go-to for bundling libraries because it emits clean ESM/CJS/UMD outputs with minimal wrapper code. Configure multiple output formats in one `rollup.config.js` via an `output` array. Mark peer deps in `external` so they aren't bundled in.

A source map (`.map` file or inline `//# sourceMappingURL=`) maps minified/transpiled output back to original source lines so DevTools shows real code in errors and breakpoints. Use `eval-cheap-module-source-map` in dev for speed and `source-map` (separate file) in prod for accuracy.

Prettier handles formatting (spacing, quotes, line length); ESLint handles code-quality rules (unused vars, bad patterns). Run `eslint-config-prettier` to turn off ESLint's stylistic rules so the two don't fight. Don't use `eslint-plugin-prettier` for new setups — running Prettier separately is faster.

`eslint --fix` auto-applies fixes for rules flagged fixable (quotes, semicolons, simple refactors) and leaves the rest as reported errors. `--fix-dry-run` shows what would change without writing. Use `--fix-type problem,suggestion` to limit which fix categories run.

`uv` is a Rust-based Python package/project manager from Astral that replaces pip, pip-tools, virtualenv, and pyenv with one fast tool. `uv pip install` is a drop-in for pip; `uv sync` installs from `uv.lock`; `uv run script.py` auto-creates and uses a venv. It resolves and installs many times faster than pip.

`pip install -e .` installs a package in 'editable' mode: it links to your source tree so code edits take effect without reinstalling. Useful for local library development. Modern editable installs read `pyproject.toml`; the old `setup.py develop` is its predecessor.

`pip freeze > requirements.txt` records exact installed versions for reproducible installs via `pip install -r requirements.txt`. But it captures the whole flattened env including transitive deps — for cleaner separation use a tool like pip-tools (`requirements.in` → compiled `requirements.txt`) or `uv`/Poetry with a real lockfile.

Poetry manages Python deps and packaging via `pyproject.toml` plus a `poetry.lock` for reproducible installs. `poetry add requests` updates both files and resolves the full tree; `poetry install` reads the lock; `poetry shell`/`poetry run` use its managed venv. It separates main and dev dependency groups.

Bun is a JS runtime, bundler, test runner, and package manager in one Zig binary. `bun install` is a drop-in for npm install that's dramatically faster and writes a binary `bun.lockb` (newer versions can use a text `bun.lock`). `bun run` executes scripts, and `bun` runs TS/JSX directly with no transpile step.

Deno runs JS/TS with no file, network, or env access unless you grant it explicitly: `deno run --allow-net --allow-read=./data app.ts`. This sandbox-by-default model is its core security feature. Deno 2 added strong npm/Node compatibility so `npm:` and `node:` specifiers work directly.

`browserslist` is a shared config (in `package.json` or `.browserslistrc`) that tools like Babel, autoprefixer, and Vite read to decide which browsers to support, e.g. `> 0.5%, last 2 versions, not dead`. Run `npx browserslist` to see the resolved browser list. It pulls usage data from caniuse.

`tsc` type-checks and emits JS, but in bundler-based projects you usually let esbuild/SWC strip types (fast, no checking) and run `tsc --noEmit` separately just for type validation. `tsc --build` (project references) caches per-project output for faster incremental monorepo builds via `.tsbuildinfo`.

Minification shrinks JS by removing whitespace/comments and renaming local variables to short names ('mangling'). Terser is the standard JS minifier (a maintained uglify-es fork); esbuild and SWC also minify much faster. Mangling only touches locals — it can't safely rename your public API exports.

`peerDependencies` declare a package the host app must provide (e.g. a React plugin needs React) rather than bundling its own copy, avoiding duplicate/incompatible instances. npm 7+ auto-installs missing peers; conflicts surface as `ERESOLVE` errors you can override with `--legacy-peer-deps` as a last resort.

`dependencies` are needed at runtime; `devDependencies` (build tools, test frameworks, types) are only needed to develop. `npm install --omit=dev` (or `NODE_ENV=production`) skips devDeps for leaner production/Docker installs. Bundled apps can often demote build-only libs to devDeps since they're inlined at build time.

PostCSS is a CSS transformer driven by plugins; the most common is `autoprefixer`, which adds vendor prefixes based on your browserslist targets. Tailwind also runs as a PostCSS plugin. It parses CSS into an AST and lets each plugin rewrite it, similar to how Babel works for JS.

Husky manages git hooks in-repo so a `pre-commit` hook runs on every machine after `npm install`. Pair it with `lint-staged`, which runs linters/formatters only on staged files (not the whole repo), keeping commits clean without slowing things down on large codebases.

To force a specific version of a deep transitive dependency (e.g. to patch a vulnerable sub-dep), use `overrides` in package.json (npm/pnpm) or `resolutions` (Yarn). This rewrites the resolved version across the tree regardless of what intermediate packages requested, useful for security patches before upstream updates.

Cache misses come in three flavors (the "3 C's"): compulsory (first-ever access, cold), capacity (working set bigger than the cache), and conflict (too many addresses map to the same set). Increasing associativity kills conflict misses; a bigger cache kills capacity misses.

An N-way set-associative cache splits into sets; an address maps to one set and can live in any of its N ways. Direct-mapped = 1-way (fast, conflict-prone); fully associative = any line anywhere (flexible, expensive). L1 is typically 8-way; an address's set index comes from the middle bits of the physical/virtual address.

Typical x86 hierarchy: L1 ~4 cycles (32-48 KB, per core, split I/D), L2 ~12-15 cycles (256 KB-2 MB, per core), L3 ~40 cycles (tens of MB, shared), DRAM ~200-300 cycles. Each level trades capacity for latency; a single DRAM miss can cost as much as 100+ arithmetic ops.

The CPU guesses the direction of a branch before the condition is computed and speculatively executes down that path. A correct guess is nearly free; a mispredict flushes the pipeline and costs ~15-20 cycles on modern cores. Predictable branches (loop bounds) are cheap; data-dependent random branches hurt.

Branchless code replaces an unpredictable branch with arithmetic or a conditional-move (`cmov` on x86) so there's nothing to mispredict. Example: `x = cond ? a : b` may compile to `cmov`. Worth it only when the branch is genuinely unpredictable — a well-predicted branch is faster than always doing both sides.

Out-of-order cores execute instructions as their inputs become ready, not in program order, then retire them in order via the reorder buffer (ROB). This hides latency: while one load misses to memory, independent instructions keep executing. The ROB size (hundreds of entries on big cores) bounds how far ahead the CPU can look.

A classic RISC pipeline has 5 stages: fetch, decode, execute, memory, write-back — so up to 5 instructions are in flight at once. Modern x86 cores have ~15-20 stages. Deeper pipelines clock higher but pay more on a flush, which is why branch misprediction penalties scale with pipeline depth.

A superscalar CPU issues multiple instructions per cycle through several execution ports (a wide core does 4-8). This exploits instruction-level parallelism: independent instructions run simultaneously. IPC (instructions per cycle) above 1 only happens when the code has enough independent work to fill the ports.

Hardware prefetchers detect access patterns (sequential or fixed-stride) and pull cache lines in before you ask, hiding memory latency. This is why linear array scans are fast and pointer-chasing (linked lists, random access) is slow — the prefetcher can't predict the next address. Software can hint with `__builtin_prefetch`.

Huge pages (2 MB or 1 GB on x86 vs the default 4 KB) let one TLB entry map far more memory, slashing TLB misses for big working sets like databases and JVMs. Linux offers explicit hugepages and Transparent Huge Pages (THP); THP can cause latency spikes from compaction, so latency-sensitive apps often disable it.

MESI keeps per-core caches consistent: each line is Modified, Exclusive, Shared, or Invalid. A core writing a Shared line must invalidate other copies first (gaining exclusive ownership). This bus/directory traffic is why heavily shared mutable data scales poorly across cores.

Writes go into a store buffer and drain to cache asynchronously so the core doesn't stall waiting. If a later load reads an address still in the store buffer, store-to-load forwarding feeds it directly. The store buffer is also why x86's memory model allows a store to be reordered after a later load (StoreLoad reordering).

SIMD instructions (SSE 128-bit, AVX2 256-bit, AVX-512 512-bit on x86; NEON/SVE on ARM) apply one operation to many data lanes at once — e.g. 8 floats per AVX2 op. Compilers auto-vectorize simple loops with `-O3 -march=native`; check with `-fopt-info-vec`. Branch-free, contiguous, aligned data vectorizes best.

Register renaming maps architectural registers to a larger physical register file, eliminating false (write-after-write / write-after-read) dependencies so out-of-order execution isn't blocked by register reuse. It's why `xor eax, eax` (a recognized zeroing idiom) breaks the dependency chain better than `mov eax, 0`.

CPU clocks stalled around 3-5 GHz because power scales roughly with frequency × voltage² and heat became unmanageable — the end of Dennard scaling. That's why performance now comes from more cores, wider SIMD, and bigger caches rather than raw GHz. Single-thread gains today come mostly from IPC, not clock.

SMT (Intel calls it Hyper-Threading) runs two threads on one physical core, sharing execution units to fill bubbles when one thread stalls on memory. It boosts throughput ~20-30% on mixed workloads but the two threads contend for L1/L2 and ports, so compute-bound or latency-sensitive code sometimes runs faster with SMT off.

A write-back cache updates only the cache line (marking it dirty) and writes to the next level later on eviction — fewer memory writes, standard for L1/L2/L3. Write-through writes to cache and the next level immediately — simpler coherence, more bandwidth. Modern data caches are write-back; dirty lines are flushed on eviction.

Spectre and Meltdown exploit speculative execution: the CPU speculatively reads data it shouldn't and, even after rolling back, leaves a measurable footprint in the cache that an attacker times to recover secrets. Mitigations (retpolines, KPTI, microcode) cost real performance, which is why some are tunable in the kernel.

The L1 instruction cache (often 32 KB) is separate from the data cache. Bloated or scattered hot code thrashes the I-cache and stalls the front-end. Aggressive inlining can hurt by exploding code size; profile-guided optimization (PGO) lays out hot paths contiguously to keep them resident.

Array-of-Structures (AoS) interleaves fields; Structure-of-Arrays (SoA) groups each field into its own array. When a loop touches only one field across many elements, SoA packs that field densely into cache lines and vectorizes cleanly, while AoS wastes bandwidth pulling in unused fields. Hot inner loops often prefer SoA.

Pointer-chasing (linked lists, trees, hash chains) is slow because each node is at an unpredictable address: the prefetcher can't help, and each dereference can be a full cache (or TLB) miss serialized behind the previous one. Contiguous arrays beat linked lists for traversal even at large sizes for this reason.

Compare-and-swap (`lock cmpxchg` on x86) atomically sets a memory word to a new value only if it still holds the expected old value, returning success/failure. It's the building block of lock-free data structures and spinlocks. Contended CAS is expensive because it requires exclusive ownership of the cache line.

Naturally-aligned data (an 8-byte value at an 8-byte boundary) is read in a single access. A misaligned value can straddle two cache lines, requiring two reads, and some SIMD/atomic instructions fault on misalignment. Compilers align structs by padding to the largest member; reorder fields largest-to-smallest to shrink padding.

`rdtsc` reads the Time Stamp Counter, a cycle-accurate clock useful for microbenchmarks. Gotchas: it can be reordered (pair with `rdtscp` or a fence), and on modern CPUs the TSC is invariant (counts at a fixed rate regardless of turbo/frequency), so it measures wall-time, not actual core cycles executed.

Modern x86 is CISC on the surface but RISC inside: the decoder cracks variable-length x86 instructions into fixed-size micro-ops (uops) that the out-of-order back-end actually executes. A uop cache stores decoded uops so hot loops skip re-decoding. ARM is natively fixed-width, simplifying decode and enabling more parallel decoders.

Turbo/boost clocks a core above base frequency when thermal and power budget allow, then throttles down (DVFS) as more cores activate or temperature rises. AVX-512-heavy code can trigger lower "AVX offset" frequencies. Benchmarks vary run-to-run because boost depends on temperature, so pin frequency for stable measurements.

The roofline model says performance is capped either by compute (peak FLOPs) or by memory bandwidth, whichever you hit first. Arithmetic intensity (FLOPs per byte loaded) decides which: low intensity (like vector add) is bandwidth-bound, high intensity (dense matmul) is compute-bound. Optimize the binding constraint, not the other.

When a cache set is full, a replacement policy picks the victim line. True LRU is expensive at high associativity, so caches use pseudo-LRU or other approximations (some recent designs add adaptive/RRIP policies). This is why a streaming scan larger than the cache evicts everything useful — it has no temporal reuse.

A chain of instructions where each needs the previous result (e.g. `a = a + x` repeated) is latency-bound: the CPU can't parallelize it regardless of how wide it is. Breaking one long sum into several independent partial sums (loop unrolling with multiple accumulators) lets the superscalar core run them in parallel.

A spinlock busy-waits in a loop instead of sleeping — fast when the lock is held briefly, wasteful otherwise. Inside the spin, emit the `pause` instruction (x86) / `yield` (ARM) to hint the spin-wait, reduce power, and avoid memory-order violations. For long or contended waits a sleeping mutex is better; it lets the scheduler reuse the core.

Virtual memory is managed in pages (4 KB default on x86 and ARM). The page table maps virtual pages to physical frames; allocation, protection, and swapping all happen at page granularity. Touching one byte commits a whole 4 KB page, which is why sparse data structures can waste large amounts of physical RAM.

Loop unrolling replicates the body N times per iteration, cutting branch/counter overhead and exposing independent operations the superscalar core can overlap. Compilers do it automatically at `-O2/-O3`; manual unrolling rarely helps modern compilers and can bloat the I-cache. The bigger win is usually multiple accumulators to break the dependency chain.

x86 and most ARM are little-endian (least-significant byte at the lowest address); network protocols use big-endian ("network byte order"). Convert with `htons`/`htonl`/`ntohl`. Endianness matters when reinterpreting raw bytes across machines or in binary file formats — within one machine's normal arithmetic you never notice it.

The working set is the memory a program actively touches over a time window. If it fits in a cache level, accesses stay fast; once it spills past L2/L3 into DRAM, latency jumps an order of magnitude. Performance often has cliffs exactly where the working set crosses each cache size, visible in a size-vs-time sweep.

Non-temporal (streaming) stores like `movntdq` / `_mm_stream_si128` write straight to memory and bypass the cache, avoiding read-for-ownership and not polluting the cache with data you won't reread. Use them when writing a large buffer you won't touch again soon (memset of huge regions, frame buffers); misuse hurts if the data is reread.

DRAM stores bits as leaking capacitors that must be periodically refreshed, and access goes through a row buffer: opening a new row (row miss) is slower than hitting an already-open row. Sequential access within a row is cheap; scattered access pays row-activation latency repeatedly. This row-buffer locality is another reason linear access beats random.

Amdahl's Law: if a fraction s of a program is inherently serial, max speedup with infinite cores is 1/s. A workload that's 10% serial caps out at 10× no matter how many cores you throw at it. It's the reason adding cores hits diminishing returns and why reducing the serial section often matters more than parallelizing the rest.

Raft splits time into terms, each with at most one leader. A follower that hears no heartbeat before its randomized election timeout (typically 150-300ms) becomes a candidate, increments the term, and requests votes. Randomizing the timeout per node makes split votes rare, so one candidate usually wins a majority quickly.

In Raft the leader appends a client command to its log and sends `AppendEntries` to followers. An entry is committed once it is stored on a majority of nodes; only then is it applied to the state machine and acked to the client. The leader tracks each follower's `matchIndex` and never commits an entry from a prior term by counting replicas alone (it must commit a current-term entry).

Basic Paxos decides one value in two phases. Phase 1: a proposer sends `prepare(n)`; acceptors promise not to accept anything numbered below `n` and return any value they already accepted. Phase 2: the proposer sends `accept(n, v)`, where `v` is the highest-numbered previously-accepted value if one exists, else its own. A value is chosen once a majority accepts it.

Multi-Paxos runs a Paxos instance per log slot but elects a stable leader so the prepare phase is skipped for steady-state writes, leaving one round trip per command. Raft is essentially Multi-Paxos with a stronger leader and a contiguous-log invariant, which is why it is considered easier to implement correctly.

The FLP result proves no deterministic consensus protocol can guarantee termination in a fully asynchronous network if even one process may crash, because you cannot distinguish a slow node from a dead one. Real systems sidestep it with timeouts/failure detectors (partial synchrony) or randomization, trading guaranteed liveness for high-probability liveness.

Quorum systems guarantee freshness when read and write quorums overlap: with N replicas, choosing R + W > N forces at least one read replica to have seen the latest write. W > N/2 additionally prevents two concurrent writes from both succeeding. Dynamo-style stores expose N, R, W as tunable knobs per operation.

3PC adds a `pre-commit` phase between vote and commit so participants learn the outcome is decided before any of them commits, making it non-blocking on coordinator failure under a synchronous-network assumption. It is rarely used in practice because it fails under network partitions and adds a round trip; consensus (Raft/Paxos) is preferred.

Linearizability is the strongest single-object consistency: every operation appears to take effect instantaneously at some point between its invocation and response, respecting real-time order. If write A completes before read B starts, B must see A. It composes (a system of linearizable objects is linearizable) but requires coordination, costing latency.

Serializability means a set of transactions produces a result equivalent to some serial (one-at-a-time) execution; it concerns multi-object transactions, not real-time order. Linearizability concerns single-object real-time order. `Strict serializability` is the combination of both — what you want from a strongly-consistent distributed database.

Sequential consistency requires a single global order of operations that respects each client's program order, but unlike linearizability it ignores real-time across clients — a read may legally miss a write that finished earlier on another client. It is the model behind many shared-memory systems and is weaker (and cheaper) than linearizability.

Causal consistency guarantees that operations causally related (via the happens-before relation) are seen in that order by all nodes, while concurrent operations may be seen in any order. It is the strongest model achievable while staying available under partitions (per the CAP-adjacent results), and `causal+` adds convergence of concurrent writes.

A Lamport clock is a per-process counter: increment on every event, and on receiving a message set the clock to `max(local, received) + 1`. It guarantees if event A happens-before B then `LC(A) < LC(B)`, but the converse fails — equal-ordered timestamps don't prove causality, so it gives a total order but can't detect concurrency.

A vector clock holds one counter per node; a process increments its own slot on an event and takes the element-wise max on receive. Comparing two vectors detects causality precisely: if every component of V1 <= V2 (and one is strictly less) then V1 happened-before V2; if neither dominates, the events are concurrent. Storage grows with the number of writers.

A Hybrid Logical Clock (HLC) packs a physical-time component plus a logical counter into one timestamp, staying close to wall-clock time while preserving happens-before like a Lamport clock. CockroachDB and YugabyteDB use HLCs so timestamps are meaningful to humans and monotonic across the cluster without perfectly synchronized clocks.

Google Spanner achieves external (strict-serializable) consistency using TrueTime, an API returning a time interval `[earliest, latest]` bounded by GPS/atomic-clock uncertainty. After choosing a commit timestamp, Spanner does `commit wait` — it sleeps until the uncertainty bound passes — so no later transaction can get an earlier timestamp.

Dynamo-style stores reconcile divergent replicas two ways: read repair fixes stale replicas inline when a read detects them returning old versions, and background anti-entropy (often Merkle-tree comparison) periodically syncs replicas that reads rarely touch. Cassandra also runs scheduled `nodetool repair` to bound divergence.

Anti-entropy compares replicas with Merkle trees: leaves hash data ranges, parents hash children. Two nodes exchange root hashes; if they match, the ranges are identical and no data moves. Mismatches are drilled down the tree so only the differing ranges are transferred, making repair cost proportional to divergence, not dataset size.

Gossip spreads state by having each node periodically pick random peers and exchange updates, so information reaches all N nodes in roughly O(log N) rounds with no central coordinator. SWIM is a popular variant separating failure detection (random ping + indirect ping via proxies) from dissemination; Cassandra, Consul, and Serf use gossip for membership.

Rendezvous (HRW) hashing assigns a key to the node maximizing `hash(key, node)`; removing a node only reroutes that node's keys and needs no ring of virtual nodes. It is simpler than consistent hashing and supports weights cleanly, at the cost of O(N) hashes per lookup (fine for small/medium N).

Split-brain is when a partition lets two nodes both believe they are leader and both accept writes, corrupting state. Defenses: require a majority quorum so a minority side can't elect a leader, and use monotonically increasing fencing tokens that resource managers check to reject writes from a stale leader (STONITH — shoot the other node in the head — is the hardware version).

A lease grants exclusive rights (e.g. leadership) for a bounded time, after which the holder must renew or lose them. Unlike a plain lock it self-expires, so a crashed holder doesn't block forever. Correctness depends on clock-drift assumptions; pair leases with fencing tokens so an old holder whose lease expired during a GC pause can't still write.

ZooKeeper uses ZAB (ZooKeeper Atomic Broadcast): a single leader assigns each transaction a monotonic 64-bit `zxid` (epoch + counter) and broadcasts in order; followers ack and the leader commits after a quorum. ZAB guarantees that a new leader's history is a superset of any committed state, giving primary-order, linearizable writes.

Exactly-once message delivery is impossible over an unreliable network; what systems actually provide is at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing (or transactional dedup) to achieve effectively-once results. Kafka's 'exactly-once' is real only within its ecosystem via idempotent producers (PID + sequence numbers) and transactional consume-process-produce.

CDC streams a database's committed changes by tailing its replication log (MySQL binlog, Postgres WAL/logical replication) rather than polling tables, so it captures every change in commit order with low overhead. Debezium is the common open-source connector, emitting per-row before/after images to Kafka for replication, search indexing, and the outbox relay.

When a target replica is down, a sloppy quorum writes to the next available node, which stores a `hint` and replays it to the real owner once it recovers (hinted handoff). This keeps writes available during partitions but weakens the quorum guarantee — a read might briefly miss a write that's only sitting as a hint. Cassandra caps hint storage to avoid unbounded buildup.

Last-Write-Wins resolves concurrent updates by keeping the one with the highest timestamp and silently discarding the other. It's simple and used by Cassandra cells, but clock skew can drop a logically-newer write, and there's no merge — for counters or sets it loses data, which is why CRDTs or vector-clock sibling merges are preferred when correctness matters.

Byzantine fault tolerance handles nodes that lie or behave arbitrarily (not just crash). Tolerating `f` Byzantine faults requires `3f + 1` total nodes and quorums of `2f + 1`. PBFT achieves it in partial synchrony with three message rounds (pre-prepare, prepare, commit); blockchains use BFT variants because participants are mutually untrusted.

Crash detection via fixed heartbeat timeouts is brittle: too short causes false positives, too long delays detection. The phi-accrual failure detector instead outputs a continuous suspicion value phi from the distribution of recent inter-arrival times, letting each consumer pick its own threshold. Akka and Cassandra use phi-accrual for adaptive failure detection.

A network partition splits nodes into groups that can't communicate while each may still serve clients. A CP system keeps only the majority side writable (the minority rejects writes to avoid split-brain); an AP system lets both sides serve and reconciles afterward. Always test partition behavior — `iptables`/`tc` or tools like Jepsen and toxiproxy inject partitions deliberately.

Jepsen is a testing framework that hammers a distributed database with concurrent ops while injecting partitions, clock skew, and crashes, then checks the recorded history against a consistency model (e.g. linearizability via the Knossos/Elle checker). Its public reports have exposed real consistency bugs in many production databases under partition.

Raft logs grow unbounded, so nodes periodically snapshot the state machine and discard log entries up to that point. A leader that needs to bring a far-behind follower up to date — but has already compacted the needed entries — sends an `InstallSnapshot` RPC with the snapshot bytes instead of replaying individual log entries.

State-based (convergent) CRDTs replicate by periodically shipping full state and merging via a function that must be commutative, associative, and idempotent — a join over a semilattice — so replicas converge regardless of message order, loss, or duplication. A G-Counter merges by taking the per-node maximum, then sums entries to read the total.

Operation-based (commutative) CRDTs replicate by broadcasting each operation; merges work because the operations themselves commute. They send less data than state-based CRDTs but require the delivery layer to guarantee each op is delivered exactly once and in causal order, whereas state-based CRDTs tolerate arbitrary message loss and duplication.

Distributed systems must assume wall clocks drift and jump (NTP steps, VM pauses), so never order events across machines by comparing `System.currentTimeMillis()`. Use a monotonic clock for measuring elapsed time on one node, and logical/hybrid clocks or quorum timestamps for cross-node ordering. Spanner's whole design exists to bound this uncertainty.

PACELC extends CAP: if there is a Partition, choose Availability or Consistency; Else (normal operation) choose Latency or Consistency. It captures the everyday cost CAP ignores — even with no partition, synchronous replication for strong consistency adds latency. Dynamo is PA/EL, fully consistent systems are PC/EC, and Spanner is PC/EC by design.

Total-order (atomic) broadcast delivers the same messages to every node in the same order. It is equivalent to consensus — you can build either from the other — which is why a replicated state machine (every replica applying the same ops in the same order) reduces exactly to running consensus on the command log.

Changing a Raft cluster's membership naively can elect two leaders during the transition. Raft solves it with joint consensus: a transitional config requiring majorities in both the old and new sets simultaneously, so no decision can be made without overlap. Many implementations instead restrict changes to one server at a time, which is simpler and avoids the dual-majority window.

Even with R + W > N, strict quorums aren't linearizable: a read concurrent with a write may catch some replicas updated and some not, and two clients reading at the same instant can disagree. Read repair eventually converges them, but if you need real linearizability you must add consensus or a coordinator-assigned order, not just overlapping quorums.

`zoxide` is a smarter `cd` that learns your most-used directories: after visiting `~/projects/api`, just type `z api` from anywhere to jump back. It ranks by 'frecency' (frequency + recency). `zi` opens an interactive fzf picker over the database, and `z foo bar` matches a path containing both terms.

`tldr` shows community-maintained example-driven summaries instead of full man pages: `tldr tar` gives you the five flag combos you actually use rather than a wall of prose. It's a great complement to `man`, which has the exhaustive reference. Clients exist for many languages; cache updates with `tldr --update`.

`jq` is a command-line JSON processor. `jq '.items[].name'` extracts a field from each array element, `jq -r` strips quotes for raw string output, and `jq 'select(.age > 30)'` filters. `jq -c` emits compact one-line-per-object output ideal for piping. Use `jq 'keys'` to discover an object's fields fast.

`delta` is a syntax-highlighting pager for git/diff output with side-by-side mode, line numbers, and word-level highlighting. Wire it in with `git config --global core.pager delta` and `git config --global interactive.diffFilter 'delta --color-only'`. `delta -s` toggles side-by-side; it also prettifies `git blame` and merge conflicts.

`git commit --amend` rewrites the most recent commit — add staged changes you forgot or fix the message with `--amend -m 'new msg'`. Use `--amend --no-edit` to fold in changes without changing the message. Don't amend commits you've already pushed and shared, since it rewrites history and forces collaborators to reconcile.

In VS Code, `Ctrl/Cmd+D` selects the next occurrence of the current word and adds a cursor there — keep pressing to edit several matches at once. `Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+L` selects all occurrences at once. `Alt+Click` drops an extra cursor anywhere, and `Alt+Shift+drag` does a column (box) selection for editing aligned text.

The VS Code command palette (`Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+P`) runs any command, setting, or extension action by name — the fastest way to do anything without hunting menus. Type `>` for commands, `@` to jump to a symbol in the file, `#` to search workspace symbols, and `:` to go to a line number. Plain `Ctrl/Cmd+P` is quick file open.

Neovim ships a built-in LSP client (`vim.lsp`), so editors get completion, go-to-definition, and diagnostics from language servers without a wrapper plugin. Most users pair it with `nvim-lspconfig` for server presets and `mason.nvim` to install servers. `:LspInfo` shows attached servers; `gd`, `K`, and `<C-]>`-style mappings are wired to LSP requests.

In Vim, `q` followed by a register letter starts recording a macro of your keystrokes; press `q` again to stop, then replay with `@a` (for register `a`) and `@@` to repeat the last. Prefix with a count to run it many times: `100@a`. Macros are stored in normal registers, so you can paste, edit, and re-yank them like text.

Generate a modern SSH key with `ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C 'you@example.com'` — Ed25519 keys are shorter and faster than RSA with strong security. Copy the public key to a server with `ssh-copy-id user@host`, or paste `~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub` into GitHub. Never share the private key (no `.pub`); add a passphrase and load it with `ssh-add`.

`entr` runs a command whenever watched files change — feed it filenames on stdin: `ls *.c | entr make` rebuilds on every save. `find . -name '*.py' | entr -c pytest` clears the screen and reruns tests; `-r` restarts a long-running server, and `-d` exits when a new file appears so a wrapping loop can re-scan. Tiny, fast, no config.

`watch` re-runs a command on an interval and shows the latest output full-screen: `watch -n 2 'df -h'` refreshes disk usage every 2 seconds. `watch -d` highlights what changed between runs, and `watch -t` hides the header line. Great for tailing a metric or polling a status without writing a loop.

`http` (HTTPie) is a human-friendly curl alternative with colorized JSON output and intuitive syntax: `http POST api.example.com/users name=joe age:=30` sends JSON (`:=` for raw non-string values, `=` for strings). Add headers as `Header:value`, query params as `param==value`, and `-a user:pass` for basic auth. `--download` saves the response body.

`direnv` automatically loads and unloads environment variables based on your current directory via a `.envrc` file, so secrets and project-specific `PATH` tweaks apply only inside that project. After editing `.envrc` you must run `direnv allow` to authorize it (a security gate). Common for pinning tool versions or sourcing a virtualenv on `cd`.

The `pre-commit` framework manages git hooks via a `.pre-commit-config.yaml` listing linters/formatters to run before each commit. `pre-commit install` wires the hook; thereafter staged files get checked (and often auto-fixed) on commit. Run against everything with `pre-commit run --all-files`, and skip once with `git commit --no-verify`.

Man pages are split into numbered sections: 1 = user commands, 2 = system calls, 3 = library functions, 5 = file formats, 8 = admin commands. When a name exists in several, specify it: `man 2 open` (syscall) vs `man 3 printf` (libc). `apropos keyword` searches descriptions, and `whatis cmd` prints the one-line summary.

`shellcheck script.sh` statically analyzes shell scripts and flags real bugs: unquoted variables that word-split, useless `cat`, missing `--`, and POSIX-vs-bash mismatches. Each warning has an `SC####` code you can look up for an explanation, and `# shellcheck disable=SC2086` silences one inline. Catch it before it bites in production.

`git log --oneline --graph --all --decorate` draws an ASCII commit graph across all branches with refs labeled — the fastest way to see how branches diverged and merged. `--all` includes branches you're not on, `--decorate` shows branch/tag names, and adding `--simplify-by-decoration` collapses to just the commits that carry refs.

`Ctrl-R` in bash/zsh starts a reverse incremental search of your command history — start typing and it finds the most recent match; press `Ctrl-R` again to step to older matches. `Enter` runs it, `Esc`/arrow edits it first, and `Ctrl-G` cancels. Replacing it with `fzf`'s `Ctrl-R` gives fuzzy, full-history search.

`asdf` manages versions of many runtimes (node, python, ruby, etc.) through one tool and plugin system, so a `.tool-versions` file pins exact versions per project. `asdf install nodejs 20.11.0` then `asdf local nodejs 20.11.0` writes the pin; `asdf global` sets the default. The newer `mise` is a faster, mostly drop-in alternative.

`git diff` shows only unstaged changes (working tree vs index); to review what you've actually staged for commit use `git diff --staged` (a.k.a. `--cached`). A clean workflow is `git add -p` to stage hunks interactively, then `git diff --staged` to proof-read the exact snapshot before `git commit`.

`git add -p` (patch mode) walks you through each change hunk so you can stage some edits and leave others for a separate commit. Answer `y`/`n` per hunk, `s` to split a hunk into smaller pieces, and `e` to hand-edit which lines go in. It's the key to small, focused commits when one file has unrelated changes.

Useful curl flags: `-L` follows redirects, `-s` silences the progress meter, `-o file` writes to a file (`-O` keeps the remote name), `-I` fetches headers only, and `-i` includes them with the body. `-H 'Header: val'` adds a header, `-d` sends a POST body, and `-w '%{http_code}'` prints the status code for scripting.

VS Code settings live in JSON: user settings apply globally, while `.vscode/settings.json` in a repo overrides them per-project and can be committed to share team config. Open the JSON directly with the command palette's 'Open Settings (JSON)'. Per-language blocks like `"[python]": { "editor.formatOnSave": true }` scope a setting to one language.

A 'permission denied' when running a script usually means it isn't executable: `chmod +x script.sh` sets the execute bit, then `./script.sh` runs it. The kernel reads the `#!/usr/bin/env bash` shebang on the first line to choose the interpreter; using `env` finds the interpreter on `PATH` instead of hardcoding `/bin/bash`.

`git blame file` annotates each line with the commit, author, and date that last touched it. Limit to a range with `git blame -L 40,60 file`, and use `-w` to ignore whitespace-only changes and `-C` to follow lines copied from other files. To dig into why, grab the SHA and run `git show <sha>` for the full diff and message.

To find which binary a command resolves to, `command -v foo` is the portable POSIX way (also tells you about aliases/functions); `which foo` is common but not in POSIX, and `type foo` in bash/zsh distinguishes aliases, functions, builtins, and files. `type -a foo` lists every match on `PATH` so you can spot shadowing.

`make(chan int, 5)` creates a buffered channel holding 5 values. Sends block only when the buffer is full; receives block only when it's empty. `len(ch)` reports queued items, `cap(ch)` reports capacity. Use buffering to decouple producer/consumer speed, not as a synchronization crutch.

`close(ch)` signals no more values will be sent. Receiving from a closed channel returns the zero value immediately; the two-value form `v, ok := <-ch` sets `ok=false` when drained. Closing a closed channel or sending to a closed channel panics. Rule of thumb: only the sender closes.

`for v := range ch { ... }` receives values until the channel is closed, then the loop ends cleanly. This is the idiomatic consumer pattern. If the channel is never closed, the loop blocks forever after the last value.

`select` waits on multiple channel operations and runs whichever is ready first. If several are ready it picks one at random (for fairness). An empty `select {}` blocks forever; add a `default:` case to make it non-blocking.

A `default:` case in `select` runs when no other case is ready, making the operation non-blocking. Pattern for a non-blocking send: `select { case ch <- v: ; default: /* dropped */ }`. Useful for best-effort sends to a full buffer.

`sync.WaitGroup` waits for a set of goroutines: `wg.Add(1)` before launching, `defer wg.Done()` inside the goroutine, `wg.Wait()` to block until the counter hits zero. Call `Add` before `go`, never inside the goroutine, or `Wait` may return early.

`sync.RWMutex` allows many concurrent readers OR one writer. Use `RLock/RUnlock` for reads, `Lock/Unlock` for writes. It only pays off when reads vastly outnumber writes and the critical section is non-trivial; otherwise a plain `Mutex` is faster.

Go's proverb: "Don't communicate by sharing memory; share memory by communicating." Prefer passing data through channels over guarding shared state with mutexes. That said, a `sync.Mutex` is often simpler and faster for protecting a single struct's fields — use the right tool.

`context.Context` carries cancellation, deadlines, and request-scoped values across API boundaries. `ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(parent)` returns a cancel func; calling it (or `defer cancel()`) closes `ctx.Done()`, signaling all downstream goroutines to stop.

`context.WithTimeout(parent, 5*time.Second)` auto-cancels after the duration; `WithDeadline` cancels at a fixed time. Always `defer cancel()` even when the timeout fires, to release the timer goroutine and avoid a context leak.

`ctx.Done()` returns a channel that closes on cancellation. Idiomatic loop: `select { case <-ctx.Done(): return ctx.Err(); case v := <-work: ... }`. `ctx.Err()` returns `context.Canceled` or `context.DeadlineExceeded` to tell you why.

By convention `Context` is the first parameter of a function, named `ctx`. Never store a Context in a struct field — pass it explicitly. Pass `context.TODO()` when you haven't wired one up yet, `context.Background()` at the top of a goroutine tree.

A goroutine leak happens when a goroutine blocks forever on a channel that's never sent/received or closed. Leaks accumulate memory and never show as a crash. Prevention: give every goroutine a clear exit path via context cancellation or a closed channel; verify with `goleak` in tests.

`sync.Once` runs a function exactly once across all goroutines: `once.Do(func(){ ... })`. Subsequent calls block until the first completes, then return without re-running. Standard for thread-safe lazy initialization of singletons.

A worker pool bounds concurrency: launch N goroutines that all `range` over a shared jobs channel, and collect results on a results channel. This caps parallelism at N regardless of how many jobs arrive — essential when each job uses scarce resources like DB connections.

Fan-out: multiple goroutines read from one input channel to parallelize work. Fan-in: merge several output channels into one using a goroutine per source plus a `sync.WaitGroup` to close the merged channel after all sources finish.

Send/receive on a nil channel blocks forever. This is a feature: set a channel variable to `nil` to dynamically disable its `case` in a `select`, since a blocked-forever case is never chosen. Handy for toggling inputs without restructuring the select.

`errgroup.Group` runs goroutines and collects the first error: `g.Go(func() error {...})` then `g.Wait()` returns that error. `errgroup.WithContext` cancels the shared context when any goroutine errors. `g.SetLimit(n)` (Go-modern) bounds concurrency.

`GOMAXPROCS` sets how many OS threads can execute Go code simultaneously, defaulting to the number of CPUs (`runtime.NumCPU()`). It controls parallelism, not the number of goroutines, which is effectively unlimited. In containers, set it to your CPU limit or use `automaxprocs`.

Channel types can be directional: `chan<- int` is send-only, `<-chan int` is receive-only. Use them in function signatures to document and enforce intent — e.g. `func produce(out chan<- int)`. A bidirectional channel converts to a directional one implicitly, but not back.

`time.After(d)` returns a channel that fires once after duration `d`, perfect for a `select` timeout case. Caveat: the underlying timer isn't garbage-collected until it fires, so in a hot loop use `time.NewTimer` with explicit `Stop()` to avoid pile-up. (Go 1.23 relaxed this with GC-able timers.)

`time.NewTicker(d)` sends on its `C` channel every `d`. Always `defer ticker.Stop()` — a leaked ticker keeps its timer alive. Prefer it over `time.Tick`, which has no Stop and leaks for the life of the program.

`sync.Cond` coordinates goroutines waiting for a condition: `cond.Wait()` atomically unlocks and sleeps, `Signal()` wakes one waiter, `Broadcast()` wakes all. Always re-check the predicate in a `for` loop after `Wait` returns to guard against spurious wakeups. Channels usually read clearer; reach for Cond rarely.

`sync.Pool` caches temporary objects to reduce GC pressure: `p.Get()` returns a pooled or freshly-`New`'d item, `p.Put(x)` returns it. The pool may drop entries at any GC, so only pool things that are cheap to recreate — never use it for connections or stateful resources.

Before Go 1.22, `for i := range xs { go func(){ use(i) }() }` captured one shared `i`, so all goroutines saw the final value. Go 1.22+ gives each iteration its own variable, fixing this classic bug. On older code, copy into the loop body or pass as an argument.

`chan struct{}` is the idiomatic signal channel — `struct{}` is zero-width so it carries no data, only the event. Pattern: `done := make(chan struct{})`, then `close(done)` to broadcast "stop" to every goroutine selecting on `<-done`. Closing (not sending) lets unlimited receivers see it.

The Go memory model defines when one goroutine is guaranteed to see another's writes via "happens-before" edges. A channel send happens-before the corresponding receive; an unlock happens-before the next lock. Without such an edge, there's no ordering guarantee — that's a data race.

A pipeline chains stages, each a function taking an input channel and returning an output channel, running in its own goroutine. Each stage closes its output when its input drains. Propagate a `done`/context channel through every stage so cancellation tears the whole pipeline down without leaks.

`runtime.Gosched()` yields the processor, letting other goroutines run. Rarely needed since Go 1.14 added asynchronous preemption (a goroutine can be interrupted even in a tight loop). It exists mainly for fairness in rare hot-loop edge cases.

A panic in a goroutine that isn't recovered crashes the entire program — you cannot recover it from a different goroutine. Each goroutine that might panic needs its own `defer func(){ recover() }()`. There's no parent/child propagation; goroutines aren't a tree for error handling.

An unbuffered channel is a synchronization point (a rendezvous): the send completes exactly when the receive does, so it doubles as a handoff guarantee. A buffered channel decouples them, trading that guarantee for throughput. Use unbuffered when you need to know the other side received it.

To return both a value and an error from a worker goroutine, send a struct: `type result struct{ val int; err error }` over a `chan result`. Channels carry one type, so bundle related outputs. Receivers then check `r.err` per result.

Go uses an M:N scheduler (the GMP model): G = goroutines, M = OS threads, P = logical processors (count = GOMAXPROCS). Each P has a local run queue; idle Ps steal work from busy ones. Goroutines parking on I/O don't block their M thanks to the netpoller.

When several `select` cases are ready simultaneously, Go chooses one uniformly at random rather than top-to-bottom. This prevents starvation but means you can't rely on case order for priority. For true priority, nest selects: try the high-priority channel first with a default that falls through.

`context.WithValue(ctx, key, val)` attaches request-scoped data, retrieved via `ctx.Value(key)`. Use unexported custom key types (not strings) to avoid collisions. Reserve it for cross-cutting request data like trace IDs — never for passing optional function parameters.

For request/response, send a request that carries its own reply channel: `type req struct{ arg int; resp chan int }`. The server processes and sends back on `req.resp`. Each caller gets a private channel, so responses never get mixed up between concurrent callers.

Goroutine stacks start tiny (~2KB) and grow automatically: when more space is needed, the runtime allocates a larger stack and copies the existing one over, updating pointers. This is why deeply recursive goroutines work yet idle ones stay cheap — there's no fixed thread-stack reservation.

Using a pointer after `free()` (or after the object's lifetime ends) is undefined behavior, even just comparing or printing it. Set freed pointers to `NULL` so a later deref crashes deterministically instead of silently corrupting the heap. Catch it with `gcc -fsanitize=address`.

Calling `free()` twice on the same pointer is undefined behavior; modern glibc detects many cases and aborts with `free(): double free detected in tcache 2`. `free(NULL)` is always safe and a no-op, which is why nulling after free prevents double-frees.

A local automatic variable that's never initialized holds an indeterminate value; reading it is undefined behavior (and for some types can even be a trap representation). The compiler may assume it's never read and optimize accordingly. `gcc -Wmaybe-uninitialized -Wuninitialized` flags many cases.

Signed integer overflow is undefined behavior in C and C++; `INT_MAX + 1` is not guaranteed to wrap. Compilers exploit this: `x + 1 > x` may be optimized to `true`. Use unsigned types (which wrap by definition modulo 2^N) or `__builtin_add_overflow` for safe arithmetic.

The strict aliasing rule says you can't access an object of one type through a pointer of an incompatible type (except `char*`, which may alias anything). Type-punning via casted pointers is UB; use `memcpy` or a `union` instead. Disable with `gcc -fno-strict-aliasing` if you must.

Dereferencing a null pointer is undefined behavior, not guaranteed to segfault. Worse: if the compiler sees a deref before your null check, it may delete the check entirely (since deref implies non-null). Always test for null *before* dereferencing.

A leak is allocated heap memory you lose the last pointer to without freeing. It's not UB, just a resource bug. Find leaks with `valgrind --leak-check=full ./prog` or `gcc -fsanitize=address` plus `ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_leaks=1`.

Writing past the end of an array is undefined behavior and a classic security hole. Stack overflows may corrupt the return address; `-fstack-protector-strong` adds a canary and aborts with `stack smashing detected`. Out-of-bounds reads/writes are caught at runtime by `-fsanitize=address`.

`malloc` returns `NULL` on failure; dereferencing that without checking is a null-deref crash. `malloc(0)` may return either `NULL` or a unique freeable pointer — both are valid per the standard, so don't assume. Always check the return before use.

In C++, memory from `new[]` must be freed with `delete[]`, and `new` with `delete`. Mixing them (`delete` on a `new[]` pointer) is undefined behavior. Better: avoid raw `new`/`delete` entirely and use `std::vector` or `std::make_unique`.

Never `free()` memory from `new`, nor `delete` memory from `malloc` — the allocators are separate and mixing them is undefined behavior. C++ objects from `new` also need destructors run, which `free` won't do. Keep each allocation paired with its matching deallocator.

`realloc(ptr, n)` may move the block and return a new address, so `ptr = realloc(ptr, n)` leaks the original on failure (returns NULL but old block still valid). Assign to a temp first. After a successful `realloc`, the old pointer is invalid — using it is UB.

You may form a pointer to one-past-the-end of an array (for loop bounds), but dereferencing it is UB, and computing a pointer two-or-more past the end is itself UB. Subtracting pointers into different arrays is also undefined. Differences use `ptrdiff_t`.

Arithmetic on `void*` is not allowed in standard C/C++ because `void` has no size; GCC permits it as an extension treating `sizeof(void)` as 1. Cast to `char*` for byte-level pointer math to stay portable.

`memcpy` has undefined behavior if source and destination regions overlap — use `memmove` for overlapping copies. `memcpy` is faster precisely because it assumes no overlap. Passing `NULL` to either (even with length 0) is also technically UB.

C strings need a `'\0'` terminator; `strlen`/`strcpy` read until they find one, so a missing terminator causes an out-of-bounds read (UB). `strncpy` does NOT null-terminate if the source is too long — a common bug. Allocate `strlen(s)+1` bytes for the terminator.

Deep recursion or huge local arrays exhaust the stack (typically ~8MB default on Linux, `ulimit -s`), causing a crash that's technically undefined behavior. `alloca`/VLAs allocate on the stack with no failure check — overflowing them silently corrupts memory. Heap-allocate large buffers instead.

Modifying a variable more than once between sequence points is undefined behavior: `i = i++ + 1;` and `a[i] = i++;` are classic examples. Function argument evaluation order is unspecified, not just unsequenced. `-Wsequence-point` flags some cases.

Shifting by an amount >= the type's bit width is undefined behavior (`x << 32` for a 32-bit int). Left-shifting a negative number, or a positive value into the sign bit of a signed type, is also UB. Cast to `unsigned` before shifting for well-defined results.

`std::unique_ptr` gives single-owner RAII with zero overhead vs raw pointers; `std::shared_ptr` adds an atomic refcount (heavier). Prefer `make_unique`/`make_shared` so allocation is exception-safe. A `unique_ptr` is moved, not copied — copying it is a compile error by design.

Two `shared_ptr`s pointing at each other form a reference cycle that never hits refcount zero, leaking both objects. Break the cycle with `std::weak_ptr` for the back-reference; call `.lock()` to get a usable `shared_ptr` only if the object is still alive.

`std::vector::push_back` may reallocate and invalidate all iterators, pointers, and references into the vector when it grows past capacity. Using one afterward is UB. `reserve()` upfront, or re-fetch iterators after insert. `std::erase` invalidates everything at and after the erased position.

In C++, an object's lifetime begins only when storage is acquired AND a constructor (or trivial init) runs. Casting raw bytes to a non-trivial type and using it without `placement new` (or C++20 `std::start_lifetime_as`) is UB, even if the bytes look right.

`restrict` (C99; `__restrict__` in C++ as an extension) promises a pointer is the only access path to its data, letting the compiler skip reload/aliasing guards. Violating that promise (two `restrict` pointers aliasing) is undefined behavior — the optimizer will produce wrong results.

`calloc(n, size)` zeroes the memory and checks `n*size` for overflow, unlike `malloc(n*size)` which can silently wrap and under-allocate. Note: zeroed bytes are all-zero bits, which is NOT a valid null pointer or `0.0` double on every exotic platform, but is in practice everywhere mainstream.

`const_cast` removing const and then writing through the pointer is undefined behavior if the underlying object was actually declared `const`. It's only legal when the original object was non-const and const was added along the way. Treat `const_cast`-to-write as a code smell.

An array decays to a pointer when passed to a function, so `sizeof(arr)` inside the callee gives the pointer size (8 bytes), not the array size. Pass the length separately, or take the array by reference in C++ (`T (&arr)[N]`) to preserve the size.

`volatile` tells the compiler a value may change outside program flow (hardware registers, signal handlers), forcing each access to actually load/store. It does NOT provide atomicity or thread synchronization — use `std::atomic` for threads. Misusing `volatile` for concurrency is a common bug.

In C, reading a union member other than the one last written is allowed (type-punning is well-defined). In C++ it's technically UB to read an inactive member, though most compilers support it. For portable punning use `memcpy` or C++20 `std::bit_cast`.

Calling a function through a function pointer of an incompatible type is undefined behavior, even if the calling conventions happen to match. Casting `void*` to a function pointer is also not guaranteed by the C standard (POSIX requires it for `dlsym`).

C++20's `std::bit_cast<To>(from)` reinterprets the bits of one trivially-copyable type as another of the same size, with no UB and `constexpr` support. It replaces the old `memcpy` trick and the illegal union/pointer-cast punning. Sizes must match exactly.

In C++ use `nullptr`, not `NULL` or `0`: `NULL` is often `(int)0` and picks the wrong overload (e.g. `f(int)` instead of `f(char*)`). `nullptr` has type `std::nullptr_t` and converts only to pointer types, resolving overloads correctly.

Storing a pointer to a stack variable and using it after the function returns (or the block scope ends) is undefined behavior. `-fsanitize=address` with `ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_stack_use_after_return=1` catches it. Common with lambdas capturing locals by reference that outlive the scope.

Struct padding bytes between members hold indeterminate values, so `memcmp` of two structs can report 'unequal' even when all named members match. Compare members individually. `#pragma pack` or `__attribute__((packed))` removes padding but can cause misaligned-access UB on some CPUs.

A flexible array member (`int data[];` as the last struct member, C99) lets you allocate `sizeof(struct) + n*sizeof(int)` and index `data` legally. The old 'struct hack' with `data[1]` or `data[0]` is technically UB but widely tolerated; FAM is the standard fix.

Passing `free()` anything other than NULL or a pointer returned by `malloc`/`calloc`/`realloc` (e.g. a pointer to the middle of a block, or a stack address) is undefined behavior. glibc may abort with `free(): invalid pointer`.

Undefined behavior in a C++ `constexpr` context must be diagnosed by the compiler — the program is ill-formed if UB (signed overflow, OOB access, null deref) occurs during constant evaluation. This makes `constexpr` a handy UB detector: force evaluation at compile time.

Binding a temporary to a `const&` (or `T&&`) extends its lifetime to that of the reference — but ONLY for the immediate temporary, not one buried inside a function return or a member access. `const std::string& s = getVec()[0];` dangles. Returning such a reference does not extend lifetime.

`-fsanitize=undefined` (UBSan, gcc/clang) instruments for runtime UB: signed overflow, null deref, misalignment, bad shifts, OOB on VLAs, and more. Combine with `-fno-sanitize-recover=all` to abort on first hit. Pair it with `-fsanitize=address` for the broadest coverage during testing.

If a class manages a resource and needs a custom destructor, it almost certainly needs a custom copy constructor and copy assignment too (Rule of Three) — otherwise the default shallow copy causes double-free. C++11 adds move ctor/assignment (Rule of Five). Or follow the Rule of Zero: own nothing raw, let members manage themselves.

Unlike `malloc`, C++ `new` throws `std::bad_alloc` on failure rather than returning null, so checking `if (p == nullptr)` after plain `new` is dead code. Use `new (std::nothrow) T` if you want a null return instead of an exception.

Process substitution `<(cmd)` turns a command's output into a temporary file path. `diff <(sort a.txt) <(sort b.txt)` compares two sorted streams without temp files. `>(cmd)` works in the other direction, feeding a command's input. It's a bash/zsh feature, not POSIX sh.

A here-string `<<<` feeds a string to a command's stdin: `grep foo <<< "$myvar"` or `bc <<< '2+2'`. It avoids the `echo "$x" | cmd` pipe, which spawns a subshell. Cleaner and faster for single-line input.

A heredoc feeds a multi-line block to a command: `cat <<EOF
line1
line2
EOF`. Quote the delimiter (`<<'EOF'`) to disable variable expansion inside. Use `<<-EOF` to strip leading tabs so you can indent the body in a script.

`${VAR:-default}` expands to `default` when VAR is unset or empty, without changing VAR. `${VAR:=default}` also assigns it. `${VAR:?msg}` aborts with an error message if VAR is empty — great for required arguments at the top of a script.

Replace text in a variable with no external tools: `${VAR/old/new}` replaces the first match, `${VAR//old/new}` replaces all. `${VAR#prefix}` strips a leading prefix, `${VAR%suffix}` strips a trailing suffix (double `##`/`%%` for the longest match). Pure bash, no `sed` fork.

`sed -i 's/foo/bar/g' file.txt` edits a file in place. GNU sed takes `-i` with no argument; BSD/macOS sed requires a backup suffix, even empty: `sed -i '' 's/foo/bar/g' file`. For portability, write to a temp file and move it instead.

`awk '{print $2}'` prints the second whitespace-separated field of each line. Set a different separator with `-F,` for CSV. `awk -F: '{print $1}' /etc/passwd` lists usernames. `awk '{print $NF}'` prints the last field whatever its number.

Sum a numeric column with awk: `awk '{s+=$1} END {print s}'`. Average: `awk '{s+=$1} END {print s/NR}'` where `NR` is the row count. awk keeps state across lines, so it's ideal for one-pass aggregation that `wc`/`grep` can't do.

`cut -d',' -f2,4 file.csv` pulls fields 2 and 4 using comma as the delimiter. `cut -c1-10` takes characters 1-10 of each line. Unlike awk, cut needs a single-character delimiter and won't collapse repeated whitespace, so use awk for ragged columns.

`grep -rn 'pattern' .` searches recursively and shows line numbers. Add `-i` for case-insensitive, `-w` to match whole words, `-l` to list only filenames, and `--include='*.js'` to limit by glob. `-E` enables extended regex (`+`, `|`, `()` without backslashes).

`grep -v pattern` prints lines that do NOT match — useful for filtering noise: `... | grep -v '^#' | grep -v '^$'` drops comments and blank lines. Chain multiple `-v` or use `grep -Ev 'a|b'` to exclude several patterns at once.

`tee` writes stdin to a file AND passes it through to stdout: `make 2>&1 | tee build.log` shows the build live while saving it. `-a` appends instead of overwriting. `sudo tee` is the trick for writing to a root-owned file from a non-root pipe.

`2>&1` redirects stderr to wherever stdout currently goes — order matters, so `> file 2>&1` works but `2>&1 > file` leaves stderr on the terminal. Bash shortcut: `&> file` redirects both. Discard everything with `&> /dev/null`.

`find . -name '*.tmp' -exec rm {} +` runs `rm` once with many files (the `+` batches them); `\;` instead runs the command once per file. `find . -type f -mtime +30` finds files older than 30 days. Combine with `-exec` to act on them in one pass.

`$(command)` captures a command's output into a value: `today=$(date +%F)`. Prefer `$(...)` over backticks — it nests cleanly: `$(dirname $(which node))`. Trailing newlines are stripped automatically. Always quote the result (`"$(...)"`) to preserve spaces.

Always quote variable expansions: `"$var"`. Unquoted, bash splits on whitespace and expands globs, so a filename with a space becomes two arguments and `*` matches files. The single most common shell bug. Quote `"$@"` to pass all script args through intact.

Brace expansion generates strings before the command runs: `mkdir {src,test,docs}` makes three dirs, `touch file{1..5}.txt` makes file1 through file5, and `cp file.txt{,.bak}` copies to file.txt.bak in one token. It's lexical, so it happens even with no matching files (unlike globbing).

`trap 'rm -f "$tmpfile"' EXIT` runs cleanup whenever the script exits — normally, via error, or Ctrl-C. Trap specific signals like `trap handler INT TERM`. Combine with `mktemp` so temp files always get removed even when the script dies.

`mktemp` creates a uniquely-named temp file and prints its path: `tmp=$(mktemp)`. `mktemp -d` makes a temp directory. It avoids race conditions and predictable names that `/tmp/myfile.$$` schemes suffer from. Pair with `trap ... EXIT` to clean up.

In bash use `[[ ]]` over `[ ]`: it doesn't word-split unquoted variables, supports `&&`/`||` inside, `=~` regex, and `<`/`>` string comparison without escaping. `[[ $x == a* ]]` does glob matching on the right side. `[ ]` is the POSIX builtin and is far easier to misuse.

`$(( ))` does integer arithmetic: `echo $((3 * 4))`, `i=$((i + 1))`. Inside, you don't need `$` on variable names: `$((a + b))`. It's integer-only — for decimals pipe to `bc -l` or use `awk 'BEGIN{print 3/4}'`. `(( i++ ))` is a standalone arithmetic command.

Declare an array `arr=(a b c)` and expand all elements with `"${arr[@]}"` (quoted, so each element stays one word). `${#arr[@]}` is the length, `${arr[0]}` the first element. Append with `arr+=(d)`. Use `"${arr[@]}"` not `${arr[*]}` when passing to a loop.

Bash 4+ has associative arrays (hashmaps): `declare -A m; m[foo]=bar; echo "${m[foo]}"`. Iterate keys with `"${!m[@]}"`. macOS ships bash 3.2, so `declare -A` fails there unless you install a newer bash via Homebrew.

Read a file line by line: `while IFS= read -r line; do ...; done < file`. `-r` stops backslashes being mangled and `IFS=` preserves leading/trailing whitespace. Never `for line in $(cat file)` — that splits on every space, not just newlines.

`$?` holds the exit status of the last command — `0` means success, nonzero means failure. Check it immediately: `cmd; if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then ...`. Cleaner is `if cmd; then ...`. In a pipeline `$?` is the last stage's status unless `set -o pipefail` is on.

`cmd1 && cmd2` runs cmd2 only if cmd1 succeeds; `cmd1 || cmd2` runs cmd2 only if cmd1 fails. Combine: `make && ./run || echo failed`. Use `;` to run sequentially regardless of outcome. Group with `{ a && b; }` (note the spaces and trailing `;`).

`nohup cmd &` runs a command immune to hangup (HUP) so it survives logout, redirecting output to `nohup.out`. Alternatively background with `&` then `disown` to detach it from the shell's job table. For anything serious prefer `tmux`/`screen` so you can reattach.

`cd -` jumps back to the previous directory (it prints the path too). It toggles, so repeating it swaps between two dirs. `pushd`/`popd` maintain a whole directory stack if you bounce among several. `$OLDPWD` holds the prior path as a variable.

`!!` re-runs the last command — `sudo !!` retries it with sudo. `!$` is the last argument of the previous command (`mkdir foo; cd !$`), and `!*` is all of its arguments. `!abc` reruns the most recent command starting with `abc`. These expand at the prompt before execution.

`tail -f file.log` streams new lines as they're appended — the standard way to watch a live log. Use `-F` (capital) so it keeps following across log rotation when the file is recreated. `tail -f log | grep ERROR` filters the live stream.

`ssh -L 8080:localhost:5432 user@host` forwards your local port 8080 to port 5432 on the remote side — reach a remote DB as if it were local. `-R` does reverse forwarding (expose a local service to the remote host). Add `-N` to forward without opening a shell.

`rsync -avz src/ user@host:dest/` syncs directories efficiently, transferring only changed parts. The trailing slash on `src/` copies its contents (no slash copies the folder itself). Add `--delete` to mirror exactly (remove extras on the destination) and `-n`/`--dry-run` to preview first.
